D1.justification: v2 Appendix A substantially expands configuration disclosure with model-specific iterations, batch sizes, weight decay, augmentation, and sampling settings. It identifies the controllable-generation ViT adapter and its exclusion from parameter counts. Appendices D–E add text-to-image sampling details and explicit decoder-pass pseudocode. Some earlier specifics, including the 0.1 class-conditioning dropout, are no longer stated.

E1.justification: v2 retains ImageNet generation at both resolutions, edge/depth conditioning, and zero-shot manipulation. It adds caption-conditioned generation using a 4M-image BLIP-3o subset, GenEval evaluation, and diverse text-to-image examples (Sections 4.1–4.2; Figures 7 and 12), substantially extending the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds NAR-L/XL/XXL and removes the 256-resolution LDM-4, VQGAN-re, RQ-Transformer-re, and AiM comparisons; ADM disappears from the 512-resolution comparison. New Table 3 compares text-to-image ARPG with LlamaGen-XL, Chameleon, and SD-v1.5. ControlVAR-d24 is also removed from Table 4.

E3.justification: v2 introduces text-to-image training for 50 epochs and GenEval evaluation, causal-versus-block-wise inference controls, and sampling at 16 and 24 steps. For retained experiments, reported AdamW beta1 changes from 0.99 to 0.9, and v1 Algorithm 2's cosine sampling schedule becomes arccos in v2 Appendix A. These documented revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Existing decoder-allocation, KV-sharing, sampling-step, and generation-order analyses are retained or relocated. v2 adds positional-encoding ablation, controlled attention-pattern comparisons (Figure 9 and Table 8), training-loss scaling analysis (Figure 10), and RandAR/ARPG attention maps (Figures 3 and 11), substantially expanding investigation of the method's mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, statistical error bars, or significance tests. The additional curves and attention maps in v2 introduce no statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 2's reported ImageNet FIDs at 64 steps change from 2.44/2.10/1.94 to 2.37/1.99/1.86 for L/XL/XXL. The 512-resolution XL FID changes from 3.38 to 2.82. v2 also adds text-to-image results, including overall GenEval 0.31, and extensive attention-control results. Because reported settings change, these replacements cannot uniformly be interpreted as gains under identical protocols.

M1.justification: The two-pass decoder, randomized training, and shared KV design already appear in v1. v2 adds text conditioning through pretrained FLAN-T5-XL embeddings (Section 4.2), extending the input procedure. Its fuller description of block-wise Pass-1 inference does not establish whether that behavior was already present in v1's underspecified inference implementation.

P1.justification: The introduction and method are extensively rewritten around content representation and position-guided prediction, with revised terminology and experimental organization. Controllable-generation and zero-shot implementation explanations move into the main method; the gradient proof and generation-order study move into appendices. The conclusion is substantially shortened, and the pseudocode is reorganized.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to a single-column layout, with redrawn comparison and architecture diagrams. v1 Tables 2–3 merge into v2 Table 2, and the architecture table becomes an expanded appendix configuration table. Sample grids are consolidated, while attention maps, decoding/scaling plots, and text-to-image panels substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around acceleration, comparing fixed-block methods, flexible schedules, and attention patterns in Section 2.2 and Table 1. New references include SAR, NAR, speculative Jacobi decoding, and the text-to-image dataset, encoder, and evaluation framework. Several broader masked-modeling and linear-attention references are removed; the changes exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1 Insight 2 makes an unqualified claim that unmasked-token queries receive no gradients. v2 Section 3.1 and Appendix C restrict the zero-gradient derivation to the final layer and explicitly acknowledge indirect gradients in shallower layers. The derivative calculation is largely retained, but its scope is substantively corrected.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in v1 through substantially fuller configuration disclosure, a properly qualified gradient argument, and controlled attention-pattern experiments that better test the proposed mechanism. Text-to-image experiments also validate an application previously left untested. Together these substantially strengthen reproducibility, mathematical precision, and empirical support. Reporting weaknesses remain, including unexplained IS discrepancies between Tables 2 and 8—for example, 297.7 versus 287.90 for ARPG-L at 32 steps—and incomplete text-to-image configuration details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARPG, with matching authors, core architecture, and overlapping experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison; equations, tables, figures, and qualitative samples are readable.

after.justification: v2 reports original image-generation experiments and ablations, plus text-to-image results, attention analyses, and training-loss curves (Tables 2–5 and 8; Figures 3 and 9–12).

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation results, controllable generation results, architectural ablations, decoding experiments, and zero-shot image examples (Tables 2–7 and supplementary figures).

C1.justification: The central contribution—compression-robust watermarking through anchor features, QDL, and frequency-aware growing—is retained. v6 adds a specific introductory claim that implicit MLP-generated attributes make watermark detection and manipulation difficult, and explicitly claims suitability for resource-constrained devices. v4's assertion of achieving the highest compression rate and efficiency is dropped.

C2.justification: v6 substantially expands mechanism explanations: tanh versus sigmoid bias, conflicts between low-frequency watermarking and quality optimization, median-based rejection of outlier influence, and color artifacts in sparsely represented regions. Appendices D–E add security arguments and interpretations of pruning resilience and decoder independence. The pretrained-decoder limitation is retained and expanded in Appendix B, rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents 30,000 training iterations, the 1,600–15,000 anchor-growing interval, conventional-to-frequency-aware growing, MS-COCO decoder pretraining, the stated compression setting of 0.004, gradient/opacity thresholds, and explicit HSV ranges and thresholds. Appendix D.1 documents GuardSplat's adaptation. These substantially improve implementation disclosure; they do not establish changes to previously unspecified training settings.

E1.justification: The same 25 Blender, LLFF, and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes remain the reconstruction benchmarks. However, v6 substantially expands evaluated attack environments through LightGaussian pruning-based compression, general float32-to-int8 quantization, and decoder-targeted PGD attacks in Appendices E.3–E.4. These scenarios extend the original image distortions, random model manipulations, and two anchor-based compression schemes.

E2.justification: The original WateRF, GaussianMarker, and 3D-GSW comparators remain. v6 adds GuardSplat to the compression, distortion, and capacity comparisons, including Tables 1–3 and 12–13. Appendix D.1 explains its adaptation from explicit spherical-harmonic offsets to anchor-feature offsets. This is a bounded expansion of the watermarking comparator set; LightGaussian serves as a compression attack.

E3.justification: The attribute ablation changes from HAC before compression in v4 Table 6 to both HAC and ContextGS after compression in v6 Table 4. Component controls are also redesigned. New protocols include 66% LightGaussian pruning, int8 quantization, PGD with epsilon 0.1, an alternative SSL decoder, compression-strength sweeps, and FPS evaluation. v6 also aligns image-noise prose with sigma 0.1, already specified in v4's table; this does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v6 adds dedicated embedding-feature removal, alternative-decoder testing, HSV artifact visualizations, attack-strength sweeps, compression-level analysis, and additional compression/adversarial robustness tests. Its Table 5 replaces v4's FAG/HSV/frequency-loss combination study with individual FAG/QDL/HSV removals after both compression schemes, incorporating the earlier HAC QDL comparison. The earlier frequency-loss ablation is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. Results remain point estimates or averages across datasets and compression schemes. Gaussian-noise standard deviations specify attacks, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: The headline CompMarkGS values in Table 1 are retained, but HAC+3D-GSW post-compression bit accuracy changes from 46.52% to 53.48%. Other entries change, and substantial results are added for GuardSplat, revised ablations, attack sweeps, alternative decoding, and FPS. New examples include 90.11% accuracy after int8 quantization and 84.33% after PGD. These are newly reported settings, not improvements over matched v4 experiments.

M1.justification: The stated HSV objective changes from averaging color-specific losses normalized by N_c in v4 Eq. 11 to a shared |C||Omega| denominator in v6 Eq. 8; Appendix C.6 identifies Omega as the image domain. This is a localized revision of the reported loss specification. The bounded additive watermark feature, QDL, frequency-aware anchor growing, decoding pipeline, and other loss components remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method rationale, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries are shortened, technical explanations are reorganized between the main text and appendices, limitations move to Appendix B, and ethics, discussion, and implementation sections are added. The narrative restructuring is substantial.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout, with redesigned and relocated displays. v4 Table 2 becomes the expanded appendix Table 12, accompanied by new radar plots in v6 Figure 4. Ablation tables are restructured, GuardSplat is added to qualitative comparisons, and new HSV visualizations, robustness curves, compression-size plots, and multi-scene image panels substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v6 substantially revises positioning by distinguishing steganography from ownership watermarking and adding a detailed comparison with SecureGS in Appendix D.1. It also expands distinctions from 3D-GSW and GuardSplat and discusses additional compression research such as CAT-3DGS and PCGS. Earlier coverage, including CopyRNeRF, is removed. These changes extend beyond bibliography formatting.

T1.justification: The HSV-loss normalization receives a limited mathematical revision between v4 Eq. 11 and v6 Eq. 8. The central feature-addition, quantization-noise, high-pass-filter, and SSIM-error constructions otherwise match across renumbering and relocation. Appendix C largely formalizes previously described masks and supplies parameter definitions; neither version presents new theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v6 substantially reduces important documentation and validation gaps: Appendix C supplies implementation details absent from the supplied v4, and the revised ablations test components after both compression schemes. Additional robustness, decoder, and efficiency experiments strengthen assessment of the central compression claim. Reporting weaknesses remain: PGD settings are incomplete, and Appendix E.4 incorrectly calls GaussianMarker the strongest ContextGS baseline despite Table 11 reporting WateRF at 90.36% versus 87.95%. Neither version reports statistical uncertainty. These limitations temper the expanded claims but do not outweigh the substantial gains in reproducibility and empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CompMarkGS with the same research objective, authors, and core pipeline. All pages, including figures and tables, support comparison. The supplied v4 ends after its references; v6 includes Appendices A–G, which were also inspected.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original empirical results, while Appendices E–G add ablations, robustness experiments, rendering-speed measurements, and qualitative outputs.

before.justification: Section 5 and Tables 1–7 report original rendering-quality, watermark-accuracy, compression, robustness, capacity, and ablation results.

C1.justification: Both versions claim language-guided adaptation to changing anomaly definitions, two regularization strategies, the 35,279-video PreVAD dataset and strong zero-shot generalization. v2 emphasizes the already-used weak supervision and adds targeted evidence without materially changing these central claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of LAVAD's event-understanding failure and Qwen2.5-VL's localization limitations in Section 6.4. Appendix F explains the applicability of video-specific prompts, while Appendix A acknowledges limitations in temporal and multimodal modeling and benchmark coverage. These qualify the retained generalization argument.

D1.justification: Appendices B–E newly document substantial implementation and reproduction information: RTX4090 hardware, AdamW training for 40 epochs, batch size 64, architecture dimensions, sampling, synthesis parameters, curation models and prompts, annotator procedures and baseline adaptations. v2 also provides a repository address and specifies annotation/download-script release and usage restrictions; actual online availability is not established.

E1.justification: PreVAD training and the seven evaluation datasets are retained. v2 extends variable-definition testing from illustrative UCF-Crime cases to systematic category-subset scenarios on XD-Violence and MSAD. This is a bounded extension of test scenarios within the existing dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and HolmesVAU to the concept-drift comparison alongside VadCLIP and LAVAD. In the matched trashcan case, LAVAD and Qwen2.5-VL replace PEL as comparators alongside VadCLIP. The MIL baseline is also removed from Table 2.

E3.justification: Protocol 2 introduces evaluation under category subsets, relabeling excluded categories as normal and computing both frame-level AUC and AP. Appendix E specifies conversion of Qwen temporal predictions into binary frame scores. Appendix F additionally documents controlled changes to synthesis settings, prompting and training-data fractions; these extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations, v2 supplies quantitative concept-drift robustness results, synthesis sensitivity tests, prompting comparisons and a training-data usage analysis (Table 4, Tables D–E and Figure E). It also revises the trashcan case, removes the cattle-stealing example and supplies further diagnostic examples in Figures H–I.

E5.justification: v2 introduces averaging over five randomly sampled category subsets for drift@5, explicitly motivated by reliability in Appendix D.2. This adds scenario-level sampling and estimation, not repeated training runs. Neither supplied PDF reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The retained cross-dataset scores and main component-ablation values are unchanged. New Table 4 reports LaGoVAD AUC/AP of 0.857/0.371 on XD-drift@5 and 0.856/0.401 on MSAD-drift@5. Appendix F adds sensitivity and detailed ablation results. v2 also removes MIL's 49.50 UBNormal result and the explicitly marked ground-truth-segment CLIP and ActionCLIP classification rows.

M1.justification: The documented core procedure retains language-conditioned detection, CLIP features, temporal and fusion modules, two prediction heads and the same four losses. Appendix B supplies architecture details and synthesis pseudocode, but does not establish a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: v2 adds 'under Weak Supervision' to the title, streamlines introductory and dataset prose, combines dataset and architecture ablation discussion, and reorganizes experimental setup around two protocols. The main section sequence and substantial passages remain recognizable; much of the expansion documents additional evidence and technical details.

P2.justification: The document switches from two-column to single-column layout and substantially reorganizes its displays. Figure 1 is redrawn, the radar plot moves into Table 2, and most earlier dataset panels merge into Figure 3 while the duration plot moves to Appendix Figure D. New comparison tables, diagrams and appendix figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning against Follow the Rules, distinguishing its one-class and few-shot setting, plus references for Qwen models, HolmesVAU and implementation tools. Some earlier citations, including Mosaic/Cutout inspiration, disappear. The central positioning around user-defined anomaly changes remains intact.

T1.justification: The concept-drift formulation, conditional-distribution assumption, optimization objectives and loss mathematics are retained. Equation regrouping and Appendix B's repeated loss and procedural elaboration do not introduce a new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: As supplied, v2 substantially strengthens the central concept-drift claim with a controlled quantitative evaluation, where v1 offered cross-dataset scores and illustrative cases. The appendices also make implementation, curation and sensitivity much more inspectable. A classification-reporting ambiguity remains: Appendix E describes abnormal-segment sampling while Table 3 retains v1's unmarked scores and drops its explicit ground-truth-segment rows. This does not outweigh the substantial gains in validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LaGoVAD and PreVAD, and their supplied text, equations, tables and figures are readable. However, v1 ends at the references despite citing supplementary Sections B–F; v2 includes Appendices A–F. This limits comparison of appendix-only material, which can establish newly documented content but not necessarily newly performed work.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and reports additional concept-drift evaluations, sensitivity analyses and qualitative results in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original zero-shot detection and classification experiments, component ablations and qualitative concept-drift examples in Section 6.

C1.justification: The introduction's contribution scope expands from six environments with IPPO validation to a broader environment-and-algorithm benchmark featuring MAPPO, SVO, parameter-sharing evaluations, and explicitly designed cooperation metrics. The central claims of JAX acceleration and a dedicated sequential-social-dilemma framework remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of MAPPO's learning difficulties and the limitation that the Harvest metric can reward leaving apples uncollected. It narrows the single-defector Harvest explanation to Open and explains Closed through its room structure, while removing Territory's credit-assignment failure discussion. Its new SVO trend interpretation overstates Table 2, which contains decreases at intermediate angles.

D1.justification: Appendices A and C add spawning probabilities, environment mechanics, API and command examples, Clean Up algorithm configurations, and sweep settings absent from v1. A direct code-repository link replaces the project-page link. Appendix B.2 newly clarifies that long Stable Baselines3/RLlib training times are extrapolated from measured throughput; the existing pixel/grid comparison caveat is retained there.

E1.justification: v2 retains five environments, removes Territory, and adds Commons Harvest: Partnership, Mushrooms, Gift Refinement, and Prisoners Dilemma: Arena. These evaluated additions introduce joint defense, differing reward-sharing incentives, token gifting, and inventory-based interactions, substantially changing task coverage (Table 1 and Figures 2–3).

E2.justification: v1's behavioral comparison contains individual- and common-reward IPPO. v2 adds MAPPO and SVO against these methods on retained environments in Figure 2, compares SVO orientations in Table 3, and compares shared/non-shared IPPO in Appendix B.1. Stable Baselines3 and RLlib remain the external runtime comparators.

E3.justification: v2 introduces environment-specific cooperation metrics beyond return, controlled parameter-sharing comparisons, and a two-stage SVO protocol selecting w at 90 degrees before evaluating five angles. These substantially expand the evaluation design. Figure 2 also changes from agent steps to environment timesteps, so its different horizon does not establish a directly comparable training-budget reduction.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's Schelling analysis, v2 adds SVO-angle sensitivity results (Table 2), parameter-sharing comparisons of learning and runtime (Figures 7–8), and behavioral-metric analyses including the Harvest proxy's failure conditions. Schelling diagnostics cover the added environments, while Territory's unsuccessful cooperation case disappears.

E5.justification: Tables 4 and 6 newly disclose SEED=30 and NUM_SEEDS=1 for the Clean Up IPPO and SVO configurations. This is additional seed reporting, without evidence of increased repetitions. The 30-episode Schelling averaging is retained, and no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds algorithm learning curves, SVO-angle returns, cooperation scores, and detailed runtime entries, while removing Territory results. For example, Table 2 newly reports Clean Up SVO returns of 0.02 at 0 degrees and 1410.53 at 90 degrees. The five retained Table 1 rows and corresponding Schelling payoff curves are unchanged; differing training-plot step units limit direct cross-version performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The implemented training suite expands beyond individual/common-reward IPPO to MAPPO with a centralized value function and SVO with an angle-dependent intrinsic-reward utility (Section 3.3). These introduce substantive learning procedures into the proposed framework. Its JAX foundation and grid observations remain.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten, replacing much of the detailed CPU/TPU and algorithm-family motivation. Environment descriptions and runtime-comparison caveats move into appendices, while the results discussion is reorganized around individual algorithms and behavioral metrics. This substantially changes the narrative and documentation structure.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one column with a redesigned author block. Figures 1–3 are rearranged and expanded, with changed plotting colors, legends, and axes; Figure 1 loses its individual environment labels. New behavioral and hyperparameter tables, runtime bar charts, and code-example figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds broader MARL benchmark context and citations including Lowe, Bard, Carroll, Samvelyan, Terry, and Yu, while removing Beattie and Yang. MAPPO and SVO receive explicit algorithmic positioning. The central relationship to Melting Pot and JaxMARL and the claimed JAX social-dilemma novelty remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The Markov-game definitions and social-dilemma inequalities in Section 3.1 remain unchanged. v2 adds the SVO angle/utility formulation and Appendix A.2's explicit Clean Up regrowth function, inventory-normalized strategies, and bilinear Arena payoffs. These are localized formal specifications, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 provides limited IPPO validation and little configuration information for reproducing training. v2 substantially improves the benchmark's reproducibility and diagnostic value through Appendices A–C, additional learning approaches, and targeted sharing, preference-angle, and behavioral analyses. Clarifying extrapolated runtime estimates also improves transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of Territory's documented failure case and new interpretive overstatements, notably the claim of uniformly increasing SVO returns despite Table 2's nonmonotonic rows.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SocialJax and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures with substantial matching material. All pages were inspected, including v2's Appendices A–C; v1 contains no appendix. No material reading gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds algorithm comparisons, SVO-angle results, behavioral measurements, and parameter-sharing and runtime experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original environment-throughput measurements in Table 1, IPPO training results in Figure 2, and cooperative/defector policy evaluations in Figure 3.

C1.justification: v2 elevates verification of intermediate reasoning outputs into a central contribution and explicitly claims the first systematic evidence-based agentic paradigm. Its headline validation claims expand from two diagnostic tasks and illustrative cases to broad disease coverage, superiority over medical-agent systems, and clinician-assessed diagnostic quality.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes indicator-specific errors, including harm from adding disc-hemorrhage estimates. v2 shifts interpretation toward complementary workflow components, the greater importance of quantitative analysis, and alignment between tool-assisted reasoning and clinicians' workflow assessments. Its conclusion newly states framework-level limitations involving unavailable visual tools and residual hallucinations in qualitative analysis.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands operational documentation through MedlinePlus corpus descriptions, document summaries, keyword filtering, top-five vector retrieval, and JSON plans dispatching predefined Python functions (Section 3.2). These are newly disclosed details, without establishing that the earlier retrieval implementation changed. Conversely, v1's explicit task-specific adapter-training and GPT-o1 coding-agent disclosures disappear. The code-access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates glaucoma on REFUGE2 and heart disease on MITEA. v2 retains these and adds MIMIC chest X-rays involving up to 12 findings per case, plus NEJM multiple-choice diagnosis across diverse anatomies, modalities, and diseases. This substantially extends the represented diagnostic tasks and environments.

E2.justification: On the retained diagnostic tasks, v2 Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-7B-VL, InternVL2.5-8B, MedAgents, MMedAgent, and MDAgent. The task-specific comparison adds Maira-2 and CheXagent for chest X-rays, while MAI disappears from the REFUGE2 comparison. These are evaluated comparator changes, beyond extending existing baselines to new datasets.

E3.justification: v2 introduces protocols using 442 MIMIC cases from 100 patients and 992 NEJM cases, including multiple-choice accuracy for NEJM. Clinician evaluation adds 1–12 complexity rankings and five diagnostic-quality dimensions scored from 1–5. Medical-agent baselines are adapted to VQA using GPT-4o. Existing MITEA three-slice sampling remains; the mACC-to-bAcc renaming does not establish a substantive metric change.

E4.justification: v2 adds cumulative planning, quantitative-analysis, and reliability-check ablations; a GPT-4o-versus-VisionUnite qualitative-tool test; segmentation-noise sensitivity; and clinician workflow and output-quality analyses. The glaucoma case study is retained. v1's detailed named-indicator ablation table is replaced by a count-based fusion comparison, retaining the weighted-versus-LLM decision question while dropping individual-subset detail.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 8 newly displays clinician-score variability through box-and-whisker plots, although their statistical definitions and rater counts are unspecified. Both versions retain ten repetitions of MITEA slice sampling with mean performance reporting. No new confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Glaucoma headline accuracy/F1 remains 90.4/76.4, with AUC 95.1. Table 1's heart-disease result changes from 66.8/52.6 to 77.8/72.3 for the revised workflow, and GPT-4o refusal markers are replaced by numerical results. v2 adds NEJM accuracy of 81.7, MIMIC average bAcc of 72.0, and extensive ablation and clinician results. These changes do not establish controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 adds intermediate-output reliability assessment with Continue, Terminate, and Complete decisions, allowing unreliable reasoning paths to stop before producing final indicators (Section 3.3). v1 executes selected tool steps and then summarizes and combines indicators without this gate. The hierarchical workflow and weighted-versus-LLM decision alternatives remain, despite their renaming.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and methods are extensively rewritten. The agent-by-agent catalogue becomes workflow-based exposition, task/case terminology becomes disease/patient terminology, and MOE/LLM deciders become structured/flat fusion. Comparisons are consolidated, the case study moves into methods, and a dedicated clinician-evaluation section and limitations paragraph replace the earlier future-work framing.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn around the reasoning loop, and v2 adds retrieval, sensitivity, fusion, and clinician-evaluation diagrams and plots. Figure 1 is relocated and relabeled; v1's glaucoma case remains as v2 Figure 4. Comparison tables are expanded and restructured, the detailed indicator table becomes Figure 6, and new component and tool-ablation tables appear.

R1.justification: v2 reorganizes medical-agent positioning into debate/voting and toolkit approaches and sharpens its novelty claim around systematic evidence-based reasoning. It adds substantial clinical-guideline and evidence-based-medicine literature, including Guyatt and Eddy, alongside sources for new tools, benchmarks, and evaluations. Earlier references such as Step-DPO and LISA++ disappear; these changes exceed bibliographic updating.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for workflow objects, selected steps, and especially the reliability-dependent three-state rule and completed-indicator set (Equations 2–4). Weighted risk aggregation and thresholding remain, but v1's explicit 0/0.5/1 indicator encoding is omitted. These are limited formal algorithm specifications; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves broader validation and clinician assessment to future work and lacks comparisons against other medical-agent systems. v2 addresses these important evidence gaps through relevant agent baselines, diverse diagnostic benchmarks, component and noise analyses, and clinician assessments (Sections 4–5). This substantially strengthens evaluation of generality and component contributions. Incomplete clinician-study reporting and lost implementation details remain weaknesses, but the evidential gains clearly outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MedAgent-Pro and contain readable text, equations, figures, and tables supporting a reliable comparison. The complete documents were inspected; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: Sections 4–5 report original diagnostic experiments on four datasets, component and sensitivity analyses, and clinician evaluations.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original REFUGE2 and MITEA diagnostic results, baseline comparisons, and glaucoma indicator ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract and central extraction, knowledge-discovery and generation claims largely persist. V2's introduction adds explicit claims of superior accuracy against state-of-the-art global explainers and 10–100 times faster runtime, while associating outperformance of original GNNs with well-structured datasets. These refine and strengthen the existing contribution claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops a structural-regularity explanation for success on molecular graphs and explicitly discusses performance gaps on less regular graphs. It adds interpretations of rule coverage and stability, and substantial criticism of baseline filtering and concept limitations. Appendix A.11 acknowledges that systematic quantitative generation benchmarking remains future work. V1's regression-extension discussion is dropped; the general oversight caution largely carries over from its Impact Statement.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents Adam with learning rate 0.005, a 500-epoch maximum, 100-epoch warm-up, 50-epoch stopping patience, dataset statistics and baseline reproduction choices, including GLGExplainer filtering and threshold handling. Hardware changes from 32 GB RAM and a 2.7 GHz processor to 128 GB and AMD EPYC 7532. However, v1's hidden dimension of 32 and explicit handling of conflicting class rules are no longer specified.

E1.justification: V2 retains Mutagenicity, BBBP and HIN, and adds BAMultiShapes, NCI1, IMDB-BINARY, PROTEINS, AIDS, BACE and SIDER, plus Cora/PubMed node classification. HIN classification moves to Appendix A.5, while its generation examples disappear. This substantially expands tested domains and tasks. MUTAG remains the papers' alternative name for the 4,337-graph Mutagenicity dataset.

E2.justification: GraphTrail becomes an evaluated classification and knowledge-extraction comparator in v2 Table 1, Figure 2 and Table 15. The HIN comparison replaces GLGExplainer with GraphTrail (v1 Table 1; v2 Table 9). GCNeuron moves from qualitative experimental comparisons to background/taxonomy discussion, while XGNN remains the molecular-generation baseline. These changes materially strengthen and revise the comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds runtime measurement, weighted precision/recall/F1, a four-architecture evaluation grid, Murcko scaffold-based 80:20 tests and fivefold rule-stability evaluation. The reported BBBP sample count changes from 2,039 to 2,050; the ordinary 80:20 split is retained. Newly disclosed optimizer and early-stopping settings do not establish changes to v1's previously unspecified training procedure.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's selected chemical and generation examples, v2 adds systematic architecture robustness, scaffold-distribution-shift and rule-stability analyses (Tables 11–13). Appendix A.10 adds clause-coverage histograms and representative-rule analyses, while A.11 expands generation case studies with multiple variants. These provide substantial new diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without run counts or uncertainty. V2 first specifies three random seeds and reports means and standard deviations for runtime, classification metrics and scaffold tests, alongside fivefold results. This introduces systematic variability reporting; it does not establish how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive accuracy, runtime, classification-metric and robustness results. Reported BBBP rule-classifier accuracy changes from 81.37% to 83.58%, and Mutagenicity discriminative clause counts change from 198/167 to 184/158 (v1 Table 1; v2 Tables 1 and 15). These are revised reports, not established identical-setting gains. V1's training accuracies, predicate counts and descriptive-rule counts disappear, while chemical and generated-graph findings are expanded.

M1.justification: The extraction, rule construction and grounding pipeline, including Algorithm 1, is retained. A limited generation extension appears in v2 Appendix A.11: a known molecule's descriptive clause is modified by adding or removing predicates before graph assembly. V1 describes clause sampling and reconstruction, leaving further clause manipulation to future work.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the contribution list, evaluation narrative and conclusion. Section 3.4 changes from Extensions to Analysis, and experimental setup and generation discussion are reorganized within an appendix containing eleven subsections. The standalone Impact Statement is condensed into the conclusion. The abstract and most core methodological prose remain similar.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column layout and redesigns Table 1 around accuracy and runtime, with rule-count comparisons appearing in Table 15. Figure 2 becomes a comparison across methods; Figure 3 changes generated examples and drops HIN. Numerous tables, histograms, rule panels and a generation gallery are added. The original generation walkthrough is retained as Figure 8, rather than being a new analysis.

R1.justification: V2 adds substantial positioning against GraphTrail, a functionality taxonomy, and detailed criticism of GLGExplainer's reliance on local explanations, domain knowledge and filtering (Sections 4–5; Appendices A.1 and A.3). It removes v1's explicit NEUROLOGIC lineage paragraph while retaining that citation, and adds references supporting oversmoothing, GIN/GAT, datasets and chemical interpretations.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.4 adds an informal computational-complexity argument assigning O(|V|), O(|V||G|) and O(|V|) costs to the three stages. The central predicate definitions, DNF construction and grounding mathematics remain unchanged. No formal correctness theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow evaluation through a stronger rule-based comparator, uncertainty reporting, broader task coverage, and architecture, distribution-shift and rule-stability tests. Added training details and explicit failure conditions improve assessability. Tradeoffs remain: some implementation disclosures disappear, and Table 1 supports only about 5–7 times faster runtime than GLGExplainer despite the broader 10–100 times claim. The gains in empirical support and understanding of applicability nevertheless constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LOGICXGNN framework. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated content.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification, runtime, robustness and graph-generation results in Section 4 and Appendices A.4–A.11.

before.justification: V1 Section 4 reports original classification results on HIN, BBBP and Mutagenicity, alongside extracted chemical rules and generated graph examples.

C1.justification: The core contributions remain frequency analysis of gating and the lightweight GmNet architecture. v3 explicitly claims the first systematic frequency analysis and strengthens the performance claim from competitive results to a new state of the art. Its introduction also asserts selective amplification of useful high-frequency signals while remaining robust to noise.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving shared gating representations, depth-dependent clipping effects, low-resolution limitations and the high-frequency/adversarial-robustness tradeoff. v2's standalone limitations section disappears, but its qualification about smaller benefits in larger architectures reappears with ConvNeXt evidence in Appendix A.8. These substantially expand the interpretation beyond the retained activation and bandwidth discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 supplies block pseudocode and detailed ResNet/GmNet training recipes, including normalization, layer scaling, regularization, augmentation and optimizer settings previously absent from the supplied v2. The model-configuration table is relocated unchanged. v3 also provides a code repository URL instead of v2's promise of release upon acceptance.

E1.justification: v3 documents CUB-100 classification, MSCOCO 2017 object detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and a CIFAR-10 adversarial testing scenario. v2 mentions downstream tasks but supplies no corresponding datasets or results. Existing frequency-filtered classification coverage is retained, including EfficientFormer experiments moved to the appendix.

E2.justification: The principal ImageNet comparator table is unchanged. v3 extends gate comparisons with FC-branch designs, SiLU and SwiGLU, and adds a ConvNeXt control comparison (Tables 4, 9, 11 and 13). EdgeViT and GhostNet are not new comparators: both already appear in v2 Figure 6.

E3.justification: v3 adds component comparisons controlling parameters and approximately matching FLOPs, layer-wise spectral-energy measurements using a central-quarter low-frequency region, optimizer-variation experiments using Adam at 0.001, and PGD testing. The existing ImageNet resolution, 300-epoch budget, AdamW optimizer, learning rate and batch size remain unchanged; newly disclosed recipes are documentation additions.

E4.justification: v3 adds component-attribution controls, FC and SiLU/SwiGLU gate ablations, activation replacement across model sizes, PGD robustness testing, quantitative spectra before and after gates, and optimizer sensitivity analyses. These test attribution, mechanisms and failure conditions beyond v2's activation, gate-design and kernel-bandwidth studies. Relocated threshold plots are retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages for frequency-learning experiments and five testings for selected ablations. v3 additionally reports mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds for the component breakdown in Table 5. It does not establish increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: The main ImageNet table and existing activation results remain unchanged, including GmNet-S3 at 79.3%. v3 adds substantial results: GmNet-S1 reaches 81.5% on CUB-100, ConvNeXt without/with GLU scores 82.5%/83.0%, and Table 15 reports 42.2 box AP, 40.1 mask AP and 44.6 mIoU for GmNet-S3. Additional ablation, spectral and robustness outcomes are newly reported results, not improvements over matched v2 experiments.

M1.justification: The proposed GmNet retains the ReLU6(x)·x gate, two 7×7 depth-wise convolutions, two pointwise convolutions, and the same model configurations. New pseudocode documents the existing design; alternative gates and ConvNeXt experiments do not establish a revision to GmNet.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten around spectral bias in lightweight vision models. v3 reorganizes the closing sections, replaces the NeurIPS checklist with statements, introduces a structured technical appendix, and adopts conference headers and author–year citations.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the introductory example and ResNet block diagram, separates frequency curves into clearer panels, relocates retained threshold plots and model configurations, rescales the latency plot, and recolors the bandwidth histograms. New algorithm displays, ablation tables and appendix figures substantially change the visual organization.

R1.justification: v3 removes background references including LSTM/GRU, the original Transformer, Focal Modulation and GELU, while retaining the central frequency-learning and lightweight-network literature. It more explicitly positions shared-representation gating against StarNet/EfficientMod designs and asserts an unfilled frequency-analysis gap.

T1.justification: v3 removes the explicit integration-by-parts proof of v2 Theorem 2 while retaining the differentiation identity and smoothness–spectral-decay argument in informal form. It adds a discontinuity-decay example. The convolution theorem and spectrum-broadening argument remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility through explicit pseudocode and training recipes, and strengthens the central design argument with component controls and direct spectral measurements absent from the supplied v2. Robustness and transfer experiments also make applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, although PGD settings remain unspecified, some spectral interpretations overgeneralize Table 14, and the introduction's 81.3% GmNet-S3 claim conflicts with Table 1's unchanged 79.3%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GmNet work, with matching architecture and principal experiments. All supplied pages are readable. v2 refers to supplementary material but ends with a checklist; v3 includes a technical appendix. Appendix additions are assessed as newly documented content, without assuming when the experiments were conducted.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and reports additional component ablations, spectral measurements, robustness tests, and downstream evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original frequency-filtered classification experiments, ImageNet results, activation and GLU ablations, and convolution-kernel bandwidth analyses.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same principal contributions: distributed patch artifacts motivate 'All Patches Matter, More Patches Better'; detectors exhibit Few-Patch Bias associated with lazy learning; and PPL improves generalization and robustness. Broader experiments and revised component names support or rephrase these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting matched reconstruction to preserved semantics, interpreting dropout as a weaker remedy for patch reliance, and locating similar bias in CNN decision layers. It removes v2 Section 6's substantive qualification that contemporary generators can exceed academic benchmark quality. The restriction to fully generated images remains.

D1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A newly specify reconstruction strength, denoising steps, guidance, patch size, replacement probabilities, loss parameters, prompt/mask inputs and training pseudocode. Appendix A reports V100 epoch times and 16/19 GB memory without/with PCL, replacing v2's broad 30 GB statement. Unspecified matching conditions prevent interpreting this as a demonstrated efficiency gain.

E1.justification: V3 adds evaluations on AIGCDetectionBenchmark and UniversalFakeDetect, substantially expanding generator coverage to ProGAN, StyleGAN, CycleGAN and other outputs beyond the earlier benchmarks. GenImage, Chameleon and DRCT remain; renaming DRCT to DRCT-2M does not itself change coverage.

E2.justification: The corruption comparison in Figure 6 expands from UnivFD and DRCT to also include NPR, FatFormer, SAFE, C2P-CLIP and AIDE. New benchmark tables evaluate additional comparators such as LGrad and LNP. Comparator membership in the retained GenImage, DRCT and Chameleon tables is unchanged.

E3.justification: Figure 6 changes the reported corruption metric from Accuracy to Balanced Acc and revises blur values from 0.5-2.5 to 0-3 and resizing factors from 0.6-1.4 to 0.5-1.5. New Tables 3-4 compare SDv1.4-trained PPL with GAN-trained baselines, and new ablations introduce additional experimental controls. Newly disclosed default training parameters alone do not establish changed experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds reconstruction-versus-direct-replacement controls, four hyperparameter sweeps, alternative contrastive losses, fixed-versus-random positions, patch sizes and dropout comparisons. Appendix C adds patch-effect distributions and broader CDE/Grad-CAM analyses, including ConvNeXt. V2's multi-detector masking-recall experiment in Figure 6(b) disappears; the retained single-patch occlusion analysis in Figure 3 is distinct.

E5.justification: Appendix C and Figure 10 add descriptive statistical reporting through violin distributions of normalized patch effects. This does not establish repeated-run uncertainty. No seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests are newly supplied; existing across-generator standard deviations are merely reformatted as mean plus/minus standard deviation.

E6.justification: The GenImage, DRCT and Chameleon table scores remain unchanged. V3 adds AIGCDetectionBenchmark mAcc values of 94.41/93.36 and UniversalFakeDetect values of 96.05/93.85 for DINOv2/CLIP, plus numerous analysis results. Module-ablation entries change: LoRA+RPR is 92.6 in v2 Table 4 versus 92.1 in v3 Figure 8's reconstruction series. Revised corruption curves use changed settings and cannot establish same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Random Patch Replacement becomes Randomized Patch Reconstruction, but both mix aligned real and diffusion-reconstructed patches; v3 Appendix A confirms the equivalent construction. The margin-based patch loss, combined classification objective and LoRA-tuned CLIP/DINOv2 backbones remain. Algorithm 1 and reconstruction parameters elaborate the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, motivation and methodology undergo extensive rewriting and terminology changes. The experimental narrative shifts from two explicitly named settings to dataset-based comparisons, the standalone limitations section disappears, and structured appendices are added. Author information and conference headers also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces its comparison bars with a radial display and new attention examples; Figure 2 is redesigned. Figure 6 is rebuilt, and the component-ablation table becomes an expanded grouped-bar chart. V3 adds benchmark tables, an algorithm box and numerous appendix displays, while relocating Chameleon results and combining mean/std columns.

R1.justification: V3 adds citations including Dual Data Alignment, Seeing Before Reasoning, MSCOCO, Zeiler and Fergus, and several generative-model works. It removes ZED's standalone related-work description while retaining its citation elsewhere. The local-versus-global organization and central positioning against selective patch reliance remain.

T1.justification: Appendix C introduces exponential normalization of patch effects, exp(TDE(i,j)-TDE_max), and Appendix B adds a computational-cost argument comparing contrastive losses. The core patch-intervention and PCL equations remain equivalent; renaming TDE to CDE does not itself introduce a theoretical result. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially reduces v2's training under-specification and strengthens evidence for the central mechanism through reconstruction, randomization, loss and dropout controls, plus broader patch-utilization analyses. Added benchmarks meaningfully extend transfer evaluation. Removing the limitations discussion and masking comparison weakens balance, and unequal training data limit new baseline comparisons, but the gains in reproducibility and targeted validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PPL framework and contain readable text, equations, tables and figures supporting reliable comparison. The supplied v2 ends after its references despite mentioning an appendix; v3 includes Appendices A-D. All supplied material was inspected.

after.justification: V3 retains original PPL experiments and adds benchmark results, extensive ablations, patch-effect distributions and Grad-CAM analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V2 reports original PPL results on GenImage, DRCT and Chameleon, together with component ablations, corruption tests and patch-occlusion analyses. These qualify independently of the cited baseline results.

C1.justification: v2 expands the central contribution from performance benchmarking to mechanistic interpretation and targeted compression. Its abstract and introduction add claims about final-layer up-projection importance, excessive compression of particular modules, and gains from selective protection. The parameter-count versus knowledge claim remains; the shorter-output finding persists in Appendix G but loses its headline contribution status.

C2.justification: v2 attributes important reasoning components primarily to distillation and interprets importance losses as excessive compression of gate projections and final-layer modules (Sections 4–5). It explains small MuSiQue protection gains through unchanged weight count. It also drops v1's API-security conjecture and newly uses degradation at 50% sparsity to justify excluding pruning from mechanistic analysis.

D1.justification: v2 adds an interpretation-code repository pointer and distinguishes AutoAWQ inference from original AWQ pseudo-quantization in Appendix D. It removes v1's explicit word-based response-length counting, API retry description, and MuSiQue sampling-pool provenance. Core inference platforms and decoding hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Documented task coverage remains AIME 2024, FOLIO, Temporal Sequences, and closed-book MuSiQue. Their mathematical, logical, temporal, and knowledge-intensive multihop requirements are retained. The added model configurations and analyses of reasoning behaviors do not establish a new benchmark, domain, or input scenario.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds evaluated AWQ, GPTQ, and GPTAQ variants for distilled models, plus ANY4/3 for the Qwen-32B, Llama-8B, and Qwen-7B groups. v1 Table 2 evaluated dynamic quantization, distilled models, and SparseGPT variants, with AWQ/GPTQ only discussed in the literature. v2 Table 4 additionally compares ordinary and selectively protected 3-bit AWQ.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-8B and Qwen-7B configurations and extensive 3-/4-bit quantization settings. New experiments quantize individual components using 3-bit round-to-nearest and compare AWQ with versus without 16-bit final-layer MLP restoration (Tables 3–4). Benchmark sizes, accuracy/EM/F1 metrics, closed-book answering, and the stated decoding parameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses locating important modules and tracking importance shifts after distillation and quantization, including appendix heatmaps. Five component perturbations test whether importance predicts sensitivity, and selective protection tests whether restoring identified modules helps. The earlier sparsity sweep, response-length analyses, and collapse examples are retained rather than replaced.

E5.justification: v1 specifies one pass per benchmark. v2 Table 1 reports three-pass means for student-model results, while original R1 and dynamic quantization remain exceptions; Table 2 explicitly retains one-pass sparsity results. This adds repeated evaluation and averaging, but no seeds, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds many quantization results and component-intervention outcomes. Its main-table Llama-70B and Qwen-32B averages become 81.8 and 82.2, versus v1's 80.7 and 83.0; these are three-pass summaries replacing single-pass entries, not demonstrated model improvements. New Table 4 reports 46.0 versus 52.57 average accuracy for ordinary versus protected 3-bit AWQ. The sparsity and response-length tables retain their numerical results.

M1.justification: v1 benchmarks existing compression methods. v2 adds an adapted component-level difference-of-means and attribution-patching procedure to estimate reasoning importance and compression effects (Sections 2.2–2.3). It also introduces a mixed-precision AWQ procedure that restores final-layer MLP weights to 16-bit (Section 5.2).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background and experimental setup are reorganized into Problem Formulation, and the results narrative separates performance, distillation effects, and quantization effects. Related work, implementation details, model comparisons, response-length analysis, and case studies move into expanded appendices. Author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1 to show the expanded pipeline, substantially expands the main comparison table, and adds six heatmap figures and two intervention tables. Dataset statistics and earlier response-length/collapse displays move to appendices; v1 Figure 2 becomes v2 Figure 8. Typography, table-caption placement, and boxed takeaway displays also change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the work around interpreting compression effects. It builds on Arditi and Syed, distinguishes its module-level analysis from Venhoff's layer-level work, and contrasts its up-projection finding with Shao and Wu's o-projection finding. It also adds recent compression and reasoning-model studies, while largely retaining the earlier general compression review in Appendix B.

T1.justification: v2 Sections 2.2–2.3 introduce mathematical definitions for behavior-specific steering vectors, their normalization, attribution-based importance, and relative importance shifts. They also introduce the minimal-shift hypothesis and reasoning for displaying only decreases. This formal framework is absent from v1; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited quantization comparisons and aggregate analysis through comparisons on the same model backbones and explicit component perturbation/protection experiments (Tables 1, 3–4). These provide a stronger empirical basis for compression recommendations, beyond simply reporting more scores. Important limits remain: protection is tested only on Llama-8B with additional precision, variance and annotation details are missing, and Figure 5 inconsistently names the compared model. These constrain broad causal and superiority claims but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical grounding.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepSeek-R1 compression study and provide readable text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices. Earlier experiments can be matched across renumbering and relocation, despite substantial additions in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds quantization comparisons, component-importance analyses, and selective quantization/protection experiments in Tables 1, 3–4 and Figures 2–7.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, sparsity sweeps, response-length analyses, and model-collapse examples in Section 5, Tables 2–5, and Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion broaden the three headline findings from R1-distilled Llama/Qwen models to R1 and non-R1 families. The introduction and conclusion also extend the excessive-compression finding to pruning, expanding the claimed mechanistic contribution beyond distillation and quantization. The original headline numerical gains remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of RAG gains, model-specific importance patterns, pruning-analysis feasibility, and the selective-quantization exception, which it attributes to random perturbation. It also discusses hardware tradeoffs of nonuniform compression, unmatched dynamic-quantization calibration, and uncertainty from the small annotation-validation sample.

D1.justification: Documentation expands substantially: v3 specifies the 120 annotated instances with 30 per benchmark, annotation temperature and sequence exclusions, component-specific precision in the dynamically quantized model, and calibration-information limitations. It also documents AlphaPruning's use of SparseGPT and the RAG embedding model and top-ten retrieval procedure. Existing code-access information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: The four reasoning benchmarks are retained. Appendix L adds an actually evaluated retrieval-assisted MuSiQue scenario, supplying external knowledge to the models; v2 evaluates MuSiQue only closed-book and references other work's RAG results.

E2.justification: V3 adds AlphaPruning to Table 1 for R1-Distill-Llama-70B at 50% sparsity and Llama-8B at 30% and 50%. The previous comparator set remains; rows formerly labeled 'sparse' are identified explicitly as SparseGPT.

E3.justification: V3 adds substantial evaluation designs: annotation validation at temperatures 1 and 0.1, a GPT-OSS-distilled 4B model with its GPTQ variant, retrieval-assisted MuSiQue, and selective 4-/5-bit Llama and 3-bit Qwen tests. Existing benchmark sizes and generation settings remain unchanged; the newly disclosed 120-instance annotation dataset does not establish a revised sampling protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–N investigate annotation stability, dependence on displaying only importance decreases, pruning effects, non-R1 generalization, base-model importance, knowledge provision through RAG, agreement with AWQ scaling signals, and the first-versus-final-layer quantization exception. These substantially extend validation of the central findings. V2's response-length analysis and collapse cases remain in Appendices O/P.

E5.justification: Appendix G and Table 6 introduce Spearman correlations and 95% confidence intervals for human annotation ratings, using ten instances sampled with replacement per behavior. This statistical reporting is localized to annotation validation; existing benchmark averaging and one-pass sparsity reporting remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing numerical entries in Tables 1–4 and the relocated response-length tables are unchanged. V3 adds AlphaPruning results, annotation ratings, non-R1 scores, RAG outcomes, and selective-quantization results. For example, Table 7 reports average accuracies of 71.1 and 63.2 for DistilGPT-OSS-qwen3-4B and its 4-bit GPTQ variant; Table 8 reports Llama-8B MuSiQue F1 of 4.43 closed-book versus 14.52 with RAG.

M1.justification: The steering-vector computation, attribution-patching importance scores, relative-importance normalization, and selective final-layer protection procedure remain unchanged. V3 applies this framework to additional models and compression settings without introducing a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V3 makes local wording corrections, adds cross-references, acknowledgments, and conference headers, and inserts new appendix sections. The former Appendices G/H become O/P with their substantive text preserved.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the displays with new validation and evaluation tables and importance heatmaps in Figures 8–13. Figure 2 is enlarged and rearranged into stacked groups, and Figure 1 incorporates AlphaPruning. Existing response-length tables and the collapse illustration are relocated and renumbered, with their content retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix B.5 positions the importance analysis within module-wise compression, adding AlphaPruning, OWL, and Liu et al.'s principal-weight study. This is a targeted extension of the retained literature review and research positioning. OWL is discussed but not evaluated as a baseline.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for steering vectors, attribution importance, and relative importance are retained, as is the minimal-importance-shift hypothesis. V3 adds empirical validation and conceptual explanations, without new formal results, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: V2 explicitly omitted mechanistic pruning analysis and lacked annotation-validation and non-R1 checks. V3 adds these, together with base-model and selective-quantization controls that substantially strengthen the central weight-importance argument. These additions address important validation gaps. The annotation sample remains small, and RAG comparisons do not fully isolate knowledge from reasoning, so some strengthened generalization and causal interpretations remain insufficiently supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across the revision.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds annotation validation, AlphaPruning evaluations, non-R1 experiments, retrieval-assisted evaluation, and further diagnostic results.

before.justification: V2 reports original compression benchmarks, sparsity sweeps, weight-importance analyses, and selective-quantization experiments, including Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from presenting a benchmark and multidimensional evaluation to claiming the first comprehensive anesthesiology dataset suite and dedicated reasoning-model collection. Morpheus and support for CPT, SFT, and RLVR become central contributions. The earlier emphasis on inference-search and general-model distillation findings is reduced or removed.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies v1's positive CPT interpretation with Chinese performance degradation and a possible catastrophic-forgetting explanation (Section 5.2). Appendix F acknowledges weak or nonsignificant support for some CoT, scaling, and dataset-complementarity claims. Section 6 adds limitations concerning abstract clinical scenarios and missing modalities, while Appendix G.2 newly argues for MCQs as a proxy for open-ended reasoning.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands implementation disclosure: GPU hardware, inference/training frameworks, optimization settings, generation and judging prompts, and explicit decontamination thresholds appear in Appendices A–C and G. Distribution plans now include Morpheus and HuggingFace. However, v1's specified CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license is replaced by deferred licensing information in v2 Appendix H.6; neither PDF establishes that the promised resources are already released.

E1.justification: v2 adds verifiable MCQ/CoT training through AnesR1, actually used for Morpheus, and evaluates 64 System 2 questions converted into open-ended tasks (Appendix G.2). These extend training and evaluation requirements beyond v1. English/Chinese coverage, AnesCorpus, AnesQA, and CAB MCQs already existed; CAB is retained in Appendix G.3.

E2.justification: The MCQ comparisons add Qwen3, Gemma 3, Llama 4, GPT-OSS, Gemini-2.5, and Claude-3.7 models (v2 Tables 3 and 9). R1-Distill-Llama-8B disappears from the complete English and CAB comparisons. The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reference row is also removed from the CPT/SFT ablation table, although that model remains evaluated elsewhere.

E3.justification: Reported settings change from two CPT epochs and fixed 2,000-step SFT in v1 to three CPT epochs and five SFT epochs with revised batching in v2 Appendix C.3. Benchmark and corpus sample counts also change. These descriptions do not establish reruns, and v2's equal-step claim needs reconciliation with its epoch-based settings. New protocols include SFT-only controls and open-ended evaluation using BLEU, F1, and two LLM judges.

E4.justification: v2 adds SFT-versus-GRPO controls, Chinese CPT analyses, two comparative clinical case studies, manual data-quality audits, and MCQ/open-ended validation. The explicit beam-search and model-size-dependent distillation analyses from v1 Sections 5.3–5.4 are removed. Sampling analysis now examines Morpheus self-consistency across sample counts; the existing leakage audit and word clouds are retained.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports one benchmark run and supplies point estimates without uncertainty analysis. v2 Appendix F adds bootstrap tests, 90% confidence intervals, and correlation/regression significance testing. Appendix G.2 reports three repetitions of open-ended judging. These additions do not establish repeated training runs or additional runs of the retained MCQ evaluations.

E6.justification: All 38 models shared by v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 9 retain their English scores; shared CAB totals also remain unchanged. Substantial additions include Morpheus, newer-model, open-ended, and Chinese training results. For combined SFT data, v2 Table 5 newly reports Chinese accuracy of 65.9% without CPT versus 60.0% with CPT, while retaining the earlier English values. CAB cognitive-level breakdowns and beam-search result entries are removed.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Morpheus-7B/14B, trained through SFT followed by GRPO on AnesR1 reasoning traces generated with correctness-based rejection sampling. This substantially extends v1's own CPT/SFT training procedure and evaluation of externally distilled models. The earlier mini-step, self-reflection, and beam-search procedure is no longer presented.

P1.justification: Beyond scientific additions, v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and conclusion. It reorganizes methodology into dataset overview/curation, separates evaluation and baseline models from analysis, and moves training details into structured appendices with a contents page. The title, terminology, citation style, and datasheet organization also change.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview around AnesSuite and Morpheus, adds dataset-distribution figures and numerous experimental/statistical tables, and restructures the main comparison table by model category. The scale analysis loses its CAB panel; the beam-search table and distillation chart disappear. Existing leakage and word-cloud figures are relocated, and prompts receive substantially different boxed formatting.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens its novelty positioning from structured benchmark evaluation to a comprehensive training-resource suite and the first specialized reasoning-model collection. New references connect this positioning to RLVR/Tulu 3, GRPO/DeepSeekMath, and newer model families. The earlier small-model distillation discussion and its supporting citation disappear, although much of the general related-work discussion remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix F.1 introduces an explicit interaction regression for comparing scaling slopes (Equation 2) and coefficient-based hypotheses for diminishing returns. This is a limited addition of mathematical formulation for empirical analysis. The original leakage-confidence definition in Equation 1 is unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through documented data audits and decontamination, controlled Morpheus comparisons, open-ended checks, and statistical analyses that qualify previously untested assertions. Its Chinese CPT results expose an important applicability limitation absent from v1's positive interpretation, and implementation disclosure improves substantially. Reporting problems remain: Table 3 gives Qwen3-4B a Chinese total of 0.37 below every category score, and training-budget descriptions need reconciliation. These weaken some quantitative comparisons, but the gains in validation, reproducibility, and qualified interpretation are substantial overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete and readable, including their appendices. They describe the same research lineage, retaining AnesBench, its cognitive-demand categories, and many experiments, despite v2's broader AnesSuite framing.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, Morpheus training experiments, open-ended evaluations, case studies, and statistical analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, CPT/SFT experiments, inference-strategy comparisons, and contamination analysis in Tables 1–4 and Appendix F.

C1.justification: v1's central claims concern optimal precision control and substantial welfare influence. v3 retains these while adding central claims that LLM planners reproduce theoretical policy structure, accommodate non-Bayesian behavior, and exhibit strategic reasoning relevant to studying information mediators and their regulation (abstract, Sections 1.1 and 7).

C2.justification: v3 interprets policy deviations through central tendency and non-Bayesian updating, and attributes hybrid performance losses to applying Bayesian policies to different agents. Section 7 adds applicability boundaries for heterogeneous preferences, especially the unresolved biased case. The earlier information-parity, signal-symmetry, and observability constraints remain in Remark 2.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's brief JuliaPOMDP and trajectory-budget description, Appendix E specifies EXAONE Deep 32B, prompts for all three LLM roles, an explicit parameter grid, and programmatic profile/car-fact construction. JuliaPOMDP remains the numerical tool. The earlier 100-step horizon is not restated, and message-precision calibration remains undocumented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates abstract binary-state social learning with Bayesian agents. v3 adds synthetic car-purchase scenarios with generated demographic profiles, car facts, natural-language messages, and non-Bayesian LLM agents, including good-car and bad-car trajectories in Appendix E.3.

E2.justification: v1 Figure 2 compares analytical optimal and myopic policies for both planner objectives; v3 Figure 2a compares LLM planners with analytical optimal planners. Figure 2c additionally includes Hybrid comparisons using analytical policies with LLM agents, alongside Analytical and LLM settings under both myopic and long-term objectives.

E3.justification: v3 introduces single-signal belief-update probes, measurement of LLM-reported beliefs and percentage policy deviations, and analytical/LLM/hybrid evaluation designs. Figure 2c explicitly conditions welfare comparisons on the true state B. These introduce substantial new evaluation procedures beyond v1's numerical trajectory study.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's aggregate welfare comparison and example policies, v3 investigates deviations from Bayesian updating in Figure 1b, policy discrepancies in Figure 2b, and analytical-policy robustness to LLM agents in Figure 2c. Appendix E.3 adds trajectory case studies examining resistance to information cascades.

E5.justification: v1 reports 1,000 trajectories per parameter combination and 125,000 per policy; v3 omits these replication counts without establishing that actual run counts decreased. Figure 1b introduces shaded bands, but their statistic and uncertainty level are unspecified.

E6.justification: v1 reports optimal biased/altruistic welfare changes of -26.34%/+96.97%. v3 Figure 2c replaces these summaries with state-B-conditioned comparisons, showing approximately -35%/+80% for long-term analytical planners and additional Hybrid/LLM outcomes. The conditions differ, preventing direct performance-change claims. Figures 1b, 2b, and 4 add belief-update, policy-deviation, and trajectory findings.

M1.justification: The underlying MDP remains, but v3 adds an operational LLM planner–oracle–agent procedure: the planner selects precision, and the oracle generates profile-specific messages for LLM decision-makers. Prescribed analytical controls also change through the corrected altruistic threshold and biased obfuscation policy.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled from Controlled Social Learning: Altruism vs. Bias to Steering the Herd: A Framework for LLM-based Control of Social Learning. The abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes a standalone section, applications move to Appendix A, and proof material is reorganized into appendices.

P2.justification: The two-column presentation becomes single-column, and the original policy and welfare displays are substantially reworked into Figure 2's multipanel comparison. v3 adds a system diagram, belief-update plot, deviation histogram, decision-tree illustration, trajectory plots, and a parameter table.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning beyond social-learning control into information design, Bayesian persuasion, and LLM economic agents. Section 2 adds works including Kamenica and Gentzkow, Bergemann and Morris, and Dutting et al., explicitly distinguishing its repeated social-learning setting from framing-and-signaling research.

T1.justification: Appendices B–C supply extensive derivations and proofs beyond v1's sketches, including continuity and epsilon-optimality analysis. Theorem 1 changes the investment condition from beta(1) < C to beta(1) < C(1-p). Biased-policy results replace 1-b-epsilon with b-epsilon, recognize nonattainment, and weaken several bounds. Appendix D adds a formal extension to observable heterogeneous preferences.

improvement.justification: The decisive gains are substantially more checkable theory and corrections to important policy statements: v3 supplies previously omitted derivations, corrects the altruistic threshold, and addresses biased-policy nonattainment. LLM/hybrid analyses and disclosed prompts add useful empirical scrutiny. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including missing replication and precision-calibration details and Section 6.3's 40–50% welfare-loss claim exceeding Figure 2c's roughly 35% analytical result.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' sequential social-learning framework with planner-controlled signal precision, despite substantial retitling and expansion. All pages, equations, and figures support comparison. v1 contains no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A–E.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix E report original LLM simulations and numerical comparisons, including belief updates, planner policies, welfare outcomes, and example trajectories.

before.justification: Section V and Figures 1–2 report original numerical evaluations and simulated trajectories comparing altruistic and biased planners, including measured welfare changes.

C1.justification: The abstract and first contribution shift from proposing a taxonomy of 13 functions to evaluating 12 principal score functions, modestly narrowing the headline contribution. The central claims about over 12% inactivity, AWFT underestimation, output-norm scoring and limited finetuning effects remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations of dataset stability, AWFT's decline with growing context and the role of output projection. Appendix A.14 substantially clarifies applicability: AHON requires computing head outputs, so zeroing them does not itself save that computation, and multiple-choice interventions do not establish reliable generation. It also discusses routing and cache-compression possibilities.

D1.justification: v4 adds a stated code-repository location, exact FineWeb-Edu sequence identifiers, projected-output implementation details and descriptions of the added datasets. Existing PyTorch intervention steps, model dtypes and automatic batch-size guidance are retained. These are useful but localized reproducibility additions.
