E1.justification: v2 evaluates intervention accuracy on MMLU and uses FineWeb-Edu for attention analyses. v4 adds PIQA physical commonsense reasoning and WinoGrande pronoun resolution across all 14 models, substantially broadening the evaluated task requirements beyond the original knowledge benchmark.

E2.justification: v4 Figure 7 adds circuit-based AHON and its layer-normalized variant to the MMLU comparison. Figures 2–3 exclude Last Token Head Output Norm (HN) from the overlap and ranking comparisons, although it remains in appendix intervention grids. AWFT and random-zeroing baselines are retained.

E3.justification: The existing 14-model, 5-shot MMLU and seven-threshold protocol remains. New designs include 0-shot PIQA, 5-shot WinoGrande, dataset-specific threshold calibration to identify 15% of heads for layer comparisons, and tracking growing prefixes of three FineWeb-Edu sequences of at least 512 tokens. These substantially extend the controlled evaluation procedures.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained overlap, distribution, scaling, finetuning and PCA analyses, v4 adds an output-projection ablation (A.1), cross-dataset layer profiles (4.4), examples identified by individual scoring rules (A.3), and context-dependent inactivity curves and masks (A.5). These investigate sensitivity to output definition, dataset and increasing context.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the intervention evaluations. The added experiments continue reporting point results and curves without uncertainty estimates; the score-distribution histograms are behavioral analyses.

E6.justification: MMLU Table 2 is unchanged, including average removable-head fractions of 4.61% for AWFT and 12.18% for Ours. v4 adds PIQA results of 10.01% versus 21.38% and WinoGrande results of 6.90% versus 14.45%, plus circuit-based, layer-wise and context-dependent findings. These are substantial additional results under distinct conditions.

M1.justification: The original scoring and dynamic head-zeroing procedures remain. Appendix A.1 adds implemented circuit-based AHON variants that score head contributions after output projection, changing the quantities used to select heads. Head normalization is retained in Appendix A.2 and intervention plots; its disappearance from the main text does not constitute method removal.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v4 standardizes score-function terminology, reframes Section 3, expands the normalization explanation and moves head normalization and short scoring-rule descriptions into the appendix. The new analyses receive dedicated subsections, while editing of retained material remains localized.

P2.justification: v4 adds layer profiles, circuit comparisons, example-head panels, two complete benchmark grids, context-length curves and inactivity masks, together with three result tables. It also simplifies Table 1, revises the main comparison matrices and replaces repeated legends in the full MMLU grid with a shared legend. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for PIQA, WinoGrande, transformer circuits, runtime neural pruning and mixture-of-depths. These extend discussion toward circuit interpretations and conditional computation. The main positioning relative to attention sinks, dormant heads and earlier head-pruning research remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix A.1 adds a formal definition of projected head contributions and derives the block decomposition of the output projection in Equations 2–3. It also explains why zeroing a fixed head removes its contribution under either output definition. The original scoring equations remain, and the added mathematical treatment is limited in scope.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v2's reliance on MMLU for intervention validation by adding two distinct tasks across all 14 models. The projection ablation and dataset/context analyses strengthen the evidence, while explicit computational and generation limitations improve the interpretation of retained claims. The gains concern validation and clarity rather than improved MMLU scores. Generalization remains bounded: AWFT still wins several rows in Tables 4–5, and generation is unevaluated.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, core scoring methods and original experiments. The text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison despite substantial additions in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds PIQA and WinoGrande evaluations, projected-output scoring comparisons, layer-wise analyses and growing-context experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original MMLU head-zeroing experiments across 14 models, score-function overlap measurements, attention-score distributions and attention-pattern analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain substantively unchanged: reward-guided optimization can promote unfaithful explanations, and causal-attribution augmentation can mitigate this behavior in controlled settings. Additional experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands applicability and mechanism discussion: the conclusion identifies controlled-setting limitations and difficulties constructing high-quality counterfactuals, while Section 5 explains D's label independence, C's proposed noise reduction, and avoidance of evaluator exploitation during training. Appendix F cautiously interprets mixed transfer evidence.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly documents exact-match answer extraction, invalid-output handling, and BoN counterfactual sampling from 16 responses. v3 also explicitly separates evaluator use from training. Existing DPO hyperparameters, hardware, software packages, prompt templates, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Math Book/AQUA-RAT and BiasQA/WINOGENERATED coverage is retained. v3 adds a limited software-reasoning transfer evaluation using 300 CodeMMLU Software Principles examples and Math Book-trained models (Appendix F, Table 4).

E2.justification: v3 adds RM_ALL, which appends disclaimers to every response, as an evaluated BoN comparator with both Skywork reward models (Appendix D, Figure 7). Existing base-model and default-RM comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 expands the evaluation design with full BoN/DPO experiments using Llama-3.2-3B, a blanket-disclaimer control, and cross-domain evaluation of Math Book-trained models. Appendix C also replaces classwise evaluator F1 reporting with macro-F1 and accuracy. Existing Llama-3.1-8B splits and training hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds a mechanism-focused ablation testing whether disclaimer wording alone explains mitigation (Figure 7), evaluator agreement and error examples (Tables 2–3), and a transfer analysis (Appendix F). These substantially extend the diagnostic evidence beyond v2's evaluator validation and generation examples.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three experiments with different seeds and report means and standard deviations. The additional results follow this existing practice; no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased run counts are reported.

E6.justification: v2 Tables 1–4 retain their numerical values in v3 Tables 1, 5, 6, and 9. v3 adds extensive 3B results, RM_ALL curves, transfer results, and revised evaluator metrics. For example, new Table 10 reports 3B BoN@16 stereotype rates of 68.1% with SK-Gemma-27B RM versus 55.5% with RM_C; these are new configurations, not improved earlier scores.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same counterfactual prediction tests, strategies D and C, and disclaimer augmentation for BoN and DPO. v3 clarifies the evaluator's evaluation-only role and counterfactual sampling without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative and much of the results prose remain. v3 makes localized rewrites and explanatory reorganizations, particularly in the introduction and Sections 3.2 and 5, revises appendix organization, and adds an LLM-usage statement.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from a two-column workshop layout to a single-column conference layout. It combines the introductory diagram with a reward-distribution panel, moves the original full distribution figure to Appendix B, adds counterfactual explanatory diagrams and experimental displays, and substantially rearranges appendix tables and plots.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds comparison with Turpin et al. (2025), distinguishing pre-alignment generator training from alignment-stage RM augmentation and discussing possible complementarity. A CoT Monitorability paragraph and additional citations broaden context while retaining the original research positioning.

T1.justification: The prediction-disagreement criterion, unfaithfulness condition, and background BoN selection expression are retained. New diagrams and explanations introduce no substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked a control testing whether disclaimer wording alone explained mitigation. v3's RM_ALL experiment (Figure 7) addresses this important gap, strengthening support for selective causal attribution. Second-generator experiments, evaluator error examples, and explicit counterfactual limitations further improve credibility. Transfer evidence remains preliminary and mixed, and classwise evaluator F1 detail is lost, but the stronger validation of the central mechanism provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, figures, tables, mathematical expressions, and appendices. Retained content can be reliably matched despite reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original results for another generator model, a disclaimer ablation, and CodeMMLU transfer evaluation.

before.justification: v2 reports original BoN and DPO experiments on Math Book and BiasQA, including numerical results and manual validation of its acknowledgment evaluator.

C1.justification: The central diagnosis, two-component i-LN contribution, and claims about restoration quality, feature stability, and low-precision robustness remain. v3 explicitly extends the introduction's applicability claims to real-world IR and presents theoretical insights as an additional contribution in the abstract.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism discussion: it explains cumulative outlier growth through residual paths, connects normalization bypassing to equal-statistics degeneracy, interprets SRFormer's permutation as partially holistic normalization, and discusses why gradient clipping fails while KLD sacrifices reconstruction fidelity. These extend the original bypassing and bias-alignment interpretations.

D1.justification: Beyond v2's brief settings paragraphs, v3 supplies a model-variant inventory, detailed architecture and optimization tables, degradation implementations, channel-entropy pseudocode, computational costs, and a code-repository link. This substantially improves implementation disclosure. Some inconsistencies remain: Table 5 describes HAT2 training as 300K iterations, whereas Table 14 specifies 500K.

E1.justification: The original training corpora, benchmark datasets, and four restoration tasks are retained. Appendix E.2 adds a complex synthetic degradation scenario for ×4 super-resolution, applying the Real-ESRGAN pipeline to DF2K training images and the same five SR test sets. This is a bounded extension of input conditions within the existing SR task.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original normalization comparator set. v3 adds LN with gradient clipping and LN with KL-divergence regularization as evaluated alternatives in Table 8, and compares SRFormer with LN versus i-LN in Table 7. These extend the comparisons without replacing the original comparison framework.

E3.justification: v3 introduces full-sized HAT experiments using 500K iterations for ×2 SR followed by 250K iterations of warm-start ×4 fine-tuning, an SRFormer configuration, and batch-size 2/4/8 tests. These substantially expand the evaluation design. The old HAT† results are retained under HAT2; newly disclosed settings for those existing experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v3 completes the component ablation by adding LN plus rescaling without spatial holisticness (Table 3). It extends RPE analysis across ablation variants, shallow/deep layers, and training stages (Figure 12), and adds gradient-clipping/KLD analyses, seed-stability tests, batch-size sensitivity, and additional qualitative cases. These address questions beyond the retained v2 analyses.

E5.justification: v2 does not document a repeated-seed evaluation protocol. v3 introduces multi-seed training trajectories in Figure 11 and five individual seed results with averages in Table 9. This substantially expands repeatability and variability reporting, although formal confidence intervals and significance tests are not supplied.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the previously reported ablation and low-precision scores are retained. v3 adds rescaling-only, full-sized HAT, SRFormer, regularization, and complex-degradation results; Table 9 reports average Urban100 PSNR of 21.95 for LN versus 22.14 for i-LN under the new degradation protocol. Some normalization-specific Set5 results disappear from Table 1. Table 6 prints Set14 ×2 SSIM as 0.8276 for i-LN versus 0.9274 for LN while bolding i-LN.

M1.justification: v2 Equations 3–5 and v3 Equations 2–3 specify the same method: joint spatial-channel normalization followed by rescaling attention/FFN outputs using the preceding normalization's standard deviation. The new theory, backbone experiments, and ablation variants do not revise the proposed i-LN procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially condensed and rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, observations become a standalone section, and experiments are reorganized into ablation and LN/i-LN property sections. Terminology changes from spatial consistency to spatial holisticness, and indexed backbone names clarify model variants.

P2.justification: The original Table 3 is split into separate ablation and quantization tables, Table 1 loses its Set5 columns, and existing plots and panels are rearranged or reformatted. v3 adds numerous experimental and configuration tables, entropy pseudocode, multi-run plots, expanded RPE displays, and qualitative comparison panels. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or page-count growth.

R1.justification: The original IR-transformer and abnormal-feature positioning largely remains. v3 adds references to Real-ESRGAN, SRFormer, BasicSR, and rate-distortion/VAE research supporting its new experiments and regularization discussion. It also adds a specific interpretation of SRFormer's normalization behavior, without broadly redefining the paper's research position.

T1.justification: v2 provides normalization equations and intuitive motivation without formal propositions or proofs. v3 adds definitions of inter-pixel structure and structure preservation, propositions concerning LN and holistic LN*, and derivations in Appendix G. The new analysis explicitly concerns normalization before the learned affine transformation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reproducibility and experimental support through detailed configurations, a complete component ablation, full-sized model tests, and repeated-seed and batch-size analyses. These address important gaps in v2 concerning component contributions, scaling, and training reliability while retaining its original benchmark results. The gains outweigh the added reporting problems, including the HAT2 training-duration conflict and Table 6 SSIM/bolding inconsistency. The expanded 'real-world' evidence remains entirely synthetic.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same i-LN research work. Their text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v2 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes Appendices A–G and detailed configuration tables, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds component ablations, regularization comparisons, repeated-seed analyses, and complex-degradation super-resolution results. The explicitly borrowed baseline scores in Table 6 do not negate the original results elsewhere.

before.justification: v2 reports original restoration experiments, normalization comparisons, feature-statistics analyses, ablations, and low-precision inference results in Tables 1–3 and Figures 1–10.

C1.justification: The central text-aligned tokenization contribution remains. However, v2's abstract adds comparative superiority on generated speech continuation, and its introduction adds precise speech editing and few-shot spoken QA as demonstrated capabilities. v1's explicit claim of substantially reduced computation during training and inference is no longer advanced in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning latency and streaming, English-only evaluation, and missing robust turn-taking and instruction following. It interprets new QA results as preservation of text-model capabilities and listening results as evidence of perceptual reconstruction quality. v1's speculation that successful embedding modeling could permit eliminating quantization is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A.4 newly documents Mechanical Turk sampling, 20 samples per method, more than 10 ratings per sample, MUSHRA reference conditions, complete human/GPT-4o instructions and transcription steps. Existing optimizer, hardware and epoch details are retained in relocated Appendix A.3. Conversely, v1's explicit Distil-Whisper aggregator initialization and two-decoder-block specification disappear. The resource pointer changes from a repository to a project website.

E1.justification: English Emilia and LibriTTS training coverage is retained. Beyond v1's reconstruction and likelihood-based benchmarks, v2 evaluates prompted speech generation, spoken question answering on Web Questions and LLaMA-Questions, and editing between utterances with the same transcript. Appendix Table 4 also adds SALMON background-domain and random-background scenarios.

E2.justification: Reconstruction comparisons add EnCodec and Mimi. The matched likelihood comparison adds TWIST 7B and removes pGSLM and ASR+LLM (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4). New continuation comparisons include two cascade systems, while question answering compares Mini-Omni, Moshi, Llama-Omni and their corresponding text models.

E3.justification: Reconstruction WER switches from Whisper to HuBERT-Large; duration consistency switches from Whisper alignment with 25 ms tolerance to Montreal Forced Aligner with 50 ms tolerance. Emotion consistency is removed, while DNSMOS, ViSQOL and MUSHRA are added. LoRA alpha changes from 64 to 128. New continuation and few-shot QA protocols are introduced. v2's reconstruction prose names LibriSpeech, but Table 1 still names LibriTTS, leaving the actual corpus uncertain.

E4.justification: Section 4.1.2 and Figure 3 add a focused editing case study absent from v1. Swapping selected tokens between utterances with different speaking rates tests whether word-specific duration information transfers; alignment visualizations show changes concentrated in the exchanged words. This is a limited qualitative mechanism analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates only. v2 adds uncertainty values to retained SALMON/StoryCloze results in Table 4 and reports values labeled standard deviations for reconstruction, continuation and QA in Appendix Tables 5–7. The estimation procedures are not explained sufficiently, and no training-seed counts or repeated-training evidence are supplied.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial continuation, QA, editing and background-consistency results. TASTE's reconstruction entries change from approximately 190 bps and 3.8% WER to 150 bps and 4.4% WER under revised evaluation conditions. Matched TASLM SALMON/StoryCloze point estimates are retained, but TWIST 1.3B's sSC/tSC scores change from 55.4/76.4 to 52.4/70.6 (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 4).

M1.justification: The core TASTE pipeline remains, but v2 adds an editing procedure that swaps selected word-aligned speech tokens before decoding (Section 4.1.2). The stated SLM objectives also change: Equation 6 omits v1's word-start loss mask, and Equation 8 explicitly includes text cross-entropy in the embedding objective. These equation revisions do not establish that training was rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial method passages are rewritten, with simplified notation and explanations. Related work, vocabulary alignment, training details and detailed benchmark descriptions move into dedicated appendix sections. The results narrative is reorganized around reconstruction, editing, continuation and question answering.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual overview and an editing diagram with spectrograms, redraws the tokenizer schematic, and removes v1's dedicated vocabulary-alignment/SLM-variants figure. Reconstruction tables are redesigned with different columns and highlighting. Detailed likelihood results move to Appendix Table 4, while new continuation, QA and uncertainty tables substantially expand the displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around speech representation learning and generative tokenization, adding works such as SUPERB, UniWav and Align-SLM while removing several earlier multimodal-LLM references. Appendix A.1 explicitly distinguishes TASTE from Chen and Rudnicky's prior text-speech attention for TTS. Much of v1's related-work section is retained through relocation.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 7 replaces v1 Equation 12's abstract KL expression with an explicit Gaussian expansion. Its printed first variance term is sigma rather than sigma squared, inconsistent with the stated sampling parameterization. This introduces a mathematical discrepancy beyond notation changes. Neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 claims natural speech continuation but evaluates its SLMs through likelihood-based selection. v2 addresses this important evidential gap with direct generation tests using human and automated ratings, alongside perceptual reconstruction, editing and QA evidence. Evaluation instructions and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the paper. The conflicting reconstruction-corpus labels, new KL-formula discrepancy and unclear uncertainty estimation temper the improvement, but the substantially stronger evidence for the central generative capability outweighs these reporting weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TASTE/TASLM research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison. Internal inconsistencies in v2 limit interpretation of particular settings, rather than material completeness.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, speech continuation, human listening, spoken question answering and speech-editing results in Tables 1–4 and Figure 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original speech reconstruction experiments and TASLM evaluations on SALMON and StoryCloze in Tables 1–2.

C1.justification: v2's abstract claims comparable SALMON/StoryCloze performance; v3 broadens this to outperforming pretrained SLMs on likelihood-based next-speech selection, despite unchanged scores. v3 also makes avoiding redundant textual information an explicit token-design principle. The central contribution remains text-aligned tokenization for joint spoken language modeling.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking reconstruction WER to paralinguistic information and weak ViSQOL to the flow-based vocoder, interprets ASR robustness, and discusses SALMON background weaknesses. Its limitations additionally identify untested generalization to other generative tasks and unsupported overlapping speakers and non-lexical events. These substantially expand the scientific interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies the shallow-layer choice l=6 and normalized embeddings with learned softmax fusion weights, and explicitly confirms ASR transcription use in the main experiments. Training hyperparameters, hardware, and access statements remain substantially unchanged. The earlier explicit tokenizer checkpoint specification and RVQ straight-through-estimator note are omitted.

E1.justification: Training datasets and the original reconstruction, continuation, SALMON, StoryCloze, and QA tasks remain. v3 adds reconstruction under white noise at 20, 15, 10, and 5 dB SNR (Table 8). Table 1's change from LibriTTS to LibriSpeech resolves v2's caption/prose inconsistency rather than establishing different dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the evaluated codec comparators through DAC, DM-Codec, and BigCodec in the new noise comparison (Table 8), alongside retained SpeechTokenizer, Mimi, and S3. The comparator sets in the original reconstruction, language-modeling, and QA tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include module and encoder-layer controls measured by S3 top-5 reconstruction accuracy, ground-truth versus ASR transcription controls, Parakeet replacing Whisper before GPT-4o scoring, and controlled white-noise reconstruction (Tables 4–8). These extend the evaluation protocol; the original training budgets, benchmark metrics, and human-evaluation sample counts are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained editing case study, v3 adds component ablations, ASR-dependence and evaluator-sensitivity tests, noise robustness comparisons, attention-map inspection, and layer-wise representation analysis (Section 5.2.3 and Appendices A.1.1–A.1.4). These directly examine information retention, alignment, layer selection, and robustness.

E5.justification: v3 introduces canonical correlation analysis between Whisper layers and S3 embeddings, adding a statistical association analysis (Appendix A.1.3, Figure 6). Existing standard-deviation tables and human-rating counts are unchanged. No additional repeated runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance-testing procedure are reported.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores and standard-deviation tables are retained, but substantial diagnostic results are added. Examples include module-wise top-5 accuracies of 0.98, 0.88, and 0.76 versus 0.65 for text-only (Table 4), Parakeet-based TASLM scores of 3.20/3.37 (Table 7), and TASTE's 11.1% WER at 5 dB SNR (Table 8). These are new conditions, not version-to-version performance gains.

M1.justification: The Whisper encoder, attention aggregator, RVQ quantizer, speech decoder, token/embedding language-modeling objectives, and word-level alignment algorithm are retained. Appendix A.5 specifies the previously described weighted-sum fusion; it does not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and result interpretations are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from the appendix into the main text; results are reorganized into main and additional results; and the appendices are reordered. Ethics, acknowledgements, and an LLM-use disclosure are added, alongside conference-format and affiliation edits.

P2.justification: v3 adds five diagnostic tables and three figures containing attention maps and a layer-correlation curve. Table 1 gains a token-frequency column and expanded caption, Table 3 is placed beside the new ablation table, and existing figures and appendix tables are relocated or reformatted. Figures 1–3 retain their underlying visual evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on newer joint SLMs, codecs, continuous-token modeling, ASR, and representation analysis, while removing some general representation-learning and subword-tokenization references. The central positioning against length-mismatched speech tokens and the distinction from Chen and Rudnicky's TTS cross-attention remain. Moving related work into Section 2 is principally structural.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(8), the vocabulary-alignment algorithm, and the substantive mathematical assumptions are retained. Appendix A.5 writes out the already described weighted-sum implementation; it adds no substantive theoretical result, proof, or revised derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 largely supported its ASR assumptions and component choices through end-task results. v3 directly investigates these central dependencies through component ablations, transcription and evaluator controls, attention/layer analyses, and noise tests (Tables 4–8, Figures 4–6). Together with clearer applicability limits, this substantially strengthens validation of the retained method. The new analyses lack quantified uncertainty, and the abstract's broader superiority claim exceeds the unchanged SALMON evidence, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TASTE and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained method and experiments can be matched reliably across the revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds component ablations, ASR checks, representation analyses, and controlled noise experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original speech reconstruction, text-aligned editing, speech continuation, benchmark evaluation, and spoken question-answering results, including human listening tests.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central contribution: a three-stage framework generating faithful, useful repositories directly from machine-learning papers, supported by benchmark and original-author evaluations and claims of outperforming baselines. Updated headline percentages and rewritten reproduction language do not materially redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1’s domain and proxy-evaluation caveats, v4 adds a top-down explanation of baseline differences, interpretations concerning paper underspecification and packaging failures, an explicit text-only input limitation, and concrete partial-reproduction failures. It emphasizes repositories as starting points for reproduction. Conversely, the unchanged Oracle comparison is interpreted more strongly as performance parity without significant differences, replacing v1’s acknowledgment of a remaining gap (Section 4.2).

D1.justification: v4 supplies previously absent evaluation prompts, debugging and refinement prompts, API costs, execution hardware and Docker information, debugging-model and fallback choices, and disclosures about resource-driven adjustments. Appendix A.4 newly documents generation of reproduce.sh for PaperBench. It adds a project code URL and statements about supplementary code and README instructions, and replaces the human-compensation placeholder with $15/hour. External resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The original 90-paper benchmark and 20-paper PaperBench Code-Dev coverage are retained. Added human-evaluation papers include trigger-free data poisoning and continual audio-video pretraining (v4 Table 20). v4 also tests a distinct incomplete-input scenario by removing Methodology sections (Table 11). Coverage expands within the existing machine-learning domain.

E2.justification: The main ChatDev, MetaGPT, Abstract, Paper, Basic Agent, and Iterative Agent comparisons remain. v4 adds a direct comparison with Self-Refine-augmented PaperCoder (Table 7). Abstract is no longer reported in the sequential component-ablation comparison (Table 6), although it remains in other comparisons. Additional backbone configurations do not constitute new baseline methods.

E3.justification: v4 adds full-rubric reproduction testing on 10 PaperBench papers and author-rubric testing on 10 human-evaluation papers, including debugging conditions and different judges. It also adds 30-paper refinement and missing-methodology protocols and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1, and o3 configurations. Human evaluation expands from 13 papers to 21 listed papers, while reporting 25 preference judgments without explaining their mapping. Execution experiments permit hardware-driven hyperparameter and data adjustments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and five-repository execution checks, v4 tests whether refinement improves downstream outputs, removes Methodology sections, stratifies performance by presentation type and research category, categorizes runtime failures, and compares reproduction with and without debugging. Its case studies now distinguish successful execution from faithful or partial reproduction (Section 4.3; Appendix B; Tables 7 and 11–16).

E5.justification: v4 newly reports three-run means and standard deviations for PaperCoder on PaperBench, except o1 and o3, and adds p≤0.05 markings and Cohen’s kappa of 0.79. Existing eight-sample judge averaging and other dispersion reporting remain. The retained Basic/Iterative Agent error bars change description from standard errors in v1 to standard deviations in v4 without explaining recalculation; significance-test details are also unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 1 scores remain unchanged. PaperCoder’s PaperBench result changes from 44.26 to a reported three-run 45.14±0.3, with additional model results; notably, o1 scores 38.31 versus Iterative Agent’s 43.3 (v4 Table 10). The expanded human study reports 88% preference and 92% helpfulness versus 77% and 85%, which are not matched-cohort gains. New reproduction, refinement, and failure results substantially expand the evidence. Code-availability and manual-edit summaries also change.

M1.justification: The default planning–analysis–coding algorithm and original generation prompts remain substantively unchanged. v4 adds experimental extensions: verification and Self-Refine of planning/analysis outputs, and execution-triggered LLM debugging (Sections 4.2–4.3; Appendix D). These introduce actual feedback and repair procedures, while remaining auxiliary to the retained generator.

P1.justification: The method and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Previously separate experimental-setup and results sections become one Section 4 with dedicated reproduction analysis. Human-evaluation instructions move into Appendix A.2, limitations move to Appendix C, and the appendices gain an explicit hierarchy for analyses, prompts, and planning examples. This is substantial editorial reorganization beyond the added science.

P2.justification: v4 adds refinement, reproduction, failure, and cost tables; presentation/category plots; debugging examples; and planning-artifact diagrams and prompt panels. Existing displays are also reorganized: Table 1 changes conference order, the PaperBench table gains backbone columns, and executability statistics separate Python and configuration edits. Main-text panels are regrouped and the retained human-evaluation forms are resized and relocated.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including Self-Refine, SciReplicate-Bench, S2ORC, ReAct, and the Transformer paper, while removing CodeT and CodeScore citations. The central positioning relative to software-development agents and PaperBench remains similar. ML-Bench is retained despite its changed author/year attribution, and publication-metadata updates do not represent new related work.

T1.justification: v4 makes the notation more explicit through prompt templates, file sets, and previously generated code context, but these restate dependencies already described in v1. Neither version supplies substantive theoretical guarantees, proofs, or derivations that are added or revised in the comparison.

improvement.justification: v1 relied chiefly on proxy scores and five manual execution checks. v4 substantially improves validation and auditability through full-rubric reproduction tests, broader runtime-failure analysis, a missing-methodology control, and complete evaluation/debugging prompts. The case studies expose the distinction between execution and faithful reproduction. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: execution settings are adjusted, Table 13’s reported average does not match its five entries, and the Oracle-parity interpretation exceeds the documented statistical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PaperCoder research, with matching authors, task, framework, and core experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection, including all appendices, support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and additions.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds refinement experiments, reproduction tests, runtime failure analyses, and expanded human and model evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original Paper2Code and PaperBench results, author evaluations, component ablations, and manual executability checks.

C1.justification: The central RL post-training contribution and thirteen-benchmark accuracy/sparsity claim remain. V1's 80% to 25% token retention and v2's 20% to 75% token reduction express the same claim. V2 adds quantified claims of up to 3× lower memory and 3.3× faster decoding to the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation beyond v1's brief performance discussion. It explains the all-incorrect-group reward failure, argues for grouped RL and layer-dependent sparsity, and interprets budget, context-length, and hallucination results. Its new limitations discussion identifies sequential multi-budget rollouts and incompatible KV-cache trajectories as barriers to batching and efficient training.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial previously absent implementation information: eight A100 GPUs, Adam with learning rate 1e-6, KL weight 0.04, training/evaluation frame and token counts, the 10k LLaVA calibration subset, and baseline block/budget settings. It also details ZipVL token selection and sequential rollout execution. These disclosures do not themselves establish changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: The original thirteen benchmarks and Qwen calibration dataset remain. V2 adds HallusionBench for hallucination/visual-illusion evaluation and a subset of LLaVA-Video-178k for video calibration. These extend coverage within the existing image/video domains; adding the LLaVA backbone alone is not new task coverage.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only full attention and ZipVL as comparators. V2 adds FastV and VisionZip to Qwen2.5 image comparisons; its LLaVA video comparisons also include MInference. Table 3 evaluates MOBA, post-trained ZipVL, and sharpness-loss baselines, while Figure 4 adds FlashAttention-2 resource comparisons.

E3.justification: V2 adds LLaVA-Video-7B evaluation, cross-benchmark averages, a FLOPs-equivalent ratio for MInference, budget/context-length sweeps, and controlled training-range/group-size experiments. The original training p range and inference p=0.975 remain. Newly disclosed Qwen frame/token counts do not establish changes to earlier settings, and the MLVU heading change from dev to M-avg does not establish a split change.

E4.justification: V1 contains no corresponding diagnostic experiments. V2 adds attention-mechanism ablations (Table 4), training-range and rollout-group-size ablations (Table 5), budget and context-length sensitivity tests, attention-map/layer-wise analyses, and low-budget HallusionBench robustness evaluation (Figures 3–6). These test component choices, adaptability, and preservation of visual evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V2's group-size ablation concerns GRPO training rollouts, not repeated experimental runs or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 revise many retained Qwen results. For example, Qwen2.5-VL-7B's proposed-method image ratio/MME is 24.3%/2320 in v1 and 24.7%/2286 in v2; full-attention MME also changes from 2337 to 2303. V2 additionally reports LLaVA, expanded baseline, ablation, robustness, and resource-use results. These are revised or new reports, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The GRPO/ZipVL framework remains, but v2 replaces v1's unconditional performance-plus-efficiency reward with a group-success gate: efficiency is rewarded only if at least one rollout answers correctly (Section 3.2, Equations 8–9). This is a localized objective refinement; the rename and expanded ZipVL description do not establish additional method changes.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, and method explanations are expanded. V1's compact Experiments section becomes separate Experimental Setup, Main Results, and Ablation Study and Discussion sections, alongside new Related Work and limitations text. The title and method terminology change throughout.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 with a visual query and clearer rollout-group annotations, adds Figures 2–6, and introduces Tables 3–5. Tables 1–2 gain comparator rows, average columns, and a LLaVA model block. Multipanel plots, heatmaps, and text-wrapped displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated Related Work section covering methods including VisionZip, SparseVLM, SeerAttention, MMinference, and additional attention regularization work. It substantially develops its positioning against teacher-forced SFT, fixed sparsity patterns, and proxy objectives, and adds discussion of DPO and DAPO.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the mathematical group-success indicator and conditional reward in Equations 8–9. The common masking equations, attention-retention constraint, cited approximation bound, and GRPO objective remain substantively unchanged. Additional ZipVL equations largely formalize an existing component; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V1 largely supports efficiency through accuracy/token-ratio tables against full attention and ZipVL. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence with broader baselines, measured resource use, diagnostic experiments, and implementation details. New reporting inconsistencies temper the gains: Table 3 lists Sparsity Forcing/Full averages as 70.0/70.2, contrary to the prose's 70.3/70.0, and Figure 4 labels the timing measurement as prefill despite the abstract's decoding-speedup claim. These errors weaken precision but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-based token-sparsity work, renamed from ZipR1 to Sparsity Forcing. All pages, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons, ablations, robustness analyses, and latency/memory measurements in Tables 1–5 and Figures 3–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original accuracy and token-retention results for three Qwen models across seven image and six video benchmarks in Tables 1–2.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—camera-agnostic representation learning, joint spectral/spatial SSL and cross-domain validation—remain. Section 6 replaces v2's broader priority claim of being the first work explicitly designed for spectral heterogeneity with the more specific claim to combining camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding and SSL.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations that spectral SSL prevents representation collapse and that learned features separate organ semantics from sensor identity. It also interprets embedding dimension as more useful than increasing representation count beyond eight. The discussion adds computational cost as a limitation and identifies spatial-resolution differences and additional sensor metadata as an applicability issue and possible remedy.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly specifies satellite dataset composition, 78,000 pre-training iterations, NVIDIA H200 hardware, weight decay, and linear-probe optimization, epochs, augmentation and resolution adjustment. Other implementation settings and GPU-memory information are revised. Section 7 adds a reproducibility statement identifying public datasets and existing documentation; the pseudocode was already present in v2.

E1.justification: Satellite pre-training expands from HySpecNet-11k hyperspectral imagery to mixed EnMAP and Sentinel-2 data, adding SpectralEarth and BigEarthNet. Evaluation adds m-forestnet classification and m-SA-crop-type and m-cashew-plantation segmentation, including Landsat-8 coverage. Medical evaluation additionally uses real-world filter responses for synthesis and previously unseen simulated cameras.

E2.justification: DOFA is added to medical, automotive, satellite and computational comparisons; Early Fusion is added to the medical comparison in Figure 5. The SegMunich comparison removes ViT and ViT-22k. Its previously retrained SpectralGPT+ comparator remains under the shorter SpectralGPT+ name, rather than being a newly introduced baseline.

E3.justification: Satellite experiments switch from the small model to a base configuration with spatial embedding dimension 768 and expand pre-training from 11,483 to 808,001 images. Appendix A revises SSL channel processing, mask counts and proportions, batch size from 16 to 64, and final learning rate from 10^-5 to 10^-6. New protocols include linear probing, k-NN evaluation and class-removal controls; DOFA input resolution is doubled for linear probing.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests using real-world filter responses and withheld HSICity traffic-class annotations, plus spatial-only versus joint spectral/spatial SSL ablation (Table 3). Table 6 adds aggregation and embedding-dimension ablations while retaining the existing positional-encoding and representation-count results. Appendix E adds unseen-camera feature analysis using t-SNE and regression-based variance estimates.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence-interval reporting continues, without new seed or repeated-training-run counts. Appendix E adds a statistical estimation procedure: separate regressions on organ class and sensor identity, with R2 averaged across embedding dimensions to estimate explained variance.

E6.justification: HSICity HyperFree mIoU changes from 40.1 to 44.6; CARL and CARL-SSL remain 48.6 and 50.1, while newly added DOFA scores 49.6. SegMunich CARL-SSL changes from 50.7 to 50.9 under different model and pre-training conditions. The matched SpectralGPT+ Mine/dump entry changes from 48.2 to 38.2. Substantial new results include linear probing, transfer tests, SSL ablation accuracy of 22.1 versus 32.6, and organ/sensor explained variance of 61.6% versus 0.6%.

M1.justification: Sections 3 and Algorithms 1–2 retain the wavelength encoding, alternating attention, representation aggregation, teacher–student predictors and summed VICReg objectives. Query representations Q are renamed spectral representations S. Model scale and masking settings change, but no new algorithmic component or objective is introduced.

P1.justification: Related work, experimental descriptions, ablation discussion and the closing discussion are extensively rewritten. Query terminology changes throughout the method and pseudocode. The document adds a reproducibility section, a satellite implementation subsection, feature-analysis and LLM-usage appendices, and moves existing medical protocol details into Appendix D.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned, Figure 5 gains comparator curves and changes its horizontal axis from subject counts to fractions, and Figure 6 adds a t-SNE visualization. New tables present method capabilities, transfer and SSL tests, linear probes, dataset composition and explained variance. Existing benchmark and ablation tables are reorganized and expanded, alongside widespread header, typography and float-layout changes.

R1.justification: Related work substantively incorporates DOFA, AnySat and Galileo, distinguishing camera-agnostic spatial methods from CARL's joint spectral/spatial approach. New Table 1 organizes positioning around four capabilities. Conversely, v3 removes explicit methodological links to Avilés et al.'s wavelength encoding and BLIP-2's query inspiration, changing attribution as well as citation membership.

T1.justification: The wavelength positional encoding, VICReg equations and synthetic-filter construction remain mathematically equivalent. Naming the two loss components and renumbering equations do not alter their definitions. The new regression analysis is empirical; neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked direct ablation of its central spectral SSL contribution and offered limited evidence about the learned representations themselves. v3 substantially addresses these gaps through the SSL ablation, controlled transfer tests and unseen-camera feature analysis, while adding stronger comparators and broader downstream validation. These strengthen support for the existing scientific claims. Limited drawbacks remain: Table 3b's CARL class-drop deltas are not reconciled with Table 9, and some methodological attribution is removed. The overall evidential gains outweigh these drawbacks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARL and CARL-SSL, with matching architectures and identifiable corresponding experiments. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds satellite classification and segmentation evaluations, controlled transfer tests, SSL ablations and feature analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original medical, automotive and satellite segmentation experiments, architectural ablations and computational measurements.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and concluding discussion retain the same central claims: camera-agnostic spatio-spectral encoding, joint spectral/spatial self-supervision, and cross-domain robustness. Changing 'wavelength-aware' to 'camera-agnostic' within the first contribution aligns with its existing heading and surrounding claims. The expanded experiments support the retained contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations that channel subsampling preserves information through learned spectral relationships and acts as stochastic regularization against missing or shifted bands. It also connects expanded unseen-sensor results to the accuracy–compute tradeoff. Existing limitations concerning computational cost and spatial-resolution heterogeneity remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents public access to code and model weights through a repository identified in the abstract, materially extending the reproducibility information beyond v3's pseudocode and training recipe. Table 8 also supplies benchmark sensor, channel, wavelength, class, and task metadata. This assesses documented access; external resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: Satellite evaluation expands from four to eleven benchmark entries. Additions include m-bigearthnet, m-eurosat, urban and rural LoveDA, WHU-OHS, Wuhan, and Beijing, extending evaluation to RGB imagery and unseen Orbita and Gaofen-5 hyperspectral sensors. The earlier datasets, including renamed m-cashew-plantation, remain. Medical, automotive, and pretraining coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds Galileo, Croma, Copernicus-FM, and SMARTIES to satellite linear-probe comparisons where applicable, including retained benchmarks. Table 10 adds SMARTIES to SegMunich fine-tuning and retains SatMAE, despite Appendix C's narrower baseline description. The computational comparison removes EVA-02, HyperFree, Hyve, and Spectral Adapter and adds Copernicus-FM and SMARTIES.

E3.justification: The FLOP comparison changes from standardized-depth/width encoders at 128×128×48 in v3 Appendix B to base-size models with a fixed 16×16 patch grid and 3/12/32/116 channels in v4 Appendix D. v4 also introduces average benchmark rank and a separate 16-channel training experiment. Table 8 reports 13 rather than 12 channels for the retained cashew and crop-type datasets; this revises reported inputs without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: v4 Appendix D extends the efficiency analysis across channel configurations and adds a targeted subsampling test: 16-channel training yields 68.8 versus 69.1 validation mIoU with roughly 75% fewer training FLOPs. The architectural ablations, SSL-loss ablation, medical heterogeneity tests, and t-SNE/feature-variance analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 4 reports 95% confidence intervals for satellite linear probing; corresponding results in v4 Tables 4, 5, and 9 omit them. Confidence intervals remain for medical robustness, automotive segmentation, and SegMunich fine-tuning. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, or a confidence-interval estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive satellite results, including WHU-OHS mIoU of 21.7 for CARL versus 1.5 for each evaluated baseline and an average rank of 1.6. Added SMARTIES results exceed unchanged CARL scores on m-forestnet (49.8 versus 47.0) and SegMunich linear probing (39.1 versus 38.9). DOFA's cashew entry changes from 18.7 to 18.2 alongside revised reported channel counts. Computational results are replaced under different settings; CARL's fine-tuned SegMunich score remains 50.9.

M1.justification: The wavelength encoding, spectral self-attention/cross-attention architecture, aggregation, spatial encoder, masking objectives, and Algorithms 1–2 are retained. Channel subsampling already appears in v3 Appendix A.1; v4's 16-channel experiment changes an experimental setting without introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: v4 revises the satellite-results narrative, expands related-work explanations, rewrites the complexity discussion, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. Satellite model labels are simplified, and headers change to conference-publication status. Most introductory, methodological, medical, automotive, ablation, and concluding prose remains substantially intact.

P2.justification: The satellite results presentation is substantially reorganized: v3 Table 4 becomes expanded tables separating seen and unseen sensors across the main text and appendix. Fine-tuning moves from main-text Table 5 to appendix Table 10, a dataset-description table is added, and the FLOP table gains sensor-specific columns and performance ranks. The six figures are retained, with limited diagram, caption, sizing, and placement adjustments.

R1.justification: v4 adds an expanded related-work appendix and substantially elaborates distinctions among channel invariance, wavelength awareness, spatial versus spatio-spectral encoding, and SSL strategies. Added works include Copernicus-FM, SMARTIES, Panopticon, TerraMind, Croma, OmniSat, and FlexiMo. This broadens and sharpens research positioning beyond citation or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix D adds explicit asymptotic reasoning distinguishing O(C²) spectral self-attention, O(CK) cross-attention, and O((HW)²) spatial attention from SpectralGPT's O((HWC)²) attention. v3 provides only qualitative complexity discussion and linear cross-attention scaling. The wavelength, loss, and synthetic-filter equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the central camera-generalization claim by testing unseen real RGB and hyperspectral sensors against additional camera-agnostic competitors; v3's satellite evaluation covered Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 only. The LoveDA and WHU-OHS results directly support this broader applicability. Expanded efficiency analysis and documented code/weight access also improve assessability and reproducibility. Dropped linear-probe confidence intervals and unexplained channel-count revisions weaken reporting, but the new evidence addresses an important limitation of the earlier validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CARL and contain readable methods, equations, experimental results, figures, tables, and appendices. Inspection of all 19 pages of v3 and 23 pages of v4 supports comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds satellite benchmark comparisons, revised computational measurements, and a channel-subsampling experiment.

before.justification: v3 reports original medical, automotive, and satellite experiments, architectural and self-supervision ablations, computational measurements, and feature-representation analyses.

C1.justification: The o3-specific accuracy and masking contributions become a broader cross-model privacy-risk claim. v3 foregrounds DOXBENCH, three risk levels, CLUEMINER, GEOMINER and GLARE, claims advantages over non-expert humans, and identifies clue-based reasoning and insufficient privacy alignment as two principal causes.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes revealing clues and the potential of targeted masking, qualified by residual-clue leakage. v3 adds interpretations of CoT answering harder previously refused cases, tool amplification and reflection-related exposure. Its defense discussion develops noise-dependent failures and privacy–utility tradeoffs from prompt-based refusal, substantially expanding applicability and limitation analysis.

D1.justification: v3 documents camera/EXIF data collection, framework and defense prompts, default model parameters, geocoding/Census/pyproj evaluation, and noise-processing libraries and settings. It adds a project URL and removes v1's explicit dataset non-release statement. The PDFs alone do not establish that code or data actually became downloadable.

E1.justification: The benchmark changes from Google Maps residential imagery across US cities to researcher-captured California imagery spanning three privacy-risk levels. New coverage includes private spaces without individuals, 46 reflection cases and explicit benign defense controls. Public travel scenes themselves are not wholly new: v1 already includes such appendix demonstrations.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates o3 without model or human comparators. v3 adds comparisons involving o4-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4, QVQ-Max and Llama 4 models. GEOMINER is compared with vanilla and CoT prompting, and Table 4 introduces non-expert human performance.

E3.justification: v1 Figure 3 selects the most accurate prediction across four prompts; v3 separately evaluates structured Top-1/Top-3 and vanilla/CoT conditions. Distance bins and one-/five-mile labels give way to geodesic AED/MED, Census-based geographic accuracy, VRR and GLARE. v3 also introduces API-versus-web/tool controls and a 30-image human comparison with a 300-second limit.

E4.justification: v1's paired Suzhou and Cleveland masking demonstrations are removed. v3 adds reasoning-pattern audits, CoT and tool-use comparisons, CLUEMINER convergence analysis, reflection case studies, Gaussian-noise sensitivity, and prompt/guardrail defense tests. These substantially broaden the mechanisms and failure conditions investigated.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports IQR-based outlier filtering for Table 1, changing the documented statistical treatment of errors. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's headline results are 60% within one mile and 84% within five miles. Under its different dataset and protocol, v3 Table 1 reports o3 vanilla Top-1 VRR of 80.8%, AED of 13.56 km and 34 correct census-block predictions; these are not comparable performance changes. Extensive new results cover other models, reflections, GEOMINER, humans and defenses.

M1.justification: v1 queries o3 and manually categorizes its clues. v3 introduces CLUEMINER's iterative analyzer and category-memory procedure, plus GEOMINER's two-stage Detector–Analyzer inference pipeline (Sections 5.3 and 6; Appendix B). These are new procedural components, beyond renaming the earlier clue analysis.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around three research questions. The earlier compact methodology/experiment narrative becomes separate threat-model, evaluation, mechanism, attack, human-comparison and defense sections. The screenshot appendix is replaced by organized Appendices A–D covering ethics, methods, mathematics and prompts.

P2.justification: The opening illustrative example is retained, but most displays are redesigned or replaced. v1's collection workflow, clue-frequency plots and full-page appendix chats give way to risk-level examples and radar charts, multi-model tables, convergence/attack/noise plots and prompt boxes. This substantially changes visual organization beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds engagement with VLMs as GeoGuessr Masters and Image-based Geolocation Using Large Vision-Language Models, criticizing image resolution, privacy coverage and evaluation practices. Positioning expands around a risk-tiered benchmark, legal/privacy-policy context and information-theoretic measurement, while retaining the earlier distinction between inference-time and training-data privacy.

T1.justification: v1's autoregressive factorization and image-set formalization are removed. v3 introduces GLARE's mutual-information definition, entropy bound, uniform spatial assumptions, spherical-cap approximation and geometric-mean error radius (Appendix C). This is substantial new mathematical content, although the derivation unjustifiably replaces the bound I(L;R) ≤ H(R) with equality.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical foundation beyond v1's single-model pilot through model/human comparators, refusal reporting, Census-based accuracy and controlled mechanism/defense tests. These address important weaknesses in interpreting the original leakage claims. The new GLARE contribution remains materially flawed: Appendix C substitutes an entropy bound with equality, and Table 4's bit values are roughly 100 times those implied by its formula. This weakens information-theoretic claims, but the independent conventional metrics and comparisons still provide substantial overall gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same image-geolocation privacy study, substantially expanded in v3. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including v1's screenshot-based appendix.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations on DOXBENCH, reasoning and tool-use analyses, GEOMINER experiments, human comparisons and defense results.

before.justification: v1 reports original o3 geolocation results on 50 images, visual-clue frequencies and paired masking demonstrations.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on balanced exact-k training and generalization beyond trained complexity levels. v2 reframes the contribution around informative synthetic questions and complexity-aware data efficiency, dropping the headline unseen-complexity gains. Matching full-data performance with approximately 10% of the data remains a central claim.

C2.justification: v2 explains implicit object recognition and overlapping capabilities, qualifies the taxonomy as a practical choice, and discusses tradeoffs between simple and complex training examples. Revised Table 3 supports attributing roughly half the gain to complexity, replacing v1's 'most' interpretation. Appendix A.6 adds substantive remaining failure conditions, including incorrect answers and ambiguous spatial or occluded attributes.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies generation temperature 0.1, top-p 0.9, a 1,000-token limit, average generation runs, 32 parallel processes, approximately two hours, and $86.5 cost. These are useful disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to existing settings. The project URL and promise of a future data release remain.

E1.justification: Both use LLaVA-665K images and the same eight main benchmarks. OK-VQA, MMMU, and MMMU-Pro are retained from v1 Table 4 in v2 Figure 9. New complexity breakdowns and generator experiments remain within this existing task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands beyond full LLaVA-665K, Random, and ICONS by adding evaluated 65K-data comparisons with EL2N, Perplexity, SemDeDup, D2-Pruning, Self-Sup, and Self-Filter. This substantially broadens the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds k+0/k+1 regeneration controls, two additional complexity-range settings, TextVQA stratification, and a Qwen3 generator configuration. The distribution-matched control now matches capability and k distributions. LLaVA complexity analysis changes from 5,668 to 5,400 questions, and its annotation prompt replaces object relationship with scene understanding. The main one-epoch LLaVA training setup remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled complexity augmentation, TextVQA difficulty analysis, MMStar category and complexity breakdowns, capability correlations, token efficiency, generation failures, and generator robustness analyses. It removes v1's direct COMPACT-versus-full-VIT high-k analysis in Figure 4. The leave-one-capability-out analysis is retained as Table 7, rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v2 Table 8 newly reports token-length means with ± terms, without defining the spread statistic. The complexity-range display also drops v1 Figure 7's unexplained shaded bands. Neither version documents repeated-training uncertainty or evaluation seeds; v2's average three runs per question concerns data generation.

E6.justification: Original Table 2 rows are unchanged, but added results change rankings: EL2N scores 33.53 on MM-Vet versus COMPACT's 31.74, and D2-Pruning scores 36.63 on MMStar versus 36.13. Table 3 replaces the 96.62% unbalanced-control result with 97.55% under revised matching conditions. New Qwen3 results reach 98.31% relative performance. Complexity estimates and supplementary findings also change, while v1's direct high-k generalization results disappear.

M1.justification: The four-step recipe, atomic taxonomy, and trained model remain. However, v1 explicitly rejects questions requiring extra capabilities, whereas v2 describes the sampled count k_gen as a lower bound on actual complexity. Its appendix still requires exactly k capabilities. The PDFs do not establish whether verification changed or its behavior was reinterpreted.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, interpretation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around information density and complexity-aware curation. Analyses are reorganized between the main text and appendix, which gains numbered subsections and a contents page. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column layout and extensively redesigns displays. Figure 1 becomes an experimental comparison; capability heatmaps become frequency bars; the capability ablation becomes a table; complexity-range curves become heatmaps; and the instruction-ratio plot shows separate benchmarks. New analytical displays and revised sample illustrations further change presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions COMPACT around data curation and complexity-controlled efficiency. It adds the six data-reduction baseline works and a compositional visual reasoning survey, while removing several compositionality and diagnostic references, including Fodor and LePore and Zhao et al. Taxonomy provenance shifts from benchmark literature toward LLaVA data curation and manual inspection.

T1.justification: Both retain complexity k as the number of required atomic capabilities. v2 introduces a distinct sampled count k_gen and explicitly states k_gen ≤ k, replacing v1's identification of requested and realized complexity. This is a limited revision to the mathematical characterization; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the data-efficiency contribution through broader baselines, regeneration controls, and an open-source generator test. It also replaces the strict unseen-complexity framing with a more qualified account and documents generation failures and settings. These gains outweigh remaining exact-k prompt inconsistencies and newly erroneous example answers in Figure 12, although those defects still weaken clarity and confidence in the illustrations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COMPACT and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments and relocated material can be matched despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline evaluations, controlled complexity experiments, token and failure analyses, and an open-source generator evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training evaluations across eight main benchmarks, ablations, dataset analyses, and additional knowledge-intensive benchmark results.

C1.justification: v3 adds cognitively interpretable determinants of decoding performance as an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Its prominent model contribution expands to commercial fine-tuning and zero-/few-shot reconstruction. The original claims about decoding text-specific goals and the difficulty of free-form reconstruction remain.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantive interpretations involving resource-efficient reading, task adaptation, feature redundancy, fixation ordering, and the inferential character of OneStop questions. Reconstruction discussion now distinguishes model-specific benefits from eye movements and their limits on unseen texts. These extend v2's mainly aggregate performance and generalization discussion.

D1.justification: v3 supplies Gemini demonstration-selection prompts, GPT fine-tuning settings and model versions, and detailed LLaVA encoder layers. It corrects feature-table attribution and removes v2's conflicting candidate-loss training description. Code instructions now identify a named repository, and Appendix G.2.2 announces access to generated questions and annotations through generated_questions.csv.

E1.justification: The OneStop population, passages, and goal-decoding tasks remain unchanged. Appendix A adds SQuAD question–passage data for a comparative lexical-overlap analysis, providing limited additional dataset coverage while gaze-model evaluations remain on OneStop.

E2.justification: Reconstruction comparisons add DalEye-GPT, Gemini variants, DalEye-LLaVA, and GPT-4o-mini/LLaVA text-only controls. Arbitrary GPT-4o questions are replaced by arbitrary Gemini 3 questions (v2 Table 12; v3 Tables 14–15). v2's 'Llama 3.1 arbitrary question' is retained as Text-only Llama 3.1; selection comparators remain available in the appendix.

E3.justification: Question-word and category evaluation changes from Cohen's kappa to accuracy, and Gemini introduces zero-shot and regime-matched ten-example protocols. v3 also reports LLaVA LoRA rank 16 instead of 8 and early-stopping patience 7 instead of 8 epochs. These are reported setting revisions; rerunning is not established. The ten-fold splitting design remains.

E4.justification: v3 adds RoBERTEye feature-group ablations (Table 13), an eleven-predictor analysis linking decoding to reading behavior (Figure 4), and lexical-overlap checks (Appendix A). It expands the existing generation example across models (Table 16). v2's DalEye-Llama prompt/input sensitivity experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Reconstruction reporting changes from means with 1,000-bootstrap confidence intervals to mixed-effects intercept estimates and intervals accounting for paragraph/participant structure. v3 adds reconstruction significance comparisons and an eleven-test Bonferroni correction for the cognitive analysis. The ten cross-validation splits are retained.

E6.justification: Reconstruction results are substantially expanded and revised: DalEye-Llama's New Participant BLEU summary changes from 0.602 to 0.556, and Gemini few-shot newly reports QA accuracy 0.804 (v2 Table 12; v3 Tables 14–15). Changed metrics and estimation prevent treating revised scores as same-setting performance gains. RoBERTEye's aggregate selection scores remain 49.3%, 70.9%, and 57.3%.

M1.justification: v3 substantially extends generation beyond v2's fine-tuned models by adding DalEye-GPT and zero-shot/ten-example few-shot Gemini procedures, with regime-dependent demonstration selection (Sections 4.2 and C.1.2). The existing discriminative models and DalEye-Llama remain; DalEye-LLaVA is retained in the appendix.

P1.justification: The generative-model and reconstruction-results narratives are substantially rewritten, related work is condensed into three thematic discussions, and appendix organization changes. LLaVA and generative selection discussion move out of the main narrative, while prompt variations are regrouped with their results. Goal/question and text/item terminology is also standardized.

P2.justification: v3 adds the cognitive coefficient plot and overlap/ablation tables, redraws the reconstruction chart with expanded comparisons and revised axes, and expands v2 Figure 7 into Table 16. Selection tables are split or relocated, and the LLaVA diagram is revised and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations on perceived relevance, GazeXplain, synthetic gaze feedback, and supporting datasets/statistical tools. The central positioning against procedural reading-task classification remains unchanged. OneStop and LLaVA publication updates refer to retained works.

T1.justification: The task mappings and embedding/fusion mathematics retain their substance, with no new theoretical results or proofs. Appendix E expands the explanation of chance probabilities already presented in v2 Table 1; the new regression formulations concern statistical analysis.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence about what gaze contributes and when decoding succeeds through feature ablations, cognitive analyses, additional text-only controls, and explicit dependence-aware reconstruction statistics. These address important explanatory and evidential gaps in v2. Replacing kappa with accuracy loses chance correction, and revised LLaVA settings remain incompletely reconciled, but the gains in experimental scrutiny and reproducibility outweigh these limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OneStop reading-goal decoding work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support comparison, including material relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds generative-model evaluations, feature ablations, cognitive analyses, and dataset overlap measurements in Section 6 and Appendices A and G.

before.justification: v2 reports original goal-selection experiments, DalEye-Llama reconstruction results, and prompt/input comparisons in Section 6 and Appendix E.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain hierarchical motion representation, coherent parallel generation and scale-specific guidance. v2 strengthens the existing efficiency claim to state-of-the-art sampling efficiency and generation of over 2000 frames within two seconds in the introduction. This extends a retained contribution rather than redefining the research objective.

C2.justification: v1 describes explicit body-part conditioning as unavailable; v2 asserts and illustrates body-region guidance, while reframing the limitation as poor semantic interpretability across scales. It removes the parameter-scalability warning and interprets PM/guidance results through reconstruction-versus-interaction trade-offs and collision failures. Finger omission was already disclosed in v1; v2 emphasizes its expressive consequences.

D1.justification: v2 provides baseline adaptation recipes and newly specifies 200 autoencoder and 1500 diffusion epochs, while revising hardware from RTX 4090 to L40 and changing optimizer/scheduler details. It omits v1's parameter counts, wall-clock training durations, masking-rate formulas/examples and precise ten-joint, 100-dimensional cross-distance specification. Reproducibility documentation therefore changes substantially, with both additions and losses.

E1.justification: Both versions use DD100's 1.95 hours of paired dance/music spanning ten genres for leader- and music-conditioned reactive dance generation. Long-sequence generation is already evaluated in v1. The revised skeleton, guidance configurations and participant count change settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands from Duolando and InterGen to also evaluate GestureLSM, EDGE and TCDiff. v2 substantively adapts InterGen through music conditioning and independent dancer networks. The representation ablation changes from VQ-VAE to RVQ-VAE. Figure 9 also evaluates the expanded baseline set, while v1's user-study ground-truth comparison is absent.

E3.justification: v2 reports SMPL-based baseline retraining, adds MPJPE, MPJVE and inference-time evaluation, and marks diversity and beat metrics as targeting proximity to ground truth. The user study changes from 15 participants making binary choices to 20 participants providing five-point ratings on three criteria. Reported diffusion optimization changes from Adan with cosine scheduling to AdamW with a different learning rate and exponential decay.

E4.justification: v1 tests residual depths, removes BLC/dense-window training, and crosses guidance settings with PM removal. v2 drops the depth sweep and PM-by-guidance grid, tests training strides 16/64 and a latent-stitching control, and revises guidance analysis for two layers. Appendix Figures 6–8 add qualitative HFSQ/PM failure analyses and body-region guidance demonstrations.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 9 introduces error bars around mean perceptual ratings, whereas v1 reports preference percentages without uncertainty. The error bars' meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither version reports training-run counts, random seeds or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces ReactDance's FIDk/FIDg/FIDcd values of 41.61/10.95/8.24 with 5.57/7.63/14.17 under revised representation and training settings; these are not same-setting gains or losses. v2 adds MPJPE 132.99, MPJVE 15.68, inference time 1.75 seconds, and numerous baseline/ablation results. Figure 9 replaces preference percentages with naturalness/music/coordination ratings of 4.32/4.16/4.24.
