M1.justification: Beyond renaming GRFSQ to HFSQ, v2 changes the representation from 25-joint SMPL-X global positions to 22-joint SMPL with root-relative reactor coordinates, adopts two residual stages instead of three, and adds foot-contact and relative-orientation losses (v2 Equation 7 versus v1 Equation 8). Upper/lower-body separation, progressive masking, BLC and LDCFG are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methods and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. v2 changes the title and terminology, consolidates v1's fragmented and repeated ablation discussion, adds a related-work subsection, and organizes supporting material into an appendix. The narrative structure changes substantially.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column layout, replaces the opening and qualitative-comparison figures, revises and relocates shared architecture diagrams, and substantially restructures the tables. Appendix Figures 6–9 add ablation illustrations, body-region guidance examples and a perceptual-rating chart. These exceed numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated long-motion discussion positioning BLC against MotionStreamer, priorMDM, EDGE and Lodge. It introduces DuetGen, GestureLSM, Co3Gesture and robotics/application references while removing substantial older solo/group-generation and quantization coverage. This materially revises research positioning beyond citation-format or publication-metadata updates.

T1.justification: The written quantization mathematics changes: v2 Equation 1 explicitly maintains cumulative residuals, and reconstruction includes scaling factors, replacing v1's recurrence over previous quantized outputs and unweighted sum. v2 also explicitly defines the autoencoder latent loss with stop-gradient operations. These are localized mathematical revisions; neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's unquantified sampling-efficiency claim and narrow two-baseline evaluation are materially strengthened by v2's timing comparisons, reconstruction metrics and five explicitly adapted baselines. Revised controls, appendix failure analyses and the three-criterion perceptual study provide more informative evidence, while clearer methods and organization improve assessability. Some implementation details and previous ablations are lost, and the user-study error bars remain undefined, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReactDance and provide readable methods, equations, figures and experimental tables. All supplied material was inspected, including v2's appendix, Sections 6.1–6.5. v1 ends with references and contains no appendix. The substantial revision remains reliably comparable.

after.justification: v2 reports original DD100 comparisons, reconstruction and timing results, revised ablations, qualitative analyses and a perceptual study, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original DD100 benchmark results, component ablations, guidance experiments and user-study preference percentages in Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain HFSQ for hierarchical motion representation, BLC for coherent parallel generation and LDCFG for multiscale control. Both versions claim high-quality long-form generation exceeding 2000 frames within two seconds. Frequency terminology and revised future-work framing do not materially change these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds frequency-based decomposition, phase-agnostic decoder smoothing and scalar-grid explanations, together with interpretations of depth/cost trade-offs, hand denoising, conditioning roles and generalization. Some interpretations overreach: A.7 describes consistently improving jitter, although Table 6 reports 17.18 at stride 240 and 17.99 at stride 64.

D1.justification: v3 discloses fourfold temporal downsampling and independent per-layer condition dropout with probability 0.2. It also supplies relative training-cost information and a project-page pointer. The hardware, optimizers, learning rates, epoch counts and batch size in the training appendix remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained DD100 body-motion evaluation, v3 adds hand-motion modeling, reversed leader/follower roles and zero-shot reactions to FineDance solo-dance inputs (Appendices A.8, A.10–A.11). These expand output requirements and input conditions; the generalization outcomes are reported descriptively without embedded demonstrations.

E2.justification: The five main baselines remain GestureLSM, EDGE, TCDiff, InterGen and Duolando. Table 2 adds VAE and RVQ-VAE with progressive masking as tokenizer comparators. The old 'w/o HFSQ' results are retained under RVQ-VAE without masking, rather than replaced.

E3.justification: The original DD100 splits, 8-second clips, 30 fps and default stride 4 remain. v3 adds PFC and IPR evaluation, boundary-jitter measurement, separate reconstruction evaluation, residual-depth settings R=1–4, additional strides 1/240/360 and conditioning-removal controls. These substantially broaden the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v3 expands the tokenizer/masking analysis into reconstruction and generation comparisons, tests residual-depth scalability, and extends stride analysis to boundary continuity and training cost. Appendices A.8–A.11 additionally investigate hand-motion stability, conditioning roles, role swapping and distribution shift.

E5.justification: Figure 9 retains the same user-study means and error bars, with the same participant and comparison counts. Neither version specifies what those error bars represent, and v3 adds no seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing main-table scores, retained ablation entries, guidance results and user-study ratings remain unchanged. v3 adds physical metrics, including ReactDance PFC 0.6039 and IPR 7.84%, plus reconstruction, depth, stride, hand-motion and conditioning results in Tables 2 and 5–8. Role-swapping and FineDance successes are newly reported qualitative findings.

M1.justification: HFSQ quantization, progressive masking, diffusion losses, BLC sampling and the LDCFG inference equation are retained. v3 newly documents independent layerwise conditioning dropout, but does not establish that it replaces a different v2 procedure.

P1.justification: Sections 3.4–3.5 receive focused rewriting into explicit mechanism and training/inference explanations, with smaller terminology and conclusion edits. The main section order and much retained prose remain stable. The appendix is relabeled from Section 6 to Appendix A and its outline and cross-references are expanded.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains physical-quality columns, Table 2 is substantially restructured into reconstruction and generation panels, and Tables 5–8 add displays for the new analyses. Figures 1–9 are retained, with relocation and page reflow; v3 also adds conference headers.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to MoMask, generalized winding numbers and FineDance. It contrasts MoMask's residual vector quantization and serial generation with HFSQ, and refines the DuetGen comparison to conditional response diversity. The broader related-work organization and positioning remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.7 newly defines boundary Jitter as mean L2 velocity change around block boundaries, using a 30-frame half-radius. This is a limited mathematical metric definition. Equations 1–9 otherwise retain their substance, including equivalent W-to-T notation in positional encoding; no proofs or theorems are added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices: Table 2 supplies a masking-matched RVQ comparison missing from v2, while Tables 5–6 test residual depth and directly connect boundary continuity to training cost. These address important gaps in component validation. Unexplained reconstruction MPJPE differences between Tables 2 and 5 (28.66 versus 24.32), overstated jitter monotonicity and video-dependent generalization evidence temper, but do not outweigh, those gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReactDance work. All pages, including appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. Added video-linked demonstrations can be compared only through their descriptions in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds physical-quality measurements, expanded ablations, hand-motion results and reported generalization experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original DD100 benchmark results, component and guidance ablations, qualitative comparisons and a 20-participant user study.

C1.justification: The introduction narrows effectiveness 'regardless of the task' to effectiveness on several tasks as a step toward generality, and explicitly foregrounds the unified formulation as a contribution. It also qualifies the primary scope as perception itself. The central claim of jointly learning perception and exploration across classification and regression remains.

C2.justification: V4 substantially expands interpretation through explanations of the component ablations, qualified conclusions about sparse supervision and downstream control, and discussion of tactile sim-to-real obstacles. Section 5 adds interpretations of less recognizable digit-exploration behavior, while Appendix H distinguishes within-episode information gathering from curiosity-driven policy training. The existing sample-efficiency and single-sensor limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V3 promises a future code release upon acceptance; v4 instead directs readers to source-code access through the project page. V4 also documents CIFAR-10 observation/action processing and sparse-label bookkeeping. Table 1, hardware specifications, replay-buffer details, and training-time disclosures are substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: V4 retains the five original benchmarks and adds active classification of natural CIFAR-10 images using local glimpses (Appendices B.5 and C.6). CircleSquareHideAndSeek additionally introduces a downstream control objective requiring class-dependent approach or avoidance, extending coverage beyond property prediction alone.

E2.justification: V4 adds comparisons against APPLE-GRID, APPLE-SAC-PURE-RL, and APPLE-CrossQ-PURE-RL on CircleSquare, plus APPLE-CrossQ-NO-PRED on HideAndSeek (Figures 16–19). These introduce fixed-search and prediction-supervision controls beyond the retained HAM, random-policy, and PPO comparisons.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 1M-step component comparisons, terminal-only prediction supervision, cumulative base-return evaluation for HideAndSeek, and CIFAR-10 test-split evaluation through 2.5M steps. The original benchmark protocols are largely retained; changed curves do not establish reruns. Figure 18 leaves the sparse experiment's duration ambiguous: its caption states 1M steps, while its axis ends at 0.25M.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds direct plotted evidence about transformer versus LSTM backbones, supervised prediction versus pure RL, and learned versus grid-search exploration. It also tests terminal-only supervision and the usefulness of prediction supervision for downstream control. The earlier long-run PPO/HAM analyses are retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeds and one-standard-deviation bands for the main comparisons; v4 uses the same practice for CIFAR-10. No increased replication or new statistical estimation or significance-testing procedure is documented. Changes to plotted means and uncertainty bands concern results.

E6.justification: V4 adds CIFAR-10 final accuracies of 76%, 73%, and 67% for APPLE-SAC, APPLE-CrossQ, and APPLE-RND, respectively, plus the new ablation and task-variant results. Some retained curves also change: notably, HAM rises substantially above chance in v3 Figure 9 but remains near chance in v4 Figure 14 under the same stated setting. Main-text numerical summaries remain unchanged, and the reason for these curve revisions is unspecified.

M1.justification: The main APPLE architecture, SAC/CrossQ adaptations, and joint optimization procedure remain unchanged. Appendix C.3 adds a specific adaptation for missing labels: storing an availability flag and masking the prediction loss, tested using only terminal supervision.

P1.justification: V4 tightens the introduction, rewrites portions of related work, reorganizes contribution bullets, and adds acknowledgments. Supplementary experiments previously embedded in environment details are grouped into a dedicated Further Experiments appendix. The main section sequence and much of the methods/results prose remain intact; much of the expansion consists of new scientific content.

P2.justification: V4 adds a CIFAR-10 illustration and substantial new graphical evidence for component ablations, sparse supervision, downstream control, and CIFAR-10 performance (Figures 13, 15–19, and 21). Existing plots are resized and repositioned, including the old PPO and MHSB figures becoming Figures 14 and 20. Table 1 retains its structure.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially broadens coverage of imitation learning, visual active perception, scene understanding, and haptic curiosity. New positioning relates APPLE to internally rewarded RL, while Appendix H contrasts it with RND and ICM. The conclusion also introduces relevant sim-to-real literature; these are substantive additions beyond publication-metadata updates to existing citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the prediction factor from pi(o|h) to pi(y|o) and adds transition and target-conditional factors to the trajectory distribution. The main objective, gradient decomposition, and appendix derivation are retained. Appendices C.3–C.4 introduce a masked-loss definition and downstream reward; the latter's distance signs conflict with the stated approach/avoid objective.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses an important evidential gap by directly testing supervised prediction and learned exploration against pure-RL and grid-search controls, while CIFAR-10 extends support to natural images. These additions strengthen the central methodological case, and expanded research positioning clarifies the contribution. Unexplained revisions to retained curves and the HideAndSeek reward/prose contradiction limit confidence in specific results, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in component validation and coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APPLE research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V4 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds CIFAR-10 results, component ablations, sparse-supervision experiments, and a downstream control experiment.

before.justification: V3 reports original evaluations of APPLE and baselines on five benchmarks, with learning curves, prediction metrics, and supplementary PPO/HAM experiments.

C1.justification: V2 removes v1's categorical claim that foundation models fail to develop meaningful representations of physics, replacing it with the narrower conclusion that they underutilize context. It also elevates identifying shared failure modes into the stated contributions. This materially recalibrates the paper's central claims while retaining the baseline and scaling-law contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds local-trend continuation as an explanation for Chronos's short-context advantage, interprets sampling changes through time rescaling, and proposes benchmarks without nearly repeating motifs. The conclusion explicitly frames parroting as a diagnostic baseline rather than a replacement for foundation models. Mean-collapse explanations and the nonstationarity limitation already appeared in v1.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents zero-mean, unit-standard-deviation trajectory normalization, Gaussian-mixture KL estimation, and source and processing details for added datasets, including Reynolds number 900 and PCA modes for vortex-flow data. The normalization disclosure alone does not establish that preprocessing changed. No new code-access information is provided.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds von Karman vortex-flow data, QT Database ECG recordings, experimentally measured electronic circuits, and coupled Kuramoto oscillators beyond the retained low-dimensional dysts benchmark. Appendix E additionally evaluates noise-corrupted trajectories, substantially broadening the represented systems and input conditions.

E2.justification: Both versions evaluate Chronos, Chronos Bolt, TimesFM-2.0, and Time-MoE. V2 extends this same comparator set to its additional experiments. Farmer-Sidorowich forecasting is newly discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds attractor KL divergence and correlation-dimension accuracy to the evaluation protocol. New scientific-task tables evaluate MAE and MSE at 50 steps, while sampling-rate experiments introduce 10 and 50 points per Lyapunov time alongside the retained 30-point setting. These substantially extend evaluation beyond the original forecasting metrics and protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendix E systematically tests Gaussian-noise levels of 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1 and sampling granularities of 10, 30, and 50 points per Lyapunov time across five metrics. These add substantial robustness and sensitivity evidence; the original embedding-dimension and context-length analyses remain present.

E5.justification: V2 adds shaded variability bands to the existing MSE/MAE and scaling plots. Figure 10 explicitly specifies 100 trajectories per system for the embedding study, whereas v1 supplied only a general 20-trajectory protocol; an actual increase is not explicitly documented. The main comparisons retain 20 trajectories, and some new tabular ± quantities remain undefined.

E6.justification: Tables 1–13 and the attractor-reconstruction plots add substantial results; for example, Figure 8 reports correlation-dimension accuracy of 0.80 for Parrot and 0.85 for Chronos. Retained forecasting curves also change, and the inverse-scaling correlation is revised from 0.44 ± 0.08 in v1 Figure 7 to 0.51 ± 0.08 in v2 Figure 11. These are reported additions and revisions, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains nearest-motif matching, exclusion of the final D candidate motifs, and copying and repeating the matched continuation. Explicit Euclidean-distance wording and harmonized notation clarify the existing procedure rather than introduce a new component.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract, contributions, and conclusion, expands embedding and metric explanations, and harmonizes notation across the theoretical appendix. Related-work subheadings become inline headings and several analyses receive separate appendices. Most existing exposition and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 introduces 13 tables, an attractor-KL violin plot, and a correlation-dimension comparison plot. Figure 2's VPT panel becomes a separate appendix figure, and the embedding and scaling-correlation figures move from the main text to appendices. Revised axes, captions, uncertainty displays, and table highlighting substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Eight references are added, covering transformer circuits, in-context learning, attractor evaluation, and the new datasets. Sections 3 and 5.2 now discuss Farmer-Sidorowich forecasting and acknowledge its related scaling law. The existing related-work themes and overall positioning remain recognizable.

T1.justification: Appendix F.2 distinguishes input- and output-kernel dimensions where v1 C.2 supplied a single dimensionality statement. Appendix F.4 restricts the existing mixing/scaling discussion to stochastic series. The invariant-preservation proposition, derivation, and principal scaling arguments otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's broad conclusions rested on clean, low-dimensional simulations without direct attractor-reconstruction comparisons. V2 tests broader simulated and real systems, adds noise and sampling sensitivity checks, and directly evaluates attractor statistics. Together with the narrower physics-related claim, these changes substantially strengthen empirical support and claim calibration. Some new protocol details, uncertainty definitions, and explanations for revised plots remain incomplete.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same context-parroting study. Their text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on broader scientific datasets, attractor reconstruction, observational noise, and sampling rates.

before.justification: V1 reports original forecasting experiments on 135 chaotic systems, inference-cost measurements, and embedding-dimension and scaling-law analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and three central contributions remain substantially the same. The introduction broadens the superiority claim to the expanded comparator set, including classical methods. The conclusion adds the stronger interpretation that a foundation model unable to beat parroting has arguably failed to learn the underlying physics.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes periodic forecasts' asymptotic Lyapunov behavior from finite-time estimates and attributes DynaMix's long-term geometric fidelity to its recurrent architecture. It qualifies transformer-specific context limits, expands stationarity and stochastic-system limitations, and proposes parameter-inference and unseen-bifurcation tests beyond reconstruction. These substantially develop the paper's mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 adds a reproducibility statement pointing to a Python implementation and benchmarks, plus technical specifications for added models and spectral-estimation procedures. It removes v2's CPU-only timing description and explicit VPT definition and threshold despite retaining VPT results. The PDFs establish the new code-access statement, not the external resource's availability.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 135-system dysts benchmark and the same vortex-flow, ECG, electronic-circuit, and Kuramoto data. 'Turbulence' and 'Circuit' rename existing table rows. Longer rollouts and the 129-system spectral-analysis subset change evaluation settings within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Moirai-2.0 and DynaMix to the main comparisons, including Figure 2 and Tables 1–3. Appendix B also evaluates simplex projection and AutoARIMA in Figures 7–8. v2 compared against Chronos, Chronos Bolt, TimesFM, and TimeMoE; simplex projection was discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: The standard 300-step benchmark pipeline remains, but v3 adds 9,488- and 10,000-step rollout protocols, spectral Hellinger distance, and Lyapunov-exponent evaluation. Figure 4 changes the reported embedding dimension from 10 to 5 and extends the plotted context range from 32,768 to 65,536. These are substantial evaluation additions and revisions.

E4.justification: New Figure 3 and Appendix D investigate whether periodic parroted forecasts preserve spectra and dynamical invariants over long rollouts. Figure 12 adds spectral sensitivity to context length. Conversely, v2's cross-model VPT-versus-context analysis is removed. The noise and sampling-rate analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: v3 Table 1 identifies its existing uncertainty values as standard deviations. New Table 4 reports standard deviations and correlation bounds described as p-value-based; Figure 12 specifies standard-deviation bands. The corresponding scaling analysis loses v2 Figure 11's bootstrap standard error and regression uncertainty band. Retained experiments still state 20 or 100 initial conditions.

E6.justification: v3 adds comparator and long-rollout results and revises several Parrot error and VPT curves. The scaling-dimension correlation changes from 0.51±0.08 in v2 Figure 11 to approximately 0.85 in v3 Section 5.2. These revisions are not fully explained as comparable-setting gains. Existing-method scores in Tables 1–3 and the noise/sampling tables are retained, while added competitors change some rankings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 is identical: match the final length-D motif using Euclidean distance, exclude nearby motifs, and repeat the continuation following the closest match. The mathematical formulations are retained. Different experimental choices of D do not change the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 makes focused rewrites in Methods, Results, and Conclusion, moves the mathematical overview from Section 3 to Appendix F.1, and adds a reproducibility section. Headings and citation style change throughout. Much of the prose and the main section sequence remain closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the runtime figure with multipanel spectral forecasts, redesigns Figure 5, and relocates the aggregate scaling display to Appendix Figure 10. It expands comparison plots and tables, splits Figure 8, adds long-rollout Table 4 and Figures 11–12, and removes v2's VPT-context figure. The document template and ranking highlights also change.

R1.justification: v3 extends discussion and citations to DynaMix, Moirai-2.0, Chronos-2, recurrent forecasting, language correlation dimension, and generalization beyond observed state space. It adds invariant-estimation references and replaces Huke's embedding guide with Takens. The existing related-work framework and central research positioning remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Section 5.2 corrects the geometric scaling argument to concern a point's nearest neighbor, replacing v2's statement about distances between two random points. v3 also introduces an explicit attention-versus-nearest-neighbor complexity comparison. The scaling relation, kernel formulations, and appendix propositions and proofs remain; relocating the mathematical overview introduces no new theorem.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in v2's evidence by evaluating a specialist dynamics model and classical forecasting baselines, and by directly testing invariant preservation far beyond the original 300-step forecasts. The finite-time versus periodic-behavior discussion also clarifies a central limitation. Removing the runtime plot, VPT definition, and scaling bootstrap uncertainty reduces transparency, and several revised results remain insufficiently explained. Nevertheless, the more demanding comparisons and long-rollout analyses substantially strengthen the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same context-parroting work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original forecasting evaluations and adds comparator results, long-rollout invariant-property measurements, and power-spectrum analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting evaluations on 135 chaotic systems and four additional SciML datasets, together with noise, sampling-rate, embedding-dimension, and scaling analyses.

C1.justification: The intervention, transfer, and super-neuron claims remain, but v2 makes unexplained, counterintuitive shared structure a central contribution. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion now emphasize that most annotated interference pairs lack recognized higher-order associations and may generate hypotheses about latent knowledge. The transfer claim also explicitly extends to 70B models.

C2.justification: V2 develops v1's open question about higher-order organization into substantive interpretations involving semantic priming, morphology, and latent knowledge. Section 3.5 adds the Beethoven/frustration hypothesis and proposes human validation. Appendices K–L identify categories without strong generalizability and acknowledge potential performance damage motivating weaker steering. The principal SAE-dependence and single-layer limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 identifies text-embedding-3-large, expands token-classification and sentence-generation instructions, details token-pool filtering and deduplication, lists a scaling grid, and supplies annotation prompts and matching tolerances. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Hardware/timing disclosures largely persist; both PDFs advertise the same repository and withholding of shared-direction matrices, so the separate reproducibility statement does not establish a new release.

E1.justification: V2 expands systematic prompt-injection evaluation beyond v1's location and hate/love tables to eight categories, including numbers, science, animals, colors, and time. It also adds HellaSwag commonsense-completion evaluation and feature-pair association judgments, substantially broadening the tested tasks and scenarios.

E2.justification: The random, target-feature/token, and interference-level controls remain, as does comparison between SAE-direction and gradient steering, although their displays change. Added language models serve as intervention targets or analysis annotators; no new competing intervention method is evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 replaces top-10, four-metric evaluation with full-distribution cosine/overlap measures and relative changes; prompt success changes from top-10 to top-30. Semantic cutoffs change from 0.5 to four thresholds between 0.40 and 0.15, with revised sampling and interference bins. V2 adds Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, matched-pair judgments, and 500 HellaSwag items tested with 174 vectors at quarter strength. Appendix I.2's positive scaling grid conflicts with the retained [-20,20] description.

E4.justification: V2 adds semantic-threshold sensitivity tests, controlled regressions, semantic/interference distributions, alternative DeepSeek-V3 feature interpretations, HellaSwag collateral-performance checks, and hidden-association analyses. These test substantial new robustness and explanatory questions. V1's independent feature/token/neuron replication panels and supplementary prompt-metric plots are no longer reported.

E5.justification: V1's standard-error displays are replaced by 95% confidence intervals, with regression estimates also showing 90% and 99% intervals. Prompt-table significance changes from z-tests to t-tests. New association analyses report Wilson intervals, an exact binomial test, and annotator agreement including Cohen's kappa. The stated 100 injection samples per prompt remain unchanged; these additions do not establish more repeated runs.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Llama-3.1-8B location high-interference success changes from 27.64% in v1 Table 2 to 20.78% in v2 Table 1 under different protocols, so this is not a directly comparable decline. V2 adds mixed transfer outcomes across categories and 70B results, HellaSwag's reported 2.77% average accuracy reduction from a 77.2% baseline, and association findings of 27.7% related pairs and 64.3% matched-choice preference.

M1.justification: The four intervention mechanisms and their SAE/gradient constructions remain. However, v2 Appendices K.1–K.2 construct transferred token pools using the union of tokens from the two small models, whereas v1 Section 3.4 and Appendix H.2 use their intersection. This changes transfer-input selection.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, and the research questions, evaluation exposition, and discussion are substantially recast. The main-text dataset subsection and boxed Finding summaries disappear, while appendices are reorganized into dedicated methodological, analysis, and disclosure sections. James Evans is added as an author.

P2.justification: Figures 3–4 replace four-metric panels with threshold-grouped bars and regression plots; Figure 5 changes from bars to distribution boxplots. V1 Table 1 moves to v2 Appendix Table 3, and the two neuron-distribution figures merge. New figures and tables display semantic distributions, interpreter comparisons, annotations, HellaSwag examples, and expanded prompt results; original replication grids disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds semantic-priming and morphology connections through Mandera and Bojanowski, supporting SAE and threshold-selection citations, and replaces v1's unresolved Appendix A.2 citation. Existing related-work organization and the challenge to incidental-polysemanticity explanations largely remain. Novelty wording strengthens from 'among the first' to 'the first.'

T1.justification: V2 substantively revises the mathematical evaluation definitions to use full output distributions and relative effects, including an epsilon-stabilized relative-overlap formula. The Kendall and Spearman criteria disappear. The SAE equations, transported steering-vector formulation, and token-gradient derivation remain unchanged after relocation; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 directly addresses v1's weak validation of semantic distinctness through stricter threshold sweeps, controlled regressions, and alternative feature interpretations, substantially strengthening evidence for the central interference finding. HellaSwag and weak-transfer categories add meaningful evidence about costs and boundaries. These gains outweigh the removed replication panels, although conclusions about human cognition remain indirect and Appendix K's union construction is insufficiently reconciled with claims about shared transfer tokens.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same polysemantic-intervention study despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison; revised experimental settings require caution when comparing scores.

after.justification: V2 reports original intervention results, additional transfer evaluations, HellaSwag experiments, and feature-pair annotation and comparison analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original feature-, token-, prompt-, and neuron-intervention experiments, including transfer results and appendix replications.

C1.justification: v2 makes unsupervised entropy-based calibration a central contribution and elevates reduced uncertainty and unlocking pretrained knowledge into main claims. Its abstract newly claims monotonic control of downstream attention entropy. The earlier claims about training-free, head-specific tuning and broad benchmark benefits are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive boundaries: entropy minimization can reinforce formatting errors or biased answers, and confident semantic errors resist correction while some confident formatting errors remain correctable. It expands explanations of extreme tuning and representation collapse. v1's explicit caveat about untested long-form reasoning is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a LlamaAttention implementation snippet in Figure 1 and code/runnable-demo access information in the abstract. Framework, prompt and default hyperparameter disclosures are largely retained or relocated to Appendix B; this is a limited reproducibility-information expansion.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 15 benchmarks covering classification, multiple-choice QA and MT-Bench conversation. The context-extension, few-shot and prompt-variation scenarios are retained. New entropy and error analyses reuse existing datasets without extending task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding benchmark comparisons retain Vanilla, ACT and Auto-PASTA, with ACT restricted to Llama-3.1-8B using eager attention. Table 3 also retains the same conversation reference models. The new supervised/unsupervised comparison evaluates ZeroTuning variants.

E3.justification: v2 introduces evaluation with calibration on unlabeled test inputs, plus entropy sweeps and confidence-stratified error testing. Appendix B also specifies 500 calibration samples for all methods, replacing v1's ACT-specific 10% validation description. This is a reported protocol revision; unchanged benchmark scores do not establish that ACT was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of entropy–accuracy relationships, correction rates by initial confidence, extreme-tuning failures and misleading sample-level entropy minima (Appendices D–E). Appendix F expands the earlier output examples into paired Vanilla/ZeroTuning cases. Most existing ablations and robustness experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 and report results without repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's new predictive-entropy and confidence analyses characterize model outputs rather than statistical uncertainty in benchmark estimates.

E6.justification: v2 Table 4 newly reports an unsupervised five-dataset average of 67.02, alongside 67.52 for supervised tuning and 59.00 for Vanilla. Entropy/confidence curves and expanded output cases add further findings. Tables 1–3 and the matched robustness tables retain their numerical results; larger headline percentages express relative improvements.

M1.justification: v2 adds an unsupervised variant that selects heads and scaling factors by minimizing average next-token entropy on unlabeled test inputs (Section 3.6). v1 uses accuracy-based calibration and explicitly identifies dependence on ground truth as a limitation. The supervised rescaling procedure remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and analysis narrative are extensively rewritten. A related-work summary moves near the beginning, detailed related work and experimental setup move into appendices, and the appendix sequence is reorganized around theory, failure analysis and unsupervised tuning.

P2.justification: v2 adds an implementation/heatmap overview, an attention schematic, entropy and error-analysis graphics, and an unsupervised-results table. It relocates the original scaling illustration to Appendix C and reformats tables, including correcting Table 1's duplicated SST-2 header to SST5. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Citation changes include adding Han et al. (2025a,b) and removing LoRA+, several prompt-tuning works and some value-state references. The central positioning relative to PASTA, Auto-PASTA, ACT and attention-sink research remains substantially the same; detailed related work is relocated to Appendix A.

T1.justification: v2 formalizes tuning-effect magnitude and adds Proposition 1 with a derivative proof of its dependence on initial attention (Section 3.1 and Appendix C). It extends output-stability and temperature/argmax reasoning while dropping v1's value-state-drain premise. The core attention-rescaling and key-scaling derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v1 Appendix I leaves label dependence unresolved; v2 addresses it with a tested entropy-only variant achieving 67.02 versus 67.52 for supervised calibration on five datasets. The expanded failure and error analyses also substantially improve understanding of when tuning helps. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including an abstract entropy-control claim not established by the pairwise-difference proof and removal of the earlier long-form-reasoning caveat.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ZeroTuning and retain matching core experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds unsupervised-calibration results, entropy analyses and confidence-dependent error evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results in Tables 1–3, token/layer/head experiments, and appendix robustness evaluations.

C1.justification: v3 claims API applicability but explicitly acknowledges a gap to attacking proprietary models. v4's abstract and introduction claim demonstrated success against Gemini-2.5-Pro, materially extending that scope. The lightweight BiasNet, attack formulation and response-quality metric contributions remain.

C2.justification: v4 removes the limitation concerning proprietary-model content monitors. It newly interprets stronger results on Gemini Pro as evidence that JULI benefits from more knowledgeable targets, and uses the BiasNet-only and benign examples to argue for knowledge extraction with preserved general abilities. Defense interpretations now emphasize API-compatible comparisons.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link, documents tokenizer reuse and sequential one-token API collection of training logits, and discloses sampling temperatures. The architecture, AdamW optimizer, 100 training pairs, 15 epochs, batch size and learning rate were already documented in v3.

E1.justification: v4 extends simulated API evaluation to actual Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Pro APIs, adds a deep-safety-alignment scenario, and includes benign instruction examples from databricks-dolly-15k. AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, the hard AdvBench subset and LLM-LAT training data are retained.

E2.justification: FLIP and the Naive prefix attack join the retained benchmark and circuit-breaker comparisons. v4 also evaluates the longer-prefix Naive+ variant and adds LINT restricted to top-5 access to an API comparison. GCG, ED, WTS, LINT and Base remain in corresponding legacy comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include top-k token-hit measurements on 100 LLM-LAT pairs and a BiasNet-only control that removes the target-output residual during training and sampling. The circuit-breaker comparison replaces unrestricted black-box JULI with restricted API JULI. Score-equals-five count metrics are dropped; the existing training budget, dataset selection and human-rating design remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds token-availability analysis (Figure 2), projection-seed robustness (A.4), a BiasNet-only ablation and benign-response cases (A.8), deep-alignment tests (A.12), and prefix-length analysis (A.13). The KL-divergence, top-k sensitivity and transfer analyses already existed in v3.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly reports an optimization-robustness experiment with five random seeds and individual results in Table A3. This does not establish repeated runs for all benchmark results. The human-rating correlation analysis is unchanged, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results, including Gemini-Pro scores of 4.19 Harmful Score and 3.19 Harmful Info Score in Table 2. It also revises retained entries, such as the Qwen hard-subset Base Info Score from 2.23 to 0.08 (v3 Table A5; v4 Table A9). Most legacy white-box means and transfer scores remain. Score-5 counts and some full-vocabulary black-box results disappear; replacement circuit-breaker API scores use stricter access and are not same-setting declines.

M1.justification: The documented training objective in Eq. 9 changes from scoring BiasNet's output alone to including the target-output residual. Section 4.2 also changes padding from the kth log probability to that value minus 10. BiasNet's architecture and additive decoding strategy remain. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction replaces the contribution bullets with a substantially revised narrative emphasizing knowledge extraction and proprietary APIs. Section 5 separates open-weight and API evaluations and moves mechanism analysis later; the appendices are reorganized. Extensive prose editing accompanies metric renaming from GPT-4 Score and Info Score to Harmful Score and Harmful Info Score.

P2.justification: v4 adds the token-hit figure and several experimental tables, moves the main open-weight and top-k tables into the appendix, removes count columns, and restructures the circuit-breaker table around API compatibility. The overview and KL-analysis figures are retained, with the latter renumbered. Conference formatting also changes headers, typography and layout.

R1.justification: v4 adds references covering Gemini 2.5, FLIP, deep safety alignment and covert malicious fine-tuning, while removing the Toxicity Detection for Free citation. The introduction expands discussion of prompt-rewriting and encryption attacks, but the main related-work taxonomy remains.

T1.justification: Eq. 9 revises the mathematical training objective to include the target-output residual, and new Eq. 10 specifies the objective without that residual for the ablation. The probability definitions and prior-attack formulations remain unchanged. No theoretical guarantees or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: Actual Gemini API evaluations address v3's central gap between simulated API feasibility and demonstrated proprietary-model attacks. Added prefix and FLIP comparisons, restricted-access LINT, and mechanism and robustness controls substantially strengthen the evidence. Removing score-5 counts and the content-monitor limitation reduces transparency, and some notation and labels remain inconsistent, but these costs are outweighed by the stronger validation of the central claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JULI and BiasNet. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated and revised material.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds Gemini API evaluations, new baseline comparisons, seed experiments and mechanism ablations.

before.justification: v3 reports original jailbreak experiments on AdvBench and MaliciousInstruct, circuit-breaker and transfer evaluations, and a 120-response comparison with human ratings.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the primary contribution around error identification and feedback for correction, whereas v1 foregrounded a self-correction framework. V2 removes the abstract's 'up to 25%' answer-improvement claim, expands claimed coverage to commonsense and categorical verification, and claims demonstrated integration with self-improvement.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the GSM8K explanation about weak numerical perturbations with a distinction between identifying arithmetic errors and recomputing faulty calculations. It adds interpretations concerning harmful correction with unreliable feedback, complementary identification and regeneration, sufficient single-bit updates, and empirical reward alignment. Natural-error benefits are explicitly described as modest, refining applicability beyond the retained synthetic-error limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds CommonsenseQA chain-generation and corruption instructions, prompt templates, and worked prompting examples. New appendices document feedback/refinement model roles, block sizes of 1–3, and examples from the unrelated-statement pool. Existing LoRA, optimizer, hardware, runtime, and search-setting disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds CommonsenseQA, extending evaluation from fictional logical deduction and arithmetic to commonsense multiple-choice reasoning, including naturally generated chains in Self-Refine. Appendix C.5 also introduces verification of True, False, and Unrelated statements. Naturally generated PRONTOQA chains and error-location scenarios already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: New Table 6 evaluates Self-Refine with Many2Many feedback against Self-Refine with AVI; Self-Refine was previously cited but not experimentally compared in this workflow. The existing Recursive, Many2Many, Voting, CoT, random-search, and Best-of-N comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 changes the reported natural-error evaluation from 100 to 1,000 PRONTOQA test problems. New protocols include AVI training on 10,000 examples and one Self-Refine iteration on 1,000 CommonsenseQA questions, categorical verification on 100 examples, and exhaustive evaluation of 128 assignments per seven-statement problem in C.6. Existing core search and fine-tuning settings remain.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses testing whether block updates help, whether verification handles unrelated statements, and whether proxy likelihood aligns with veracity accuracy. It also adds commonsense case studies and the Self-Refine application. These substantially extend methodological diagnosis; the original annealing, initialization, and error-location analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.6 introduces Pearson-correlation estimation for each problem and averaging across 100 problems. Existing mean/standard-deviation reporting continues, and C.2 still specifies five runs. Its changed deviations and larger test set do not establish an increased run count.

E6.justification: Retained entries in Tables 1–4 and plotted results in Figures 2–5 are unchanged. V2 adds commonsense, Self-Refine, block-update, categorical, and correlation results in Tables 1 and 6–9. Table 5 replaces raw/baseline/AVI accuracies of 0.71/0.71/0.76 on 100 problems with 0.712/0.697/0.730 on 1,000 problems; this is not a same-setting performance decline. V2 leaves unexplained the Qwen3-4B CommonsenseQA discrepancy between 0.935 in Table 1 and 0.860 for single-bit Metropolis in Table 7.

M1.justification: Search Corrector and Amortized Corrector become VS and AVI; their core reward, greedy initialization, annealing, and pseudo-label training remain unchanged. Appendices C.3–C.5 add bounded procedural extensions: AVI-guided Self-Refine regeneration, contiguous block flips, and categorical-state MCMC.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. V2 expands the explanation of posterior inference versus direct prompting, reorganizes contribution summaries and related-work subsections, renames the title and methods throughout, and removes the Broader Impact section.

P2.justification: V2 extensively retypesets the document with a compact author block, running headers, different heading styles, and relocated figures and prompt boxes. Table 1 reorders model columns and adds a commonsense block; Tables 6–9 are new displays. Figures 1, 2, and 4 update method labels or legends, while Figures 3 and 5 retain their original images.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused around veracity inference as feedback complementary to self-correction and self-improvement, removing the earlier system-1/system-2 comparison. V2 adds Talmor et al.'s CommonsenseQA and Zhou et al.'s noisy-rationale work while pruning discussions and references including RECONCILE, LM vs LM, and ReST-EM.

T1.justification: Appendix C.5 explicitly extends the latent-variable domain from Boolean to k-class categorical vectors, instantiated with True, False, and Unrelated labels; v1 mentioned categorical extensions only as future work. The posterior factorization, reward, Metropolis reasoning, and working hypothesis remain. V2's separate Bayes-rule equation restates existing mathematics rather than adding a proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens two weaknesses in v1: the central proxy-reward hypothesis lacked a direct test, and downstream utility was demonstrated through negation-based correction. Table 9 supplies direct alignment evidence, while Table 6 tests AVI within a regeneration workflow. The enlarged natural-error evaluation also gives a more restrained account of practical gains, and the revised framing better distinguishes verification from correction. The unexplained CommonsenseQA discrepancy between Tables 1 and 7 weakens reporting, but the gains in empirical support and clarity remain substantial.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and method names, both PDFs describe the same latent-veracity research framework and retain matching experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable in both versions and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports additional CommonsenseQA evaluations, Self-Refine integration, block-update comparisons, categorical verification, and correlation analysis.

before.justification: V1 reports original PRONTOQA and GSM8K experiments, search ablations, amortized-inference evaluations, and downstream correction results, including experiments in Appendix C.

C1.justification: The central claims linking MF and IGB and associating optimal trainability with transient prejudice remain. V3 qualifies the introductory trainability statement to wide architectures and explicitly broadens the equivalence's stated applicability beyond MLPs under mean-field assumptions. Its new empirical contribution mainly supports the retained central principle.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations involving softmax saturation and zero favoured-class gradients, Adam-mediated delayed learning in ordered phases, and residual architectures without phase distinctions. Its limitations shift from v1's emphasis on wide MLPs and finite-width breakdown to ordered infinite-width/data limits, absent feature learning and a proposed proportional data/parameter regime. These materially change the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V3 Appendix B and Table 2 add optimizer, regularization, learning-rate, batch-size, architecture and dataset-binarization details, plus residual scaling and the specific timm pretrained checkpoint. V1 mainly supplies simulation settings in captions. Reproducibility information expands substantially, although Table 2 duplicates a CIFAR10 ViT entry where Appendix B.3 distinguishes binary and multiclass tasks.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates synthetic Gaussian inputs and initialization gradients on CIFAR10. V3 adds supervised training on binarized Fashion MNIST, binarized CIFAR10 and multiclass CIFAR10, plus CIFAR100 fine-tuning of an ImageNet-21k-pretrained Vision Transformer (Section 6 and Appendix B). This substantially extends both dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: MF and IGB remain the compared analytical descriptions in matched signal-propagation experiments. No competing initialization or optimization method is newly benchmarked. Residual MLPs and Vision Transformers are additional study architectures, while initialization-phase comparisons remain the experimental controls.

E3.justification: V3 introduces training and fine-tuning protocols, train/test accuracy and classification-frequency measurements, additional model configurations, and pretrained-weight scaling controls. It also revises the existing activation-drift error sweep: v1 Figure 5 uses weight variances 1.8–2.2 and bias variances 0/0.1, whereas v3 Figure 14 uses 1.5–2.5 and 0/0.1/0.2, retaining the width set.

E4.justification: V3 adds class-specific accuracy and gradient analyses, residual-network criticality checks, pretrained-weight perturbations, and variance/covariance concentration studies across widths (Appendices B, E and G). Conversely, v1 Appendix D's width-50 MF–IGB breakdown analysis and Figure 7's pooled-network gradient panels are removed.

E5.justification: V3 Appendix G newly specifies median-over-input gradient summaries, including medians restricted to favoured and unfavoured classes; v1 does not specify this estimator. The existing 90% MF interval practice is retained. Neither version specifies repeated training runs or seeds, and v3 does not explain the statistical meaning of its training-curve shading.

E6.justification: V3 adds train/test accuracy and classification-frequency outcomes (Figures 4–13), including rapid bias absorption near the EOC in vanilla MLPs and similar learning across initializations in residual MLPs. It also adds covariance-concentration and class-specific gradient findings and replaces the activation-drift error entries on a revised parameter grid. These are new or replaced results, rather than demonstrated same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The MF–IGB framework and Gaussian initialization approach already include nonzero biases and multi-node pooling in v1. V3 introduces no new proposed optimization or inference algorithm; its additional architectures and weight perturbations serve as experimental applications and controls.

P1.justification: V3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: the former Section 6 pooling discussion moves into Appendix F, training dynamics becomes the new Section 6, and the setup and contribution list are rewritten. A supplementary contents page, extensive notation guide and reorganized appendix subsections materially change navigation and exposition, beyond the title and terminology edits.

P2.justification: V3 adds extensive training and class-specific gradient panels, covariance-concentration figures and an experimental-settings table, while removing several earlier displays. Appendix result grids are enlarged and reorganized. Matching confirms that the pooling phase diagram is retained unchanged from v1 Figure 4 as v3 Figure 19; its relocation is not a new result.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting Transformers, Vision Transformers, ImageNet, generalization, Adam and timm, while removing the Roberts–Yaida–Hanin theory book and Li–Nica–Roy covariance-SDE reference associated with finite-width discussion. The central positioning relative to prior MF and IGB research remains.

T1.justification: V3 states an architecture-general equivalence theorem with explicit limit ordering, expands MF derivations, and adds extensive pooling calculations and proofs in Appendix F. It also replaces chi1 with tilde-chi1 in the variance-map derivative (v1 Equation 56; v3 Equation 66). These substantively extend existing theory, although new Lemmas F.7/F.9 label points as EOC despite preceding formulas giving chi1 below one, conflicting with Section 2.2's criterion.

improvement.justification: V3 directly addresses an important evidential gap: v1 inferred bias absorption and learning behaviour largely from initialization theory, whereas v3 measures bias alongside training and test performance across architectures and datasets (Section 6 and Appendix B). The accompanying protocols and diagnostic analyses make the central claim substantially more assessable. Removing the width-50 failure example and introducing notation, setting-label and pooling-EOC inconsistencies weaken parts of the revision, but the gain in direct training evidence and reproducibility information provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MF–IGB equivalence and initialization/trainability study, despite the revised title. The complete 27-page v1 and 48-page v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains numerical validation and adds original training and fine-tuning results across MLPs, residual MLPs and Vision Transformers (Section 6 and Appendix B).

before.justification: V1 reports original network simulations, including MF–IGB correlation comparisons, finite-width deviations and CIFAR10 initialization-gradient measurements (Figures 2 and 5–9).

C1.justification: V2's abstract adds comparative claims about synthetic accessibility against seven generative methods, including GPT-5, and superior property performance on 122 synthesis-compatible medicines. These become central contributions alongside the retained bilingual modeling and iterative drug-repair claims.

C2.justification: V1 describes the fallen-angel proposals as suitable for automated assembly. V2 explicitly identifies those cases and the 430-drug experiment as lacking synthesis guarantees, and describes synthesis-compatible molecules as the intended application distribution. It also states the block-availability assumption for synthesis analysis and adds interpretations linking neighborhood similarity to representation quality and a DILI modification to Maji et al. (2023).

D1.justification: V2 documents Allchemy's 30-minute allowance per molecule, absence of substrate price limits, and metric definitions. It adds neighborhood-analysis details and explanations of dataset-table categories. Core implementation and training hyperparameters are retained, and code, data, and model release remain promised upon publication.

E1.justification: V2 adds a synthesis-compatible FDA-drug population and a synthesis-constrained editing scenario in Section 3.2. Coverage otherwise retains the same six ADMET endpoints, training sources, 430-drug study, and two failed-drug cases. This is a bounded extension within the existing drug-optimization domain.

E2.justification: V1 lacks competing molecule editors. V2 evaluates MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol, GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Claude-3.5-Haiku against mCLM in Tables 1 and 3. It also compares MoleculeSTM and FineMolTex in retrosynthesis evaluation and adds MoleculeSTM to the retained fallen-angel experiment. The oracle-model comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new 122-drug evaluation restricts mCLM outputs to 582 synthesis-guaranteed blocks while allowing unrestricted baseline generation. V2 adds average relative improvement, SA scores, RDKit validity, and Allchemy-based synthesizability and makeability metrics. Allchemy testing selects the three best SA models and samples 200 generated molecules per model. Existing training budgets and oracle scaffold splits are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix A.3 extends the existing fallen-angel case study with MoleculeSTM, exposing invalid outputs during iterative editing. Appendix F.2 adds six block-neighborhood examples to examine representation quality. The original mCLM cases and frequent DILI modifications remain; no systematic component-ablation or sensitivity study is added.

E5.justification: V1 Table 1 reports p < 0.05 using a Wilcoxon test. The corresponding results in v2 Table 4 omit that statement, and the statistical-test references disappear. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars for the editing evaluations.

E6.justification: The original 430-drug property scores and all 24 oracle AUCs are retained. New results include 15.0% average improvement for mCLM versus 6.98% for Gemini-2.5-Flash on the 122-drug evaluation, and Table 2 makeability of 98.23% versus 85.39% for MoleculeSTM and 84.96% for FineMolTex. V2 also adds baseline case outcomes, neighborhood similarities, and a 12.87% aggregate for the retained 430-drug scores. The 122-drug results use different conditions from v1's main evaluation.

M1.justification: V2 Algorithm 1 adds an explicit rule to select the property requiring the most improvement before proposing an edit; v1 enumerated functions without this priority rule. The tokenizers, GNN and adapter architecture, Qwen2.5-3B backbone, objectives, and training stages remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 merges vocabulary and tokenization sections, reverses the library-design and case-study order, moves Algorithm 1 and the original main experiment into appendices, and introduces a reproducibility statement. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figures 1–3 and reformats the retained molecular-editing illustrations. It adds comparative tables, a MoleculeSTM case figure, and six neighborhood figures. The original 430-drug table is transposed and relocated, other tables and figures move, and document typography and page layout change throughout.

R1.justification: Section 4 shifts from separate chemical-modeling, functional-group, and general multimodal/multilingual surveys toward protein-language-model inspiration and direct positioning against molecule editors. V2 adds substantial protein-model literature, the new evaluated editors, and synthesizability references, while removing many general vision, audio, and multilingual references.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds an assembly-step derivation yielding 2n−3 reactions for n blocks, assuming the required blocks are available. V2 also defines makeability as validity multiplied by conditional synthesizability. The existing cross-entropy formulation changes only notation, and no substantial theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: V1's central comparative and synthesizability advantages had little direct evaluation. V2 substantially strengthens their assessment through seven editing baselines, a synthesis-constrained experiment, and Allchemy route-search evidence, while clarifying where synthesis guarantees do not apply. Dropped Wilcoxon reporting and the disagreement between Table 2 and its prose about MoleculeSTM synthesizability weaken reporting precision, but the comparative evidence and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial net improvement. The evidence remains computational rather than laboratory validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mCLM research despite the revised title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds comparative drug-editing experiments, computational synthesizability evaluations, and molecular-block nearest-neighbor results.

before.justification: V1 reports original oracle-model AUCs, predicted property changes for 430 FDA-approved drugs, and molecule-editing case studies.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction and conclusion claims retain the same scope: synthesis-compatible modular tokens, joint chemical-language modeling, property improvement, unseen-block generalization, and iterative editing. The additional experiments support these retained claims rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds substantive interpretations of HierVAE's performance, possible benefits from mCLM-preprocessed training molecules, and disagreement between SA and retrosynthesis scores. It newly acknowledges restricted Allchemy discrimination on the FDA distribution. Appendix I interprets the Llama results as possible overfitting. The earlier multi-objective optimization caveat remains.

D1.justification: v3 adds front-page data/model and code links where v2 promised future release. Appendix F documents connection-point placeholders, their GNN encoding, and worked imatinib reconstruction steps. These improve access instructions and implementation disclosure; the existing core training recipe remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix H adds a QM9-based generation and synthesizability evaluation, extending the evaluated molecular population beyond FDA-drug editing. QM9 was already a training-data source in Appendix G. The existing ADMET tasks, FDA evaluations, and fallen-angel cases remain.

E2.justification: v3 adds two substantively different comparator families: HierVAE for property optimization and synthesizability in Tables 8–9, and vector-quantized DGAE for QM9 synthesizability in Table 10. The seven existing molecular-editing baselines remain, substantially broadening the comparison beyond the previous comparator set.

E3.justification: New experiments specify property-specific HierVAE training, an existing QM9-trained DGAE checkpoint, synthesis-guaranteed QM9 blocks for mCLM, and representation and 3B-backbone controls. These extend the experimental settings; the existing FDA evaluation sizes, TDC splits, metrics, and stated Allchemy search protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix I introduces direct tests of the GNN encoder, synthesis-aware tokenization through substitution with BRICS blocks, and Qwen versus Llama backbones. Tables 2 and 11 report their synthesizability and property-editing effects, with validation-loss evidence for the backbone comparison. Existing case studies and token-neighbor analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional results follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 8–11 add substantial results: HierVAE reports 10.5% average property improvement versus mCLM's retained 15.0%, and the new QM9 comparison reports 62% versus 100% synthesizability for DGAE and mCLM. HierVAE achieves better SA but lower retrosynthetic synthesizability than mCLM. New ablation outcomes are also reported. Existing table values remain; separately, Section 3.2 changes MoleculeSTM makeability from 85.4% to 84.8%, conflicting with the unchanged 85.39% in Table 2.

M1.justification: The proposed tokenization pipeline, GNN and adapter architecture, Qwen backbone, training objectives, and iterative editing procedure remain unchanged. Appendix F adds reconstruction documentation; the alternative encoders, tokenizer, and backbone are experimental ablations rather than revisions to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. v3 adds focused explanations, corrects wording, swaps the library-design and fallen-angel subsections, removes the A.1.1 subheading while retaining its text, and appends baseline and ablation sections and acknowledgments. This is a limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The experimental displays expand with dedicated baseline, QM9, and ablation tables in Tables 8–11, while Table 2 gains ablation rows and a clearer caption. Figure 3 is redrawn with numbered connection points. Figures 4–5 exchange order, and the retained token-example figures are repaginated.

R1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix H substantially expand positioning against closely relevant alternatives, including SAFE, Group-SELFIES, Reasyn, discrete molecular representations, DGAE, and HierVAE. They distinguish synthesis-compatible blocks from line representations and learned codebooks, extending the earlier, more general discussion of atom- and fragment-based approaches.

T1.justification: The mathematical loss formulation and Appendix A.1 derivation of 2n−3 synthesis steps are retained. Appendix F's added reconstruction example explains implementation rather than introducing a formal definition, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked direct tests of its central GNN/tokenizer choices and comparisons with hierarchical and vector-quantized generators. v3 supplies these evaluations, substantially strengthening scrutiny of the main contribution and exposing meaningful tradeoffs. Reconstruction details and discussion of evaluation limits also improve the paper. Differing baseline constraints, absent uncertainty estimates, and the new prose/Table 2 inconsistency temper the evidence, but the gains from addressing these important evaluation gaps are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mCLM research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated sections and figures.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds HierVAE and DGAE comparisons, QM9 synthesizability results, and component and backbone ablations.

before.justification: v2 reports original FDA-drug property-editing experiments, synthesizability evaluations, ADMET oracle results, and iterative molecule-editing case studies.

C1.justification: v4 explicitly characterizes FreeKV as training-free in the abstract and introduction. The principal contributions, near-lossless accuracy claim and approximately 13× maximum speedup claim remain unchanged; expanded latency-hiding language largely elaborates the existing contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of threshold choices, prefill-related scaling limits, generalization across architectures and training stages, and correction behavior on unfinished reasoning examples. Appendix C.2 expands the explanation of why system optimizations enable speculative overlap. Appendix B.3 also introduces a max-pooling correction-cost explanation that is not reconciled with the stated below-threshold correction rule.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-availability link, explicitly mentions scheduling across CPU threads and GPU streams, and documents InfiniGen's group-consistency adaptation and retained skewing-rank configuration. Most Appendix A settings already appeared in v3; their relocation is not new disclosure. Repository availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: LongBench v2, LongGenBench, MATH500, AIME24 and GPQA remain the principal datasets, and Figure 1 retains its NIAH and summarization demonstrations. The added analyses use existing task coverage; additional model configurations and sequence-length sweeps change settings.

E2.justification: v4 adds InfiniGen to Tables 2–3 and the latency comparisons in Figures 1 and 7, retaining the existing comparators. Appendix B.1 also evaluates an adapted last-layer-query retrieval alternative. Quest was already absent from v3's efficiency comparison.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include pooling and correction-threshold controls, 16K–128K input and 8K–64K output sweeps, additional model configurations, and correction measurements restricted to finished examples. LongGenBench drops standalone Acc reporting. Existing main-experiment settings are retained, largely relocated to Appendix A.

E4.justification: Appendices B–E add tests of previous-layer versus previous-step retrieval, selection and correction pooling, correction thresholds, sequence-length sensitivity, query-similarity generalization, and correction behavior on unfinished examples. The original system-optimization ablation is retained as Figure 9 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight generated samples per reasoning problem and report pass@k and avg@k. Neither adds confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. The new correction-rate histograms characterize behavior rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: Shared accuracy entries in Tables 2–3 remain unchanged, while v4 adds substantial comparator and diagnostic results. Table 4 newly reports AIME24 avg@k of 50.00 for previous-step reuse without correction versus 33.00 for the last-layer alternative; Section 5.3 adds speedups up to 8.5× over InfiniGen. Standalone LongGenBench Acc entries are removed.

M1.justification: Both versions use previous-step KV reuse, min-max page summaries with softmax mean pooling, similarity-triggered head-wise correction, hybrid CPU/GPU layouts and double-buffered recall. v4 evaluates alternatives without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v4 edits prose, integrates appendix references, moves detailed settings and the efficiency-ablation discussion into appendices, and adds acknowledgments and an LLM-usage statement. The main Sections 1–7 retain their order and much of their wording.

P2.justification: Tables 2–3 are transposed into benchmark/metric rows and method columns. Figures 1, 2 and 7 are revised to incorporate InfiniGen, and extensive new ablation tables, heatmaps and correction-rate histograms are added. The original efficiency ablation moves to Appendix C.2 as Figure 9, alongside the conference-format layout change.

R1.justification: v4 adds InfiniGen and a targeted discussion distinguishing its next-layer re-projection and partial overlap from FreeKV's previous-step reuse and efficient recall. The Chatbot Arena reference is removed. The broader KV-dropping versus KV-retrieval positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: The attention/GQA formulation, query-similarity definition, and FreeKV selection and correction equations are unchanged. The added appendices contain empirical comparisons and descriptive metrics, without new formal assumptions, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 provided limited direct validation of its retrieval, pooling and correction choices. v4 substantially strengthens that foundation through Appendix B's controlled comparisons, broader similarity and correction analyses, and evaluation against the relevant InfiniGen baseline. These gains address important evidential gaps while retaining the original results. They outweigh the loss of standalone LongGenBench Acc reporting and the unresolved max-pooling explanation in Appendix B.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FreeKV and provide readable text, equations, tables and figures. v3 ends with references and has no appendices; v4 includes Appendices A–F. The complete material supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these empirical results and adds InfiniGen comparisons, accuracy ablations, length-scaling experiments, and query-similarity and correction-rate analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark accuracy in Tables 2–3, inference latency in Figure 7, query-similarity measurements and an efficiency ablation.

C1.justification: The symmetry-discovery, canonical-normalization and first-3D-demonstration claims remain. V2 substantially broadens the abstract, introduction and concluding contribution statements to claim inference-only canonicalization that grants group invariance to frozen pretrained models and improves downstream performance without retraining those models.

C2.justification: V2 recognizes problematic multimodal centroids and attributes OOD improvements to easier optimization despite theoretical reference-frame invariance of likelihood. Its limitations emphasize whole-input transformations versus object-local symmetries in cluttered scenes, and dataset bias in learned natural poses. V1 instead concentrates on molecular prediction errors, density families, sampling and predefined groups.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds substantial reproducibility information: OOD score formulas, GEOM ID/OOD construction and threshold 96, classifier architectures and training settings, and recomputation of geometric features after canonicalization. Appendix C documents robust-centroid optimization. Core implementation details largely move from v1 Appendix C to v2 Appendix E unchanged. Code-release wording changes to availability upon publication, while both PDFs still provide placeholder repository links.

E1.justification: The three named benchmarks are retained, but v2 adds classification under rotated inputs using frozen classifiers and test-time canonicalization (Appendix F.2). It also evaluates centroid estimation on sampled unimodal, bimodal, five-modal and uniform SO(2) distributions (Figure 8). These introduce a substantial new task and additional distribution scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 reports RECON-only OOD scores; v2 adds an uncentered IE-AE comparator in all three OOD experiments (Figures 5c and 13). New classification comparisons evaluate no canonicalization, IE-AE canonicalization and RECON (Figure 6d).
