The earlier SGM/IE-AE qualitative canonicalization comparison is retained, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: Appendix F.2 introduces classifiers trained without rotation augmentation and held fixed during evaluation on rotated inputs, with three preprocessing conditions and an unaugmented reference evaluation. Training uses 100 epochs for ResNet-18 and 50 for the GCN. Appendix C adds simulations with 2,000 samples per distribution. Existing IE-AE training budgets and GEOM splits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds simulations testing centroid behavior around separated modes, a molecular-neighborhood purity analysis and its relationship to conformer counts, and an OOD ablation of centering (Appendices C, D.3 and F.1). The original neighborhood-size sensitivity and molecular-error correlation analyses survive as Appendix D.1 and Figure 12; their relocation is not new evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use a fixed random seed and retain prediction error bars, neighborhood mean/standard-deviation bands and molecular standard-deviation plots. V2 introduces no repeated-seed evaluation, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure. Its additional descriptive statistics and result rows do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 6d adds RECON classification accuracies of 92.94%, 80.32% and 55.70%, versus 66.90%, 57.52% and 52.40% without canonicalization, for MNIST, FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 respectively. Figure 10 adds a mean neighborhood hit rate of 0.95. Reported OOD AUCs change from 0.92/0.80/0.75 in v1 Section 5.3 to 0.92/0.81/0.80 in v2 Figure 5c. V1's sparse OOD protocol description prevents interpreting these revisions as established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The IE-AE backbone, neighbor-based normalization and learned predictors remain intact. V2 adds an optional Tukey-Fréchet centroid using a bounded biweight loss for multimodal distributions, a focused extension of the centering step (Section 3.1; Appendix C). It also corrects the written canonicalization transform from psi Lambda^-1 to Lambda psi^-1; this does not establish that the earlier implementation used the incorrect expression.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, introduction and limitations around the broader canonicalization application. Experiments change from separate imaging, geometric-graph and OOD sections to symmetry recovery and downstream applications. Longer neighborhood and partial-symmetry discussions move into Appendix D, and the appendices are reorganized into dedicated theory, analysis, implementation and application sections.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned and moved to the first page with a new train/test distribution-shift illustration. The centroid illustration gains an additional distribution and estimator. New accuracy tables, centroid simulations, neighborhood-quality plots and ROC curves are introduced. Existing density plots, neighborhood sensitivity and molecular-error correlations move into appendices, substantially reorganizing the displays without deleting those results.

R1.justification: V2 adds robust-statistics references by Shevlyakov et al., Rousseeuw and Hubert, and Shin and Oh. It also positions inference-only canonicalization against frame averaging and learned canonicalization, citing Puny et al. and Kaba et al. The central related-work discussion and positioning relative to SGM and IE-AE remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The original Wasserstein-consistency proposition and proof are largely retained. V2 adds Proposition B.2 and its proof concerning right-translation invariance of the likelihood score under a right Haar measure. Appendix C introduces population and empirical Tukey-Fréchet objectives and derives the loss gradient. The original consistency theorem is not extended to prove the robust variant's guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for normalization's practical value through frozen-classifier comparisons and an uncentered OOD control, addressing gaps in v1's qualitative canonicalizations and standalone OOD scores. Direct neighborhood validation supports a central sampling assumption, while the added likelihood-invariance proof and application details clarify mathematical scope and reproducibility. These are substantial gains, although the robust centroid extension has only simulation validation and fixed-seed reporting still limits confidence in experimental stability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RECON. All 19 pages of v1 and 26 pages of v2, including appendices A–C and A–G respectively, provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds centroid simulations, molecular-neighborhood validation, OOD comparisons and test-time classification experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original symmetry-recovery experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9, neighborhood sensitivity analyses, and OOD pose-detection results.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion remove the claim of the first symmetry-discovery demonstrations in 3D and clarify the target as instance-level pose distributions. The abstract adds a claim of matching or outperforming other canonicalizations. The central normalization, OOD-detection and inference-only canonicalization contributions remain.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds substantive discussion of stabilizer-induced pose ambiguity, inter-class latent overlap as a failure condition, and why molecular identity can remain separable despite conformational variation. It proposes targeted mitigation strategies and explains neighborhood-size tradeoffs. Appendix F additionally interprets the large gap to SEGNN as a limitation of canonicalization in the molecular setting.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the promised code release and hidden repository placeholder with a concrete repository address. It adds comparator architectures, training configurations and hyperparameter-search tables, plus pseudo-label runtimes and per-sample centering overhead. Existing RECON architecture and hardware documentation is largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MNIST, FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 for pose recovery, OOD detection and classification under rotations, alongside the same synthetic SO(2) centroid simulations. Added comparisons and diagnostics remain within this existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds EquiAdapt to the frozen-classifier canonicalization comparisons on all three datasets in Figure 6d. New Table 3 evaluates ESCNN and Partial G-CNN classifiers on the images and a SEGNN classifier on GEOM-QM9. The existing IE-AE comparisons and qualitative SGM comparison are retained.

E3.justification: The reported image pseudo-label neighborhood changes from k=25 to k=10, while GEOM-QM9 retains k=25. v3 also introduces comparator-training protocols, hyperparameter sweeps, and selection of the worst 5,000 FashionMNIST inputs for failure analysis. Appendix F explicitly selects EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters by test accuracy; existing RECON training budgets and data splits largely remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2's neighborhood-size and molecular hit-rate analyses are substantially extended. v3 adds FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 neighborhood sensitivity, worst-molecule error, image hit rates, a FashionMNIST neighbor-confusion matrix and low-hit-rate examples. Appendix D.5 adds computational-cost and inference-overhead analyses.

E5.justification: Although v2 already displays some dispersion, v3 adds ± reporting to OOD scores, downstream accuracies and reference accuracies in Figures 5c–6d and Table 2. Figure 10 explicitly identifies image sensitivity bands as standard deviations across runs with different seeds. Run counts and the meaning of all tabulated ± terms remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Figure 6d replaces RECON accuracies of 92.94%, 80.32% and 55.70% with 90.96%, 81.96% and 55.92% for MNIST, FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9. These are updated results under revised settings/reporting, including changed image k. Figure 5c revises MNIST and GEOM-QM9 OOD AUCs from 0.92 to 0.91 and 0.80 to 0.82. Substantial new comparator and diagnostic results include EquiAdapt exceeding RECON on MNIST and SEGNN reaching 98.55% on GEOM-QM9.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the class-pose backbones, Fréchet normalization, learned mappings Θ and Λ, losses and inference formulas remain unchanged. The Tukey-Fréchet extension already appears in v2. The revised image neighborhood size is a hyperparameter change, not a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion receive localized rewrites, including terminology changes to pose distributions and right translation. Appendix D is reorganized and Appendix F.2 gains domain-specific subsections. The main section sequence and most method, proof and implementation prose remain stable.

P2.justification: Figure 6d gains comparator rows and a supervision column. The neighborhood plot becomes a broader two-panel display, the hit-rate figure gains an image panel, and new confusion-matrix and neighbor-example figures are added. Four new tables present runtimes, classifier comparisons and hyperparameter searches. The existing pose-distribution visualization moves from v2 Figure 11 to v3 Figure 9.

R1.justification: Section 4 substantially expands positioning through LieGG, LieGAN, LaLiGAN, Implicit-PDF, Alignist and test-time canonicalization methods including EquiAdapt. It explicitly distinguishes instance-level pose estimation from dataset-level group discovery and explains differences in supervision and downstream-model dependence. The bibliography also adds supporting work on representation learning and efficient neighbor search.

T1.justification: New Appendix D.1 defines the stabilizer S_x and states that pose distributions are identifiable only modulo it. Appendix D.5 adds an O(N²d) complexity analysis for naive neighborhood search. Proposition 3.1, the Appendix B proofs and the Tukey-Fréchet mathematics in Appendix C are retained.

improvement.justification: The added relevant comparators substantially address v2's limited evidence for downstream utility. Expanded failure analyses, computational measurements, uncertainty reporting and concrete code-access information also make the benefits and limitations more assessable. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: Appendix F tunes baselines on test accuracy and incorrectly states that EquiAdapt lowers GEOM-QM9 accuracy, whereas Figure 6d reports 52.96% versus 52.40% without canonicalization. Uncertainty reporting also remains incompletely specified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RECON with the same authors, core method and experimental domains. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated comparators, neighborhood diagnostics, failure cases and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original symmetry-recovery, OOD-detection and classification results on MNIST, FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9, plus centroid simulations and appendix analyses.

C1.justification: The central claims about deterministic FIM bounds and efficient unbiased estimation with bounded relative variability remain. v2 explicitly promotes an empirical study demonstrating production-setting advantages as a contribution. Its conclusion additionally claims straightforward integration into libraries for FIM or Hessian evaluation.

C2.justification: v2 adds practical estimator-selection guidance based on the new accuracy comparisons, qualifies power iteration by spectral-gap-dependent convergence, and explains the locality assumption behind moving averages. Appendix B discusses numerical stability of the square-root formulation. The absence of downstream optimizer development was already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: Hardware changes from an Apple M1 laptop with 16 GB RAM to Nvidia H100 SXM5 GPUs. v2 specifies an actual 30-iteration power-method budget and gives log_softmax implementation guidance; v1 only suggested 10 iterations as an example. Conversely, v1's explicit DistilBERT checkpoint identifiers are omitted in v2.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates AG News topic classification and SST-2 sentiment classification. v2 removes AG News, retains SST-2, and adds DBpedia ontology classification, MNLI natural language inference, CIFAR-100 image classification, and SpeechCommands audio classification. Coverage expands substantially beyond the original text-classification tasks.

E2.justification: The empirical FIM, unbiased Hutchinson, diagonal-core, and rank-one estimators remain evaluated. v2 Table 2 adds the rank-two variant, including in the retained SST-2 comparison. Monte Carlo estimation was not an evaluated comparator in v1, so its explicit exclusion in v2 is not a baseline removal.

E3.justification: v1 uses the first 128 examples for illustrative estimator distributions. v2 uses a fixed random subset of 128 batches of 64 examples, computes the exact diagonal FIM, and evaluates RelMAE with epsilon 10^-12 and relative computational speed. Its single-backward-pass-per-batch comparison introduces a substantially different evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted rank-one versus rank-two comparison in Table 2 and an informal numerical comparison of the original and square-root formulations in Appendix B. Existing layerwise diagnostics are revised to examine exact FIM distributions, including zero masses and differences between model components.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly averages 10 Hutchinson samples for variance reduction. v2 describes independent minibatch probes and accumulation under a single-backward-pass-per-batch budget. This changes stochastic aggregation, without establishing additional repeated experimental runs. Neither version reports seeds or between-run confidence intervals; analytical variance guarantees are assessed under T1.

E6.justification: The original approximation-density results are replaced by ground-truth histograms and quantitative error/speed comparisons. For example, v2 Table 2 reports Hutchinson versus empirical-FIM RelMAE of 0.18 versus 1.15 on SST-2 and 0.17 versus 56.8 on SpeechCommands. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The main Hutchinson estimator is retained. v2 Section 4.4 extends the optional rank-one core approximation to top-k eigenpairs, while Appendix B adds an equivalent square-root implementation without detach(). The extension has a specification ambiguity: Equation (8) uses xi_x although the text specifies k probes per example.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around motivation and explicit contributions. Estimator construction moves from the introduction into Section 4.2; core-space variance material and two estimator propositions move into appendices. Empirical and Monte Carlo FIM notation is separated, and the experimental narrative is substantially rewritten.

P2.justification: Both original estimator-by-layer density grids are replaced by grouped ground-truth histograms across models, with logarithmic horizontal axes, explicit zero masses, parameter counts, and median/95th-percentile markers. v2 adds the accuracy-and-speed Table 2 and revises the notation table. These are substantial display changes.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially broadens positioning through pruning, transfer learning, fine-tuning, catastrophic forgetting, and foundational information geometry, with corresponding new citations. Section 3 newly contrasts the proposed bounds with monotonicity and coarse-graining bounds. The Sun–Nielsen preprint-to-publication update represents the same work, not an added research connection.

T1.justification: v2 Propositions 5 and 8 extend v1 Propositions 6 and 9 from rank one to rank k, with corresponding proof revisions in Appendices J and M. Lemma 2 adds an interior condition, and Section 4.2 adds minibatch variance reasoning under approximately equal batch contributions. The original spectral and estimator-variance results otherwise remain, sometimes relocated.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly visualizes approximations without measuring their errors against an exact reference. v2 Section 4.5 and Table 2 resolve this important evidential weakness through exact diagonal-FIM accuracy and computational-speed comparisons across text, vision, and audio. Clearer notation and organization also help. The new rank-k formula's probe-index ambiguity limits confidence in that extension, but does not outweigh the substantially stronger validation of the retained main estimator.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FIM bounds and Hutchinson estimator research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v2 reports original estimation errors and computational speed comparisons across six model-task combinations in Table 2, plus ground-truth FIM distributions in Figures 1–2 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original diagonal-FIM computations for DistilBERT on AG News in Section 4.4 and Figure 1, and on SST-2 in Appendix O and Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract adds preservation of long-term statistics as a central forecasting claim, replacing nonlinear resonance as a highlighted emergent property. The introduction also revises its claimed real-world applications, replacing chemical-reaction/electrophysiology examples with the evaluated motion and circuit applications. Zero-shot PDE forecasting and dynamical-diversity scaling claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 5.4 and Appendix M newly acknowledge Panda's regression to the mean beyond its training horizon and contrast this with Chronos parroting and geometric failures. v2 also interprets dataset diagnostics as evidence against diversity collapse and qualifies optimal patch length as data-dependent. Most earlier attention-based mechanism explanations are retained in the appendix.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the Radau integration procedure, period selection, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, clipping, augmentation frequency, expanded architecture settings and training budgets. It newly documents PDE initialization and PCA-based vorticity inputs. Dataset/checkpoint links are added, the code repository target changes, and the reported training node changes from four to eight GPUs.

E1.justification: Both cover chaotic ODE forecasting and completion, double-pendulum motion, eigenworms, electronic circuits, and KS/VKVS PDE forecasting. The enlarged training datasets vary system counts, initial conditions and integration timescales within retained coverage. Some founder-system examples separately identified in v2 were already plotted in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds Chronos 200M comparisons in Appendix D and Chronos 46M, including supervised-fine-tuned and probabilistic variants, in Appendix K. This extends the existing Chronos comparator family; the original main comparison set remains. Time-MoE is excluded from the new significance tests because of NaNs, but remains in benchmark plots.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes the reported Chronos-SFT budget from 300K iterations to ten times Panda's iterations; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include distributional evaluation over four contexts per system, patch-length comparisons with embedding removal and batch-size adjustments, and 42M/72M models with larger datasets and training budgets. The reported founder-pool size also changes from 135 to 129.

E4.justification: v2 adds dataset-diversity and chaoticity diagnostics, forecast-distribution and Lyapunov analyses, patch-length sensitivity, model/data scaling studies, and explicit comparative failure cases. These test substantial new questions about dataset quality, generalization and forecast validity. The original architectural ablations and attention analyses remain, with attention analysis relocated to Appendix G.

E5.justification: v2 adds Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Sidak adjustment in Table 5, plus mean-and-standard-deviation summaries for distributional and timing analyses. Existing median/IQR reporting, PDE standard-error bars and five-mask completion averaging were already present. These additions do not establish increased independent training repetitions.

E6.justification: Substantial new numerical and qualitative results appear. At horizon 128, Table 1 reports KL divergence of 1.18 for Panda versus 1.72 for Chronos-SFT probabilistic; Table 17 reports sMAPE 20.6 for the new 72M Panda. Prediction-only Lyapunov comparisons also reveal advantages for Chronos-SFT. The enlarged-model results use different training conditions and are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core patch embedding, temporal/channel attention, prediction heads and objectives remain. However, v1 names NoPE while v2 specifies p-RoPE, and v2 newly describes KPSS/ADF stationarity filtering. The PDFs do not resolve whether these represent procedural changes or corrected and expanded implementation documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, dataset procedure and architecture exposition undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. The main narrative replaces the attention-analysis section with long-term geometry evaluation, relocating retained attention material and reorganizing the appendices. The title, terminology and citation style also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds extensive distributional, statistical, ablation and scaling tables, together with diagnostic and failure-analysis figures. Forecast example grids are regrouped, and the main attention/resonance figures move to Appendix G. Core benchmark plots are retained, while headings, title formatting and page layout are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting stationarity tests, skew-product flows and distributional evaluation, including Dickey-Fuller, Kwiatkowski et al., Kloeden-Kozyakin and Hess et al. It removes the conserved-quantities related-work paragraph and several resonance analogies and associated citations. The principal positioning against synthetic-data and PDE foundation models remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 introduces an explicit empirical stiffness-score definition using the logarithm of the maximum-to-average finite-difference ratio. The skew-product equations receive fuller exposition, while the correlation-dimension estimator and linear-attention coupling derivation are substantively retained. No substantial new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked quantitative forecast-distribution validation and several essential replication settings. v2 supplies these, adds dataset-quality checks and adjusted significance tests, and documents comparative failures, substantially strengthening evidential support and reproducibility. Important limits remain: scale-up changes data and budgets together, while mean regression and mixed prediction-only Lyapunov results qualify the stronger long-term preservation claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Panda research project. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds dataset diagnostics, distributional evaluations, patch-length ablations, larger-model comparisons and failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments on synthetic ODEs, experimental time series and PDEs, together with architectural ablations, diversity scaling and masked-completion results.

C1.justification: The central dataset-generation, zero-shot forecasting, diversity-scaling, and ODE-to-PDE contributions remain. The abstract replaces explicit preservation of 'long-term statistics' with preservation of 'distributional measures' and elevates the already-reported resonance and experimental-data findings into its headline description.

C2.justification: v2 acknowledged mean regression while emphasizing consistent distributional advantages. v3 explains where Chronos-SFT and DynaMix outperform Panda, discusses failures for large Lyapunov exponents, and connects parroting to unstable periodic orbits. It adds substantive qualifications about DynaMix's preferred context length and the operator baselines' one-step settings, limiting interpretation of those comparisons.

D1.justification: Appendices B, F, H, and K add architecture tables, residual-block operations, KL pseudocode, operator-baseline configurations, training times, and MLM-66M training details. Section 8 consolidates code/checkpoint access and adds the 66M checkpoint pointer. However, v2's direct links to both training datasets and the smaller MLM checkpoint are absent from v3; this does not establish that those resources became unavailable.

E1.justification: Both versions cover synthetic founder/skew-product ODEs, double-pendulum recordings, eigenworms, electronic circuits, Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and von Kármán vortex-street PDEs, and masked completion. Added analyses and longer evaluations reuse this coverage; changes concern configurations, sample counts, and procedures.

E2.justification: v3 adds DynaMix to ODE forecasting and long-horizon comparisons, FNO and DeepONet to PDE evaluation, and cubic-spline, linear, and degree-3 polynomial interpolation to completion. Figure 2 replaces Chronos 20M with Chronos 200M, previously evaluated elsewhere. Long-horizon comparisons also replace probabilistic Chronos variants with an expanded deterministic comparator set.

E3.justification: Long-term evaluation changes from 128–512-step forecasts using full-trajectory or context-inclusive references to 512–3584-step, horizon-matched evaluations and tail-only scoring. Completion evaluation changes from 3584 to 4096 points and adds the 66M checkpoint; operator-baseline training introduces additional PDE protocols. Appendix B revises Adam to AdamW and Chronos-SFT settings from batch 128 and ten times Panda's iterations to batch 160 and 300K iterations. These are reported setting revisions, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a tsfresh/UMAP analysis of founder–offspring diversity. Appendix F adds KL-estimator sensitivity and tail-only mean-regression tests, replacing shorter-horizon Lyapunov correlation tables with longer-horizon distribution comparisons. Appendix N adds spline-versus-Panda case studies. The attention-resonance and patch-length analyses already existed and are not new experiments.

E5.justification: Completion evaluation changes its reported averaging from five independent masks in v2 Figure 15 to eight seeded masks in v3 Figure 18/Table 10, alongside changed model/context settings. v3 also documents Monte Carlo KL estimation. Mean/standard-deviation, interquartile-range, and Holm–Šidák-adjusted Wilcoxon reporting remain established practices.

E6.justification: Many original short-horizon table values remain, but substantial results are added or replaced. v3 Table 17 reports tail-only KL divergence of 15.25 for Panda, 7.00 for Chronos 20M SFT, and 3.50 for DynaMix. Table 10 adds completion R² values of 0.91 for Panda MLM-66M, 0.78 for Panda MLM, and 0.71 for cubic splines. Table 6 adds a nonsignificant 512-step sMAPE comparison against probabilistic Chronos 20M SFT (p=0.326). These are new evaluations, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The evolutionary data-generation procedure, dynamics embeddings, temporal/channel attention, and forecasting/MLM objectives are retained. The new 66M MLM checkpoint scales the existing architecture. Expanded residual-block and pooling descriptions do not establish a changed method; optimizer and training-budget revisions concern experimental settings.

P1.justification: The long-term section is rewritten and moved from Section 5.4 to 5.6. Appendix G's resonance and attention-map discussion becomes main-text Section 5.5, while Appendix F is reorganized into six subsections. New acknowledgements and reproducibility sections and substantial appendix restructuring change the narrative beyond routine copyediting.

P2.justification: v2's attention Figures 17–19 are recomposed as main-text Figures 7–8, and its separate main KL/Hellinger tables become a combined table. PDE Figure 6 is redrawn with additional baselines and clearer panels. New UMAP, long-horizon, and completion displays, architecture/configuration tables, and revised galleries substantially change presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds positioning relative to DynaMix and Almost-Linear RNNs, plus citations supporting parroting, periodic orbits, tsfresh/UMAP, and operator-learning implementations. References to Kloeden–Kozyakin and structured state-space models are removed. The main distinction based on evolutionary data generation and multivariate forecasting remains.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds an explicit local-bandwidth objective and Gaussian-mixture/Monte Carlo construction for KL estimation, beyond v2's brief metric description. The skew-product equations, correlation-dimension derivation, and spatiotemporal-attention derivation remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 already recognized mean regression, but its long-term argument relied largely on 128–512-step forecasts. v3 tests up to 3584 steps, checks alternative KL estimation, and isolates forecast tails, substantially improving evidence about where preservation fails. Added comparators and implementation details strengthen validation and reproducibility. Unequal comparison settings, retained blanket significance wording contradicted by Table 6, and removed dataset links are drawbacks, but the substantially more informative assessment of Panda's capabilities and limits outweighs them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Panda research work. The text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–N support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional baseline comparisons, completion results, dataset analyses, and long-horizon failure measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting, completion, ablation, scaling, and attractor-statistics experiments on synthetic chaotic systems, experimental recordings, and PDE simulations.

C1.justification: The introduction qualifies categorical statements: 'no subspace' becomes finding no evidence for an isolated linear subspace, and 'establish' nonseparability becomes observing patterns inconsistent with separability. The abstract and conclusion retain the central entanglement claim, so this is a limited qualification rather than a new contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix L newly distinguishes local activation-steering controllability from a stable, uniquely safety-specific subspace. The robustness appendices add interpretations concerning alignment-method dependence, general ability, and over-refusal. Appendix G also extends its overlap interpretation to all layers, although Figure 14 contains threshold-specific exceptions. The formal limitations paragraph is unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 documents the DPO subset size and training steps, individual-layer selection, and uses of the added datasets. Existing hardware, software, Table 3 hyperparameters, and the code link remain unchanged. The new reproducibility statement largely consolidates existing disclosures; exact early-token-window settings remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v3 adds preference-based safety training with PKU-SafeRLHF, general-knowledge evaluation with MMLU, benign-query over-refusal testing with XSTest, and harmless Extended Refusal prompts for activation analysis. These substantially broaden the represented training and evaluation tasks while retaining the earlier mathematics and harmful-prompt coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding original experiments retain Random-K and Random controls, the same model reference conditions, and the analytical random-subspace baseline. The added studies reuse these comparison approaches; newly cited activation-steering methods are discussed without being evaluated as competing methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include DPO training of Llama-3.2 1B for 5,000 steps on 10,000 PKU-SafeRLHF examples, projections restricted to ten individual Qwen-2.5 1.5B layers, and earlier-token activation measurements. MMLU accuracy and XSTest refusal rates add evaluation metrics. These supplement, rather than replace, the retained experimental settings.

E4.justification: Appendices G–K add substantial tests of dependence on layer selection, alignment procedure, token position, and benign-prompt choice. They also investigate whether general-capability loss or over-refusal explains the safety findings. Layerwise overlap plots and single-layer interventions extend the earlier selected-layer and averaged analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance-testing procedures. The additional plots retain point-result reporting, and the analytical random-subspace expectation remains unchanged.

E6.justification: The numerical entries in Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 and all original result plots are unchanged. Figures 10–26 add layerwise, DPO, token-window, and refusal-prompt results, plus largely stable MMLU accuracy and low XSTest refusal rates. These are newly reported results under additional conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: Section 2 retains the same SVD subspace construction, parallel and orthogonal projection operators, and MSO procedure. DPO-trained models and single-layer projections are additional experimental conditions rather than revisions to the study's core method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained. Changes include localized contribution wording, more specific weight/activation headings, cross-references, a reproducibility statement, and expanded appendix organization. Former Appendices G–I move to M–O; most additional prose accompanies new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figures 10–26 substantially expand the visual presentation through layerwise grids, individual-layer projection panels, and robustness plots. All nine original figure images are retained, with some relocated. Captions for Figures 3 and 7 correct 'Parallel' to 'Orthogonal'; existing table structures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix L substantially expands positioning relative to activation steering, explaining compatibility with local refusal control while challenging stronger subspace assumptions. It adds discussion and citations concerning conditional steering, manifold steering, and dimensionality, alongside new dataset references. Publication-metadata updates and the duplicated DPO reference do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations in Section 2, including projections, energy retention, MSO, and expected random overlap, are unchanged. The new appendices introduce empirical analyses and conceptual discussion without new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence that previously depended on selected layers, limited activation inputs, and fewer safety-training conditions. Appendices G–K investigate these dependencies and important capability-loss and over-refusal confounds, while Appendix L clarifies compatibility with activation steering. These gains outweigh remaining shortcomings: some new protocols are incompletely documented, and Appendix G's blanket 'never' statement overstates Figure 14, where alignment–harmful overlap is largest at some thresholds in early layers.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same safety-subspace study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix relocations.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds DPO, layer-specific, MMLU, XSTest, and alternative activation-input experiments in Appendices G–K.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning experiments, GSM8K utility and AdvBench harmfulness scores, and weight- and activation-subspace measurements in Sections 3–6 and Appendices C–F.

C1.justification: The central novelty and contribution claims about transferring passive video diffusion models into autoregressive, action-conditioned world models remain. v2 extends the claimed demonstrated applicability to navigation and explicitly argues that transferring action-free video priors can avoid costly cross-domain action-labeled pretraining.

C2.justification: v2 interprets navigation with a 20-frame context versus 16-frame training as temporal generalization and distinguishes NWM's single-shot prediction from Vid2World's accumulating autoregressive predictions. RT-1 non-autoregressive superiority is softened to 'superior or comparable.' Existing limitations concerning fine control, object identity, respawn randomness and computational cost remain.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the extrapolative implementation with kernel size 3 and m=1, p=2, newly identifies LPIPS feature networks, and documents RECON action encoding, splits and resizing. Most earlier implementation information is retained. However, Table 3 still lists 'Mixed weight transfer,' conflicting with the revised method description.

E1.justification: v2 adds RECON open-world navigation, representing 40 hours across nine environments with continuous translation-and-yaw actions. This extends the work beyond v1's robot manipulation and CS:GO domains; the earlier coverage and drawer-closing policy task remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds AVID as an evaluated RT-1 comparator; v1 cited AVID and borrowed other baseline results without reporting an AVID row. Navigation introduces comparisons with NWM, NWM + Ego4D and DIAMOND navigation variants in Table 1 and Figure 6. The earlier RT-1 comparators and CS:GO Fast/HQ comparator set remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds DreamSim and navigation protocols using 500 segments for four-second target prediction and 150 for autoregressive evaluation, with four history frames, sixteen predicted frames and 1/4 fps baseline conditions. The stated policy-evaluation sample count changes from 80 to 50 trajectories per policy. Reported RT-1/CS:GO splits and training budgets otherwise remain.

E4.justification: v1's three-row transfer/action-guidance ablation becomes a five-row comparison of Shift, Masked and Extrapolative transfer, with guidance varied for the latter two. v2 also compares navigation errors across rollout horizons and temporal rates, including context exceeding the training length. Earlier failure-case and counterfactual-action analyses are retained in Appendix D.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run uncertainty reporting. v2 Appendix C.6.1 reports five random-seed navigation runs with means and standard deviations, accompanied by uncertainty bands in Figure 6; Table 1 also includes uncertainty for NWM baselines. This does not establish increased runs for the retained robot/game experiments.

E6.justification: Reported Vid2World RT-1 autoregressive FVD changes from 21.0 to 18.5, while CS:GO FVD changes from 102.6 to 106.6 alongside the revised transfer method. DIAMOND-Fast/HQ FVD changes from 903.9/562.2 to 577.1/368.5 without an explained protocol revision. AVID, navigation, DreamSim and revised ablation entries are added. Policy success estimates change from 0.341/0.756/0.874 to 0.260/0.820/0.880, accompanying the reduced sample count rather than establishing same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 replaces Mixed Weight Transfer, which initializes additional past positions using averaged weights, with Extrapolative Weight Transfer, which redistributes future-facing weights using local linear extrapolation. Masked Weight Transfer is also introduced. This revises a central causalization component; diffusion forcing and causal action guidance remain.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses the introduction, preliminaries, methods and experimental narrative, adding explanatory subheadings. Training/sampling pseudocode moves from the main text to Appendix B, theoretical material leads the appendices, and citations change from numbered to author-year style.

P2.justification: v2 adds data-pyramid and navigation figures, redraws the transfer and training diagrams, and merges the RT-1/CS:GO tables into a three-domain table with DreamSim and inference-type annotations. The policy chart and main qualitative panel are redesigned. Earlier appendix examples are retained with relocation and caption/display refinements.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands positioning through a data pyramid, contrasting model transfer with cross-domain action-labeled pretraining in NWM/iVideoGPT and action-free co-training in AdaWorld. References add works including AdaWorld, RECON, DreamSim and RLVR-World, while dropping works including BERT, Mineworld and Tesseract.

T1.justification: New Appendix A provides a linear-sequence counterexample for Shift Weight Transfer, an ordinary-least-squares derivation of Extrapolative Weight Transfer, and Proposition 1 with a smoothness-based error bound and proof. v1 contains no corresponding theoretical analysis; its mixed-weight construction is superseded.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the methodological and empirical basis of the paper through a derived transfer construction, more informative component controls, and navigation comparisons with seed-based uncertainty. These address important gaps in v1's mechanism justification and demonstrated generality. The gains outweigh the smaller policy-evaluation sample and remaining reporting problems, including the stale transfer label in Table 3 and unexplained DIAMOND FVD revisions. Updated scores do not establish uniform performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Vid2World with the same authors and research objective. Text extraction and visual inspection of all pages, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original robot manipulation, game simulation, policy-evaluation and newly added RECON navigation results, including ablations and appendix visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original RT-1 and CS:GO predictions, component ablations and Real2Sim policy-evaluation outcomes in Section 5, with additional generated examples in Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contribution: a precise, unambiguous benchmark for molecular recognition, editing and generation across representations. The headline GPT-5 accuracies of 86.2%, 85.5% and 43.0% and the central claim that current models struggle remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretations of atom-level editing/generation failures, complexity-dependent localization difficulties, graph–language alignment limitations and SELFIES weaknesses. It also interprets structural prompting as beneficial for downstream prediction and argues for dataset representativeness from chemical-space coverage. The original annotation-cost limitation and tokenization hypothesis remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents snapshots and API providers for added models, further curation and validation details, LLM assistance with annotation wording, and a dataset contamination canary. These improve procedural disclosure without establishing changes to the retained annotation pipeline. The code and dataset links already appeared in v2.

E1.justification: v3 adds BBBP and BACE property-classification tasks and five complex-substructure recognition tasks: alpha-amino acid, glucose-like pyranose, penam, phthalimide and steroid motifs (Appendices A.13 and A.15). These substantially expand task requirements beyond the retained original benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Llama-4-Maverick, Qwen3-Max, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-Opus-4.1, plus HIGHT for recognition and Llamole for editing/generation. ChemDFM, ChemLLM and Galactica also gain reported recognition and generation comparisons beyond their v2 editing comparison. o4-mini remains evaluated in the appendices despite its replacement by Gemini in the main tables.

E3.justification: v3 adds Tanimoto similarity, pass@3/pass@5 evaluation and direct-versus-structure-first property-prediction prompts. New SELFIES, chemistry-specific-model and HIGHT recognition evaluations omit atom-index-dependent subtasks and localization accuracy (Appendices A.10–A.16). These introduce substantial additional evaluation protocols; the original core-set sizes and zero-shot evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine chemical-space coverage through t-SNE, structural complexity, SELFIES sensitivity, multiple-attempt success and the downstream effect of structural prompting. Table 3 and Figures S7–S8 add a six-category error analysis and illustrated o3 failures. Existing prompt-sensitivity, OCR-agreement, tokenization and image-generation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new property-prediction experiment explicitly reports three runs per model–task–prompt configuration and mean ± standard deviation (Table S8). Existing o3 analyses still specify five runs; no increase in that run count is established. Revised means and standard deviations are result changes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for new models, representations, metrics and analyses; Gemini-2.5-Pro, for example, ties GPT-5 at 0.430 core-generation accuracy. GPT-5's headline scores remain unchanged. The reported five-run o3 editing/generation mean accuracies change from 0.774/0.286 in v2 Table S5 to 0.754/0.246 in v3 Table S10 without an explanation. SELFIES and multiple-attempt results represent additional settings, not changes in the original SMILES pass@1 performance.

M1.justification: The three task mappings and the core and extended annotation pipelines remain unchanged. Added model architectures, representations and prompting comparisons are benchmark evaluations, without a newly proposed model or algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites related work, separates recognition and editing/generation discussions, reorders existing appendix sections and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Author affiliations and conference headers also change. The introduction, task formulations, annotation instructions and conclusion remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the error-count table, chemical-space and SELFIES figures, and extensive failure-case panels. Results tables expand and reorganize to accommodate models, similarity scores and pass@k metrics; the ranking plot gains models and a revised axis. Existing benchmark examples are retained but redistributed and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SELFIES, MoleculeNet, fingerprints, HIGHT, Llamole, additional LLMs and contamination prevention. Related work more explicitly discusses structural grounding and graph–language alignment, while retaining the original positioning relative to molecule-description datasets and specialized chemical models.

T1.justification: Section 2 retains the same mathematical task formulations. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations appear. The standard pass@k explanation and SELFIES illustrations document evaluation and representation behavior rather than new formal results.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential breadth and diagnostic value: it addresses v2's untested graph modality, broadens model comparisons and quantifies failures previously discussed mainly qualitatively. Complex-substructure and downstream-prompting experiments further test the benchmark's motivation. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including unexplained revisions to o3's five-run summaries and the new claim that Gemini has the highest generation validity, contradicted by Claude's higher value in Table S5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MolLangBench. Their complete main texts and appendices, including rendered figures, tables and task equations, support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds model comparisons, property-prediction experiments, complex-substructure evaluations and error analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations on molecular recognition, editing and generation, together with prompt-sensitivity, repeated-run and OCR-validation results.

C1.justification: The central claim that generative pretraining enables transfer to unseen mask categories and styles remains. V2 narrows v1's explicit claims about generalization beyond both pretraining and finetuning distributions to unseen finetuning supervision. Section 3.1 also explicitly disclaims novelty for the finetuning strategy.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking clean boundaries to generative priors despite polygonal supervision, locating grouping information in the decoder, and explaining why simple prompting probes representations. It also qualifies the necessary training diversity and interprets perturbation robustness. Existing small-object and background-omission limitations remain. Some new interpretations exceed the evidence: Table 5 shows EgoHOS falling from 40.0 to 28.6 despite describing timestep effects as negligible.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 documents pruning images with over 35% disallowed area or no allowed masks, and the shorter training budgets for restricted-category SD models. Appendix C clarifies previously general data-cleaning descriptions by specifying removal of maskless images and scenes with fewer than ten objects. Core hardware, optimization settings and code-access statements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V1 finetunes on Hypersim and Virtual KITTI 2. V2 additionally trains on real-world COCO and synthetic ClevrTex, evaluates five- and ten-class Hypersim supervision regimes, and tests photometrically perturbed COCO images. The original five segmentation evaluation datasets and BSDS500 remain.

E2.justification: SAM, SimpleClick, DINO-B and the Sobel edge baseline remain. However, the separately compared SD-Limited variant disappears from Table 1 and the edge comparison in Figure 6, although it remains in Figure 5. New five- and ten-class variants use different training restrictions rather than simply renaming SD-Limited.

E3.justification: V2 makes AP below 20% recall the main edge summary, replacing v1's full-range AP numbers while retaining full precision–recall curves. Added experiments introduce class-exclusion and image-pruning controls, 15,000-iteration budgets for restricted-category SD models, alternative timesteps, photometric transformations and partial-layer finetuning. These are new experimental settings, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds substantial analyses of training domain and category diversity (Table 2), timestep sensitivity (Table 5), photometric robustness (Table 6), and the necessary depth of decoder finetuning (Table 7). The original loss ablation survives as Table 4; multi-prompt and background-omission analyses are retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or run-to-run error bars. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: All 42 shared Table 1 values and the original loss-ablation scores are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive results in Tables 2–3 and 5–7 and removes the Table 1 SD-Limited row. V1 Figure 6 reports full-range edge AP of 58.8 for SD and 64.7 for SAM; v2 Table 3 reports 93.4 and 79.0 below 20% recall. This ranking difference reflects different metric coverage, not a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Equation 7 revises the stated prompting rule from inverse feature distance to min(1, inverse feature distance), introducing a cap before normalization. The architectures, generative-model adaptation and three-component instance coloring loss remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around human object generalization and narrow supervision, presenting MAE before Stable Diffusion. V2 removes the standalone qualitative-results subsection, expands the prompting explanation, moves multi-prompt and detailed edge discussion into the appendix, and reorganizes the implementation and ablation sections.

P2.justification: V2 adds five tables, relocates Figures 5–7 to the appendix, and redraws Figure 6 with additional curves and a different legend. Figures 13–19 are substantially reconfigured to display additional training variants. Figure 4 loses one example, Table 1 loses a row, and the title page, headers and document layout change.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the relatively unexplored diffusion-instance-segmentation framing with explicit distinctions from Fan et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2025). It adds substantive positioning against pseudo-mask approaches such as FreeSOLO and Cut and Learn, and credits De Brabandere et al. (2017) and Kong and Fowlkes (2018) as antecedents of its finetuning strategy.

T1.justification: Equation 7 changes the mathematical definition of query-feature similarity by adding a non-equivalent cap at 1. The instance definitions and loss formulas in Equations 1–6 remain unchanged. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central argument by testing dependence on synthetic annotations, category diversity and extensive finetuning (Tables 2–3 and 7), alternative explanations that v1 largely left uncontrolled. It also clarifies the contribution and credits methodological antecedents. Restricted edge AP and unequal training budgets limit some comparisons, and the timestep interpretation is overbroad, but full curves remain available and these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial added diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gen2seg research, with matching architectures, loss equations and core experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds training-data comparisons, timestep ablations, perturbation tests and decoder-finetuning experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation and edge-detection experiments, including Table 1, Figures 5–7 and the appendix loss ablation.

C1.justification: The central claims about the benchmark, three tasks, and VLM reliance on superficial cues remain. V3's introduction adds the claim that training on DECEPTIONDECODED improves external misinformation detection, extending its claimed utility beyond evaluation. This is a limited expansion of the retained contributions.

C2.justification: V3 interprets the new studies as evidence of realistic, intent-aligned data and broader training utility. Section 5.2 adds a guardrail-bypass risk interpretation, while Appendix B clarifies that the target is unsupported distortion while respecting diverse viewpoints. The limitations concerning open-ended intent evaluation and unmeasured societal influence are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: Appendix F.5 adds a substantial fine-tuning recipe: prompt masking, answer-span matching, data shuffling, left padding without truncation, learning rate 1e-5, effective batch size 32, bf16 precision, and the Figure 11 prompt. V3 also documents new annotation questions and explicitly specifies majority-vote aggregation. V1's release-upon-acceptance timing statement disappears, although planned access for verified researchers remains.

E1.justification: MMFakeBench, previously discussed only as related work, becomes an evaluated external dataset in v3. Its general misinformation classification task extends coverage beyond the internally generated intent benchmark. The original 12,000 instances, ten source topics, and three intent-centric tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 3 removes Claude-3.5-Sonnet from creator-desire inference, reducing that comparison from nine models to eight. The main 14-model comparison is retained; the appendices confirm that the revised Qwen and Llama names identify the same models. The new transfer experiment compares pretrained and fine-tuned variants of two existing 7B models.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a transfer protocol using 6,000 training examples, 1,000 per intent category, one epoch, binary label mapping, and evaluation on 1,000 MMFakeBench validation examples comprising 700 fake and 300 real cases. Table 6 reports Macro-F1 and Macro-Acc. New human protocols assess 120 examples per modality for standalone plausibility and 80 misleading examples per modality for pairwise plausibility and intent alignment. Retained experiments keep their settings.

E4.justification: V1's human verification checks misleading versus non-misleading labels. V3 substantially extends validation to standalone and pairwise realism, desired-influence alignment, and execution-plan alignment (Appendices E.2–E.3). It also tests downstream transfer utility. Existing modality, style, authenticity-hint, and image-fidelity analyses remain; Table 9 adds illustrative pairs to the existing style analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions specify one evaluation run at temperature zero and report human agreement through accuracy and Fleiss' kappa. V3 applies the same reporting practice to additional human studies. It introduces no repeated-run estimates, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds pretrained-to-fine-tuned MMFakeBench macro-F1 results of 44.41 to 52.37 for LLaVA and 27.96 to 58.66 for Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Table 6). New human findings include text/image standalone plausibility of 98.3%/91.7% and desire alignment of 92.5%/86.3%. Section 5.2 newly reports successful misleading image generation for all 200 cases despite guardrails. Claude-3.5-Sonnet's desire-inference results are removed. Retained detection, modality, hint, and image-generator table values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The GPT-4o/FLUX data-generation pipeline and implication-oriented and consistency-oriented inference prompts remain unchanged. V3 adds a limited training adaptation for transfer: full-parameter fine-tuning of two 7B VLMs using image-caption inputs and answer-only binary supervision (Appendix F.5).

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract and narrative, consistently emphasizes trustworthy news context, moves shortcut analyses into Section 4.3, and restructures Section 5 as Discussion. Limitations and ethics move into appendices; the existing appendices are reorganized, and an LLM usage statement is added. The author list also changes.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, substantially reflowing tables, figures, and prompt boxes. Figure 1 uses a replacement example; Figures 2 and 4 are redesigned to foreground reference context; Figure 3's labels are reformatted. V3 adds the transfer-results table, style-example table, and fine-tuning prompt figure, while relocating several retained displays.

R1.justification: The core literature comparison and creator-produced versus reader-inferred intent positioning remain. V3 omits the Radford et al. (2021) CLIP reference and adds limited positioning around broader MMD utility. NewsINT remains the same benchmark comparison despite its updated Wang citation.

T1.justification: The news-triplet formulations and desired-influence/execution-plan representation remain unchanged. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs, and v3 adds no mathematical derivation or substantive formal definition.

improvement.justification: V1 validates binary misleading labels but leaves realism and fidelity to the simulated desire and execution plan largely untested. V3 directly evaluates these central properties (Appendices E.2–E.3), substantially strengthening support for the benchmark's intent annotations. The documented external transfer experiment also supplies evidence of practical training utility. The unexplained removal of one desire-inference comparator reduces completeness, and single-run evaluation limits statistical assurance, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains in benchmark validation and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DECEPTIONDECODED and the same underlying research. Their text, tables, figures, prompts, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added studies in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds human realism and intent-alignment studies plus fine-tuning transfer results.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM evaluations, human verification, modality and prompting analyses, and an image-generator comparison.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: reference-based verification needs dedicated evaluation, VerifyBench-Hard exposes difficult cases, and benchmark performance can guide reasoning-model training. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds the interpretation that weak verifiers can degrade RL-trained models through biased reward assignment and inaccurate supervision; v1 emphasized better rejection-sampling outcomes with stronger verifiers. The five limitations remain substantively unchanged in Appendix A. Appendix C newly states that general reasoning includes commonsense subsets, conflicting with the retained domain limitation.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands reproducibility information: annotator qualifications, training, instructions and interfaces; benchmark-generation sampling settings; source-split handling; and detailed RL software, hyperparameters, hardware, evaluation, and smoothing procedures. It also adds code and project-page links. These disclosures accompany retention of the original rejection-sampling implementation details.

E1.justification: v3 adds AMC23 and MinervaMath as downstream evaluation datasets. The 41 benchmark-construction sources and the original GSM8K, MATH500, and SVAMP evaluations remain. Coverage expands within mathematical reasoning while the benchmark domains and answer types stay unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DeepSeek-V3-0324, DeepSeek-R1-0528, gpt-oss-20b, gpt-oss-120b, and seven dedicated verifiers across xVerify, Tencent-Qwen2.5-7B-RLVR, and CompassVerifier. This substantially broadens comparison beyond the original rule-based method and general LLM judges. Existing comparators, including Table 4's reward models, are retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds GRPO training of Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on DeepMath-103K, using four verifier conditions, 16 rollouts per query, and checkpoint evaluation every ten steps. Appendix H.1 specifies the new training and evaluation settings. The original rejection-sampling protocol is retained in H.2, rather than replaced.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds direct RL validation of whether verifier benchmark performance predicts downstream training outcomes, including deterioration under weaker verifiers. This substantially extends the original rejection-sampling correlation analysis. The reference-answer ablation and fine-grained error analysis remain unchanged; the taxonomy table redisplays existing categories.

E5.justification: Appendix H.1 newly specifies eight stochastic generations per test example for the RL evaluation. The retained rejection-sampling evaluation still averages sixteen generations, as in v1. This adds repeat-count information for the new experiment without establishing additional independent training runs; neither version reports training-seed uncertainty or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial verifier results and RL learning curves. Table 2's highest reported VerifyBench-Hard accuracy changes from 72.60% for GPT-4o in v1 to 87.90% for gpt-oss-120b and CompassVerifier-32B in v3 through added model entries. Shared table results and the original rejection-sampling curves remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction pipeline, answer categories, verification prompts, balancing procedure, and five-model disagreement filtering remain unchanged. The meta-annotator description expands the existing adjudication procedure. GRPO is introduced as an evaluation experiment rather than a proposed method component.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the section sequence remain intact. Section 5.2 is rewritten around RL, the original rejection-sampling discussion moves to Appendix H.2, and limitations move to Appendix A. Appendix organization, explanatory passages, terminology, and affiliation text receive localized revisions.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to predominantly single-column formatting, with extensive table and figure repositioning. v3 expands Table 2, adds annotation-interface screenshots and RL plots, and redisplays the taxonomy as Table 8. The original RFT plot becomes Figure 10, while existing examples receive larger, less abbreviated displays.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds substantive positioning against concurrent reference-based verification work, especially VerifierBench. It acknowledges similar construction and distinguishes VerifyBench through 41 versus 14 sources, finer annotation, disagreement-based hard-case selection, and reasoning-model outputs. Discussion of dedicated model-based verifiers also expands the earlier emphasis on preference and process reward systems.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the same reward mappings and accuracy definitions; changing Acc to Accuracy is not substantive. No new theoretical assumptions, theorems, or proofs are introduced. Table 8 restates the taxonomy already documented in v1's classification prompt.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's practical validation by adding direct GRPO experiments where v1 relied on rejection-sampling fine-tuning. Dedicated-verifier comparisons and detailed annotation and implementation documentation also address important evaluation and reproducibility gaps. The retained 72.4% maximum claim now conflicts sharply with Table 2's 87.90%, and some documentation remains inconsistent, but these defects do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VerifyBench research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds evaluations of further verifiers in Table 2 and direct reinforcement-learning experiments in Section 5.2 and Appendix H.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original verifier evaluations, reference-answer ablations, error analyses, and rejection-sampling fine-tuning results in Tables 2–5 and Figure 3.

C1.justification: v2 foregrounds the finding that models with MoE in every layer and no shared experts have the highest consistency. v3's abstract, contributions, and conclusion instead emphasize toy-model verification of local load-balance tradeoffs, coexistence with global balance, and expert-combination space. The domain-versus-vocabulary specialization and approximately two-times-cache recommendations remain.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies v2's speculation that dense components weaken routing: interleaved dense layers show little direct effect, and other factors may explain the earlier association. It adds shared-expert bypass and combination-space explanations, distinguishes local from global load balance, and suggests a pretraining-data explanation for domain patterns. Appendix F explicitly limits throughput implications because measured overhead correlations are weak and implementation factors also matter.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.2 documents toy architectures and training settings, including the eight-layer, 1,280-dimensional baseline, expert configurations, 10,000 steps, sequence length 4,096, batch size 1,024, and learning-rate schedule. Appendix F describes the LRU/on-demand implementation. Conversely, v2's disclosure of eight RTX 4090 GPUs and BF16 precision disappears. Evaluation-data preparation and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same 11-domain evaluation corpus is retained; changing '7' to '11' in Section 4.1 corrects the description rather than adding domains. v3 additionally uses a 20B-token sample of OLMoE pretraining data and evaluates actual offloading during prefilling and decoding in Appendix F.

E2.justification: v3 adds clairvoyant optimal replacement as the reference for the new Table 4 comparison of SCH, LRU, and LFU. Table 3 retains all three earlier comparator columns—LRU, LFU, and Fixed—even though v3's accompanying prose and caption describe only LRU and LFU.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled pretraining experiments across ten approximately 1.43B-parameter toy configurations, varying expert counts, activation counts, shared experts, dense-layer placement, and load-balancing loss. It also adds optimal-hit-rate normalization and separate prefilling/decoding overhead measurements against full-GPU inference. SCH's evaluation procedure changes, while the original 22,528 evaluation sequences of 512 tokens are retained.

E4.justification: Section 3.3 adds interventions testing which architectural and training factors affect consistency, and Appendix F tests its relationship to system overhead. v2's dedicated real-model perplexity and broader architecture analyses in Appendices E.2–E.3 are removed. Most earlier post-training, position, domain, layer, and expert analyses are retained under new numbering.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% SCH confidence intervals obtained from 1,000 bootstrap resamples and retain the deterministic-configuration statement. No changed repeated-run, seed, or uncertainty-estimation procedure is reported. Different confidence-interval values belong to the changed results.

E6.justification: v3 Table 2 adds toy-model SRPs, including Baseline 43.56, NoLB 56.42, and OverLB 36.42. SCH curves and Tables 7–8 change under the revised metric; for example, Table 7's correlation at m=16 and rho=2 changes from 98.49 to 94.87, without establishing a same-metric performance loss. Table 4 adds optimal-relative hit rates, and Appendix F reports SCH correlations with relative overhead of approximately +0.2 during prefilling and -0.3 during decoding. The earlier real-model perplexity plot is removed.

M1.justification: The computation of SCH, one of the two proposed measures, changes substantially. v2 optimizes an expert set held fixed throughout each segment; v3 simulates token-by-token loading and eviction, removing unused experts with the lowest activation frequency over the next m tokens. SRP's underlying optimization remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Section 2 replaces much of its mathematical exposition with explanatory prose and moves formal SRP material to Appendix C. Section 3.3 is extensively rewritten around the REAL/TOY distinction and individual factors. The headline narrative, appendix organization, and throughput discussion are substantially reworked.

P2.justification: v3 adds SRP/SCH illustrations, a toy-model scatterplot, expanded Table 2, and new Table 4. The main SRP and specialization plots change from horizontal four-panel displays to two-by-two arrangements. Earlier real-model perplexity and architecture-comparison displays are removed, while many retained appendix figures receive revised labels, captions, placement, and SCH curves.

R1.justification: The bibliography and Appendix B are unchanged. Positioning is modestly extended through comparison with clairvoyant optimal replacement and attribution of the expert-combination-space explanation to the already cited Muennighoff et al. (2025).

T1.justification: v2's fixed-segment SCH maximization and derivation in Equations 8–9 are replaced by a different operational definition, explicitly distinguished from clairvoyant optimal replacement. Appendix F adds an informal overhead argument under ideal-prefetching and memory assumptions. The SRP definitions and proofs are substantially preserved and relocated to Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2's architecture recommendations relied on comparisons among heterogeneous pretrained models. v3 substantially strengthens their evidential basis with controlled toy-model interventions and uses those results to qualify the dense-layer claim. Appendix F also tests the connection to system performance and acknowledges its weak correlations. These improve support and claim calibration despite reporting drawbacks, including removed hardware/precision details and Table 8 populating a SwitchTransformers decoder m=256 entry that its caption still calls invalid.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same local-routing-consistency study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated SRP definitions and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical analyses and adds pretrained toy-model experiments, optimal-cache comparisons, and measured offloading-overhead results in Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original routing analyses across 20 MoE models, cache-algorithm comparisons, and appendix results on specialization, post-training, and statistical uncertainty.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on introducing MEMENTO and diagnosing memory-utilization failures. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion additionally make a hierarchical user-profile memory architecture and its benefits on single- and joint-memory tasks central contributions, extending the paper from evaluation and diagnosis to a proposed solution.

C2.justification: v2 develops the rationale for separating personalized knowledge from episodic memory's in-context learning benefits. New interpretations concern retrieval improvements failing to ensure task success, navigation cues, and instruction cues supporting generalization. Appendix A also adds the absence of conversational clarification as a substantive limitation and expands privacy considerations.

D1.justification: v2 adds graph algorithms, node/edge schemas, construction and retrieval prompts, experimental configurations, explicit filtering criteria, complete trajectory/evaluation examples, and a code-access statement. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. Hardware and inference settings remain unchanged, while v1's separate asset-license and source-link appendix is omitted.

E1.justification: The original 12-scene, 438-episode benchmark and ambiguous-instruction tasks remain. v2 substantially extends tested scenarios to three-memory coordination, transferring user patterns to changed target locations, corrupted or incomplete memories, and retrieval without guaranteed relevant memories (Appendix E), while retaining the household simulation domain.

E2.justification: The six-model headline comparison and three memory-format alternatives are retained. v2 adds an evaluated human reference (Appendix E.1) and compares LLM pointwise reranking and query expansion against embedding-only retrieval for GPT-4o and Qwen-2.5-72b (Table 11), substantially expanding comparison approaches.

E3.justification: The main metrics, oracle skills, and top-5 retrieval with guaranteed relevant memories remain. New experiments introduce distinct protocols: four human participants on 20 tasks, reranking ten candidates into top-3/top-5 results, 30% unrelated-step injection, 20% step removal, and separate graph-memory retrieval without guaranteed gold entries (Appendices D.3 and E).

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled tests of shuffled, injected, and removed memory steps; retrieval quality versus task success; three-memory coordination; and transfer to new locations. It also expands execution-trace case studies. These substantially extend the retained top-k, memory-quality, summarization, and ambiguous-instruction analyses.

E5.justification: v2 adds inter-rater reliability estimation using Krippendorff's alpha, reporting four category values from 0.57 to 0.87 and an average of 0.69 (Appendix C.3.3). The five-attempt filtering procedure and existing 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged; no new seed counts or uncertainty estimates accompany agent-performance comparisons.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their scores, and v1's ambiguous-instruction results reappear in v2 Table 13. Substantial new results include user-profile memory gains in Figure 8 and robustness, retrieval, human, and transfer outcomes. Table 12 adds GPT-4o's 22.0% success rate on three-memory tasks; its retained two-memory result remains 63.9%, under different task requirements.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's environmental scene graph and episodic memory, v2 introduces a separate hierarchical user-profile knowledge graph. It extracts and updates personalized knowledge, represents temporal relationships, and retrieves and reformulates subgraphs alongside episodic memory (Section 6.2; Appendix D.1). This adds a substantial memory-processing component.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion around three research questions. It combines and reorganizes the task/framework exposition, separates evaluation from bottleneck analysis, restructures the discussion around memory design, and reorganizes the appendices, including moving the ambiguous-instruction experiment out of the main text.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the framework overview and case taxonomy, adds overall bars and delta annotations to retained performance displays, and introduces user-profile memory plots and diagrams, schema tables, new experimental tables, and detailed trajectory tables. Extensive relocation and a changed document template further alter the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The main related-work coverage and earlier extended discussion are largely retained. v2 adds targeted connections to ConceptNet/COMET, context engineering, long-context modeling, retrieval methods, and annotation reliability. It also clarifies the distinction between explicitly provided user knowledge and preferences inferred from demonstrations.
