The irreversible-unmasking explanation is retained and supported more systematically. v2's explicit discussion of untested complex applications and future adaptive tempering is removed.

D1.justification: v3 Appendix D.1 adds extensive training recipes: optimisers, learning rates, batch sizes, training budgets, GPU configurations, reward scaling, regularisation, LoRA and pretrained-model sources. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v2's toy architectures and sampling settings. However, v2's promised project-code link, explicit ESS/partial-resampling settings and detailed carry-over gradient construction are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates Gaussian mixtures and binarised MNIST. v3 retains these task families and adds prompted toxic-text generation, regulatory DNA design, class-conditional ImageNet256 generation, and text-to-image generation using HPDv2, DrawBench and animal prompts (Sections 4.2–4.4). Figure 1 also introduces a product-target toy scenario.

E2.justification: The corresponding MoG comparison drops v2's brute-force locally optimal oracle and adds learned-proposal variants; the base and gradient variants largely retain their identities under shorter names. v3 introduces BoN comparisons and DNA comparisons against CG, CFG, DRAKES and DRAKES without KL (Table 5). Those DNA baseline scores are attributed to Wang et al., rather than established as new reruns.

E3.justification: Reported reward-estimation sample counts change from 100 to 10 for MoG and from 1 to 10 for MNIST (v2 Section 4; v3 Table 3). Added protocols include 100-token text generation over 15 prompts with 20 generations each, and ImageNet FID/IS evaluation using 50,000 images with particle-count, denoising-step and CFG sweeps. These are changes to retained settings and newly introduced evaluation designs, respectively.

E4.justification: v3 adds temperature-schedule sweeps with an independent MNIST validation classifier and worst-run examples, reward-estimator sample-count sensitivity, proposal-training convergence curves, and particle/step/CFG analyses (Figures 7–11 and Tables 2, 6–10). ReMDM robustness receives more systematic testing. v2's MoG reward/ESS/resampling traces and UDLM experiment are no longer included.

E5.justification: v2 reports sample-set outcomes and trajectories without repeated-run uncertainty estimates. v3 reports means and standard deviations from 30 independent SMC runs per MNIST schedule (Appendix D.2.1), and means with standard deviations across three random seeds for DNA design (Table 5). This introduces substantial replication and uncertainty reporting; it does not establish increased repetition of the original v2 experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive language, DNA and image results and replaces retained toy outcomes. For example, first-order SMC MoG EMD changes from 1.72 in v2 Figure 1 to 2.36 in v3 Figure 2 under changed reward-estimation settings, so this is not a same-setting performance comparison. New Table 2 reports ImageNet FID 14.56 with 16 particles, eight steps and CFG 1.25. v3 Tables 1 and 4 disagree on eight-particle SMCamot perplexity, reporting 147.6 and 127.0 respectively.

M1.justification: v3 retains the first-order/Gumbel-Softmax proposal but adds an amortised proposal trained with a log-variance-based objective and an auxiliary mean network. It also introduces product-target/CFG weighting and a shared-position adaptation for low-confidence sampling (Section 3 and Appendix C.2). Appendix D.1 explicitly changes intermediate reward estimation from averaging rewards to log-mean-exp.

P1.justification: The title, introduction, background, method narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten, with contribution bullets and systematic base/grad/amot terminology. Related work moves from Appendix E into main Section 5, and the appendices are reorganised around proofs, sampling implementation and experimental details. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the addition of experiments.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes predominantly single-column. Toy comparison figures are rebuilt with additional panels, and training/sampling pseudocode appears in paired boxes. v3 adds numerical comparison tables, multi-panel scaling and sensitivity plots, training curves and extensive sample galleries, while removing v2's ESS figure. These are substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around large discrete models, amortised inference, log-variance training and inference-time scaling. Newly cited works include Richter et al. (2020), Richter and Berner (2023), and Dang et al. (2025). Section 5 identifies fixed-proposal SMC approaches as a central contrast, whereas v2 Appendix E emphasised guidance methods and its distinction from Lee et al.

T1.justification: v3 adds product-target importance-weight derivations, formal proofs for the existing locally optimal proposal, a uniqueness argument using chi-squared divergence, and a log-variance upper-bound proposition with its proof (Appendix A). Much of v2's continuous-time derivation survives in Appendix B and should not be counted as wholly new. Conversely, v2 Appendix D's carry-over gradient and finite-difference analysis is omitted.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2 Appendix G's central deficiency: effectiveness beyond small datasets and against broader comparators was untested. Multi-domain evaluations, controlled sensitivity studies, independent validation, uncertainty reporting and detailed training recipes now provide substantially stronger support for practical applicability and the learned proposal. The gains outweigh the loss of the carry-over gradient derivation and reporting defects, including conflicting toxicity entries in Tables 1 and 4, although those defects limit confidence in particular results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and complete enough for comparison, including figures, equations and appendices. Despite the changed title and expanded scope, the retained SMC framework, first-order proposal and toy experiments clearly establish continuity.

after.justification: v3 reports original synthetic, language, DNA and image-generation experiments in Section 4 and Appendix D. Table 5 explicitly attributes some baseline scores to prior work, but the proposed methods have original results.

before.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian-mixture and binarised-MNIST experiments, including reward, EMD, diversity, ESS traces and generated samples in Section 4 and Appendix F.

C1.justification: The central biased-counting claim remains, but v2's abstract and introduction add claims about background removal and a nonmonotonic relationship between reasoning length and accuracy. The conclusion adds claims about pointing-model advantages, inverse scaling, and human performance. These substantially broaden the paper's principal findings.

C2.justification: v1 leaves encoder failure versus language-model override as an open explanation; v2 attributes failures to language priors overriding encoded information and to background cues (Appendix A.8; Section 4.4). It adds explanations involving overconfidence and underused tools, plus pointing failures from crowding or localization. The earlier inability-to-test-tools limitation is replaced by analysis of observed tool limitations.

D1.justification: v2 expands model IDs, access platforms, and inference settings into Tables 21–23. It additionally documents LangSAM/SVG background processing, SigLIP feature pooling and logistic-regression probing, Puppeteer/data-export measurement of tool use, and the human-study procedure and interface. The existing code/data access link is retained.

E1.justification: The seven original domains are retained, but v2 adds background-removed or visually simplified test scenarios across those domains (Section 4.4). It also introduces human-participant evaluation of animal leg counting (Appendix A.19). The larger mammal dataset for probing expands sampling within existing animal coverage.

E2.justification: v2 retains the original five VLMs and adds GPT-5 and Grok-4, Pixtral and Qwen2.5-VL size variants, Molmo and Moondream pointing models, and tool-enabled o4-mini (Tables 12–17). New comparisons also include LLaVA-OneVision-S versus a SigLIP linear probe and random baseline, and human performance (Tables 8 and 20).

E3.justification: New protocols include a 5,598/300/696 train/validation/test split for probing, a 1152-pixel API-versus-ChatGPT tool comparison, and randomized human viewing conditions of 0.2–2 seconds with multiple-choice responses. v2 also adds few-shot conditions and pass@5/confidence metrics. Documented Adidas and Ebbinghaus prompts are revised, without establishing that the retained result tables were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds background ablation, encoder-versus-language probing, reasoning-length analysis, model-size comparisons, and resolution and generator-family checks (Sections 4.4–4.5; Appendices A.8, A.14, A.17–A.18). Few-shot, tool-use, pointing, and human analyses substantially deepen the investigation. Earlier text-injection and helpful-prompt analyses are retained in Appendices A.9–A.10.

E5.justification: Appendix A.11 newly reports five evaluation runs for o4-mini and Sonnet-3.7 across all tasks, with accuracies of 19.54 ± 0.68% and 16.23 ± 0.36% (Table 10). v1 has no equivalent evaluation-run uncertainty reporting. This addition is limited to two models, and the ± statistic is not explicitly identified.

E6.justification: The original Table 2 results retain their 17.05% mean accuracy. Added results include 38.14% after background removal, GPT-5's 30.72%, and 93.75% human counterfactual-animal accuracy at two seconds (Tables 4, 12, and 20). These are new comparisons or settings. Table 14 reports 23.18% to 25.08% for tool access, whereas Appendix A.15 inconsistently uses a 20.25% baseline.

M1.justification: The core counterfactual-generation framework and counting/identification design remain unchanged. Cropping, linear probing, few-shot prompting, and tool use are introduced as experimental interventions or comparisons, rather than changes to a proposed model architecture, objective, or core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main Results section is reorganized from eight subsections into five, with detailed domain results and text/prompt studies moved into Appendix A. The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Appendix ordering also changes extensively, including moving illustrative questions from Appendix A to Appendix M.

P2.justification: v2 adds reasoning and human-performance plots, study-interface screenshots, background comparisons, numerous experimental tables, and pointing/few-shot case figures. Existing displays are also revised: v1 Table 3 becomes a two-block Table 6, duplicated shoe-logo examples are consolidated, and Ebbinghaus illustrations are recolored. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v1's brief comparison with three nearby benchmarks becomes a broader treatment including ViLP and Appendix C's comparisons of bias sources, scale, and image generation. v2 acknowledges limited counting coverage in prior work and adds TallyQA, VALSE, BEAF, and reasoning, scaling, and pointing literature. This substantially expands research positioning beyond citation-format changes.

T1.justification: The image-scaling and patterned-grid mathematics are retained, with no new theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations. v2's explicit bias-rate explanation restates the measure already used in v1; the new empirical metrics and probing experiments do not introduce theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1's encoder-versus-language explanation and tool-use limitation were largely unresolved. v2's paired encoder/VLM probe, background interventions, human validation of animal images, and systematic tool comparison substantially strengthen benchmark validation and failure analysis. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including conflicting tool-gain numbers in Appendix A.15/Table 14 and incorrect success markers in Figures 32/34. Some broad causal claims still exceed what the controls establish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VLMBias study and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained tasks and results can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those evaluations and adds original background-removal, encoder-probing, tool-use, repeated-run, and human-study results (Tables 4, 8, 10, 14, and 20).

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of five VLMs across seven VLMBias domains, including counting, identification, and prompting experiments (Tables 2–5).

C1.justification: v1 presents the first nationwide general-purpose encoder spanning human and natural domains, with an approximately 35% advantage. v4 instead emphasizes human-centric functional representations, nine socio-economic tasks and a 12.9% advantage. It also newly claims, with qualification, the first empirical evidence of geospatial scaling laws, although the scaling experiment is retained.

C2.justification: v4 develops the interpretation of mobility as spatial syntax, explains the new anchor and graph controls, recommends a neighborhood-based alternative, and discusses geographically sparse task coverage. Appendix A.6 corrects the resolution interpretation: finer grids generally help, with crime as the exception, replacing v1's opposite generalization with population as the exception. The underlying resolution table is unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 adds downstream sample counts, discloses five-year crime aggregation followed by log(1 + count), and describes baseline adaptation and training/inference choices. Code-access directions change from a placeholder/anonymized address to the named MoRA GitHub repository. Core hardware, optimizer, training-time and distillation specifications remain unchanged; actual online availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v4 removes elevation and forest-coverage evaluation, narrowing the benchmark from 11 social, economic and natural tasks to nine social and economic tasks. Their distillation results and natural-domain ablation/sampling results are also removed. The pretraining modalities and Chinese geographical coverage are retained; Jiangsu was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v4 adds AlphaEarth to the nationwide comparison in Table 2 while retaining the six original baselines. New Table 3 evaluates HREP, ReCP and ReFound against MoRA in Jiangsu. These three methods were cited but not evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 revises demographic preprocessing from five-year age bands and gender to ten-year bands, gender and work-home status. Point-level evaluation changes from assigning grid embeddings to individual points to aggregating point values within grids. Added comparisons specify AlphaEarth pixel pooling and Jiangsu baseline training/inference procedures. The main split, training budget and prediction models remain unchanged; the revised descriptions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds comparisons of mobility, demographic, POI and image anchors; a mobility-versus-neighborhood graph control; and individual auxiliary-modality removals (Figure 3 and Table 6). These directly test the backbone and fusion choices beyond v1's component removals. Existing scaling, graph-sampling and grid-resolution studies are retained, while natural-domain ablation results disappear.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten repeated downstream runs and report means with standard deviations in Table 2. Neither introduces a different uncertainty-estimation practice, explicit seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Additional tables report point estimates, as supplementary tables already did in v1.

E6.justification: The nine retained proposed-model scores in Table 2 are unchanged, but new comparator results alter rankings: AlphaEarth scores 0.63 on nighttime lights versus MoRA's 0.62. v4 adds Jiangsu comparison and modality-ablation results and removes natural-task results. Scaling, grid-resolution and retained distillation numbers match v1. The headline 35% versus 12.9% advantages concern different task/comparator sets, not a same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: The LINE-initialized LightGCN, auxiliary encoders, contrastive objective and MLP distillation remain unchanged; the new 'asymmetric' terminology does not change the loss. v4 additionally evaluates and recommends a variant replacing mobility edges with direct cell-neighborhood edges (Sections 4.4–5).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and discussion are extensively rewritten around human-centric representation learning. The paper is renamed, the distillation discussion moves into evaluation, and appendices are reorganized. Dedicated ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements replace the NeurIPS checklist.

P2.justification: Figure 3 is redesigned from two panels to three, adding anchor comparisons and the neighborhood variant while dropping natural-task groups. v4 adds dataset-distribution maps and two tables, adds sample counts to Table 1, and removes natural-task and average columns from Table 2. Existing appendix tables are relocated and renumbered within the ICLR layout.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially reposition the paper around physical Earth-observation representations versus human-centric functional representations. v4 introduces AlphaEarth and citations to Brown et al., Cole et al. and Mac Aodha et al., and expands discussion of regional methods and PDFM. HREP, ReCP and ReFound are newly evaluated, rather than newly cited.

T1.justification: Equations 1–5 and the distillation objective retain the same mathematics. v4's LLM and spatial-syntax analogy supplies conceptual motivation, without adding formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for the central mobility-backbone claim by addressing v1's reliance on coordinate/image comparators and limited mechanism controls. Relevant regional baselines and direct anchor, neighborhood and modality tests make that claim more assessable; the narrower scope and corrected resolution interpretation also improve alignment with evidence. Removing natural-task results reduces documented breadth, and prose still overstates wins contradicted by Tables 3 and 6. These shortcomings temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mobility-based multimodal representation work, renamed from MobCLIP to MoRA. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines, anchor-choice and neighborhood-graph comparisons, and auxiliary-modality ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original downstream prediction results, scaling experiments, ablations, sampling and grid-resolution analyses, and distillation results.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the claimed validation from video quality and trajectory control to state-of-the-art robotic action planning. The introduction also promotes the previously documented 21k Bridge curation to an explicit dataset contribution. The central collaborative-trajectory and object-embedding claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets better interaction videos as enabling more reliable inverse-dynamics actions. Appendix B substantially expands the earlier brief limitations: 3D occlusion and annotation burden, segmentation failures requiring manual intervention, contributions of pretrained backbone priors, and unresolved generalization to unseen robot morphologies.

D1.justification: v3 documents robot-adaptation compute, the Cosmos model and fine-tuning recipe, and more explicit trajectory-annotation instructions with four transition cases. Appendix B newly discloses approximately 17,000 automatically acceptable masks plus 4,000 manual reannotations behind the retained 21k dataset; this is additional disclosure, not evidence that Bridge curation changed. The architecture table and project link remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds five RLBench and four SIMPLER simulated execution tasks involving Franka and Google Robot morphologies, plus evaluation with inaccurate subject prompts. Bridge and in-the-wild generation coverage remains; shortening Bridge V2 to Bridge and highlighting the existing 21k curated samples do not establish another dataset.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TesserAct while retaining IRASim, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, and Tora. The new action-planning comparison evaluates OpenVLA, TesserAct, and Tora, substantially extending comparison to executable policies and a 4D world model. The relocated VBench comparison retains its original comparator set.

E3.justification: New planning protocols specify fixed cameras, adaptation on 1,300 pairs excluding evaluated tasks, inverse-model training on 300 video-action samples per evaluated task, and 100 execution trials per task. v3 also introduces action-conditioned video checks including latent L2 and 10–40% prompt-replacement conditions. The existing Bridge evaluation and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds prompt-error sensitivity analysis (Table 8), validation of inferred actions through action-conditioned video generation (Table 3), and single-object versus multiple-object segmentation failure analysis (Appendix B, Table R11). Existing component, mask-sparsity, and trajectory-perturbation ablations retain their results.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across repeated runs or seeds. The new 100-episode planning evaluation specifies an evaluation sample count, rather than repeated-model-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds planning, action-validation, prompt-robustness, segmentation, and TesserAct results; TesserAct's Table 2 FVD is 261.84. Existing Bridge objective metrics, VBench scores, and earlier ablation values are unchanged. RoboMaster's preference changes from 47.33% to 45.16% with an expanded comparator set, so this is not a same-setting decline. Table 4 shows seven wins over Tora across nine tasks, contradicting the text's eight-of-ten statement.

M1.justification: The generator, collaborative trajectory representation, object embeddings, motion injector, and loss remain unchanged in Section 3. New Section 4.5 extends the downstream procedure with morphology adaptation and a trained inverse-dynamics component that converts generated videos into executable actions.

P1.justification: Parts of the abstract and introduction are rewritten, user-interaction explanations are condensed or clarified, and terminology and citation style change. References move before the appendices, VBench moves to Appendix D.1, and planning and limitations receive dedicated sections. Most existing method and experimental prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands and reorganizes displays with new action-validation, planning, prompt-robustness, annotation-case, and segmentation tables. Table 2 gains a row, and VBench moves from Table 3 to Table R12. Figure 5 removes the carrot comparison and reorders the box example; Figure S8 is redrawn. The ICLR layout separates references from retained supplementary figure pages.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused citations and discussion concerning TesserAct, Cosmos2.5, OpenVLA, RLBench, SIMPLER, MOFT, and LoRA, extending positioning toward policy extraction and morphology adaptation. Most existing trajectory-control, camera-control, and control-injection related work remains.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the mathematical definitions, conditional factorization, embedding equations, and loss. v2's motion-injection Equation 6 becomes inline mathematics in v3, renumbering the loss from Equation 7 to Equation 6. No substantive mathematical revision or new proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2's proposed utility for robot learning rested mainly on video-quality and control evaluations. v3 adds simulated task execution, action-validation checks, prompt robustness, and quantified annotation failures, substantially strengthening practical validation and transparency. The new evidence remains qualified by inverse-model training on evaluated tasks, absent uncertainty estimates, and the incorrect eight-of-ten summary of Table 4. These weaknesses limit the stronger claims but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RoboMaster research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite changes in formatting and section order.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds simulated robot execution, action-conditioned video validation, prompt robustness, and annotation-success measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original Bridge experiments, user preferences, component ablations, robustness tests, and qualitative generalization results.

C1.justification: v4 elevates memory-efficient adaptive optimization to a main contribution and adds an approximately 1.5-fold end-to-end speedup claim in the abstract. Its contribution narrative centers ALIAS, whereas v2 foregrounds SOS and ALIAS together. The underlying parameter-free, stochastic, distributed, and momentum claims remain.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly discusses ALIAS's full-gradient storage requirement, the memory variant's theoretical boundaries, and its accuracy tradeoff. Appendix A.1.2 explains how norm overestimation produces smaller steps and interprets initialization and noise sensitivity. Section 3 also adds a substantive justification for using convex theory to inform neural-network optimization.

D1.justification: v4 adds explicit stochastic pseudocode distinguishing the practical and theoretical options and documenting shared-sample gradient calculations. It replaces the anonymous code link with a named ALIAS repository link and revises the LLaMA compute description to four A100 GPUs and approximately 12 hours. Most previously reported training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 Appendix A.3 adds fastMRI reconstruction and OGBG molecular-property prediction, substantially extending the evaluated domains and tasks. C4 pre-training, TinyImageNet fine-tuning, and the four LIBSVM datasets remain; the convex and non-convex toy experiments move to Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: v4 Table 7 adds evaluated DoG, D-Adaptation with Adam, and MoMo with Adam to the LLaMA parameter-free comparisons, extending v2's comparison with Prodigy. The original language and vision comparator sets remain. Table 11 additionally compares against explicitly attributed baseline results for the new tasks.

E3.justification: v4 introduces a 350M LLaMA configuration, batch-size comparisons using 512, 256, 128, and 64 sequences, and an initial-value comparison using d0 = 1 and 0.001. New U-Net and GNN evaluations use SSIM and mAP. The existing 130M training setup and 50-epoch Swin protocol are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds exact-versus-approximated norm ablations for the memory-efficient variant, initialization sensitivity, and batch-size experiments intended to test gradient-noise robustness. These investigate substantial new questions beyond v2's stepsize dynamics and L-infinity sensitivity analysis, which remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experiments. The shaded region in v4 Figure 3 displays the gap between exact and approximated norms, without introducing repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original 130M results in Tables 1–2 and Swin accuracies remain unchanged. v4 adds memory-variant, robustness, and additional-baseline results, plus a 350M ALIAS Adam loss of 2.707 and MRI/MPP scores of 0.724 SSIM and 0.242 mAP. Table 11 reports AdamW at 0.254 mAP, so the new findings do not establish superiority over AdamW on both tasks.

M1.justification: v4 Section 3.3 introduces a memory-efficient ALIAS variant absent from v2. It exchanges the norms in the local smoothness estimator and approximates gradient differences using coordinate extrema, retaining previous gradient signs and two scalars instead of the full previous gradient. The existing SOS, ALIAS, and momentum approaches remain.

P1.justification: v4 shortens the title, extensively rewrites the abstract and introductory narrative, and reorganizes the presentation around ALIAS. SOS and its toy experiments move to Appendix B, while the experimental appendix gains a clearer study-by-study structure. A conclusion and additional explanatory passages are added.

P2.justification: v4 replaces v2's pervasive boxed presentation with a conference layout, places Tables 1–2 side by side, and moves the retained LLaMA training curves into the main text. It adds norm-approximation and 350M figures and several new tables, revises highlighting and captions, and relocates the toy plots. Table 1 also corrects the first baseline label to match the already-described constant learning rate.

R1.justification: v4 makes focused additions covering recent Sign-SGD momentum, heavy-tailed-noise and privacy research, convexity-related neural-network work, and MoMo/AlgoPerf. It removes several broad LLM-background references. The central positioning around unknown stepsize quantities and much of the parameter-free optimization review remain.

T1.justification: v4 adds L1-smoothness Assumption 3.11, Theorem 3.12, and Appendix F.4's descent lemma and convergence proof for the norm-modified ALIAS variant, including dimension-dependent bounds. Existing SOS, ALIAS, and steepest-descent analyses are substantially retained. The new guarantee explicitly covers the exact norm formulation, not its practical extrema approximation.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v2's tension between its memory-efficiency motivation and ALIAS's full-gradient storage: the new variant reports 0.41 GB versus 1.22 GB, with validation loss increasing modestly from 3.006 to 3.019. Broader parameter-free comparisons, larger-model and cross-domain evaluations, and targeted ablations materially strengthen validation. These gains outweigh the accuracy tradeoff, although the practical approximation remains outside the proved guarantee and the new 1.5-fold speedup claim lacks a corresponding end-to-end timing comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same parameter-free Sign-SGD research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching SOS and toy experiments across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains these results and reports additional memory-variant, robustness, 350M LLaMA, MRI reconstruction, and molecular-property experiments. Appendix A.3 distinguishes its original ALIAS results from externally attributed baseline scores.

before.justification: v2 reports original LIBSVM experiments, 130M LLaMA pre-training results on C4, and Swin fine-tuning results on TinyImageNet.

C1.justification: The central GSI contribution remains intact. v2 explicitly claims priority as the first test-time scaling method with guarantees to the optimal tilted distribution and extends its superiority claims to SPECS. Expected-reward approximation is promoted into the abstract but was already claimed in v1; its theorem now carries additional assumptions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of how beta balances reward and likelihood, why threshold choice depends on n, and how tilted rewards can reject correct reasoning or miss errors. It also discusses weak STEM generations, selection of short illustrative traces, runtime sensitivity to batching, and the limited comparability of SPECS scores.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the double-newline step delimiter, dataset subset sizes, full-batch timing, additional A100/H200 usage, software libraries, and RewardHub/prm800k answer grading. These refine reproducibility information. Model identities, principal decoding settings, H100 timing hardware, and the public code URL were already disclosed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluations on GSM8K and MMLU-STEM while retaining MATH500, OlympiadBench, and Minerva Math. This broadens coverage to grade-school word problems and STEM multiple-choice questions, including biology examples in Appendix B.5.

E2.justification: The main implemented baselines remain RSD and small/base-model S-BoN. v2 Figure 2 adds RSD and small-model S-BoN to the corresponding scaling/rejection comparison. Section 5.1 also introduces a quantitative SPECS comparison using published scores, explicitly without running SPECS and with different evaluation subsets.

E3.justification: Appendices B.2–B.3 add systematic MATH500 protocols sweeping beta from 0 to 1000 and rejection thresholds from 0.05 to 1.5 across n=1,4,16,64,256, including accuracy–latency and Pareto comparisons. The default models and decoding hyperparameters remain unchanged. v2's newly specified subset sizes do not establish that v1 used different subsets.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the rejection-step ablation, v2 adds acceptance-rate scaling, beta and threshold sensitivity studies, and a threshold Pareto analysis. Section 5.2 and Appendix B.5 introduce paired GSI/RSD reasoning cases examining error correction, rejection of correct steps, and failures where GSI loses or both methods fail.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages over two random seeds without confidence intervals. v2 reports three seeds and introduces 95% confidence intervals in accuracy and runtime tables and several figures. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, although the interval-construction procedure is not specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds benchmark, sensitivity, and case-study results and revises existing estimates. In Table 1, Minerva accuracy at n=16 changes from 29.6% to 28.2% for GSI and from 36.0% to 33.6% for target S-BoN. Runtime averages also change, but aggregate five rather than three datasets; these replacements do not establish same-setting speedups.

M1.justification: Both versions use draft sampling, reward-plus-log-likelihood weighting, soft selection, threshold rejection, and target-model S-BoN fallback. Algorithm 1 in v2 clarifies history conditioning and sample indices; the PDFs do not establish a new method component or changed inference procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and contribution narrative, separates related work from background, expands reward-model and method explanations, and reorganizes the appendices. New experiment subsections and a contents page improve navigation; the changes extend beyond inserting additional scientific results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with colored components and explicit acceptance/fallback branches. Figure 2 becomes a six-panel display with additional comparators and uncertainty bands. Tables are reorganized by n, and v2 adds sensitivity plots, a Pareto figure, an extended runtime table, and colored reasoning-trace boxes marking rejected steps.

R1.justification: v2 expands research positioning through a dedicated related-work discussion of parallel versus sequential scaling and a substantive comparison with concurrent SPECS, including contrasting theoretical assumptions. It also adds relevant work on self-consistency, introspection, data-constrained scaling, and smoothed best-of-n analysis.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 retains its substantive bound. For Theorem 2, v2 Appendix A.2 introduces Assumption 2 concerning golden rewards on the acceptance set and the target distribution's probability of that set. It revises the rejection-mixture decomposition, adds a third proof term and bounding argument, and adds an asymptotic remark relaxing one condition. These materially revise v1 Appendix B's reward guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's sparse empirical validation through broader task coverage, uncertainty reporting, parameter sensitivity and latency analyses, and concrete success and failure traces. These additions make the method's tradeoffs and limitations much easier to assess. The revised theorem states additional assumptions explicitly. Although the stronger SPECS superiority claim remains limited by unmatched evaluation subsets, the empirical and explanatory gains provide a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GSI research, with matching authors, core algorithm, models, and original benchmarks. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching the relocated proofs and code disclosure.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on five benchmarks, runtime measurements, parameter sweeps, and reasoning-trace analyses in Section 5 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original accuracy experiments on three reasoning benchmarks, runtime and acceptance measurements, and a rejection-step ablation in Tables 1–2 and Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements extend the empirical claim across model families and sizes, and the abstract adds up to 28% lower end-to-end latency. The novelty claim narrows from the first test-time scaling method with the stated distributional guarantee to the first speculative test-time scaling method. The central algorithmic and convergence claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 explains larger Qwen3 gains through the draft–target quality gap, identifies PRM cost as a latency bottleneck, and discusses hyperparameter transfer. It adds a practical coverage argument and cautions against using Theorem 1's loose bound for tuning. The earlier OlympiadBench-specific explanation for RSD's advantage is dropped; existing reasoning-failure discussions remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix B supplies consequential reproduction details absent from v2: dataset-specific system prompts, 512-token step limits, an 8192-token context limit, the below-0.1 reward stopping rule, and 45/100-step limits for Qwen2.5/Qwen3. Section 5 clarifies that PRM verification and target likelihood computation are not parallelized. These are newly documented details; code access and supporting libraries are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MATH500, OlympiadBench, Minerva Math, MMLU-STEM, and GSM8K with the same task coverage. Qwen3 configurations and the additional MATH500 divergence analysis introduce no new dataset, domain, or task requirements.

E2.justification: Both evaluate RSD, small-model S-BoN, and target-model S-BoN, and retain rejection-free GSI comparisons. SPECS remains an indirect comparison to published results. Newly discussed EAGLE methods are explicitly not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 adds Qwen3-1.7B/14B with thinking disabled, a 100-step generation limit, A100 timing experiments, and divergence estimation using 50 MATH500 problems with 64 drafts per step. It adds throughput and component-level timing measurements. Figure 7 also labels retained beta-ablation timings as H200, revising v2's statement that all runtime experiments used H100 without establishing that they were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 extends rejection and acceptance analyses and beta sensitivity experiments to Qwen3. It adds an empirical check of draft–target divergence underlying Theorem 1 (Appendix C.5, Table 4) and a runtime breakdown identifying model costs (Figure 4). The original threshold ablations and reasoning case studies are retained.

E5.justification: The existing three-seed, 95% confidence-interval practice is retained. Appendix C.5 adds a Monte Carlo divergence-estimation procedure, with means, plus/minus quantities, and maxima in Table 4. The meaning of those new plus/minus quantities is unspecified; no increase in repeated-run counts is established.

E6.justification: The original Qwen2.5 accuracy tables and ablation plots are retained. Substantial Qwen3 results are added: at n=16, Table 3 reports average accuracies of 66.9% for GSI, 60.9% for RSD, and 69.4% for target S-BoN; Table 1 reports respective GSI and target latencies of 1.21 and 1.82 seconds per step. These are new configurations, not same-setting improvements over v2. Divergence estimates and runtime-component results are also new.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same likelihood-adjusted rewards, soft best-of-n selection, acceptance threshold, and target-model fallback. Added explanations and newly disclosed generation constraints do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable, with localized explanatory additions and revised experimental discussion. v3 introduces an implementation appendix and additional experimental subsections, moves detailed accuracy reporting into the appendix, and updates author, acknowledgment, and conference-header text.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout and substantially reorganizes empirical displays. Figure 2 gains Qwen3 panels, acceptance and beta plots expand, and new runtime-breakdown and divergence displays appear. Runtime tables gain model-family and throughput columns, while v2's main accuracy table moves to Appendix C. The workflow figure and original reasoning examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, speculative-decoding scaling laws, and the Qwen model reports. A new passage uses batching limitations to justify excluding conventional speculative-decoding comparisons, and the novelty claim is narrowed to speculative methods. The existing related-work discussion and positioning against RSD and SPECS largely remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 substantively revises a central guarantee: Theorem 2's rejection-dependent factor changes from (1-p(u)) to (1-p(u))^(1/4), with a rewritten indicator-based derivation replacing the earlier independence argument. Associated algebra and the asymptotic remark are revised, and Section 3 restricts golden rewards to nonnegative values. Theorem 1 and the claimed O(1/sqrt(n)) rate remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence beyond v2's single model pair through Qwen3 evaluations and runtime profiling, while Appendix B fills important gaps in prompts and stopping conditions. Appendix A.2 improves the finite-n derivation using a weaker rejection-dependent bound, and Appendix C.5 clarifies limits on its practical use. These gains materially improve empirical support, transparency, and reproducibility despite retaining the original method and benchmark coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GSI research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite reformatting and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original Qwen3 evaluations, runtime profiling, and empirical divergence estimates in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark accuracies, runtime measurements, ablations, acceptance-rate analyses, and generated reasoning traces in Section 5 and Appendix B.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains sharing online features with frozen linear heads and learning successive Bellman updates to improve target-free sample efficiency while retaining a low Q-network memory footprint. The broader evaluations support this retained claim rather than redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a policy-churn analogy and interprets target-churn measurements as evidence of greater target stability. Its new limitations discussion addresses setting-dependent head counts, replay-buffer and optimizer memory, unchanged inference memory, and generally unchanged computation. Continuous control moves beyond v1's future-work status; pruning and quantization become proposed future directions.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D add DMC and Wordle setup and hyperparameter details, timing hardware and tasks, normalization placement and batching, IMPALA layer sizes, and the previously unspecified Atari CQL weight of 0.1. These disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments. The reproducibility statement additionally says supplementary code contains versioned dependencies; public release remains conditional on acceptance.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained online and offline Atari coverage, v2 evaluates seven DMC Hard continuous-control tasks and offline Wordle using the Wordle Twitter dataset. These introduce continuous actions and language-based, multi-turn decision making.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator families expand from DQN/CQL to target-based and target-free SAC with SimbaV2, and target-based and target-free ILQL (Figures 6–7). The Atari comparator sets, including ES-CQL, are retained. Figure 19 additionally compares TB-SAC with and without BatchNorm.

E3.justification: New protocols include distributional SAC with soft target updates, 500,000 training steps and action repeat 2, and GPT-2-small ILQL with 800,000 gradient steps (Tables 2–3). SAC uses BatchNorm for TF-SAC and iS-SAC but excludes it from TB-SAC. v2 also specifies cumulative, periodically reset, TF-normalized target-churn measurement. Existing Atari settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds target-churn analysis to test target stability (Figure 8), DMC representation-rank and dormant-neuron analyses plus a BatchNorm control (Figure 19), and runtime/FLOP comparisons (Appendix B). Earlier head-count, normalization, gradient-similarity, and ensemble analyses remain; the offline effective-rank analysis is relocated.

E5.justification: v2 specifies ten seeds per DMC task and five for Wordle. Five Atari seeds, IQM aggregation, and 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals are retained. This adds experiment-specific run information without establishing increased runs for existing Atari experiments.

E6.justification: Headline Atari AUC findings remain, including the 6% CNN-LayerNorm advantage and CQL gap reduction from 26% to 6%, although some plotted estimates, including cosine similarities, change. New results report DMC gap recovery with iS-SAC K=1 and 49% fewer total model parameters, and over 5% higher normalized Wordle AUC with iS-ILQL K=9 and 33% fewer parameters. Target-churn and runtime/FLOP results are also added.

M1.justification: The shared-feature architecture, frozen first head, Equation 1, and DQN pseudocode remain intact. New adaptations include discounting successive SAC losses by 0.25, corresponding aggregation of critic predictions in the policy loss, and averaging ILQL advantage weights across heads (Section 5.3 and Appendix C).

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the title shortened, and the author list updated. Existing explanations receive local refinements, while algorithmic appendix notes are regrouped and reproducibility and language-model-use statements are added. Most original prose and the main narrative sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds continuous-control, Wordle, computational-cost, and DMC diagnostic figures plus two hyperparameter tables. It recomposes the mechanism figure, relocates offline effective rank, reorganizes the CQL learning-curve grid, and adds memory annotations. Formatting and captions change throughout; Figure 15 introduces a TB-DQN caption label inconsistent with its retained TF-DQN plot.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting SAC, ILQL, Wordle, DMC, policy churn, and critic/actor sizing. It also refines its positioning against i-QN: v1 describes storing 2K networks, whereas v2 acknowledges shared online representations while identifying retained target copies as the memory burden. The main target-free literature survey remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Section 5.5 introduces target churn as the absolute difference between regression targets before and after a batch update, with cumulative reset and normalization rules. This adds a defined mathematical quantity. Existing Bellman relations and Equation 1 remain; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was restricted to Atari, left continuous control for future work, and asserted comparable training time without reporting timing measurements. v2 adds distinct continuous-control and language evaluations, directly measures target stability, and benchmarks runtime and FLOPs. These address substantive gaps in applicability and support for the resource-efficiency argument. Expanded implementation details and explicit memory/computation limitations further improve assessability. Minor new caption and cross-reference errors do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iS-QN research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original Atari results and adds original continuous-control, Wordle, target-stability, and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v1 reports original online and offline Atari experiments, head-count and normalization ablations, and gradient and representation analyses.

C1.justification: The central claims about improving target-free sample efficiency while retaining a low parameter footprint remain unchanged. The conclusion replaces the prospective pruning/quantization direction with mixed-precision training and adds a limited claim of positive pilot evidence for that combination.

C2.justification: The original target-churn, gradient-similarity, and representation explanations remain. v3 adds an explanation for large-head-count instability in streaming, interprets learned near-equal weights as support for uniform weighting, and recommends increasing K until performance decreases. Appendix B also qualifies how simulated runtime relates to real-world interaction time.

D1.justification: v3 replaces promised public code release with an explicit repository address and adds substantial implementation information for the new studies, including streaming initialization, optimizer and trace settings, MellowMax temperatures, and reduced-precision operations. It also explains Wordle budget selection and clarifies that all SAC variants use l2 normalization. Repository availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: Section 5.5 adds streaming evaluation on seven Atari games without replay buffers, batch updates, or parallel environments, substantially extending the tested learning conditions. Appendix D.1 also adds Seaquest through the MellowMax experiment. The original Atari, DMC Hard, and Wordle coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 adds TF-Stream Q(lambda) as the comparator for the new streaming evaluation and explicitly evaluates TB-Mellow and TF-Mellow against iS-Mellow in Figure 12. MellowMax was previously only discussed in related work. The original DQN, CQL/ES-CQL, SAC, and ILQL comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include streaming with NOOP starts, life-loss termination, and T=10, plus 40-million-frame appendix experiments varying update periods, feature widths, and numerical precision. Table 2 revises the reported final DMC learning rate from 3e-4 to 1e-5; Table 3 changes Wordle training from 800,000 to 600,000 gradient steps. The retained plots do not establish that these experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds direct tests of target-update sensitivity on Tutankham, the interaction between head count and feature width on two games, learned versus fixed Bellman-loss weighting on three games, and float16 versus float32 training on four games. These substantially extend v2's existing head-count, normalization, and representation analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify IQM aggregation, 95% stratified bootstrap confidence intervals, five seeds per Atari game, ten per DMC Hard task, and five for Wordle. v3 adds results without reporting a changed uncertainty-estimation practice or increased run counts.

E6.justification: Existing result plots are unchanged, but v3 adds substantial findings: improved streaming AUC, reduced MellowMax performance gaps, update-period and width sensitivity results, meta-weighting performing on par with fixed K=9, and retained relative advantages under reduced precision. Figure 8 attributes the streaming gain above 10% to K=3, although its learning-curve legend says K=4, leaving that configuration ambiguous.

M1.justification: The core shared-feature architecture, Equation 1, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. However, Appendix D.4 introduces Meta iS-DQN, which learns softmax-parameterized weights for individual Bellman losses through an additional meta-gradient optimization procedure. This is a substantive method extension beyond v2's fixed equal or discounted weighting.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. v3 inserts a streaming subsection and an Additional Experiments appendix, shifts subsequent numbering, and adds acknowledgments and carbon-impact sections. Local wording, author-name spelling, affiliations, and explanatory references are refined without extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds six multipanel figures covering streaming, MellowMax, update-period sensitivity, head-count/width sensitivity, learned coefficient trajectories, and precision comparisons. The 20 original figures retain their plot content, with later figures renumbered. Existing table structures remain, alongside conference headers and limited caption changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations supporting streaming RL, hybrid online/target estimates, meta-gradients, mixed precision, code provenance, and carbon accounting. The main positioning relative to target-free regularization and iterated Q-learning is retained. The Schneider citation's venue/year update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Appendix D.4 adds a bilevel optimization formulation and Equations 2–7 deriving the loss-weight meta-gradient through head-specific and shared parameters. The derivation assumes dependence through one update and uses SGD for simplification. This substantial mathematical addition is absent from v2; it does not establish a general convergence guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 conjectured how feature richness affects useful head counts and largely deferred alternative loss weighting. v3 directly investigates these questions, tests target-update sensitivity, and adds a replay-free evaluation closely relevant to resource constraints. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support, while code-access information and corrected Wordle budget documentation improve reproducibility. The small game subsets and Figure 8's K=3/K=4 labeling inconsistency limit some conclusions but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iS-QN research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison. All 20 original figures have matching plot content in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds streaming RL experiments, hyperparameter studies, meta-gradient weighting results, and a mixed-precision pilot.

before.justification: v2 reports original Atari, DMC Hard, and Wordle experiments, including learning curves, resource measurements, and analyses of learning dynamics.

C1.justification: The central claims about decoupled perception, reasoning-reward optimization, and retraining-free reasoner upgrades persist. v2 moderates the abstract and conclusion from state-of-the-art performance claims to significant accuracy gains. Inference-time scaling receives greater emphasis, but that capability was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of caption reward hacking, why query-relevant captions optimize better despite weaker initial performance, and small-model reasoning forgetting. Appendix H expands the earlier domain-extension limitation into concrete qualifications about required adaptations, general evaluations excluding the reasoner, automatic thinking-mode selection, and the frozen reasoning LLM.

D1.justification: v2 provides substantially richer training and checkpoint-selection documentation, including evaluation every 50 steps and selection by average benchmark accuracy. It adds the caption-checking prompt, penalty coefficient, training-token estimates, and compute-estimation procedures. These disclosures exceed v1's basic hyperparameters and prompts. The reported code-access link changes from RACRO2 to RAPID.

E1.justification: ViRL39K and the seven main reasoning benchmarks remain. v2 adds general vision-language evaluations on MME, MMBench-v1.1, MM-Vet, SEED-Image, MMStar, RealWorld-QA, MMT-Bench, and BLINK, extending coverage to general recognition, OCR, and perception tasks. These evaluations test the optimized perception model with the external reasoner disabled.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated comparators including ECSO, OmniCaptioner, ReVisual-R1, Gemma-3, and Ovis2, while removing VisualPRM best-of-eight comparisons and several earlier rows, including o1 and OpenVLThinker. Appendix D adds Keye-VL-8B and InternVL3.5-8B comparisons. The reward-reasoner ablation replaces R1-Distilled-1.5B with Qwen3-8B.

E3.justification: The main benchmark splits and metrics remain, but GRPO changes from symmetric 0.2 clipping with KL coefficient 0.001 to asymmetric 0.2/0.25 clipping without KL. v2 adds 72B configurations and changes default ablation inference from R1-7B to Qwen3-8B. New protocols include non-thinking general evaluation, compute estimation using 100 examples per dataset, and four human ratings per caption pair instead of one.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analyses of holistic versus query-relevant captions, caption-penalty effectiveness and reward hacking, sequential training and reasoning forgetting, and training/inference compute tradeoffs. Component ablations are redesigned in Tables 2 and 7. The lengthy caption and reasoning case studies from v1 Tables 7–19 are retained as v2 Tables 9–21.

E5.justification: v2 adds aggregation of four annotators' decisions and an inter-annotator agreement estimate, supplementing the existing GPT-human agreement measure (Appendix E.3). This is a localized expansion of reliability reporting; handling of 2–2 voting ties remains unspecified. Neither version reports seed-based benchmark uncertainty or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Table 1 reports 47.4% for v1's CRO-only 7B/Qwen3-8B configuration and 53.2% for v2's revised GRPO/VPO configuration; these use different training procedures. v2 adds a 72B/GPT-OSS result of 58.0%. Human win/tie/loss rates change from 60/29/11% to 62/32/6% under the revised annotation design.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming CRO to VPO, v2 adds a model-judged caption-validity penalty to the correctness reward (Equation 3). It incorporates sequential GRPO/VPO optimization into the main method and adds a GRPO recovery stage for the 3B model. GRPO combinations already appeared in v1, but its main results used CRO alone.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and method narrative are extensively rewritten, with RAPID/VPO terminology replacing RACRO/CRO. Generalization and caption evaluation become separate subsections. The appendices gain a contents list and substantial reorganization; the earlier broader-impact and future-work sections disappear, and an LLM-writing disclosure is added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is enlarged and rescaled, and the earlier hallucination illustration is replaced by a quantitative perception-strategy comparison. Main tables are restructured, with new general-benchmark, reward-hacking, training, and compute plots. Reward and caption-length plots are separated and expanded. Existing case tables are retained and reflowed within a different document layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 gains a dedicated caption-then-reason discussion, adding earlier pipelines such as those of Tiong, Guo, and Hu. Existing ECSO and OmniCaptioner citations receive substantive treatment. v2 acknowledges prior query-aware captioning and positions its distinction around tentative solutions and outcome-based optimization, revising v1's positioning around query-conditioned, reasoning-aligned representations.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the formal caption-penalty reward definition in Equation 3 and changes the VPO objective to separate lower and upper clipping parameters. The underlying GRPO formulation is retained, and neither version develops additional theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct caption-then-reason comparisons, diagnosis and mitigation of reward hacking, and explicit compute and general-ability analyses (Table 1, Figure 7, Appendices D–E). Fuller implementation details and applicability limitations substantially strengthen the paper's evidential support and transparency. Removing the VisualPRM comparison and introducing inconsistencies in training-order and ablation descriptions temper these gains, but do not outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from RACRO to RAPID, with shared authors, training data, reasoning benchmarks, and retained appendix examples. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original RAPID experiments, including revised ablations, general vision-language evaluations, compute analyses, and human caption assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, component and reward-computation ablations, training analyses, and automated and human caption evaluations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contribution statements retain the same claims about globally interpretable coefficients, per-instance corrections, parameter-elimination optimization, and competitive prediction. The conclusion's self-interaction caveat is expanded elsewhere rather than abandoned.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 replaces the inference that differing coefficients demonstrate nonlinear interactions with an explanation involving correlated predictors and unstable feature selection. Section 3.2 adds qualifications about MEM's applicability, while Section 4.4 and D.6 substantially develop the architectural self-interaction limitation and feature-engineering remedy. D.7 also interprets local SHAP agreement and disagreements.

D1.justification: V3 revises the NN dropout specification and supplies the quadratic data generator, explicit nine-feature polynomial expansion, PMLB size thresholds, and a grid-search statement. Existing implementation, hardware, and repository-access information is retained; detailed PMLB tuning grids and experiment-specific split information are not supplied.

E1.justification: V3 adds ten PMLB regression datasets, including 197_cpu_act, 503_wind, and 225_puma8NH (Appendix D.10). It also introduces a purely quadratic self-interaction scenario outside the original synthetic model structure (D.6), while retaining the previous datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: Corresponding original predictive and SHAP-ranking comparisons retain their comparator membership. The added experiments reuse Lasso, LassoNet, NN, and SHAP. NODE-GAM and Interpretable Mixture of Experts are added to related work but are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Appendix D.1 changes the stated NN dropout for superconductivity from 0.6 to 0.1. New protocols include original versus polynomial-expanded inputs, a group-penalty control, local-contribution comparisons, and a mean nonlinear-correction diagnostic. D.10 introduces PMLB size filtering and grid-search tuning; these are additional evaluations rather than revisions to all retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained masking and positional-encoding ablations, D.6–D.9 add a self-interaction failure-and-remedy study, local contributions compared with synthetic ground truth and Boston SHAP values, a diabetes/Boston nonlinearity comparison, and an ablation testing the first-layer group penalty.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the 9/9/5 seed counts in Section 4.2 and the five-run description with cross-split error bars and confidence intervals in D.4. V3 specifies no increased repeat count, significance test, or revised uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and most original results are retained, but Figures 5 and 13 replace the NN superconductivity results, shifting plotted errors from roughly 0.15 to around 0.10 alongside the dropout revision. New Table 4 reports NIMO values of 5.340 and 1.009 before and after basis expansion, versus LassoNet's 1.027 and 1.012. Figures 17–22 add substantial diagnostic and benchmark findings.

M1.justification: NIMO's masked correction networks, shared positional encoding, sparsity mechanisms, and parameter-elimination training remain unchanged. The new basis-expansion experiments apply preprocessing to the existing model.

P1.justification: Most original prose and section ordering are retained. Changes concentrate on the hybrid-model discussion, result interpretation, a dedicated limitations subsection, and new appendix subsections D.6–D.10. Author emails and the conference-publication header are also added.

P2.justification: V3 adds Table 4 and Figures 17–22, introducing original-versus-expanded-feature displays, local-explanation scatter plots, nonlinearity and penalty analyses, and a PMLB comparison chart. Existing displays are retained with some relocation and reflow, and Figure 14's caption explicitly identifies the coefficients as MEMs.

R1.justification: Related work adds NODE-GAM and Interpretable Mixture of Experts, contrasting their interpretations with NIMO's global coefficients. New citations also support the MEM limitations discussion and PMLB benchmark. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: V3 introduces the explicit nonlinearity diagnostic n_j(x) = |1 + g_uj(x_-j)| in Equation 51. The adaptive-ridge equivalence proof, parameter-elimination derivations, IRLS extension, and sub-l1 mathematics in Appendices A–B remain unchanged apart from renumbering.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence about NIMO's applicability: the previously brief self-interaction caveat becomes a demonstrated failure case with a tested remedy, while local-explanation checks and the group-penalty ablation support important design claims. Broader PMLB evaluation and the more cautious interpretation of correlated features improve credibility. New benchmark protocols remain incompletely documented, but the gains in validation and clarity about limitations are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NIMO and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably across pagination changes.

after.justification: V3 retains these empirical results and adds self-interaction experiments, local-explanation analyses, a group-penalty ablation, and PMLB benchmark results.

before.justification: V2 reports original synthetic regression and classification experiments, evaluations on diabetes, Boston housing, and superconductivity, and masking and positional-encoding ablations.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds variational forecasting and claims state-of-the-art extrapolation on two synthetic benchmarks. v2 centers smoothness-prior modeling, explicitly claims benefits from regularizing both latent and decoded trajectories, and extends its state-of-the-art claim to real-world HyperNeRF. Its abstract and contribution list also replace the earlier gain summaries with aggregate percentage claims.

C2.justification: v1 motivates variational inference through uncertain futures and the shortcomings of deterministic averaging. v2 instead attributes poor variational NVFi results to sampling/KL optimization difficulties and underfitting. Section 5 adds substantive limitations involving interpolation-error propagation, fast small objects, abrupt dynamics, and unforeseeable behavior. Appendix B.2 qualifies cross-scene generalization as preliminary and generally weaker than per-scene training.

D1.justification: v2 adds sinusoidal positional-encoding disclosure, explicit trajectory-sampling formulas, a 40,000-iteration interpolation schedule, and temperature, EMA, and adaptive-regularization settings. Most architecture, solver, tolerance, and hardware details are retained and moved to Appendix B.1. Conversely, v1's variational noise scale and KL-annealing schedule are no longer specified for the retained variational comparison.

E1.justification: v2 expands synthetic-only evaluation to six real-world HyperNeRF scenes and adds fallingball to the NVFi evaluation. Appendix B.2 introduces a distinct transfer scenario: a forecaster trained jointly on other NVFi scenes is tested on withheld whale trajectories, using whale's separately fitted interpolation model.

E2.justification: The four external comparators on the original benchmarks are retained. v2 adds NVFi itself to the NVFi benchmark comparison and introduces a pure autoregressive Transformer control. The deterministic-versus-variational comparison disappears from D-NeRF Table 1 and is newly reported on NVFi in Table 5, rather than merely relocating the same experiment.

E3.justification: The reported training recipe changes from 20 context/20 target points and a 0.3 context span to lengths of 30/10 and spans of 0.6 for D-NeRF and 0.5 for NVFi. Learning-rate and regularization settings also change. v2 adds HyperNeRF's 90/10 temporal split and shared-forecaster training with whale withheld; existing D-NeRF 80/20 and NVFi 75/25 splits remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's deterministic/variational comparison, v2 adds controlled removal of the ODE, regularizers, adaptive weighting, and dynamic sampling, with averages and per-scene results in Tables 4, 6, and 7. Figure 4 visualizes regularization effects. Appendix B.2/Table 8 additionally tests joint training and transfer to withheld scene dynamics.

E5.justification: Both versions report point metrics and scene averages without seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. Their descriptions of probabilistic latent states do not provide empirical uncertainty estimates for the reported benchmark results.

E6.justification: v1 reports D-NeRF average PSNR of 26.53 for deterministic and 27.01 for variational ODE-GS; v2 reports 27.30 for its revised deterministic model. NVFi variational results are substantially replaced: bat PSNR changes from 38.50 to 28.01. TiNeuVox's telescope PSNR changes from 24.04 to 27.04. HyperNeRF, ablation, and multi-scene results are added. Changed training recipes and coverage preclude treating these collectively as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v2 makes the existing deterministic variant the primary model while retaining variational forecasting in Appendix A.0.2. More substantively, it adds Gaussian-position acceleration regularization and EMA-controlled adaptive regularization weighting to v1's fixed-weight latent smoothness penalty. Dynamic prefix–suffix sampling already exists in v1; its expanded description alone is not a new component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around underconstrained prediction and smoothness priors. The method presentation is reorganized, related-work subsections become compact topical paragraphs, implementation and dataset details move into appendices, and the conclusion gains a limitations discussion. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds an interpolation/extrapolation schematic, redraws the workflow, expands qualitative comparisons from one D-NeRF scene to five plus five NVFi scenes, and adds a regularization visualization. Benchmark tables are reorganized into scene blocks with method rows and colored rankings. New benchmark, ablation, variant-comparison, and transfer tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The central positioning around Gaussian splatting and latent ODEs remains. v2 explicitly discusses NVFi as an extrapolation predecessor and drops v1's assertion of being the only continuous-time scene-prediction work. It adds human-prediction, Transformer, VAE, HyperNeRF, and LPIPS references while pruning portions of the efficient-rendering and ODE-variant literature.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for positional acceleration regularization, the combined training objective, and EMA-based adaptive scaling in Equations 7–11. Existing latent-ODE and variational mathematics is largely retained or relocated. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs; the additions concern limited objective and weighting definitions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the method through real-video evaluation, the relevant NVFi comparator, and controlled component ablations that address important gaps in v1. Explicit failure conditions and the qualified transfer experiment also improve scientific interpretation. Reporting weaknesses remain: the variational-score revisions lack a clear cross-version explanation, and the claimed chickchicken PSNR lead contradicts Table 3's 20.29 versus GaussianPredict's 21.94. Nevertheless, the added diagnostic evidence and applicability boundaries provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ODE-GS and retain the same foundational framework and overlapping experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–B and supplementary figures and tables were included.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on D-NeRF, NVFi, and HyperNeRF, plus component ablations, deterministic-versus-variational comparisons, and a multi-scene generalization experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original ODE-GS extrapolation results on D-NeRF and NVFI, including numerical comparisons in Tables 1–2 and qualitative results in Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the central contribution to energy-based diffusion training and introduce a claim of favorable inference-time scaling. The unification claim now includes Fokker–Planck regularization. Density estimation and inference-time control remain contributions, although density estimation receives less main-text emphasis.

C2.justification: v1 treated imperfect-model cancellation weights as exact and explained weaker performance through ESS. v4 instead explains the normalization obstruction and explicitly acknowledges biased annealing/composition in Appendix B. It also adds interpretations of score-matching blindness, energy accuracy versus diffusion sample quality, and TI errors caused by mismatch between interpolant samples and learned energies.

D1.justification: v4 adds RNC pseudocode, energy-network and Dual SM implementation details, regularization settings of 1000 and a time increment of 0.0001, and extensive stochastic-interpolant/TI training and estimation instructions. Earlier annealing and multi-target SBDD details largely remain. However, v1 Appendix D.3's controllable-SBDD implementation details disappear despite retained reward-tilting plots.

E1.justification: v4 adds energy-learning evaluations on 2D and 100D Gaussian mixtures, MCMC sampling from learned ALDP energies, and free-energy estimation between vacuum and implicit-solvent ALDP. Earlier 10D mixture, annealing and ligand-design coverage remains represented, including reward-tilting plots in Appendix F.4.

E2.justification: New comparisons evaluate standard DSM, Dual SM (Guth et al., 2025; Figure 5), and neural thermodynamic integration without RNE regularization (Table 4). Existing density-estimation comparators and FKC remain. RNC-TDS disappears from the multi-target SBDD comparison but remains in the annealing table.

E3.justification: Original annealing and multi-target SBDD settings are largely retained. Added protocols include a 100–5,000-particle scaling sweep, MCMC-versus-denoising evaluation, and learned-energy correlation measurements. Appendix I.4 specifies 40,000 training iterations and thermodynamic integration using 5,000 samples over 1,000 time steps.

E4.justification: v4 adds particle-count sensitivity analysis, comparisons with and without energy regularization, and checks of learned endpoint energies (Figures 3–6 and 15; Table 2). These examine scaling, energy accuracy and effects on diffusion sample quality. Earlier reference-process and ESS analyses remain; v1's illustrated ligand examples are removed.

E5.justification: Appendix I.4 explicitly reports three repetitions of the new thermodynamic-integration experiments and summarizes their means and standard deviations. v1 already used ± reporting in molecular-result tables. This adds a statistical reporting protocol for a new experiment without establishing additional runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: New results include ALDP MCMC W2 of 0.1836 with RNE versus 0.9472 with DSM, and TI estimates of 29.28±0.04 with RNE versus 27.30±0.45 without it, against a 29.43±0.01 reference. Original annealing and shared SBDD values are unchanged. The SBDD RNC-TDS row and v1's aggregate reward-tilting Table 3 are removed, while pocket-level reward plots remain.

M1.justification: v4 adds energy-based diffusion training: scalar energy parametrization and a stop-gradient RNE consistency loss augment denoising score matching (Section 2.2). Appendices I.3–I.4 provide reference-based and stochastic-interpolant implementations. This introduces a substantial training component beyond v1's estimation and inference-time control procedures.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are rewritten around control and energy-based training. Existing density-estimation and importance-sampling sections move into Appendix C, the experimental narrative is condensed, and limitations, connections and implementation guidance receive reorganized appendix sections. This substantially changes the narrative and document structure beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v4 adds scaling, learned-density, energy-correlation and Ramachandran plots, two result tables and a pseudocode figure. The method-connection diagram is redrawn and expanded, and existing density-estimation plots move into the appendix. v1's ligand-example figure and reward-tilting table are removed; the main experimental page uses a substantially rearranged, denser layout.
