R1.justification: Positioning expands substantially toward energy-based diffusion, force fields and free-energy estimation, including Guth, Máté and Plainer. New Appendix J distinguishes RNE from RND-based samplers with tractable intermediate densities. Appendix C.1 newly acknowledges Skreta's earlier discrete Gaussian estimator, while Appendix H.4.4 recognizes a newer Laplacian-free FKC formulation.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix C.5 explicitly retracts v1's exact-weight argument for imperfect-model annealing/product because the omitted normalization depends on the endpoint; exact cancellation is restricted to reward tilting. v4 also adds derivations connecting energy regularization to the Fokker–Planck equation and recovering a second, Laplacian-free reward-FKC formulation. Existing convergence and CTMC derivations largely survive relocation.

improvement.justification: The explicit normalization erratum corrects a consequential false guarantee in v1 and clarifies the method's actual applicability. v4 also documents and evaluates a substantial energy-training extension through DSM/Dual SM comparisons, sampling checks and repeated free-energy estimates. Removing the aggregate reward-tilting results and settings weakens documentation, and the surviving RNC-TDS annealing row is unexplained. These gaps do not outweigh the important correction and added validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RNE/RNC framework and retain matching methods and experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices F and I report retained control experiments and new particle-scaling, energy-learning and solvation free-energy results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original density-estimation, molecular annealing, multi-target ligand-design and reward-tilting experiments.

C1.justification: V1 primarily introduces the benchmark and DS-Guru and argues that existing systems struggle with end-to-end pipelines. V2 adds central claims about the benefits of agentic control flow, persistent failures with oracle retrieval, and limitations in data-dependent reasoning and prior-knowledge integration. Its abstract foregrounds the 50% full-input and 59% oracle-input results, while DS-Guru is positioned as minimal reference scaffolding.

C2.justification: V2 develops explanations involving coupled retrieval and pipeline revision, competing helpful and harmful effects of prior knowledge, and failures to infer conventions across a data lake. These substantially extend v1's speculation about wildfire memorization and debugging limitations. V2 also adds discussion of language, cultural and domain-coverage limitations and biomedical re-identification risks.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents GPT-o3's role in functionality annotation, fallback to no snippets when context limits are exceeded, evaluation token costs, and curation/reproduction scripts. It also explains source-only distribution for redistribution-restricted datasets. Existing dataset-source descriptions, the system prompt and the public repository disclosure are largely retained.

E1.justification: The underlying coverage remains 104 tasks, 633 subtasks, six domains and 1,764 files. V2 adds gold-file-only scenarios that remove discovery requirements and obscured-input scenarios covering about 20% of tasks from legal and wildfire domains. These extend tested input conditions within the existing task structures and domains.

E2.justification: V2 adds smolagents Deep Research with GPT-o3, GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 and Claude-3.7, introducing a substantial agentic comparator alongside DS-Guru. OpenAI Deep Research and Gemini remain in the trimmed-input comparison. The additional OpenAI Deep Research entry in v1 Table 4 is omitted from the corresponding overall table.

E3.justification: V2 introduces oracle controls, obscured-input evaluation, sampling sweeps of 10–150 rows and iteration-budget sweeps of 5–20. It also revises the stated task-validation workflow from two independent reconstructions to a second solver plus a third adjudicator; this does not establish that validation was rerun. Primary scoring remains unchanged, while v1 Table 8's supplementary BLEU/ROUGE and other metric evaluations disappear.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's automation-level comparisons and brief qualitative observations, v2 adds retrieval controls, sample-size and iteration sensitivity studies, and obscured-data tests of reliance on prior knowledge. Section 4.2 adds two environmental case studies and trace-based diagnosis of failures to resolve data conventions. These substantially expand investigation of failure mechanisms.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for benchmark performance. V2's additional mean token costs and iteration-budget experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting or repeated-run estimation.

E6.justification: All 126 original domain-level DS-Guru scores and 54 lower-automation scores are retained. New smolagents/Claude-3.7 results report 50% under Full, 59% under Oracle and 57.85% under Trimmed inputs; these are added comparisons, not improvements to an unchanged configuration. V2 also adds obscured-input, sensitivity and failure-frequency results, while removing v1's partially populated Table 8 and its separate 8.47% OpenAI Deep Research entry.

M1.justification: V1's naive, simple-planning and self-correcting variants correspond to v2's no-context, one-shot and few-shot variants. Sampling, task decomposition, Python execution and iterative error feedback are retained, and the appendix system prompt is unchanged. The newly named One-Pass Sampling mechanism does not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and much of the explanatory narrative are rewritten. Benchmark design, evaluation and reference implementation are consolidated into Section 2; setup and results are reorganized, and appendices are reordered. V1's unfinished evaluation-mode appendix is replaced with established evaluation descriptions, and ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn, and Figure 2 adds illustrated environmental case data. Results are reorganized into Full/Oracle/Trimmed displays, with new mechanism-comparison and ablation tables and extended results in Appendix A. V1's partially populated final table is removed, and appendix prompts receive boxed formatting.

R1.justification: The QA discussion replaces examples such as QASPER, HotpotQA and MMQA with agentic retrieval benchmarks including FanOutQA, CRAG and BrowseComp. V2 adds agent-system and failure-analysis references and drops v1's explicit first-benchmark claim. The central positioning against existing data-science benchmarks and the substantive comparisons in Table 1 remain.

T1.justification: The end-to-end averaging formula, functionality-coverage score and six answer-type scoring schemes are retained. Detailed equations move from v1 Section 3 to v2 Appendix E. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation through a capable agentic comparator, oracle controls, obscured-input tests and concrete failure analyses, addressing v1's largely untested explanations of retrieval and memorization failures. Reorganization also removes the unfinished evaluation appendix. Some new interpretations remain unreliable—for example, Table 12 falls from 23.36% at five iterations to 21.33% at twenty despite prose claiming improvement—and uncertainty reporting remains absent. These limitations temper individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in diagnostic evidence and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KramaBench and DS-Guru. All 23 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison of text, figures, tables and equations despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original evaluations and adds smolagents comparisons, oracle-input experiments, obscured-input tests, sensitivity studies and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of DS-Guru configurations and proprietary systems, including benchmark scores, automation-level comparisons and runtimes in Tables 4–6.

C1.justification: V1 primarily claims a novel visual-option benchmark, difficult model performance and analytical insights. V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion additionally elevate image-text misalignment and positional heuristics into central diagnoses and claim effective alignment-oriented interventions, including fine-tuning. The original benchmark novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: V2 develops the earlier discussion of weak visual-textual binding into a dominant-failure explanation supported by shuffling and error analysis, and interprets fine-tuning gains as evidence of insufficient alignment-oriented training data. It adds explicit K–12 applicability limits and model-version qualifications. V1's correlation-based transferability and dedicated deep-thinking interpretations are removed.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C newly provide hardware and software versions, closed-model release identifiers, exact prompts, zero-padding and 50-pixel label-strip details, and fine-tuning settings including learning rate, batch size, gradient accumulation and training steps. The reasoning-data generation and augmentation pipeline is also documented. These substantially expand v1's sparse reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The original evaluation benchmark and K–12 mathematics domain remain. V2 adds a web-collected training pool of 1,072 multi-image problems, filtered to 500 exemplars and augmented to 1.3k samples, plus evaluation with permuted option-image correspondences. These extend coverage within the existing task. Table 1's added English-language label does not establish a separately conducted bilingual evaluation.

E2.justification: V2 adds GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Seed1.6-Thinking, GLM-4.5V, Vision-R1 and R1-OneVision, expanding the benchmark comparison from 36 to 42 LMMs. All earlier models remain in Appendix Tables 6–7. Figure 4 also changes participants in the retained merging/labeling comparison, removing models such as Doubao and Mantis while adding newer reasoning models.

E3.justification: V2 adds substantial experimental designs: fixed-image-order testing with permuted textual labels and adjusted answers, manual inspection of 50 sampled errors, and evaluation after supervised fine-tuning with a specified 336-step budget. The retained benchmark protocol still specifies zero-shot prompting, temperature zero, accuracy and GLM4-Flash answer extraction; newly disclosed implementation details do not establish changes to those existing evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds controlled option-shuffling tests, a GLM-4.5V error audit with representative cases, and a fine-tuning comparison (Sections 3.2–3.3 and Appendix D). It retains and revises the merging/labeling probes. V1's cross-scenario Pearson analyses and similarity-correlation heatmap are removed, rather than relocated.

E5.justification: V1 reports Pearson significance tests for accuracy across stem conditions, including r = 0.89, p < 0.01 and r = -0.39, p = 0.39. V2 removes these tests. Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seed-based uncertainty or confidence intervals for benchmark accuracy.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including Gemini 2.5 Pro at 80.9%, its shuffled-option accuracy of 72.2%, and Qwen2.5-VL-3B fine-tuning from 25.4% to 38.0%. Doubao's reported overall accuracy changes from 59.0% to 66.3%, with revised subgroup scores; v1 lacks snapshot identifiers, so a same-snapshot gain is not established. Most retained benchmark rows are numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 introduces Strategy 3: supervised fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL-3B using caption-derived, DeepSeek-refined, correctness-filtered and option-shuffled reasoning data (Section 3.3 and Appendix B). This adds a substantive training procedure. Image consolidation and explicit option labels already appear in v1 and are retained strategies.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, benchmark construction and analysis narrative. It organizes construction around three principles, moves related work after experiments, introduces a dedicated strategies section, and adds limitations, reporting statements and Appendices A–E. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column layout, redraws dataset examples, adds a construction pipeline, combines dataset statistics into a multi-panel figure, and redesigns Figure 4 with error proportions and intervention results. It adds input-format and error-case illustrations, version and prompt tables, and presents selected benchmark rows in the main text with full tables in the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for newer evaluated models and the fine-tuning framework, and explicitly contrasts its focus with Vision-R1 and R1-OneVision's predominantly single-image reasoning. References to MathQA, MathBench and OBELICS disappear. The central positioning around independently presented visual answer options remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: V2's Equation 1 expresses the same minimum pairwise cosine-similarity definition already stated in v1's Data Cleaning passage. This formalizes existing mathematics without changing it. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens diagnostic evidence and reproducibility. Controlled shuffling, error cases and the training experiment extend v1's largely observational analysis, while Appendices A–C supply previously missing prompts, model identifiers and implementation settings. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: the error audit covers only 50 failures from one model, and Section 3.3 claims consistent image-consolidation benefits although Figure 4 shows declines, including 6.3 percentage points for Gemini 2.5 Pro.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisioMath, retaining 1,800 questions and 8,070 images. Their text, figures, tables and mathematical content support comparison. V2's Appendices A–E are readable; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark evaluations and adds model results, controlled option shuffling, manual error analysis and a fine-tuning experiment, including supplementary results in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 36 LMMs, image-merging and option-labeling experiments, and correlation analyses in Tables 3–4 and Figures 3–4.

C1.justification: The three principal claims remain: style patterns inflate ASR, superficial style tuning increases matched-style vulnerability, and style-matched safety data mitigates that vulnerability while preserving utility. v2 updates the experimental scope in the abstract and introduction, providing broader evidence for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains predefined styles as a control against noise, interprets natural-data results as evidence of robustness, and notes limited improvement headroom from low initial ASR. It drops the PTST/Constrained utility-failure hypotheses and the explicit limitation about unexplored styles beyond prefixes/suffixes. Attention-based interpretation caveats survive in Appendix A.2.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly documents the source safety corpus: 2,000 Anthropic red-team questions converted into instructions with GPT-3.5-turbo refusal responses. New tables illustrate style transformations. Reported hardware changes from four to eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. The code-access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Dolly-15K instruction data, news/legal response-style conditions, and HumanEval programming evaluation. It also evaluates SafeStyle on natural Alpaca instructions; Alpaca itself, the seven jailbreak datasets, and AlpacaEval were already used in v1. These additions substantially broaden the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: Both Table 1 comparisons contain No Defense, Vanilla, PTST, SPPFT, Constrained, and Paraphrase against SafeStyle. v2 extends this same comparator set to its new style conditions and natural-data comparison in Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 adds a natural-data protocol using Dolly-15K and Alpaca-52K with GPT-4o responses, one training epoch for Alpaca-52K, and evaluation on original, untransformed queries. The equal four-style mixture and its averaged evaluation are removed. HumanEval Pass@1 and readability-change measurement are also added; the retained controlled experiments keep their stated settings.

E4.justification: Targeted extensions add a readability-based complexity analysis, news/legal tests of matched-style vulnerability, and news/legal safety-data alternatives in the existing style ablation. Appendix C.2 checks whether code-style tuning harms programming capability. The original attention, length, mixing-ratio, position, and safety-data-quantity analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both Section 4.1 descriptions specify three repetitions and reporting mean scores. Correlations with p-values and the existing distribution plots remain the reporting practice. The new complexity correlation adds a result, without a new uncertainty-estimation procedure or changed seed/run disclosure.

E6.justification: All shared Table 1 scores for list, poem, Shakespeare, and code match. v2 adds news/legal results and the natural-data Table 2, while removing mixture results. New Llama SafeStyle ASR changes are -0.045 on Dolly and -0.049 on Alpaca. Appendices add a complexity correlation of 0.078 and HumanEval Pass@1 of 72.6 before versus 73.1 after code-style tuning within v2. These are newly reported experiments, not performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core defense remains fine-tuning with 50 style-matched safety examples. Section 5.2 adds an adaptation for natural instruction data: extract styles using GPT-4o, sample ten bigrams according to frequency, and incorporate them into safety examples. This extends the augmentation procedure without changing the underlying training method.

P1.justification: The main progression from ASR inflation to style tuning to SafeStyle is retained. v2 revises introductory and related-work framing, moves detailed factor and utility discussion into subdivided appendices, adds a natural-data subsection, and replaces the closing Discussion with a shorter Conclusion.

P2.justification: The displays and layout are substantially reorganized. Figure 1 is redrawn; Figure 3 loses its length panel, which joins the expanded appendix Figure 7; the utility grid moves to Figure 9. Safety-style legends expand, Table 1 replaces mixture with news/legal columns, and new Table 2, Figure 8, and style-example tables accompany document-wide formatting changes.

R1.justification: v2 distinguishes benchmark-intrinsic style effects from engineered jailbreak transformations and discusses h4rm3l and Constitutional Classifiers. It adds journalism/legal, Dolly, HumanEval, readability, and safety-data references while removing mathematical-task and nuanced-style references. The overall alignment, safety-risk, and defense positioning remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. The operational definitions of ASR inflation and attention difference are retained. The added readability-based empirical analysis does not introduce a formal theoretical result or derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 validates the defense only on predefined styles and their synthetic mixture. v2 specifies an adaptation for naturally occurring styles and evaluates it on Dolly and Alpaca across the retained models and baselines (Sections 5.2–5.4, Table 2), addressing an important applicability gap. Additional robustness and programming-utility checks strengthen the evidence. Removing mixture results and shortening explicit limitations are costs, but the new validation provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeStyle research, with matching authors, research questions, and retained experiments. The complete main texts and appendices, including rendered figures and tables, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds natural instruction-tuning evaluations, news/legal style experiments, and appendix analyses including HumanEval results.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 32 LLMs across seven jailbreak benchmarks, controlled fine-tuning experiments, and SafeStyle safety and utility comparisons.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: styles inflate ASR, superficial style alignment creates safety vulnerabilities, and style-matched safety data mitigates them while preserving utility. Updating the survey from 32 to 36 models expands supporting evidence without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands mechanism and applicability interpretation: Appendix B.2 characterizes the effect as semantic style compliance rather than exact-token triggering, and Appendix C.2 discusses protection when attacker styles differ from training. New qualifications explain the stress-test role of poetry/Shakespeare styles. Section 6 expands the limitations discussion and recommends benchmarking malicious intent and style as separate evaluation dimensions.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 newly discloses that identical-intent exclusions account for 4% of queries. The appendices document construction of the new curated-intent and prefix-overlap controls. The original hyperparameter grid, LLaMA-Factory implementation, eight A100 GPUs, safety-data provenance, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: The seven jailbreak benchmarks, Alpaca/Dolly training data, AlpacaEval, HumanEval, and six principal styles are retained. Appendix C.2 extends SafeStyle's evaluation from matched training/attack styles to a scenario including attack styles unseen during its fine-tuning. News/legal analyses already appeared in v2.

E2.justification: The comparator set remains No Defense, Vanilla, PTST, SPPFT, Constrained, and Paraphrase. The new defense comparisons reuse this set. DeepSeek models are evaluated backbones, while Llama-Guard and Qwen3Guard are judges, not additional defense baselines.

E3.justification: The survey expands from 32 to 36 models by adding three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models and GPT-4o-mini; SafeStyle is additionally tested on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B. New evaluation designs introduce two alternative judges, 50 manually curated intents with synthetic styles, semantic/syntactic overlap controls, cross-style averages, and joint safety/utility rankings. Existing fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds substantial checks of judge dependence and benchmark-extraction artifacts in Appendix A.2, semantic versus syntactic trigger effects in Figure 11, SafeStyle robustness to unseen attack styles in Table 10, and safety/utility ranking analysis in Table 9. The earlier news/legal extensions, utility curves, and HumanEval check are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 adds a paired t-test for ASR inflation, reporting p = 0.0002. Appendix A.2 newly reports Cohen's kappa agreement with alternative judges: 0.767 and 0.858. The existing three-run mean-reporting statement is unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: All 336 numerical entries in Tables 1–2 are unchanged. The expanded survey reports inflation in 32/36 models instead of 28/32, and Figure 3's attention correlation changes from 0.571 to 0.456 under the expanded model set. New Tables 4 and 7–10 and Figure 11 add extensive results; for example, Table 8 reports SafeStyle delta ASR of -0.007 for news and -0.004 for legal, the latter tied with Constrained. Figure 9 updates length/complexity correlations to 0.125/0.076, although Appendix A.3 retains v2's 0.129/0.078.

M1.justification: SafeStyle retains the same intervention: incorporate 50 safety examples augmented to match fine-tuning styles. Section 5.2 also retains GPT-4o style extraction and frequency-based sampling of ten bigrams for real-world datasets. The additional evaluations introduce no method component, objective, or procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained, with targeted rewrites and expanded explanations. Conclusion becomes Discussion with Conclusion, Future Works, and Broader Impacts paragraphs; Appendix A gains a subsection and B.2 is retitled. Acknowledgements and the ICLR publication header are also added.

P2.justification: v3 adds three figures for alternative judges and semantic/syntactic controls, plus five tables for controlled styles, judge comparisons, reasoning-model results, rankings, and cross-style evaluation. Existing survey/correlation plots gain model entries and revised legends. Main tables and retained appendix displays are relocated, producing a substantial expansion of the visual evidence while preserving the overall design.

R1.justification: New citations cover DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3Guard, BackdoorLLM and a backdoor survey, linguistic style research, and hierarchical safety benchmarks such as SALAD-Bench and SafeDialBench. These support the added controls and benchmark recommendations; the central positioning relative to alignment and fine-tuning defenses remains stable.

T1.justification: The definitions of ASR inflation and attention difference remain substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. The new semantic-backdoor discussion is an empirical interpretation, and the added rankings and agreement measures are evaluation analyses.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps: alternative judges test dependence on GPT-4o, controlled experiments test benchmark artifacts and exact-wording explanations, and Table 10 evaluates SafeStyle beyond matching attack styles. These additions substantially strengthen the central empirical argument and practical applicability while preserving the original comparisons. Appendix A.3's stale correlation values introduce a small reporting defect, but the corresponding qualitative trends remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeStyle study. The main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C are readable and matchable across the additions, relocations, and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and reports additional model evaluations, alternative-judge checks, controlled style experiments, and SafeStyle robustness results.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 32 LLMs across seven jailbreak benchmarks, controlled fine-tuning experiments, and SafeStyle comparisons, with additional empirical analyses in the appendices.

C1.justification: The central claims about RL/SFT complementarity and selective interleaving remain. V2 expands its headline comparison to joint-loss and sequential hybrid methods and adds a claim of reduced training time. V1's specific 13% demonstration and nearly tenfold response-length framing gives way to broader data and computational-efficiency claims.

C2.justification: V2 explains entropy regularization as protecting exploration during fine-tuning. Appendix E interprets keyword frequencies as evidence of confidence and stronger planning. Appendices B–C add concrete Llama limitations: the full training set is too challenging and the Qwen prompt cannot be followed. The original interpretation of adaptive hardest-question training largely remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds filtering instructions, the SFT hyperparameter-search grid and LLaMA-Factory implementation, hybrid-loss construction, sequential-training details, Llama-specific instructions, and per-method GPU costs. Reported hardware changes from 16 to 8 A800 GPUs. Conversely, v1's explicit RoPE/context-extension settings, RL entropy coefficient, and VERL disclosure disappear; omission does not establish that those settings changed. The repository link target is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both use OpenR1/NuminaMath-derived mathematical training data and evaluate AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, MATH500, OlympiadBench, and MMLU-Pro. V2's Llama experiments and differently filtered subsets change model configurations and protocols within this retained coverage. Its new behavioral analyses use existing AIME25 tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds RL w/ SFT loss and two SFT then RL variants, including a demonstration-matched sequential control. The original pure SFT/RL, LUFFY, and four prior RLVR comparators remain. These additions substantially expand the comparison against alternative ways of combining SFT and RL.

E3.justification: The reported main training subset changes from 45k to 46k examples, with correctness/length filtering specified in v2. The Qwen2.5-Math-7B budget changes from 500 to 600 steps, and SFT batch size/learning rate from 128/1e-5 to 64/5e-5. V2 adds sequential-training controls, Llama settings using 11k short solutions and a 2048-token cap, and GPU-hour and normalized-keyword measurements.

E4.justification: V2 retains the all/uniform/random ablations, moving their detailed table to Appendix D. It adds an entropy-coefficient sensitivity study, AIME25 keyword-frequency analysis, and a worked case comparing completeness and verbosity across methods. The hardest-question-count trajectory previously shown in Figure 3c is removed.

E5.justification: The avg@32 reporting for the small competition test sets is retained. Neither version specifies repeated training runs or seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical significance procedures. V2's additional plots do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Main ReLIFT overall accuracy/length changes from 51.1/1061 in v1 Table 1 to 52.6/3502 in v2 Table 1, alongside changed training conditions. Many baseline and model entries also change. Scheduling-ablation accuracies are retained but their lengths are revised. Hybrid, Llama, resource, coefficient-sweep, and behavioral results are added; these are not isolated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 uses plain cross-entropy for interleaved fine-tuning. V2 adds token-distribution entropy regularization in Equation (4), with alpha set to 0.0001. This changes the fine-tuning objective, while retaining the hardest-question selection, verified-demonstration buffer, GRPO training, and adaptive interleaving procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and results narrative are extensively revised, with an explicit contribution list added. Experimental setup and results become separate sections, much implementation material moves into Appendix B, and the original appendix is reorganized into several thematic appendices.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1, reorganizes the main tables into method/model groups, and changes Figure 3 from four panels to three. The detailed ablation table moves to Appendix D and gains a main-text bar-chart summary. New displays include the resource table, entropy sweep, Llama prompt, keyword plots, and boxed case-study responses.

R1.justification: V2 adds discussion and citations concerning entropy-limited exploration, online difficulty filtering, and DAPO, alongside newer model and implementation references. It elaborates the cited arguments about RL's capability limits, while retaining the central positioning of ReLIFT relative to sequential SFT/RL and LUFFY.

T1.justification: V2 adds the mathematical definition of the entropy-regularized fine-tuning objective and its weighting parameter in Equation (4). The GRPO objective, hardest-example buffer definition, and cross-entropy formulation remain substantively unchanged. No theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: The new joint-loss and sequential SFT/RL controls, including a demonstration-matched variant, address a major gap in v1's evidence for adaptive interleaving. The entropy ablation and measured GPU costs further strengthen that central comparison. These gains outweigh omitted earlier implementation settings and remaining overstatements: Table 1 does not support universal top-two rankings, and Table 2 limits training-time savings to hybrid baselines.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReLIFT study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, revised, and newly added material.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations and ablations, including additional hybrid baselines, Llama experiments, resource measurements, entropy sensitivity, and reasoning-behavior analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original RL/SFT training-dynamics experiments, ReLIFT benchmark evaluations, scheduling/data-selection ablations, and experiments with additional Qwen models.

C1.justification: v1 claims the first use of draft models for approximate inference generally. v2 narrows the abstract and introduction's priority claim to SpecKV's KV-cache optimization, describes the framework as generalizing SpecPrefill, and calls SpecPC an iterative improvement of it. The conclusion also removes the combined first-method claim.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 adds explanations concerning task-dependent windows, avoiding static chunks that split related tokens, and position reassignment permitting inputs beyond the target's context limit. Sections 6.3 and E.1 attribute advantages over SpecPrefill to shorter lookahead. The explicit limitations and future-work discussion remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents contiguous position-ID reassignment, clarifies window weights, corrects Algorithm 2's index, and supplies SpecPrefill hyperparameters, including window size 1, kernel size 13, lookahead 8, and chunk size 32. Hardware, software, decoding instructions, and code/data access disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same RULER tasks, selected English/code LongBench tasks, and six MileBench datasets. SpecPrefill is evaluated within retained task coverage; no new domain, population, or task is demonstrated.

E2.justification: v2 adds SpecPrefill, a directly related draft-attention and lookahead method, to the central RULER, LongBench, latency, and memory comparisons (Figures 5–7 and 9; Tables 3–4 and 9–10). This substantially strengthens comparator relevance. The KV-dropping, multimodal, and larger-model comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added SpecPrefill evaluations use eight lookahead tokens and settings listed in Table 8. Figure 7 narrows the reported memory-measurement range from 128K to 64K input tokens. Table 8 also changes SpecPC's Pool entry from Max to Avg, consistent with v1's prose and pseudocode; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The token-importance case study, attention-correlation diagnostics, and draft-quality, lookahead-length, and sparse-prefill ablations remain unchanged (Figures 3–4, 8, and 11–13). The expanded window-size motivation in Section 5.2 supplies no additional ablation results.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The attention-correlation fitting and reporting practices are unchanged.

E6.justification: The added SpecPrefill results substantially change the comparative picture. At Cmax = 1024, its LongBench aggregate scores are 43.00 for Qwen and 42.86 for Llama, versus unchanged SpecPC scores of 43.73 and 43.76; v1's best prompt-compression baselines scored 37.17 and 37.58 (Tables 3–4). Additional SpecPrefill results cover larger budgets, RULER, latency, and memory. Figure 7 removes the 128K memory results.

M1.justification: The SpecKV and SpecPC procedures remain substantively unchanged. Window weighting and pooling already appear in v1; v2 corrects Algorithm 2's weighting index and explicitly documents position-ID reassignment, without establishing that the implemented procedure changed.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, contribution list, related-work discussion, and SpecPC explanation, with smaller edits to results and conclusions. The overall section order, narrative organization, and appendix structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Existing figures and tables are retained. SpecPrefill adds curves and legends to Figures 5–7 and 9, rows to Tables 3–4 and 9–10, and a column to Table 8. Figures 6–7 have axis adjustments, and Tables 3–4 and Figure 6 move with text reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liu, Chen, and Zhang's Speculative Prefill and substantially revises positioning around this closely related work. Sections 1–3 and 5 acknowledge shared draft-model lookahead and attention scoring, distinguish windowing, chunking, and positional handling, and reposition SpecPC as an improvement of SpecPrefill.

T1.justification: The importance-score definitions, Lemmas 1–2, Theorems 1–3, assumptions, and Appendix B proofs are retained. Equation-formatting and index-notation corrections introduce no substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: Acknowledging and evaluating SpecPrefill substantially addresses v1's omission of closely related prior work from its novelty discussion and central comparisons. Tables 3–4 now reveal much smaller LongBench advantages over this comparator, making SpecPC's contribution more accurately assessable. These gains outweigh the limited loss of 128K memory evidence. The correction remains incomplete because Section 2 retains a conflicting broad first-use claim.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Draft-based Approximate Inference with SpecKV and SpecPC. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–E support reliable comparison after matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds accuracy and efficiency comparisons with SpecPrefill.

before.justification: v1 reports original RULER, LongBench, and MileBench evaluations, latency and memory measurements, attention-correlation experiments, and ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contributions to include SpecKV-PC and its combined accuracy, latency, and memory benefits. They also reframe the framework as unifying and extending recent lookahead work, narrowing the earlier broad novelty positioning. The central draft-based importance-estimation claim remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of cascade pre-filtering, failures under aggressive prompt compression, and SpecPC's sensitivity to cross-family attention mismatch. It explicitly requires a reasonably accurate draft and distinguishes the empirical centroid proxy from the theorem's assumptions. Earlier discussion favoring mean correlation versus max retrieval aggregation is removed.

D1.justification: v3 documents LAQ++ hyperparameters and the authors' own implementation, cross-tokenizer processing, and settings for the new H200 timing experiments. Most original pseudocode, implementation-stack information, and hyperparameters remain. The public code link is retained; the added reproducibility statement does not establish newly available code.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 13 RULER tasks, included English/code LongBench tasks, and six temporal/semantic MileBench datasets. The added cross-family and output-length experiments use retained tasks with different model configurations or controls; they do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds LAQ++ throughout the KV comparisons. Existing large-model experiments gain H2O and PyramidKV comparisons, plus SpecPrefill and, in selected comparisons, LLMLingua-2, beyond v2's narrower SnapKV/CPC/R2C sets. StreamingLLM and AdaKV remain in the smaller-model appendix comparisons rather than being removed.

E3.justification: Efficiency evaluation changes from H100/Qwen2.5-14B time-to-first-token measurements to H200/Qwen2.5-32B generation timing, including 64–512 output-token sweeps. v3 also adds cross-family and oracle-importance protocols, varies cascade compression strength, and replaces the Qwen72B SpecKV draft configurations with 1.5B. Larger target models already appeared in v2's appendix.

E4.justification: v3 adds output-error versus accuracy tests, importance-correlation versus downstream-score analyses, cross-family robustness tests, cascade compression sensitivity, and stage-level efficiency breakdowns. It extends the lookahead ablation through EOS and adds a zero-lookahead SpecKV control. The earlier needle heatmap and multi-family mean/max attention-correlation suite are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both report benchmark point estimates and R-squared correlations. Additional correlation plots and dataset sample counts do not establish a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Many matched LongBench scores are retained: Llama70B/3B SpecKV at Cmax=256 remains 48.80. v3 adds 51.60 for SpecKV-PC-2048 and 48.43 for LAQ++ in that comparison (Table 2), alongside cross-family, correlation, and new efficiency results. Qwen72B SpecKV entries are replaced under different draft settings, preventing direct performance-change attribution.

M1.justification: v3 introduces SpecKV-PC, which compresses the prompt with SpecPC before applying SpecKV to the target KV cache, using shared draft information (Section 4.3). It also adds cross-family adaptations involving retokenization, word-level importance aggregation, and chat-template replacement (Appendix E.5). The original standalone algorithms remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, framework discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Theoretical motivations move into Sections 3.1–3.2, methods are consolidated under Section 4, and Appendix E is substantially reorganized. v3 also adds an appendix contents page, reproducibility statement, and LLM-usage disclosure.

P2.justification: The framework figure gains a performance panel, the SpecKV schematic is redrawn, and a cascade schematic is added. Main LongBench results use a combined table, while memory and latency share a redesigned figure. New correlation grids and stacked timing plots, expanded ablation axes, revised palettes, and ICLR formatting substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: LAQ++ becomes a central related method, with Sections 2–4 distinguishing SpecKV from its target-generated queries and full-cache requirement. v3 explicitly unifies LAQ++ and SpecPrefill and drops the broad claim of being first to use drafts for target-model approximate inference. GPT-3 and gpt-oss citations are added; the distillation citation is removed.

T1.justification: Theorems 1–3 and their Appendix B proofs are substantively retained. Table 1 corrects prompt-prefill complexity from O(Cmax) to O(Cmax^2) and adds prefill-space bounds. Section 3.1 introduces a centroid-distance proxy while explicitly distinguishing it from Theorem 1's token-wise error condition.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central accuracy–efficiency argument through the directly relevant LAQ++ comparison, tests linking importance-estimation quality to accuracy, and end-to-end timing with stage-level overhead analysis. Cascade sensitivity and cross-family experiments also expose useful applicability limits. These gains outweigh removal of the older mean/max correlation diagnostics. Reporting weaknesses remain: Section 5.1 names a 14B Qwen target while Figure 5 and Table 2 show 32B, and some superiority claims exceed what individual table entries support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Draft-based Approximate Inference work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds cascade, cross-family, importance-estimation, and extended efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original RULER, LongBench, and MileBench evaluations, attention-correlation experiments, ablations, and latency and memory measurements.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain, but v3 explicitly expands the adversarial resource to include 1,080 expert-labeled responses. It also removes the introduction's 'among the largest' claim and corrects '100 licensed' professionals to 'licensed or professionally trained.' The principal quality, safety, and judging-reliability claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets 72.9% agreement as supporting GPT-4.1 as a practical adversarial-labeling proxy; v3 emphasizes substantial misalignment even with explicit failure definitions and examples. Section 6 adds substantive discussion of clinician-data scarcity, privacy constraints, and multi-turn challenges involving context tracking and longitudinal coherence. The pretraining explanation for limited few-shot benefits remains in Appendix H.

D1.justification: v3 adds the adversarial-question survey screenshot, annotation allocation and instructions, Google Sheets fields, recruitment compensation, and KeyBERT implementation settings. Appendix I also explicitly identifies GPT-4.1 as the judge for the retained domain-specific adversarial results. Existing generation hyperparameters, hardware information, prompts, and code/data access link remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use 100 CounselChat questions covering 20 topics and 120 expert-authored adversarial questions targeting six failure modes. v3's keyword table characterizes existing questions. Multi-turn dialogue and patient simulation are discussed as future extensions, not evaluated scenarios.

E2.justification: The adversarial human-agreement comparison expands from GPT-4.1 validation alone to eight judges in v3 Table 4: GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, LLaMA-3.1, LLaMA-3.3, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, and Gemini-2.0-Flash. Existing CounselBench-Eval comparators, nine adversarial response models, and domain-specific pilots are retained.

E3.justification: v2's principal adversarial evaluation uses GPT-4.1 labels on three generations per question/model, with 96 responses checked by one professional. v3 adds a principal expert evaluation of one generation per question/model, totaling 1,080 responses distributed across five professionals. It also introduces judge accuracy, F1, and per-failure TPR/FPR evaluation. The original three-generation experiment remains in Appendix H.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands validation of adversarial failure detection against expert labels and adds per-failure false-positive/true-positive analysis in Figure 8. Appendix E.1 adds a keyword-based characterization of question diversity. The existing few-shot analysis, annotator-behavior analyses, and domain-specific pilots are retained rather than removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly specifies seed 42 for the 96-response pilot and documents single-generation expert evaluation alongside retained three-generation GPT-4.1 averages. Existing standard deviations, inter-rater reliability, and significance-testing practices remain unchanged; no confidence intervals are added.

E6.justification: v3 adds expert-assessed adversarial failure rates, including GPT-5 medication advice at 0.47, and judge F1 scores ranging from 0.35 to 0.50. The earlier GPT-4.1-assessed rates, including GPT-5 medication advice at 0.97, remain in Table 17. These are additional results under different labeling and sampling conditions, not same-setting performance improvements. CounselBench-Eval numerical results are retained.

M1.justification: The two-part benchmark, six evaluation dimensions, six adversarial failure definitions, and response-generation prompts remain unchanged. Expanded expert labeling and judge comparisons change the evaluation protocol without introducing a new algorithm or model component.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify annotation counts, credentials, single-turn scope, and the term 'online human therapists.' Few-shot discussion moves to Appendix H, and v3 adds an LLM-usage statement and conference header. The main section sequence and most existing methodological and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the expert failure-rate table, judge-performance table, question-keyword table, adversarial-authoring screenshot, and TPR/FPR plots. v2 Table 3 is retained as v3 Table 17, while several existing tables and figures move. These additions substantially change the presentation of adversarial and appendix evidence; the original six figure graphics are preserved.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the cited context for clinician-data scarcity, de-identification, patient simulation, multi-turn red-teaming, and downstream alignment in Section 6. Section 2 also replaces Elyoseph and Levkovich with Song et al. and Li et al. when positioning post hoc mental-health studies. These are substantive literature additions and positioning refinements.

T1.justification: Neither version presents theoretical propositions, proofs, or derivations. The benchmark rubrics and failure-mode definitions are retained; newly reported classification metrics introduce no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important validation weakness by grounding its principal adversarial results in 1,080 expert annotations instead of relying on GPT-4.1 with only a 96-response check. Table 4 and Figure 8 directly examine judge reliability, while Appendix H preserves the earlier experiments. Although the new adversarial study does not report inter-rater reliability or confidence intervals, the stronger expert foundation substantially improves the credibility of a central benchmark component.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CounselBench study and provide readable main text, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Matching retained and relocated material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds expert annotations of 1,080 adversarial responses and evaluations of eight LLM judges against these annotations.

before.justification: v2 reports original expert ratings, LLM-judge evaluations, adversarial failure rates, few-shot experiments, and domain-specific model pilots.

C1.justification: V2 foregrounds a novel physics-integrated flow-matching framework and up to eightfold residual improvement. V3 instead foregrounds first recognition of the physics–distribution trade-off and a Pareto-optimal balance, explicitly claiming that unrolling mitigates Jensen's gap. Presenting the approach as adapting established techniques also revises the headline novelty claim.

C2.justification: V3 explains unrolling through Jensen's gap, develops Pareto trade-off interpretations, and adds explanations involving deterministic-sampler bias, mode collapse and alignment between physics gradients. It adds memory-cost limitations and interpretations of normalization, noise and variant trade-offs. V2's explanation that numerical residual noise compensates for zero added Gaussian noise is omitted.

D1.justification: V3 adds Darcy normalization constants, comparator implementation disclosures, memory measurements and variant implementation details. Core optimizer, EMA, architecture and training hyperparameters remain unchanged, as does the code/data availability statement. V2's explicit pixel-independent 1D Wasserstein description and exact CPU model number are omitted, slightly reducing specificity.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Darcy, Reynolds-conditioned Kolmogorov, pitching-airfoil dynamic-stall and unit-circle tasks. Dataset populations, resolutions and conditioning ranges remain unchanged. The toy experiment moves from v2 Section 2.4 to v3 Appendix B; new sensitivity experiments use retained coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated DiffusionPDE and D-Flow comparisons across the PDE benchmarks, ECI on Darcy and PCFM on dynamic stall (Tables 2 and 4), including D-Flow's failed Kolmogorov evaluation. DM disappears from the Darcy comparison but remains in the toy experiment. FM-OT and the ConFIG-only variant match earlier FM and PBFM-1 terminology.

E3.justification: V3 adds Jensen-Shannon divergence, alternative Darcy normalization, sampler-threshold sweeps and dynamic-stall noise and gradient-flow protocols. New comparator settings include boundary-only ECI enforcement and D-Flow filtering at RE < 5, retaining 888 Darcy samples or 403 under alternative scaling. Original splits and training budgets remain unchanged. V3's conflicting Darcy MAE/MSE labels prevent an unqualified cross-version metric comparison.

E4.justification: V3 adds sampler-threshold, noise-level and normalization sensitivity studies, measured gradient conflicts/alignment, and separate-loss and final-step-backpropagation ablations (Tables 3, 5, 8 and 11–14; Appendices F and J). Earlier toy, architecture and loss-weighting analyses remain. V2's Darcy uniform-versus-logit sampling-time comparison in Figure 5 is removed, although corresponding toy variants remain.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 6 explicitly displays Kolmogorov residual variation across conditioning values using violin plots; v3 replaces this comparison with point metrics in Table 4. Sample/condition error bands remain elsewhere, including Figures 10 and 16. Neither version specifies independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive numerical baseline, sensitivity and variant results. For example, Table 4 reports dynamic-stall residual MSEs of 0.339e-6 for PBFM and 0.143e-6 for newly evaluated PCFM, with inference times of 60.47 and 3906 ms. Darcy and dynamic-stall training-time entries are exchanged between v2 Table 3 and v3 Table 6. These additions and revisions do not establish same-setting gains over v2.

M1.justification: The core ConFIG updates, unrolling, residual weighting, DiT architecture and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. V3 Appendix J introduces two tested variants: separating the physics residuals into distinct losses and backpropagating the residual loss only through the final unrolling step. These are limited procedural extensions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method explanations and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before methodology, the toy ablation moves into Appendix B, and the conclusion becomes a discussion with explicit limitations. Terminology is revised throughout, including FM-OT and the renamed ConFIG-only variant.

P2.justification: V3 adds a gradient diagram, Pareto plot, method-comparison table and numerous quantitative, sensitivity and memory tables. Darcy plots are recombined, several histogram/violin displays disappear, and field comparisons lose some no-unrolling panels. The main dynamic-stall visualization is simplified, while many appendix plots are retained with relocation or relabeling.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around constrained generation, discussing FFM, ProbConserv, D-Flow, ECI, PCFM, PIDDM, PIRF and PCFT. New Table 1 contrasts constraint enforcement, inference gradients and loss balancing. Earlier topology-optimization discussions and citations are removed, while Jensen's-gap literature and the revised trade-off novelty claim become central.

T1.justification: Following the unchanged gradient-update equations, v3 replaces v2's assertion of equal positive gradient inner products with separate positivity conditions. It also adds approximate residual-MSE scaling with sigma_min squared and a dynamic-stall noise bound. The underlying flow-matching and PDE mathematics remains, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical support: conditional benchmarks previously compared mainly FM variants, whereas Table 4 adds external competitors and exposes accuracy–cost trade-offs. New sensitivity, gradient and variant analyses test important design choices, and memory reporting improves transparency. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent Darcy MAE/MSE labels and prose reversing the Kolmogorov standard-deviation-error comparison in Table 4.

A1.justification: Despite retitling and substantial reorganization, both PDFs describe PBFM and the same physical benchmarks. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark experiments and adds baseline comparisons, sensitivity studies and method-variant results, including Appendix J.

before.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the unit-circle toy problem, Darcy flow, Kolmogorov flow and dynamic stall, including ablations and computational timings.

C1.justification: The central dataset, automation, spatial-multigraph novelty, and algebra-to-graph universality claims remain. The quantitative efficiency claim is narrowed from v1's million-fold speedup and 20–40-fold memory advantage to approximately hundred-thousand-fold speedup without a fixed memory-improvement factor.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantial interpretations concerning edge-feature utility, attention overhead, parameter efficiency, and Top-k retrieval for inverse design. Appendix H explicitly discusses information lost by the reference edge summaries and narrows the claimed practical relevance of fragmentation. Some interpretations overreach: the claimed consistent GINE superiority contradicts one-band accuracy in Table 2, where GIN scores 0.799 versus GINE's 0.764.

D1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands implementation documentation with per-model widths, activation and attention-head settings, and distributed-training configuration. V2 newly describes an auxiliary HSG-12M package supporting reproduction and custom featurization. Existing access locations and most Poly2Graph tutorial content are retained, but the explicit Python-version requirement is removed.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on balanced HSG-three-band and full HSG-12M. This extends testing to higher-band geometric variations beyond the topology-deduplicated population evaluated in v1, although HSG-topology already represented all 1401 classes. Dataset construction and sizes remain unchanged, and neither version evaluates temporal tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 expands from GCN, GIN, GAT, and GraphSAGE to eight comparators by adding GATv2, GINE, Molecular Fingerprints, and CGCNN. These additions participate in comparisons on the original three subsets as well as the newly evaluated subsets.

E3.justification: V1's five-epoch runs become runs capped at 100 epochs and 1000 steps. Batch sizes change from 256/64 to 6000, dropout from 0.1 to zero, and initial learning rate from 0.01 to 0.001. V2 introduces model-specific widths targeting parameter counts within 4%, two-GPU DDP, revised edge preprocessing, and Top-5/test-loss evaluation. The 80/10/10 stratified split ratio is retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C.5 adds an analysis of computation time as polynomial degree range increases from two to six; v1 provided only aggregate speed claims. The fragmentation gallery and extraction-quality checks are retained. The additional classification tables do not introduce a separate controlled ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions report classification means and standard deviations over three seeds, but seed identities change from 42/624/706 to 42/2025/666. V2 additionally reports standard deviations for throughput and GPU memory, whereas v1 reported averages only. There is no documented increase in classification run count.

E6.justification: Classification and resource results are extensively replaced under revised settings. For example, GraphSAGE one-band accuracy changes from 0.694±0.010 to 0.854±0.003; this is not a same-setting improvement. V2 adds full-dataset results, test loss, Top-5 accuracy, and timing measurements showing approximately 120,000–230,000-fold spectral-potential speedups. GraphSAGE retains the best Top-1 and Macro-F1 ranking.

M1.justification: The reference GNN input representation changes from 13-dimensional edge features containing five sampled coordinate pairs to six-dimensional summaries containing length, endpoint distance, midpoint, and average potential/DOS. Poly2Graph's extraction procedure and Algorithm 1 remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially reorganized around physical-science motivation and automated extraction, and the contributions are reordered. Related Work moves to Appendix A, the mathematical and benchmark material gains extensive subsection structure, and limitations move into an expanded Appendix H. An appendix contents list and reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: Table 2 is transposed and expanded, and the appendices add timing, conceptual-summary, feature, configuration, test-loss, and Top-5 tables while separating throughput and memory displays. The document template and figure placement change throughout. The tutorial plots are retained as unnumbered inline images rather than deleted; the underlying raster images match across versions.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting the four additional baselines and a related graph-transformer study, while pruning background citations including GOOD, PowerGraph, and The Well. The substantive positioning against existing spatial and multigraph resources remains largely intact; relocating Related Work is principally organizational.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the binary z-support definition of polynomial classes with bivariate monomial support modulo parity. Appendix B also revises multiband matrix dimensions and Hermiticity conditions, distinguishes hopping range from determinant degree, and adds degree bounds and examples. Appendix F newly asserts that a smallest graph multiset gives a canonical signature, without establishing uniqueness.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's explicitly minimal validation by evaluating the balanced higher-band and full datasets, adding edge-aware comparators and parameter-count controls, and supplying direct extraction-timing evidence. Revised class definitions and expanded implementation documentation improve assessability and reproducibility. New interpretive overstatements and the unproved canonical-signature assertion are weaknesses, but the stronger empirical foundation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HSG-12M dataset and Poly2Graph pipeline. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and matchable despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports expanded original classification experiments, resource measurements, and a Poly2Graph timing comparison in Appendix C.5.

before.justification: V1 reports original GNN classification experiments in Table 2 and GPU memory and throughput measurements in Appendix D.

C1.justification: v1 presents channel tokens as the key innovation; v2 frames existing token and patching ideas as repurposed within a unified mask-guided framework. The conclusion adds practical-efficiency claims supported by scalability experiments. The central contribution of jointly handling dependency, asynchrony, and missingness remains.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 replaces Weather's multi-scale explanation favoring more tokens with a correlation/redundancy explanation favoring one. Section 6.3 newly attributes CTF–TimeXer gaps exclusively to interpolation. Appendix C.3 and the conclusion recast scalability as adequate at realistic sizes, while Appendix G retains the earlier quadratic-attention and MSE limitations.

D1.justification: v2 documents an FFT search range and 70th-percentile threshold, new dataset settings, irregular-baseline integration, ContiFormer's solver approximation, and modified-TimeXer implementation. New statements promise code upon publication and explicitly prohibit private-data release. Documentation expands substantially, although the claimed software-version details are not actually specified.

E1.justification: v2 adds ETT2-practical and EPA-Air covering four regions, including short-gap testing on Los Angeles and Hillsborough. ETTm2 already appeared in v1's conventional evaluation, but its asynchronous setting is new. The original practical datasets and five conventional benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: TimeMixer is replaced by TimeMixer++ in retained comparisons. Tables 1–2 add Hi-Patch and t-PatchGNN, with ContiFormer and BiTGraph additionally evaluated for SolarWind missingness. Appendix C.4 introduces an evaluated TimeXer variant adapted for asynchronous inputs.

E3.justification: Section 5 changes regular baselines' test-time missing-block treatment from zero-filling to linear interpolation. The six-mask comparison changes missingness from 0.125 to 0.375. New protocols evaluate fixed patch lengths 8/16/32, channel counts up to 280, and input lengths up to 2048. These are reported protocol changes, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds fixed-versus-FFT patching ablations, channel/input-length scalability analyses, and a modified-TimeXer control examining architectural versus interpolation effects. Missingness testing extends to EPA, and Figure 10 revises the forecast examples. Conversely, v1's forward-fill versus linear-interpolation comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Both Appendix E sections describe error reporting over five random seeds. v2 adds a reproducibility statement saying each experiment used three seeds and reports averages. This introduces conflicting run-count reporting; it does not establish an actual reduction in runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises retained results, including CTF Weather CMSE from 0.269 to 0.275, and adds ETT2/EPA outcomes. SolarWind missingness results are replaced under revised evaluation conditions. Table 4 changes Weather's optimal token count from three to one. New comparator and scalability results appear; forward-fill results and horizon-specific ETT1 short-gap entries disappear. Tables 5–6 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture, loss, decoder, and attention/masking components match. However, v2 Appendix A.2 introduces a sampling-factor division in patch-length calculation while retaining v1's 48/18-step SolarWind patches. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents a procedural change or an inconsistent clarification of units.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, method motivation, analysis, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Contribution bullets become an integrated narrative, terminology shifts toward repurposing and mask-guided attention, Appendix C is reorganized and expanded, and new ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and substantially restructures comparison tables with additional datasets and method groups. It adds Tables 9, 12–14, and 20, removes the forward-fill table, compresses ETT1 short-gap results to averages, and redraws Figure 10 with updated comparisons and a different SolarWind example. Most architecture and attention-mask figures remain.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and 4 substantially revise positioning around prior channel-summary and auxiliary tokens, frequency-guided patching in Moirai/LightGTS, and repurposed PatchDropout. Related work expands with Hi-Patch, Time-IMM, SAITS, BiTGraph, S4M, and other references, making the relationship to existing components more explicit.

T1.justification: The written patch-length formula changes from floor(L_i/f_i*) in v1 Section 4 to floor(p_i*/r_i), with p_i*=L_i/k_i*, in v2 Appendix A.2. This adds a sampling-factor division under the stated definitions, although its intended units remain unclear. Section 3's mathematics and Appendix B's spectral derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens the central evaluation by replacing potentially disadvantageous zero-filled baseline inputs with interpolation, adding relevant irregular/missing-aware comparators, and introducing a modified-TimeXer control. EPA evaluation and scalability measurements also address important applicability gaps in v1. These gains outweigh lost ETT1 result detail and new seed-count/patch-unit ambiguities. Nevertheless, blanket superiority language needs qualification: Table 2 now includes a TimeXer CMAE advantage at missingness 0.375.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChannelTokenFormer study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G are readable, including the rotated results tables, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original CTF experiments and reports additional EPA and asynchronous ETT2 results, patch-length ablations, scalability measurements, and modified-TimeXer comparisons.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and the appendices report original forecasting results, component ablations, missingness experiments, and spectral analyses for CTF.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contribution: intention-conditioned flow occupancy learning and implicit GPI for offline pre-training and adaptation. The reported 1.8× return and 36% success-rate improvements on the original benchmark suite remain unchanged; added experiments primarily support existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations involving reward sparsity, BC protection against out-of-distribution actions and overestimated values, data requirements, and Monte Carlo estimation variability. It interprets t-SNE clusters as intention alignment and newly discusses poor end-to-end pixel learning on RT-1. The original limitation concerning intention inference from adjacent transitions is retained.

D1.justification: New disclosures include fourfold scaling of jaco returns for aggregation, RT-1's 73,499 episodes and reuse across training stages, and frozen β-VAE versus DINO representations. The reproducibility statement largely relocates existing JAX, A6000 hardware, runtime and code-access information from v1's appendix.

E1.justification: The original 36 state-based and four image-based benchmark tasks are retained. Appendix F.1 adds training on real robot data from RT-1 and evaluation on SimplerEnv's google_robot_pick_coke_can task, substantially extending coverage beyond the original simulated datasets.

E2.justification: The eight main baselines and existing FB/HILP intention-encoder comparisons are retained. The new robotics comparison evaluates standalone behavioral cloning alongside ReBRAC and DINO+ReBRAC; standalone BC was not a reported comparator in v1.

E3.justification: V2 adds protocols using the entire RT-1 dataset for both training stages, frozen image embeddings, dense-reward ReBRAC controls, and pre-training/fine-tuning dataset-size sweeps. It extends the future-state sampling sweep to N=1 and additional tasks. Existing benchmark training budgets remain unchanged, while jaco's previously stated dense rewards are redescribed as sparse without establishing a rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds intention-clustering case studies, dense-versus-sparse reward controls, removal of BC regularization, and dataset-size sensitivity studies (Figures 4, 6, 10–13). The existing future-state-count ablation is expanded to eight tasks in Figure 14. Original encoder comparisons, convergence analyses and other hyperparameter ablations are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across eight seeds for state-based tasks and four for image-based tasks. V2 extends this existing practice to additional experiments without changing uncertainty estimation or documenting increased repetitions of retained experiments.

E6.justification: All 344 mean-and-standard-deviation entries in Table 4 are identical. V2 nevertheless adds substantial results: a reported 34% advantage over DINO+ReBRAC in the new robotics comparison, improved ReBRAC performance with dense jaco rewards, dataset-size trends, BC-removal outcomes and intention-clustering findings. These are additional results rather than improved scores on the original benchmark comparison.

M1.justification: V2 changes the SARSA bootstrap target's conditioning from (s,a) to (s′,a′) and reverses the expectile residual from Q−Qhat to Qz−Q, with corresponding pseudocode changes (Sections 4.3–4.4; Algorithms 1–2). Appendix F.1 also adapts InFOM to frozen β-VAE image embeddings. These are bounded revisions to the documented procedure; the PDFs do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: background formulations and algorithms move to appendices, Section 5.2 foregrounds intention visualizations, and the original encoder and convergence studies move to Appendices F.2–F.3. The supplement is reorganized around problem-setting discussions, visualizations and additional experiments, with document-wide citation and terminology edits.

P2.justification: V2 adds trajectory/t-SNE panels, a robotics comparison and several controlled-analysis plots. The original sampling-count bars become an expanded line plot in Figure 14, while other hyperparameter panels are rearranged in Figure 15. Existing figures and algorithm displays are relocated, alongside substantial typography and layout changes.

R1.justification: Appendix B.2 newly distinguishes the setting from meta-RL and multi-task RL through task-description and reward-supervision requirements. Related citations are added, alongside references for RT-1, SimplerEnv, t-SNE and latent-space generative modeling. Positioning relative to TD flows and successor-representation methods remains stable.

T1.justification: Reversing the residual under the unchanged asymmetric-loss definition corrects its mathematical consistency with the claimed upper-expectile maximization. Target-field conditioning is also corrected in the flow equations. The consistency assumption, ELBO/information-bottleneck derivation and asymptotic GPI argument otherwise remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 adds controlled tests of reward sparsity, regularization removal and data requirements that v1 lacked, alongside intention visualizations and expanded sampling analysis. These substantially strengthen evidence for the design choices, while corrected bootstrap conditioning and expectile direction improve mathematical clarity. The robotics extension remains limited to one simulated task with fixed embeddings and an inconsistent return/success-rate label, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same InFOM work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds intention visualizations, RT-1/SimplerEnv evaluation and further controlled analyses.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original ExORL and OGBench evaluations, method comparisons and hyperparameter ablations.

C1.justification: v3 adds Core-Cocktail training for LLM knowledge retention as a principal contribution. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from SOTA spoken-QA performance with relatively little data to SOTA on OpenAudioBench and Big Bench Audio, with comparable performance on VoiceBench and UltraEval-Audio among approximately 7B models.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting training-stage recovery, instructional-data quality, ASR augmentation, and selective forgetting to model performance. The speech-quality limitation changes from inadequate tokenization and naturalness to weaker speech-text alignment than Qwen2.5-Omni, hypothesized to arise from SRH lacking explicit text input. Full-duplex interaction and broader multimodality remain future directions.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix A newly specify frozen tokenizer/detokenizer components, a 2K sequence limit, interpolation weight alpha = 0, unit loss weights, and stage-specific learning rates. Reported hardware changes from 32 to 64 A800 GPUs, and v3 documents WER-based synthetic-data selection. The explicit v2 promise to release all code and checkpoints disappears; neither PDF establishes actual release availability.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond Llama Questions and Web Questions to instruction following, refusal behavior, real-speech interaction, and reasoning through OpenAudioBench, VoiceBench, UltraEval-Audio, and Big Bench Audio. The original QA tasks remain within the expanded suites. Training adds real-speech ASR corpora, while Appendix C evaluates additional instruction datasets, including coding and mathematics data.

E2.justification: The overlapping Llama/Web comparisons add Step-Audio2-Mini and remove comparators including Moshi, MinMo, VITA-Audio, and Stream-Omni. Table 3 replaces the previous speech-quality comparator roster with MiniCPM-o 2.6, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Kimi-Audio, and Step-Audio2-Mini. Appendix C additionally uses the original Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct text model as a reference.

E3.justification: Reported pretraining decreases from 210K to 100K hours; 17.8K conversation hours are replaced by mixtures including 26K S2S and 20K S2T hours. Learning-rate schedules become two-stage, and warmup changes from 1% to 2%. New evaluations introduce G-Eval and refusal rate. Table 2 mostly uses checkpoint inference instead of literature-sourced baseline scores. The stated Qwen backbones remain unchanged despite revised size labels.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds comparisons of training stages, instructional-data mixtures, ASR augmentation, and retention versus forgetting after text fine-tuning across multiple corpora (Tables 6, 8–9). Existing component ablations, grouping-factor experiments, and data-scaling analyses are retained: v2 Tables 5 and 4 become v3 Tables 4 and 7, and Figures 2–3 move to the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the two-QA headline results with expanded results, including overall scores of 69.24 on OpenAudioBench and 66.3 on Big Bench Audio.
