Table 3 changes DrVoice's UTMOS/ASR-WER entries from 3.86/6.75 to 4.29/11.2 under a revised pipeline and benchmark collection, preventing a controlled performance comparison. Appendix C adds numerous training and forgetting results; the original component and grouping ablation values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 replace HuBERT tokenization and direct token-to-HiFi-GAN synthesis with S3Tokenizer and speaker-conditioned flow matching followed by HiFi-GAN. Figure 1 also removes the discrete-token branch from user speech inputs. v3 introduces Core-Cocktail training: high-learning-rate fine-tuning, parameter merging with the base LLM, and low-learning-rate fine-tuning. The grouping/SRH architecture and CoM-Mixing remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, results discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Section 3.3 broadens into Training Strategy, main results and ablations become separate subsections, and existing implementation details, prompts, analyses, and future-work material are reorganized into Appendices A–D.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with revised input pathways and a more compact arrangement. Table 2 changes from model rows with two QA datasets to model columns with four benchmark blocks. New Tables 6, 8, and 9 display training/data analyses; existing grouping and prompt tables are relocated or reformatted, and Figures 2–3 are resized and moved to Appendix C.

R1.justification: The tokenization discussion shifts from HuBERT's lightweight, diffusion-free synthesis to S3Tokenizer/CosyVoice and SenseVoice. v3 credits LM-Cocktail for parameter merging and adds references for Step-Audio2, VoiceBench, G-Eval, and ASR corpora. The main text-driven versus joint-model taxonomy and positioning of dual-resolution modeling remain.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds the mathematical definition of the merged model, Mr = alpha M1 + (1 - alpha) M0. The existing joint-generation, grouping, ungrouping, and loss equations (1–8) remain unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 supports a broad voice-conversation claim mainly through two QA benchmarks and literature-sourced comparator scores. v3 substantially strengthens the evidence through instruction-following, refusal, real-speech, and reasoning evaluations, mostly direct checkpoint comparisons, and explicit data-quality/forgetting analyses against the text backbone (Tables 6, 8–9). Some earlier comparators are dropped, uncertainty reporting remains absent, and the merging effect is insufficiently isolated. Nevertheless, the broader evaluation and diagnostic analyses substantially improve the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DrVoice. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and ablation results, including additional training-strategy, data-quality, and forgetting experiments in Appendix C.

before.justification: v2 reports original DrVoice benchmark results, component ablations, grouping experiments, and data-scaling results in Tables 2–5 and Figures 2–3.

C1.justification: Both versions make the same central contributions: curvature-based characterization of heterogeneity gains and gradient-based environment-parameter search for favorable reward regimes. v2 clarifies the behavioral meaning of heterogeneity and provides broader experimental support, but does not substantively replace or redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets football results as evidence of applicability when double aggregation forms only part of the reward, explains Softmax parameter variance through saturation, and expands discussion of convergence and non-differentiable alternatives. It also sharpens the neural-versus-behavioral distinction. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation concerning inseparable tasks disappears without a corresponding extension of the theory.

D1.justification: v2 adds a supplementary website and visualization links, documents the new task reward constructions and training settings, and reports single-L40 iteration timings of approximately 15 seconds without environment backpropagation versus 20 seconds with it. MAPPO, VMAS/TorchRL, two-layer 256-unit Tanh networks and the supplementary code/YAML disclosure remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds two materially different evaluated tasks: 2v2 tag with moving heuristic escapees, obstacles and sparse capture rewards, and a football drill requiring scoring and opponent blocking under a composite reward. Matrix games and Multi-Goal-Capture remain. Colonel Blotto and level-based foraging remain analytical examples.

E2.justification: The experimental comparison remains MAPPO with shared versus independent agent parameters. The added environments reuse this comparison and existing aggregator choices. PAIRED, Designer-RL and evolutionary approaches are discussed, but no experimental comparison against another environment-search algorithm is added.

E3.justification: New protocols include football training for 500 iterations of 240,000 frames with opponent speed annealed from 0% to 100%, and tag training for 30 million frames. Appendix J adds an eight-agent/eight-task matrix configuration; Appendix Q adds adverse Softmax initialization and measurements through 100 million frames. These supplement the retained protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds scalability analysis at N=M=8, an initialization-robustness test starting with unfavorable aggregator temperatures, and football controls testing whether heterogeneity benefits depend on reward structure. Figures 8–9 add behavioral case studies. The original observability analysis is retained and relocated, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit replication counts for the new studies: eight seeds for the larger matrix game, six for football and three for adverse initialization. Retained experiments keep their previous seed counts and mean/standard-deviation reporting. This documents additional replication designs, not increased runs for the original experiments or new significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Tables 5–8 retain their numerical values. New results include tag gains in Figure 4b, larger-team gains in Table 9, and football gains of 1.76±0.72 for (U=min,T=max) and 1.18±0.11 for (U=mean,T=max), alongside near-zero control means in Table 10. Table 11 reports recovery from adverse initialization. These are results under added settings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: HED is renamed HetGPS, but Algorithm 1 retains the same rollouts, heterogeneity-gain objective, environment-gradient update and policy-training steps. The policy architecture also remains unchanged. Appendix P expands discussion of possible non-differentiable variants without specifying a substantive new algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 renames HED to HetGPS, refines terminology and introductory explanations, and condenses the experimental narrative by moving Multi-Goal-Capture details and observability discussion into appendices. The principal section sequence and most theoretical and algorithmic exposition remain intact; this is a targeted reorganization rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, revises curve styling and legends, adds the tag panel, Figures 8–9 and Tables 9–11, and relocates the original observability panel to Figure 10. These substantially change the visual presentation. New problems include incorrect duplicate legend entries in Figures 3 and 4a and an extra Figure 11 caption attached to the observability plot.

R1.justification: v2 adds Amir et al. on RECODE, Simaan and Cruz on Stackelberg games, and Stanley et al. on neuroevolution, supporting expanded co-design and optimization discussion. The main diversity literature and relationship to PAIRED remain. The System Neural Diversity preprint-to-journal update concerns the same cited work.

T1.justification: Theorems 3.1–3.4, their proofs and the existing aggregator derivations are retained. v2 removes v1's explicit conjecture that the Softmax lower bound is exact and removes 'Exact' from Theorem 3.4's title. Appendix P.1 explicitly formulates the optimized-policy Stackelberg objective, without adding a convergence theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical bridge between the theory and embodied learning. Tag tests sparse discrete rewards; football tests a composite reward with controls; and Appendix Q addresses whether search succeeds from unfavorable initialization. These resolve important gaps in v1's narrower validation, while clearer behavioral-versus-neural distinctions improve interpretation. The legend/caption errors and removed inseparability caveat are drawbacks, but do not outweigh the added targeted evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, research questions, core theory, algorithm and retained experiments. All 25 pages of v1 and 30 pages of v2, including appendices and visual material, support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds tag, football, larger-team matrix-game and adverse-initialization experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original MARL experiments in discrete and continuous matrix games and Multi-Goal-Capture, including observability tests and HED parameter-search results.

C1.justification: The original distribution-shift generalization claim remains. v2 adds a central claim that value estimates trained on real-world trajectories support zero-shot simulated reward shaping and yield offline policies outperforming Meta-World's dense rewards. Expert-versus-non-expert discrimination also becomes an explicitly claimed capability.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations linking sampling diversity to reduced redundant-frame shortcuts and explaining real-to-simulation reward transfer. It qualifies scripted trajectories as lacking quantified suboptimality and adds limitations involving execution variability, long durations and deployment-time updates. These substantially extend v1's brief discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds concrete IQL/d3rlpy hyperparameters, training and evaluation schedules, generic descriptions for unannotated scripted data, and batched GPU distance computation for sampling. Most original encoder, optimizer and hardware details are retained. Reproducibility remains limited by ambiguous sampling defaults and the absence of an explicit value-to-reward construction.

E1.justification: The original BridgeData coverage is retained. v2 adds four randomized-controller subsets for expert versus non-expert discrimination and Meta-World MT10 for simulated offline policy learning, extending both behavioral coverage and downstream task requirements.

E2.justification: The principal VLM comparators remain, with CLIP renamed VLM-CL, while TTT-EX disappears from Table 1. v2 adds META-WL as the native-reward comparator and full-trajectory/random sampling controls. GVL's offline-RL entries are unevaluated dashes; the Qwen and GPT-4o trials already appeared in v1 Appendix B.3.

E3.justification: v2 introduces BinVOC discrimination evaluation and an offline-IQL protocol using 20 demonstrations per task, 100,000 training steps and 20 evaluation rollouts per task with horizon 150. Appendix D.1 also changes the default sampled-window count from eight to sixteen, although Section 4.1 retains eight; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test expert-versus-scripted discrimination and the effects of full-trajectory, random and dissimilarity sampling, including window-length and window-count variations. The temporal-adaptation analysis in v1 Appendix C is retained in v2 Appendix F.2 with renamed methods and identical numerical results, rather than being a new ablation.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run or uncertainty information. For its new offline-RL experiment, v2 reports ten seeds covering data generation and policy training, plus 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 task-stratified bootstrap resamples. The retained VOC experiments still lack uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds BinVOC, sampling-ablation and offline-RL results; Table 2 reports VITA's IQM as 0.815 versus META-WL's 0.779. Original VOC results mostly change only by rounding, but GVL-1S on dt_tk_pnp changes from 0.2151 to 0.211, and TTT-EX entries are removed. Table 4's full-trajectory average of 0.25 conflicts with its two successful cases out of four.

M1.justification: v2 narrows the proposed configuration to implicit-memory TTT-IM, renamed VITA, removing the explicit-window/reset TTT-EX option. The encoder, reconstruction loss, regression head and meta-learning core remain unchanged. The newly documented sampling heuristic does not establish that its implementation changed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around VITA and zero-shot value functions. v1's compact organization becomes separate preliminaries, expanded method and experiment subsections, related work, and discussion with limitations and future work. Existing appendix material is regrouped alongside additions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and Figure 1 is redrawn around training and inference. v2 adds a main-text trajectory gallery, scripted examples, a two-panel results table and a sampling-ablation table. Existing appendix illustrations are retained, while the dataset table replaces shift checkmarks with embodiment names.

R1.justification: A substantial Related Work section newly positions VITA against RoboCLIP, ReWiND, Video-Language Critic, DecisionNCE and prompt-based adaptation. The introduction also expands discussion of world models and latent-action learning, substantially broadening v1's shorter inline research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 adds the diversity-score/top-k formulation in Equation 5, the BinVOC indicator definition and a sampling-complexity derivation in Appendix G. Core value and reconstruction-loss definitions are retained; the latter already appeared in v1 Figure 1. No shortcut-learning theorem is added, and Appendix G's numerical cost estimate contains an arithmetic error.

improvement.justification: The new sampling ablations directly test a central component that v1 did not isolate experimentally. Scripted-trajectory checks and ten-seed offline-RL experiments substantially strengthen evidence beyond expert-trajectory rank correlation, with useful uncertainty and implementation reporting. These gains outweigh the new reporting weaknesses, including Table 4's inconsistent average and Appendix G's cost arithmetic. The overlapping RL confidence intervals and incomplete reward-construction details nevertheless qualify the strength and reproducibility of the claimed downstream superiority.

A1.justification: Both PDFs support comparison of text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Despite retitling and expansion, they share the authors, core method and original BridgeData experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds scripted-trajectory discrimination, sampling ablations and offline reinforcement-learning results in Tables 2 and 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original progress-estimation experiments in Table 1 and adaptation-strategy experiments in Appendix C, Table 3.

C1.justification: The central claims about efficient probing, accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs and broad applicability remain. V2 extends the framing to generative representations, claims greater attention complementarity than competing methods, and raises the stated maximum ImageNet gain from 13.6 to 24.3 points using DiT. The abstract's 10× speed-up claim is removed.

C2.justification: V2 interprets complementarity as potentially arising from attentive probing rather than solely backbone architecture, and connects diffuse backbone attention with larger EP gains. New Appendix D explicitly limits conclusions to frozen-backbone classification and characterizes the mechanism analysis as diagnostic. It also discusses untested fine-tuning interactions, structured tasks and multimodal extensions, while Section 4.2 clarifies that reported compute savings exclude the backbone.

D1.justification: V2 adds LUMI/AMD MI250X hardware information and discloses patch sizes, the Table 2 EP32 default, GAP-based LP entries and different-setting FT sources. Comparator descriptions gain detail, although Table 1 gives DELF softmax while its prose specifies softplus. V2 removes v1's explicit code-access link; this does not establish that the code itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: The SUN397 evaluation in v1 Figure 9f is absent from v2. The other seven classification datasets remain, including results relocated into the appendix. Newly evaluated generative backbones still perform image classification; they do not introduce generation tasks.

E2.justification: V2 explicitly adds MHCA to the reference comparisons, co-plotted with AIM in Figures 2–3, while retaining the existing named pooling methods. Table 5 also introduces a Vanilla Matryoshka comparison using separate classifiers. Newly added pretrained backbones are evaluation targets rather than competing probing algorithms.

E3.justification: V2 adds evaluation configurations for DiT, AIMv2, Franca, DINOv3 and DINOv2-L. New protocols match predictor counts for complementarity comparisons and test projected-map counts, multiple representation dimensions and Matryoshka loss weights. The established 90-epoch schedule, warmup, batch sizes and low-shot subsets remain substantially unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative complementarity comparisons across backbones and probes, worst-pair redundancy measurements, checks across all 12 MAE blocks, and a cross-backbone entropy analysis. Appendix C.3 also tests attention mixing and Matryoshka tradeoffs. Existing projection ablations, dimensionality sweeps, low-shot and layer-wise analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, experimental error bars or significance tests. The retained standard-deviation attention maps summarize variation across heads, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial new results, including DiT LP/EP accuracy of 32.7/57.0 and complementarity, mixing and Matryoshka outcomes. DINO LP/EP entries change from 78.2/78.7 to 77.3/77.8; SigLIP and SigLIP2 LP change from 85.9/86.9 to 84.1/85.2, now explicitly labeled GAP. These revisions do not establish identical underlying settings. SUN397 results disappear, while low-shot and layer-wise values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The main EP procedure and Equations 1–10 remain unchanged. Appendix C.3 adds auxiliary attention mixing through a linear-plus-softmax projection and Matryoshka variants using joint losses with shared nested or separate classifiers. These extend EP experimentally; attention mixing is explicitly excluded from the final design.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around broader representation evaluation. Preliminary method sections are merged, competitors move into experimental setup, analyses are regrouped, and implementation details move earlier in the appendix. Pooling-related work is relocated, and an appendix contents page and new concluding appendix sections are added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a single-column layout and extensively regroups benchmark panels between the main text and appendix. It adds an algorithm-comparison table, expands the pretraining-results table with parameter and gain columns, introduces complementarity and entropy plots and variant tables, and replaces the main attention visualization with color-coded maps across bird images. Many earlier appendix visualizations are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens the research framing beyond its original MIM emphasis through discussion of vision-language, autoregressive and diffusion representations. Added connections include AIMv2, DiT/SiT, DINOv3, Franca and Matryoshka learning, alongside new support for fine-tuning cost arguments. Existing pooling, slot-attention and PEFT positioning is largely retained.

T1.justification: The original attention derivations and complexity arguments are retained. V2 newly defines complementarity through one minus average or maximum off-diagonal cosine similarity and specifies joint Matryoshka losses. It adds no theorem or proof establishing why complementarity emerges.

improvement.justification: V1's complementarity argument relied mainly on qualitative maps; v2 adds quantitative comparisons, matched predictor counts and checks across all 12 MAE layers, substantially strengthening its evidential basis. Clearer FLOP and FT qualifications and explicit applicability limits also improve interpretation. The removed code pointer and new DELF table–prose inconsistency weaken reproducibility, but these limited drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger analysis.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same efficient probing (EP) study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite retitling and extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds backbone evaluations, quantitative attention-complementarity analyses, and attention-mixing and Matryoshka experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification benchmarks, computational-cost comparisons, localization analyses, ablations, and appendix low-shot and layer-wise experiments.

C1.justification: The systematic benchmark, efficient EP mechanism, and complementary-attention contributions remain central. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a claim that EP complements PEFT and that LoRA+EP improves accuracy–parameter trade-offs over either alone. Low-shot and layer-wise gains lose their explicit abstract emphasis, although their results remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning EP's cross-dataset generalization relative to LoRA, diversity regularization accelerating convergence without improving final EP accuracy, and Matryoshka as exploratory rather than matching dimension-specific probes. It expands cached-feature trade-off discussion. However, some new retrieval and convergence generalizations exceed their tables, and Appendix D retains outdated statements about PEFT interaction and retrieval remaining future work.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-page access pointer, explicitly identifies the default depth-1 AbMILP implementation, and documents LoRA target layers, projection matrices, ranks, and the transfer configuration. Retrieval dataset sizes and query construction are specified. Existing optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size, augmentation, and hardware information is retained; the PDF does not establish what resources the project page contains.

E1.justification: The seven classification datasets are retained, but Appendix C.2 substantially expands task coverage: cross-dataset transfer among ImageNet-1K, StanfordCars, and Food101; object localization on ImageNet-1K; and zero-shot retrieval on CUB200 and Cars196. These introduce new task requirements and transfer scenarios using existing datasets.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds evaluated LoRA, BitFit, and LayerNorm-tuning comparators, extending the main comparison beyond pooling/probing methods. Appendix C also adds deeper AbMILP variants and LP with and without Matryoshka as controls. The original probing comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: The original 90-epoch classification protocol is retained. New experiments introduce LoRA layer/projection/rank sweeps, cross-dataset k-NN evaluation, WSOL MaxBoxAccV2 localization, full-dataset retrieval with every image serving as a query and Recall@1–32, and 10-versus-90-epoch checkpoint comparisons. These are added evaluation designs, not evidence that existing benchmarks were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds AbMILP depth ablations (Table 3), cross-dataset generalization analysis (Table 5), an intervention encouraging attention complementarity (Figure 13), convergence analysis (Table 9), and LP Matryoshka controls (Table 12). These test baseline selection, transfer, diversity, training efficiency, and dimensional truncation beyond v2's retained analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The retained standard-deviation visualizations summarize attention across heads, not experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the matched low-shot, layer-wise, attention-mixing, and EP Matryoshka results are retained. Substantial new results include LoRA+EP reaching 76.99% with 850K parameters, localization and retrieval scores, transfer results, and training analyses. These are additional configurations and evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v2. Results include exceptions: BEiTv2 Cars196 retrieval R@1 falls from 48.3 to 44.2 with EP.

M1.justification: The base EP pooling procedure remains unchanged. Section 4.2 adds a hybrid combining EP with LoRA adapters on value projections across backbone layers, and Appendix C.3 tests an auxiliary attention-similarity loss. These are extensions rather than a redesign of EP; the effective-query explanation restates the existing reparameterization.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the introduction and conclusion incorporate PEFT, and selected method and Matryoshka explanations are refined. The key/value ablation moves earlier within Section 4.3, while the overall section structure remains. Conference headers, acknowledgments, affiliation text, and bibliography formatting are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 adds the PEFT trade-off plot and auxiliary-loss learning curves, plus seven tables covering the new evaluations and controls. Figure 1 is redrawn with clearer labels, and Table 1 removes the separate vanilla-MHCA row while retaining its formulation in the text. Existing plots and attention visualizations are largely retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds the two Choe et al. localization-protocol references and develops EP's relationship to PEFT through explicit competition and complementarity claims. LoRA, BitFit, and LayerNorm tuning were already cited in v2. Most other reference changes update publication metadata rather than introduce different prior work.

T1.justification: The underlying equations, complexity arguments, and complementarity definitions are retained. The explicit effective-query identity clarifies algebra already present in v2. Likewise, adding lambda to the illustrative Matryoshka loss reflects weighting already described and evaluated there. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 explicitly left PEFT synergy and applications beyond classification open. v3 substantially strengthens the paper by testing those questions through PEFT comparisons, hybrid configurations, transfer, localization, and retrieval, alongside useful controls. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses: Table 8 contradicts uniformly positive retrieval wording, Table 9 shows MAE EP@10 at 60.0% versus LP@90 at 67.7%, and Appendix D was not reconciled with the added experiments.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attentive-probing study and EP method. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds PEFT comparisons, cross-dataset evaluation, localization, retrieval, and additional ablations.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification benchmarks, efficiency comparisons, low-shot and layer-wise results, and attention analyses in Section 4 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The three central contributions and claims of improved personalization, generalization, and adaptation remain. V2's abstract strengthens the privacy assertion to collaboration 'without privacy risks,' beyond v1's statement that collaboration avoids sharing data. The title and SIMA-to-RELA renaming otherwise preserve the central contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations of public-data robustness, privacy–accuracy tradeoffs, communication frequency, model assignment, and NBS's weaker personalization. V1's ten-client limitation is replaced by limitations concerning untested speech/time-series modalities and broader architectures (v1 Section A.19; v2 Section A.26).

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously missing alignment details: LLaVA-Instruct-158K, 5,000 examples, one epoch, batch size four, Adam, a cosine scheduler, and learning rate 5e-5 (Section A.17). It also adds consolidated model configurations and EMA/sanitization defaults. These substantially improve reproducibility documentation; code release remains promised rather than established.

E1.justification: V2 adds Fed-LLM-Large, combining instruction-following data from Fed-ChatbotIT, Fed-Aya, and Fed-FLAN, and uses ChatbotIT and VisualStorytelling in alignment-data experiments. DRAKE's tasks remain unchanged. Fed-Scope matches the earlier five-client general-capability, mathematics, and coding coverage; its new name alone does not establish added coverage.

E2.justification: The main FL comparator roster remains. V2 adds an adapted NBS comparator in Table 33, adds FedSim, TAKFL, and FedDAT to the corresponding five-client text evaluation, and replaces PerAda with FedDAT in the Fed-Aya comparison (v1 Tables 4 and 14; v2 Table 20). Other newly discussed methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a 52-client Fed-LLM-Large protocol with two tasks per client, four communication rounds, ten local steps, and ROUGE-L evaluation (Section A.6). It also adds mixed Llama/Qwen configurations, randomized client-model assignments, fixed-budget communication/local-step comparisons, and auxiliary-model quantization settings.

E4.justification: V1's rank, block-count, gradient-source, and alignment ablations are retained. V2 substantially extends analysis to public-data size and domain mismatch, randomized model assignment, temperature, EMA, noise and compression sensitivity, lighter auxiliary models, and computational and communication scaling. The main component ablation replaces HFLB with Fed-Scope.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three random seeds and report means with standard deviations in Section 6.1. V2 extends this reporting practice to additional experiments without introducing new confidence intervals, significance tests, or an increased run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds cross-family, 52-client, and extensive sensitivity results. Existing entries also change: FedMosaic's DRAKE-Static Self AAUC changes from 64.24 to 64.64, and HFLB-Dynamic Self Alast from 80.90 to 80.80. The heterogeneous HFLB-Static comparison is removed. Many original DRAKE-Dynamic and appendix results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: RELA retains SIMA's EMA-gradient-based similarity weighting but adds Gaussian noise and random coordinate subsampling to the gradient pipeline (Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1). This changes the information transmitted and used for aggregation. PQ-LoRA's architecture and block-wise alignment approach remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten around collaborative personalization. SIMA becomes RELA, preliminary material is condensed, and appendix analyses are reorganized. The NeurIPS checklist is removed, while ICLR ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements are introduced.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn to show the sanitization pipeline, a CKA example is redisplayed in the main text, and new cost and sensitivity plots are added. Main results and model-validation tables are split or regrouped, with substantial caption and layout changes. Many original appendix graphics are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: New Sections A.22 and A.25 substantially expand positioning against similarity-aware FL, multi-task learning, and alternative multimodal benchmarks. They distinguish RELA from pFedSim, pFedHR, Flashback, FEDLAW, NBS, and RotoGrad, alongside new privacy references and benchmark comparisons. This exceeds the accompanying citation-style changes.

T1.justification: Theorems 1 and 2 and their proofs are retained. Section 4.2.2 specifies rectangular CCA projections and replaces the ordinary inverse with an explicit pseudoinverse in the back-projection formula, a limited mathematical correction. The appendix still retains the older inverse formula.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central heterogeneous-collaboration claim through mixed-family experiments, a 52-client evaluation, and public-data mismatch and randomized-assignment tests absent from v1. These address important validation gaps, while the alignment recipe improves reproducibility. The gains outweigh the omitted heterogeneous HFLB-Static comparison. However, stronger privacy claims remain unvalidated, and Equation 3 and Algorithm 1 disagree about whether noise precedes or follows EMA.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FedMosaic, PQ-LoRA, and DRAKE despite the revised title and SIMA-to-RELA renaming. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds cross-family evaluations, Fed-LLM-Large experiments, and extensive sensitivity and robustness analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, adaptation experiments, client-level results, and ablations on DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Aya, and its named Fed-LLM setup.

C1.justification: V2 makes human behavioral alignment a central contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. It changes v1's broad reasoning-performance improvement claim to matching or exceeding comparable baselines while retaining interpretability. Correlation with human judgments becomes supporting evidence for the central specialization claim, and the introduction's test-time compute-scaling claim is removed.

C2.justification: V2 revises the localizer interpretation to emphasize early language-expert and later world-expert selectivity, and proposes scale-dependent emergence as an explanation for ToM localization. It adds architectural failure conditions, interprets behavioral alignment across scales, and specifies obstacles to neural validation involving suitable fMRI data. The scaling limitation moves from beyond 1B to beyond 3B base models; the earlier test-time-scaling tradeoff discussion disappears.

D1.justification: Core training hyperparameters and the detailed expert-data table are retained. V2 adds the GPT-5 stimulus-generation prompt, human-rating analysis details, and more explicit benchmark metric specifications. It removes the four-A100 hardware disclosure and v1's explicit randomized-routing baseline description, and changes the project access address. Revised sampling prose agrees more closely with the retained appendix mixture; it does not establish a changed training dataset.

E1.justification: V2 adds CogBench psychological tasks, independently human-rated sentences, generated domain-specific probes, HellaSwag and ARC evaluations, and preference training data for DPO. PIQA gains evaluation coverage after already appearing in the training mixture. EWoK, ToMi, and DROP evaluations disappear. The curated expert-training mixture, core reasoning benchmarks, Empathy routing evaluation, and medical benchmarks are retained.

E2.justification: Dense and unspecialized full-block baseline roles persist under the Dense and MoB names. V2 adds a MoB ablation comparator in Figure 7 and a conventional FFN-only MoE comparator in Table 6. Conversely, v1's standard OLMo benchmark comparison against No Experts and General is absent from v2's corresponding benchmark results, although OLMo medical comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 expands model configurations beyond the two original 1B backbones and introduces CogBench evaluation using log-probability choices and human-normalized similarity. Localizer selection changes from the top 1% to 10% of units, and routing aggregation changes from modal expert assignments to aggregation across layers. GPT-4o-defined ablation clusters are replaced by standard MMLU categories and aggregate BBH results. Figure 7 also selects the best result after ablating up to one expert, replacing v1's intuitive benchmark-level selection.

E4.justification: V2 adds correlations between routing and human judgments, DPO robustness tests, and architectural analyses identifying failed specialization in larger MiCRo-MoE models. Expert ablations and qualitative steering examples are expanded and revised. Training-stability analysis now probes all four generated domains instead of Empathy alone. V1's analysis of varying the number of active experts at inference is removed.

E5.justification: Although v1 already displays some error bars, v2 adds explicit standard errors in benchmark tables, pairwise Welch's t-tests in Figure 7, and five random seeds for CogBench experiments. Routing captions also identify variation across samples. These substantially expand statistical reporting; the five-seed statement concerns behavioral evaluation, not repeated model training.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial behavioral, correlation, DPO, MoE, and expanded benchmark results, while removing earlier benchmark and test-time-scaling entries. Reported Llama-1B Dense GSM8K accuracy changes from 35.7 in v1 Table 1 to 36.8 in v2 Table 3, whereas MiCRo remains 34.7. New Figure 15 reports a 0.70 social-routing/mental-state correlation in middle layers. CogBench advantages vary by model scale. Medical results remain numerically unchanged between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 5.

M1.justification: The four-expert full-block architecture and three-stage training curriculum remain intact. V2 adds a MiCRo-MoE adaptation with FFN-only experts and shared attention (Appendix G), plus optional DPO post-training (Appendix F). These are limited extensions of the retained framework; the MoB and MiCRoSFT terminology does not itself change the method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, results narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work moves into the early background section, and performance evaluation follows specialization and behavioral analyses. Dataset and baseline terminology changes throughout, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. These changes exceed the prose needed merely to insert new experiments.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redesigned, and main benchmark comparisons shift from a table to Figure 7's bar charts with significance annotations. Routing, ablation, and localizer displays are rebuilt or expanded, with new behavioral and correlation figures. Medical results move to an appendix table. The unchanged pseudo-labeling prompt and examples are relocated, while the overall figure organization and document layout change substantially.

R1.justification: V2 updates citations for emergent modularity, Switch Transformers, CogBench, human ratings, and DPO, while removing some earlier references such as Continuous Thought Machines and Topoformer. Section 2.2 adds an explicit first-model claim for inducing this brain-network specialization. These refine the retained positioning within modular and brain-inspired language modeling.

T1.justification: V2 Section 5.4 introduces BRE_i = |s_i - 1| / max(1, s_i) and S_BRE = 1 - mean(BRE_i), together with a boundedness claim intended to handle superhuman scores. This is a limited mathematical definition absent from v1. The existing training notation is substantively unchanged, and no broader theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit absence of behavioral validation through CogBench and independent human-rating correlations (Figures 6, 15, and 18). Architectural failure analyses, broader scale testing, and more explicit statistical reporting substantially strengthen evidence for the central specialization argument and clarify its boundaries. Some earlier benchmark coverage and hardware disclosure are lost, and behavioral advantages are not uniform across scales. Nevertheless, the gains in independent validation and characterization of failure conditions outweigh these losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MiCRo framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material that was renamed, redrawn, or relocated.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations and analyses, including CogBench experiments, correlations with human ratings, architectural comparisons, and DPO experiments, alongside retained results.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, expert ablations, routing analyses, neuroscience-localizer experiments, and medical-domain and test-time-scaling results.

C1.justification: The central contribution broadens from superior image/text generation to a systematic conversion framework spanning classification, masked diffusion, and recurrent-depth architectures. v2 adds single-pass recurrent training and up-to-K-fold training-computation savings as main contributions. Its abstract and conclusion emphasize competitive performance across architectures, whereas v1 emphasizes outperforming end-to-end training on its generative tasks.

C2.justification: v2 introduces matching input/output dimensions as an applicability restriction and flags U-Net difficulties, whereas v1 describes U-Nets as ideally suited. It explains the difficulty of ordinary perplexity evaluation and newly acknowledges that concatenated language sequences double sequence memory. It also interprets optimal block count as task-dependent. Conversely, v1's explicit warning about multiplicative autoregressive inference overhead and real-time applicability is removed.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D newly specify numerical EDM defaults, conditioning and attention details, architecture-specific configurations, warmup schedules, and implementation/checkpoint references for added experiments. These disclosures do not establish changes to previously unspecified settings. Some existing reproducibility information is lost: v1 explicitly identifies clean-FID, guidance scale 2.0, layer-forward budget matching, and LM1B prompt-length/filtering rules; v2 does not retain those details.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 image classification, text8 character modeling with masked diffusion, and OpenWebText language generation. CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation and LM1B language generation remain. These additions expand actual task and data coverage beyond v1's image generation and LM1B experiments.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's end-to-end baselines, v2 evaluates ViT and Forward-Forward for classification, MD4 for masked language modeling, Huginn for recurrent-depth generation, and NoProp-DT, NoProp-CT, NoProp-FM, and their associated Backprop comparator on CIFAR-100. These methods appear in reported comparisons, not merely citations. The DiT end-to-end comparator remains.

E3.justification: Main image experiments change from four blocks with overlap 0.1 to three with overlap 0.05; ImageNet also changes VAE checkpoint and learning rate from 1e-4 to 5e-5. Autoregressive text generation changes from 50 to four diffusion steps and adds teacher-model generative perplexity. New protocols include the 10% OpenWebText holdout and Huginn's unequal 15-versus-five-epoch training budgets. These are reported setting changes, not evidence that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 expands the partitioning study to four layer allocations, adds an LM1B block-count sweep, and compares NoProp variants on their CNN architecture to examine continuous-time block independence. The CIFAR-10 block-count analysis remains with revised settings. Conversely, v1's five-setting overlap-sensitivity sweep is removed, although overlap remains part of the method.

E5.justification: Both experimental appendices report the minimum of three FID evaluations. Neither supplies training-seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The three evaluations do not establish three independent training runs, and v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced and added. CIFAR-10 baseline/DiffusionBlocks FID changes from 41.87/41.39 in v1 Table 1 to 39.83/37.20 in v2 Table 2; LM1B MAUVE changes from 0.595/0.779 to 0.50/0.71. These are results under revised settings, not same-setting gains or losses. New classification, text8, Huginn, and OpenWebText results appear; OpenWebText MAUVE favors AR, 0.85 versus 0.82. Ablation values change, and v1's generated examples disappear.

M1.justification: The continuous-noise block-training core remains, but v2 introduces substantive adaptations: noisy label embeddings for ViT classification, masking-schedule partitioning for discrete diffusion, and single-pass denoising training of recurrent-depth networks without block partitioning. Sections 5.1, 5.3, and 5.5 and Appendices A/C describe these procedural extensions; the rewritten conversion recipe also clarifies existing components.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The method becomes a three-step conversion narrative, related work moves before experiments, and experiments are organized by architecture. Appendix material is substantially reorganized, including moving overlap details out of the main method. The title, author list, and document headers also change.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws the overview, adds conversion and architecture-specific diagrams, and presents training/inference algorithms in comparative panels. The partition plot is updated as Figure 4. Tables gain dataset, metric, and layer-allocation structures, while the overlap table and generated-image/text displays are removed. These are substantial visual changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against stage-specific diffusion experts, recurrent-depth models, and discrete language diffusion. Its NoProp discussion shifts toward architectural transfer and experimentally evaluated comparisons. Meanwhile, v1's survey of deep equilibrium models, synthetic gradients, feedback alignment, and target propagation is dropped. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix C adds a masked-diffusion objective and derives its decomposition into independent block losses, with boundaries defined by equal decrements of the unmasking probability. This extends the mathematical treatment beyond v1's continuous VE formulation. Section 3.1 also explicitly assumes dimension-preserving token maps. The shared residual/Euler argument is largely retained.

improvement.justification: The explicit conversion recipe, architecture-specific instructions, and masked-diffusion derivation make the framework substantially more actionable. Direct Forward-Forward/NoProp comparisons address v1's reliance on end-to-end baselines, while broader experiments strengthen support for applicability. These gains outweigh losing the overlap sweep, generated examples, and some evaluation specifics. Neither version supplies measured-memory results or confidence intervals, so important limits on the efficiency and performance evidence remain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiffusionBlocks work despite retitling and substantial expansion. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and generation experiments across several architectures, including CIFAR-100, image generation, text8, LM1B, and OpenWebText, with additional analyses in Tables 6–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet generation results, LM1B language-generation results, and partitioning, overlap, and block-count ablations in Tables 1–5.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction explicitly define criminal potential as harmful behavior under adversarial conditions that could facilitate unlawful activity, refining v2's criminal-capability framing. The framework contribution, unprompted trait-expression claim and headline expression–detection mismatch remain.

C2.justification: Section 6 and Appendix C.1 explicitly interpret criminal potential as a context-conditioned misuse indicator and distinguish exploitation from intrinsic criminal agency. v3 also explains second-person framing and adds observations supporting the previously proposed self-moderation and contextual-dilution explanations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies scenario provenance, GPT-4o rewriting and recognition prompts, simulation and judging templates, persona profiles, and the 6,000-sentence validation sample with its contingency table. It also adds a dataset/framework release statement and access link, plus logging and LLM-use disclosures. These substantially improve documentation of the retained experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate 60 scenarios from ten films across individual planning, collaboration and detective-criminal confrontation. Neutral scenarios and five persona conditions already appear in v2; v3 newly identifies their topics and sources without establishing expanded task coverage.

E2.justification: The same eight models participate in both principal experiments, and the same three models receive persona testing. Qwen-Max in v3 matches the comparator already labeled Qwen-Max in v2's figures, despite v2's setup calling it Qwen2.5-Max.

E3.justification: Five-turn dialogues, default inference settings, paired instruction conditions, information access and CTAR/OTDA metrics are retained. Recognition-prompt variants, exact validation sampling and persona specifications are newly documented, without evidence of revised protocols or reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix C.2 adds extended output cases illustrating trait expression in single-character and multi-turn simulations. Section 4.2 adds model-specific thought-text observations to the existing dialogue-turn analysis. The neutral calibration and persona-sensitivity experiments were already reported in v2.

E5.justification: Both report Cohen's kappa of approximately 0.65, judge accuracy of 91.6%, and Pearson r = -0.776 with p = 0.0237. Appendix D.2 explains the existing agreement calculation; neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or additional significance tests.

E6.justification: Section 4.2 corrects Qwen-Max's Frame-Up increase without instruction from 2.26% to 1.26%, consistent with Table 10's 0.1083 versus 0.1209. Section 5.2 corrects 'most' models exceeding 50% detection accuracy to 'only a subset.' Appendices add numerical persona and neutral-test entries and underlying counts, while the principal plotted findings remain stable.

M1.justification: The five traits, Criminal/Detective/God perspectives, information asymmetry, Thought/Response generation and GPT-4o judging remain unchanged. The later formalizations and prompt templates document the existing framework without establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, scenario-construction explanation, several results paragraphs and discussion are extensively rewritten around adversarial misuse. Scenario construction gains explicit subheadings, and a structured appendix with a contents list provides a substantial new documentation hierarchy.

P2.justification: Figures 2–7 become much smaller displays wrapped by text, with revised captions and bar-chart label orientation; Table 1 is relocated. Appendices add Tables 2–15 and numerous prompt boxes, combining new documentation with numerical redisplays of existing plots.

R1.justification: v3 adds supporting literature on recognition prompting, perspective-taking and role-play, including Wilf et al. and Kong et al., and identifies CoSER as the persona source. The central positioning between ethical evaluation and realistic social interaction remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Beyond v2's verbal criteria and two evaluation equations, Appendix A.2 supplies a formal scenario representation, Intent/Induce/Blame predicates, and conjunctive mathematical definitions for all five traits in Equations 3–7. This substantially expands the mathematical specification without introducing performance theorems.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves a substantial auditability gap in v2, whose referenced appendices were absent, by supplying prompts, scenario provenance, validation counts and detailed sensitivity results, together with a code/data access statement. It also more carefully bounds the misuse interpretation. Smaller figures and unresolved inconsistencies, including Detective criteria requiring THOUGHT information withheld by Section 5.1, limit the gains; nevertheless, the evaluation becomes substantially more transparent and reproducible.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRISON study, with matching methods, experiments and readable figures and equations. v2 ends after the references despite citing appendices; v3 supplies Appendices A–G. These constitute newly available documentation in the supplied pair.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and supplies detailed numerical results, validation counts, persona comparisons and simulation outputs in its appendices.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and Figures 3–7 report original eight-model experiments on criminal-trait generation and detection, alongside human validation and supplementary checks.

C1.justification: The framework, lower-variance estimator, and ICL contributions remain central. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace the TD3-focused empirical summary with competitive or sometimes better performance across continuous, native discrete, and hybrid control. Hybrid evaluation is no longer future work, and the introduction drops v1's claim of performance without hyperparameter tuning.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that ICL is generally biased because it omits importance weights, explaining its updates as off-distribution learning (Section 4.3). Appendix B adds substantive applicability discussion, including loss of exploitable discrete-action structure and possible planning extensions. Conversely, v1's warning that clipped Gaussian actions can disadvantage AC-RP disappears, although clipping remains documented.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's CleanRL implementation provenance and existing settings, v2 reports a project-specific code release and reproducibility statement. Appendices D–G document new CNN/action encoding, benchmark adaptations, deterministic hybrid evaluation, extensive comparator hyperparameters, and EAC pseudocode. These substantially expand the information available for reproduction; the code link itself was not externally verified.

E1.justification: v2 retains the bandits and 20 MuJoCo/DMC environments in continuous and discretized forms, while adding four Gym tasks, five MinAtar games with visual observations, and seven parameterized-action hybrid tasks. These substantially expand the evaluated domains, observation types, and action requirements beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds SAC and PPO to continuous-control comparisons and PPO to the retained discretized-control comparisons. Its new Gym/MinAtar evaluations include EAC, DSAC, and DQN, while hybrid evaluations compare against PATD3, PDQN, and HHQN (Figures 3, 5, and 6). AC-RP/AC-LR/AC-ST are retained under reordered names.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 500,000-step Gym and 5-million-step MinAtar budgets, benchmark-specific network and training settings, and hybrid evaluation using highest-probability discrete actions and continuous means, reporting evaluation returns or success rates (Appendices D–E). Existing MuJoCo/DMC budgets remain one million steps. For retained bandit policy evaluation, the reported batch size changes from 32 in v1 Appendix B.2 to the Table 4 default of 8 in v2 Appendix D.2; this establishes a documentation-level setting revision, not necessarily a rerun.

E4.justification: The existing ICL-versus-standard-update ablation is extended to Gym, MinAtar, and hybrid control (v2 Figures 7, 14, and 16). Representative bandit critic landscapes and discrete training checkpoints are revised. The underlying analysis questions remain largely unchanged, and the actor-target-network and alternative-learning-rate analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use 10 seeds for control tasks, 50 for bandit optimization, and 95% bootstrap intervals with 10,000 resamples. v2 additionally specifies pooling across seed-environment trials and adds two-sided paired t-tests within settings and across seven setting means (Appendix D.8, Table 1). The Gym row's n=30 is unexplained relative to the stated four tasks and 10 seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new tasks and comparators. Figure 3 shows the newly evaluated SAC ahead of DA-AC on aggregate MuJoCo performance; Figure 6 shows DA-AC with the highest hybrid-control aggregate. Table 1 newly reports an across-setting ICL mean difference of 0.0508 with p=0.0088. Bandit critic landscapes are also replaced, while the principal retained continuous/discretized-control findings largely persist.

M1.justification: DPPG/DPAC become DA-PG/DA-AC with the central gradient and ICL updates retained. v2 introduces benchmark-specific adaptations: CNN-feature/action outer-product encoding for MinAtar and disabling double Q-networks for Gym (Appendix D.5). Appendix B also specifies optional, unevaluated entropy-regularized update and reward-shaping variants.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, terminology is systematically changed to distributions-as-actions, and empirical summaries and explanatory passages are edited. Detailed bandit discussion moves to the appendix, and hyperparameters, plots, and pseudocode are reorganized. The main framework-to-estimator-to-ICL narrative and much of the existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn; Figure 4 expands from four to six panels with a shared legend; and Figure 5 replaces its per-task difference panel with a broader four-benchmark aggregate display. v2 adds hybrid-control displays, a statistical-test table, and numerous configuration tables, expands and rearranges appendix learning curves, and relocates bandit plots. These constitute substantial visual and layout revisions.

R1.justification: v2 adds an extensive related-work appendix covering discrete, continuous, hybrid, and representation-driven approaches. It explicitly compares its formulation with Todorov's concurrent D-MDP work and distinguishes its decision boundary from RepRL, positioning its contribution around practical algorithms and empirical breadth. This substantially expands research positioning beyond v1's shorter discussions.

T1.justification: The gradient theorem, variance propositions, and convergence bound are retained, including corrections to the cited DPG analysis already present in v1. v2 makes Proposition 3.2's premises more explicit by placing continuity conditions in Assumption 3.1 and explicitly requiring U to be continuous. Much of this consolidates assumptions previously stated in Assumption 4.1, rather than introducing new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its diverse-action-space claim primarily through continuous tasks and their discretizations, leaving hybrid evaluation to future work. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence with native discrete, visual, and hybrid tasks and stronger comparators (Sections 5.1–5.4). Expanded reproducibility information, closer research positioning, and explicit acknowledgment of ICL bias further improve transparency. These gains outweigh the removed RP-clipping caveat and the unresolved Gym sample-count inconsistency in Table 1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same framework, policy-gradient estimator, and interpolated critic learning algorithm, despite the changed title and terminology. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and additionally reports Gym, MinAtar, and hybrid-control experiments, expanded baseline comparisons, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original bandit simulations, continuous and discretized MuJoCo/DMC evaluations, and critic-learning and actor-target-network ablations.

C1.justification: v1 presents NAPE as an introduced contribution; v3 explicitly treats it as a practical default rather than a contribution. The abstract and conclusion also broaden the central empirical claims to preserving short-context performance and achieving language-model extrapolation at eight times training length, beyond the retained synthetic extrapolation claims.

C2.justification: Sections 5.2 and H.9 add substantive applicability qualifications concerning near-random downstream performance, PubMed degradation at eightfold extrapolation, and difficult retrieval settings. They interpret RoPE base-frequency adjustment's short-context costs as supporting NAPE's robustness. The conclusion replaces v1's explicit multi-phase, production-scale validation caveat with more optimistic extrapolation from the 420M experiments.

D1.justification: New Appendix G.3 documents language-model dimensions, layers, heads, torchtitan, tokenizer, optimizer, training steps, warm-up/cooldown, learning rates, batch size, and precision. v3 also adds a reproducibility statement explicitly naming FlashAttention-2 and changes the advertised code reference from bigfish to asentmax. These are substantial additions to the documented reproduction setup.

E1.justification: v3 adds DCLM-Edu training and evaluation on LAMBADA, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-C, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, The Pile's ArXiv/PubMed subsets, and RULER S-NIAH-1/2. This substantially expands coverage beyond the retained synthetic tasks and FineWeb scaling analysis into natural-text modeling and retrieval.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates Top-K attention on Max Retrieval, MQMTAR, Copy, Reverse, and Sort, and Stick-Breaking Attention on the latter four tasks. The MQMTAR comparison drops SEntmax (v1 Table 6; v3 Table 9), although it remains in other comparisons. RoPE comparisons omitted from the main table remain in the appendix.

E3.justification: The added language-model protocol uses 420M-parameter models trained for 7B tokens at length 2048, with evaluation extending to 16K, 500 documents per long-text dataset, and 500 RULER samples per length. Appendix G.3 specifies exponential ALiBi slopes and RoPE testing with a 500,000 base frequency. The retained scaler-fit analysis also changes its logarithmic control from beta log n to delta + beta log n.

E4.justification: New Tables 16–17 compare NAPE, RoPE, and RoPE with adjusted base frequency, testing extrapolation robustness alongside short-context costs. Appendix H adds Top-K sensitivity comparisons, including fixed and length-dependent K on Reverse, while Section 4.1 revises the scaler-fit analysis. Existing representation, gradient, alpha/gamma, RoPE-scaling, and attention-map analyses largely remain.

E5.justification: Both versions' Appendix G.2 reports the single best synthetic model selected across three random seeds and various learning rates. v3 introduces no additional run-count or uncertainty-reporting practice for its language-model results. Confidence intervals, standard deviations, and significance tests are not newly supplied.

E6.justification: The MQMTAR tables change reported NAPE accuracy at 65K from 76.7% to 95.3% for ASEntmax and from 1.0% to 26.7% for SSMax (v1 Table 6; v3 Table 9), without explaining the update history. Numerous comparator and language-model results are added, including ASEntmax's 10.77 ArXiv perplexity and 97.4% S-NIAH-1 accuracy at 16K. Some v3 MQMTAR entries disagree between Tables 1 and 9, limiting precise comparisons.

M1.justification: The ASEntmax scaling rule, content-dependent per-head beta/gamma projections, and alpha-entmax transformation are retained (v1 Equations 9–10; v3 Equations 8–9). The hybrid NoPE/ALiBi design also remains. New model configurations and NAPE's changed contribution status do not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: it refocuses the abstract and conclusion, consolidates Section 3.3, folds the standalone NAPE section into experimental setup and positioning, divides experiments into synthetic and language-model subsections, and exchanges Appendices C and D. Expanded related work, a reproducibility statement, and an AI-assistant disclosure accompany these structural revisions.

P2.justification: Five language-model tables are added and Table 1 is rebuilt with new comparator rows and without its RoPE blocks. Figure 1 replaces the Reverse panel with the previously separate Max Retrieval comparison, and the scaler-fit figure is redrawn. The redundant main-text representation/gradient figure disappears while its appendix evidence remains. Typography, running headers, and figure/table placement also change throughout.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds an attention-scaling discussion covering YaRN, InfoScale, and Scale-invariant Attention, and expands positioning around KERPLE, FIRE, Stick-Breaking, Top-K, and chunk-based attention. NAPE is explicitly connected to Hard-ALiBi's zero-slope configuration instead of claimed as novel. Publication updates to retained works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: v3's consolidated Proposition 2 replaces v1's main-text preservation bound 'for any constant c > 0' with existence of a positive constant, matching the earlier appendix's quantification, and explicitly states bounded-support assumptions. The detailed counterexamples and proofs are otherwise retained after the Appendix C/D exchange. This is a localized formal refinement.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited direct evidence for natural-text applications: the earlier FineWeb experiment analyzed scaling parameters, whereas Section 5.2 and Tables 2–4 and 16–17 directly evaluate language modeling, retrieval, and extrapolation tradeoffs. Added sparse comparators and withdrawal of the NAPE novelty claim strengthen the paper's support and positioning. Reporting problems temper these gains: for example, Top-K MQMTAR accuracy at fourfold length is 6.2% in Table 1 but 99.9% in Table 9, and uncertainty reporting remains limited. These issues weaken exact margins without outweighing the broader empirical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ASEntmax research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content. Internal numerical inconsistencies limit particular result interpretations but do not prevent identifying the revisions.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 420M-parameter language-model evaluations reporting downstream accuracy, long-context perplexity, and RULER retrieval performance in Section 5.2 and Appendix H.9.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-task results, representation and gradient experiments, and attention-scaling analyses from a 120M-parameter model trained on FineWeb, including results in Appendices C, F, and H.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain MLE-Live, CoMind and community-driven iterative exploration. v2 emphasizes specialized multi-agent collaboration and updates the headline performance claims to the full benchmark and new live competitions. It drops v1's explicit contribution claim about overcoming context-window limitations and its introductory human-evaluation endorsement. These refine the contribution framing while preserving the central research thesis.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about contamination from public datasets and failure caused by unreliable popularity signals, validation on only ten examples, saturated feedback and inadequate component assessment (Appendix F). It also attributes live progress to distinct exploration and refinement phases. v1's report-only interaction limitation and broader-impact discussion are removed, while the earlier explanation of Seq2Seq failures under runtime constraints remains.

D1.justification: Appendices G-H add role prompts, evaluator scripts' specifications, 90/10 splitting and stratification instructions, monitoring prompts, generated code and detailed example hyperparameters. Appendices B and E add token/cost measurements and per-competition resource inventories. These greatly expand documentation beyond v1's brief setup. However, v1's explicit CoMind code-release statement and repository link are omitted; this does not establish that the repository became unavailable.

E1.justification: The 20-task, seven-category evaluation expands to all 75 MLE-Bench competitions across low, medium and high difficulty, covering additional requirements such as segmentation, object detection and question answering. The original four live competitions are replaced by eight different competitions, including MABe Behavior, Impostor Hunt and RSNA Aneurysm. The original 20-task coverage remains as an ablation study.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds comparisons with Neo, R&D-Agent, ML-Master, OpenHands and MLAB, using attributed leaderboard results. AIDE and its Code/RAG variants remain in the 20-task comparison. The live evaluation replaces v1's AIDE comparison with comparisons against the strongest public kernels.

E3.justification: v1's principal setting uses 4 vCPUs, five hours per competition, one hour per execution and 20 implementation steps. v2's main setting specifies 32 vCPUs, 24 hours, five-hour executions, 30 steps per coder and four parallel agents. Its main leaderboard comparison includes heterogeneous backend models, whereas the retained 20-task study keeps a common o4-mini backend and the five-hour/4-vCPU budget. Appendix A also introduces additional code-quality metrics.

E4.justification: The public-resource ablation and retrospective time-course analyses are retained. v2 adds cyclomatic complexity, Pylint and Halstead analyses, live validation trajectories, a kernel-vote distribution analysis, an Impostor Hunt failure analysis and a detailed denoising workflow case study. Conversely, v1 Section 5.5's expert assessment of solution novelty is removed; automated code-complexity measurements assess a different question.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly reports means and standard deviations for token usage and cost across 75 competitions, including cost of $32.25 ± $19.43. Appendix H discloses seed 42 in example splitting and training code. These additions do not establish additional repeated runs; benchmark performance still lacks repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds a 36.00% medal rate on 75 tasks, compared with Neo's 34.22%, and new live standings averaging top 7.35%. These are expanded or replaced evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1. The retained category win rates are unchanged, including CoMind's 0.668 overall. Human novelty rankings and explicit valid-submission results disappear. Code-length assignments also change: image-classification AIDE changes from 5192.1 to 4624.3, with AIDE+Code receiving the former AIDE value; the PDFs do not explain this apparent label swap.

M1.justification: v1 specifies a four-stage loop with idea/report pools and report-level collaboration. v2 expands the specified system to share kernels, datasets and checkpoints through a resource-dependency graph, and introduces dedicated evaluation and execution-monitoring components. These change shared state, coder inputs and execution control beyond merely assigning names to existing roles; the underlying ideation and ReAct loop remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, benchmark description and method exposition are extensively rewritten, and the title gains the CoMind prefix. The former unified experimental section is reorganized into benchmark evaluation, ablation and analytical sections, with substantial supporting material organized into Appendices A-H. This changes the narrative structure beyond simply appending new results.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the workflow diagram and replaces the introductory radar chart with paired comparison plots. It adds difficulty-based benchmark tables, live leaderboard displays, validation trajectories and resource visualizations. The original ablation table is incorporated into a revised bar chart that omits the valid-submission panel, while the code-length table is expanded and moved into Appendix A.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to ML-Master, R&D-Agent and Wuchty et al.'s study of teamwork, and positions CoMind against newer competing systems. The worked example also references CBAM. The main related-work discussion and its distinction between isolated agents and community-aware research remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 newly defines the evolving community state (K_t, D_t, T_t) and a resource-dependency graph T_0 = (V, E), adding a formal representation of relationships absent from v1's idea/report-pool account. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees, and v2 adds no theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evaluation coverage and sparse operational documentation through the full 75-task evaluation, detailed prompts and code, evaluation instructions, cost reporting and concrete failure analysis. These make generality, implementation and failure boundaries much more assessable. The gains outweigh the loss of the human novelty study and code-release link, although the apparent code-length label swap weakens reporting reliability. The heterogeneous-backend leaderboard comparison also leaves the architecture's independent contribution unresolved.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MLE-Live and CoMind. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection support comparison of the methods, results and displays. v1 ends after its references; v2 includes Appendices A-H. The substantial revision does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: Sections 5-7 report CoMind results on 75 past and eight ongoing competitions, alongside the retained 20-task evaluation. The appendices add original code analyses, resource measurements, validation trajectories and case studies.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original experiments on 20 past competitions, a public-resource ablation, submissions to four ongoing competitions and human novelty assessments.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction redefine the contribution from a single compact model with a model-soup stage to a model series with progressive contrastive distillation. The introduction additionally claims industrial generalization, robustness at reduced embedding dimensions, and improved discrimination and cluster separation. The broad claim of competitive performance below 1B parameters is retained.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantive interpretations of KL as the primary learning signal, component complementarity, and temperature effects through overly peaked or smoothed teacher distributions. Appendix C distinguishes tasks tolerating small embeddings from retrieval/reranking tasks needing higher dimensions. The earlier explanations of unsuccessful model soup, latency equivalence, and limited exploration under computational constraints disappear.

D1.justification: Appendix A/Table 9 newly document Adam, warm-up settings, teacher-embedding caching, and detailed distillation settings. Section 3.4.1 newly describes 550k persona-based synthetic examples, although their relationship to the unchanged dataset table is unspecified. Conversely, v3 replaces named Ascend 910B/A800 hardware with generic GPU reporting and removes the explicit model/code URLs and MTEB-overlap-filtering statement; these omissions do not establish changed availability or filtering practice.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond MTEB to real-user Chinese customer-service FAQ retrieval and game-documentation search in Appendix B. These introduce industrial input conditions and domain-generalization coverage absent from v1. The 31 Chinese and 56 English MTEB tasks and the tabulated training datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The MTEB comparisons retain the earlier baselines and add Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and, for English, NV-Embed-v2 in Tables 2–4. The new industrial comparison also evaluates Qwen3-Embedding-8B. These are targeted additions within the existing comparison landscape of general-purpose embedding models.

E3.justification: New distillation experiments introduce a one-epoch, approximately 24k-step stage, learning rate 1e-5, KL temperature 0.05, and contrastive/KL weights of 0.3/0.7. Additional protocols include temperature and embedding-dimension sweeps and industrial evaluation using MRR and Recall at 1, 5, and 10. The retained MTEB task selection and original pre-training/fine-tuning budgets remain stable.

E4.justification: v3 retests focal reweighting on V2.5 and adds ablations of negative mixing, bidirectional attention, adding example-based labeling, contrastive versus KL objectives, and temperature. Appendices B–E add industrial generalization tests, dimensionality/MKL ablations, HotpotQA cases, and UMAP analyses. v1's model-soup and inference-latency studies are removed.

E5.justification: v3 adds a fitted logarithmic relationship between baseline model size and performance in Figure 1, plus boxplots summarizing seven hard-negative scores per case in Figure 4. These introduce descriptive statistical summaries, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across evaluation runs.

E6.justification: The original V1/V2 benchmark entries, including the full per-dataset tables, are retained. v3 adds the distilled V2.5 variant with Chinese/English MTK scores of 70.93/69.33, alongside retained V2 scores of 68.15/67.47. It also adds industrial, ablation, dimensionality, and qualitative results, while removing the original model-soup, latency, and V2-specific focal-ablation entries.
