M1.justification: The proposed third training stage changes from model-soup parameter averaging to contrastive distillation from Qwen3-Embedding-8B, producing KaLM-Embedding-V2.5. v3 combines contrastive and KL objectives and extends the existing matryoshka training to KL loss. The undistilled V2 variant and its bidirectional Qwen2-0.5B architecture, mean pooling, focal reweighting, and negative mixing remain.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, contributions become an explicit four-part list, and method explanations gain descriptive subheadings. Experimental settings move from Section 4.1 to Appendix A, while the original appendices become F/G alongside new analysis appendices. Training-data prose is substantially condensed and reorganized, and the author/affiliation block changes.

P2.justification: The original training diagram is expanded into contrastive-learning and distillation workflows. v3 adds a performance overview, a training-stage diagram, case-study boxplots, and UMAP panels. Benchmark tables gain model rows/columns, new analysis and hyperparameter tables appear, and headers, typography, caption placement, and table formatting change throughout.

R1.justification: The related-work framework remains centered on general text embeddings and adapting LLMs. Targeted additions include Hinton's distillation work, Gecko, Persona Hub, and embedding/data-synthesis surveys; model-soup, LM-Cocktail, LoRA, and FlashAttention-2 references are removed. The introduction also places greater emphasis on open, reproducible, commercially usable research.

T1.justification: v3 introduces the mathematical definition of teacher/student similarity distributions and their KL objective in Equation 8. Equation 6 also corrects the mixing-weight normalization from a sum over batch size N to the M hard negatives. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 offered limited direct validation of several central training choices. v3's Tables 5–8 test those components and compare distillation against additional contrastive training, while Appendices B–C provide evidence about industrial generalization and dimensionality tradeoffs. This substantially strengthens the empirical justification and practical guidance. Removing latency measurements and some reproducibility disclosures is a loss, and repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, but the added controls and documented distillation procedure provide a clear overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KaLM-Embedding-V2 research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained methods and results can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark results and reports additional V2.5 results, controlled ablations, industrial retrieval evaluations, dimensionality experiments, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original KaLM benchmark results, model-soup experiments, attention-latency measurements, and a focal-reweighting ablation in Tables 2–9.

C1.justification: The central checkpoint-based unlearning and ideal-model-recovery claims remain. V2 qualifies blanket superiority as competitive performance with frequent improvements, narrows the highlighted checkpoint-gap claim from trillions to hundreds of billions of tokens, and replaces the prominent no-retain-set contribution with claims about membership inference and privacy metrics.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of checkpoint availability, why earlier vectors may better isolate data influence, and tradeoffs between ideal-model recovery and aggressive content removal. It gives benchmark-dependent checkpoint limits, interprets repeated exposure as favoring checkpoints before first exposure, and acknowledges possible MUSE/pretraining overlap in Appendix I. These substantially expand v1's limitations and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 documents more detailed baseline search grids, MUSE vector-training recipes, and C4 exposure settings, and reports two A100 GPUs instead of four RTX A5000s. It additionally describes supplementary reproduction scripts while retaining the repository link. However, v1's selected α/β table disappears, and Appendix E inconsistently names the MUSE Llama model as Llama-3-8B versus Llama-3.1-8B in Table 9.

E1.justification: V2 adds MUSE-Books document unlearning and TOFU scenarios involving subsequent C4 training and repeated exposure to forget data. Conversely, v1's combined TOFU-to-RESTOR experiment assessing collateral damage to TOFU knowledge is replaced by RESTOR-only evaluation. These substantially change the domains and training-history scenarios tested.

E2.justification: TOFU comparisons add SatImp and UNDIAL; the Llama-3.1-8B comparison also adds RMU and GradDiff beyond v1's NPO comparison. RMU is omitted from the corresponding 1B forget01 table. Appendix H adds checkpoint-augmented comparators. Task Vector corresponds to v1's final-checkpoint MSA variant, so that name alone does not establish a new baseline.

E3.justification: V2 changes standard TOFU training to five epochs, replaces validation on 10% of forget questions with a 15%/85% validation/test split, and selects configurations using a multi-metric score instead of Forget Quality. Searches are expanded, OLMo-2-1B is replaced by OLMo-2-7B, forget05 and Extraction Strength are added, and retain-set ROUGE is dropped. New MUSE and temporal-exposure experiments introduce additional protocols.

E4.justification: Appendices F-H newly test continued training after target exposure, repeated target exposure, and whether competing algorithms benefit from historical checkpoints. Checkpoint-distance analysis extends across benchmarks. V1's explicit TOFU no-retain-vector comparisons, longer-training ablation, and parameter-sensitivity plots are removed. The 200-example judge validation is retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or error bars. Forget Quality p-values remain in v2's appendix, and both versions report the same 200-judgment check with 96% agreement. No new uncertainty-estimation practice is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 replaces substantial TOFU and RESTOR results and adds MUSE and temporal-exposure findings. For Llama-3.1-8B forget10, MSAinstruct recovery/retention changes from 0.43/0.97 in v1 Table 9 to 0.46/0.91 in v2 Table 2. Training and selection settings differ, so these are revised results rather than a demonstrated same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The core MSA procedure—subtracting a checkpoint-derived forget vector and optionally adding a retain vector—is unchanged. Appendix H introduces a limited procedural adaptation for baselines: perform unlearning at an earlier checkpoint, then transfer its scaled parameter update to the target model.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and substantially reorganized: v1's separate evaluation and experimental sections become an Experiments section followed by a finding-led Results and Discussion section. The introduction and benchmark descriptions are extensively rewritten, preliminaries are separated, and the appendices are reorganized. Ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with example outputs, and the earlier ROUGE example table is replaced by two illustrated figures containing different examples. Checkpoint and sensitivity plots are removed. Results tables gain percentage annotations, color highlighting, and reorganized columns, alongside new benchmark and analysis tables and a conference-style layout.

R1.justification: The new extended related-work appendix compares MSA with Amnesiac Unlearning, Unrolling SGD, and Rewind-to-Delete, explicitly acknowledging earlier use of previous model states for forgetting. It positions MSA through post-hoc applicability, storage and computational requirements, and LLM-scale evaluation. Additional citations support new baselines, metrics, and checkpoint-access discussions.

T1.justification: V2 introduces nonstandard mathematical definitions of composite validation scores in Appendices C.3 and E. The core MSA equations remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. The printed MUSE score includes (1−KnowMem_r)^2, which conflicts with its stated higher-is-better retention objective.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for historical-checkpoint unlearning by testing subsequent training, repeated exposure, and checkpoint-augmented competitors, addressing important gaps in v1's evaluation. Its expanded comparison with earlier trajectory-based methods also improves research positioning. MUSE adds privacy and memorization evidence beyond factual QA. These gains outweigh the removed ablations and sensitivity results, although the contradictory retention term in Appendix E leaves the MUSE model-selection procedure partly unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MSA research despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable. Revised experimental settings can be distinguished from retained content.

after.justification: V2 reports original TOFU, RESTOR, and MUSE-Books results, including experiments on repeated exposure, subsequent training, and checkpoint-augmented baselines.

before.justification: V1 reports original TOFU and RESTOR experiments, checkpoint-distance evaluations, ablations, and a manual validation of its GPT-4o judge.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution summary qualify one-epoch pretraining as near single-pass. The abstract also changes zero cost to near zero cost and describes reduced reliance on instruction tuning and benchmark evaluation. The central local-grokking and pathway-monitoring claims, including the conclusion, remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations that correlations reflect intrinsic pretraining dynamics rather than LoRA artifacts, and that pathway convergence reflects local semantic organization rather than global routing balance or regularization. Appendix E.6 further interprets nanoMoE results as evidence of an architecture-intrinsic MoE property, extending the earlier mechanistic explanation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 substantially expands grouping and matching details: delta=0.05, domain-specific epsilon selection targeting 20–25% memorization, test-group criteria, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, and SciPy Hungarian matching. v4 also specifies the main routing cutoff of 0.7 and nanoMoE budgets, H100 hardware, Qwen3 filtering, and repository information. Conversely, Section 4.2 drops the explicit token-averaging description of consistency weights.

E1.justification: Appendix E.6 adds OpenWebText training data and a filtered commonsense subset, with evaluation on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, and OpenBookQA. This substantially extends the evaluated data and task coverage into additional science reasoning and contextual completion benchmarks. The original four-domain datasets and synthetic Gaussian-cluster experiment remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains training loss, moving-average training loss, and validation loss as comparators. The added LoRA and nanoMoE comparisons reuse existing loss comparators. Routing entropy is examined as a possible explanation for pathway distance, rather than evaluated as a competing generalization monitor.

E3.justification: New protocols include training 55M-parameter nanoMoE on approximately 25B tokens for 50k iterations, sampling ten checkpoints, and evaluating them zero-shot. Additional settings include rank-64 LoRA, routing and memorization threshold sweeps, and an entropy analysis of 141,530 pairs. These supplement existing experiments; the revised near-single-pass description does not establish that OLMoE pretraining was rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices E.1–E.5 add tests of routing-threshold sensitivity, LoRA-rank dependence, and memorization-threshold sensitivity. They also examine math–code pathway distances and the relationship between routing entropy and edit distance, testing possible global routing explanations. These robustness and mechanism checks were absent from v3.

E5.justification: Both versions report correlation significance through p-value coloring and retain Appendix C.4's independent random-router runs and Figure 8's standard-deviation band. The new correlation tables follow the existing reporting approach; no additional repeated-run or uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Original results in Tables 1 and 3 and Figures 1–8 are retained. Table 4 adds rank-64 commonsense Pearson correlations of -0.9927 for pathway distance and 0.9559 for consistency. Table 5 adds nanoMoE correlations across four benchmarks, and Figure 13 reports entropy–distance r=0.244. Threshold robustness and cross-domain findings are also new. These are additional results under additional settings, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The pathway edit-distance construction, routing-embedding consistency formula, and monitoring approach are retained. Specifying the routing threshold and elaborating group construction document existing procedures. Applying the same metrics to nanoMoE introduces no new proposed method component.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are largely retained, with targeted wording qualifications, expanded explanations, and appendix cross-references. New material is organized into Appendix B.1 and E.1–E.6, followed by an LLM usage statement. This is an extension rather than an extensive rewrite or reorganization.

P2.justification: v4 adds Figures 9–15 and Tables 4–5, including multipanel sensitivity plots, a cross-domain plot, an entropy hexbin display, and nanoMoE dynamics and correlation displays. Original figures are retained, Figure 2's caption is expanded, and existing figures and tables move with text reflow.

R1.justification: Section 4.1 newly distinguishes Lo et al.'s static depth-dependent specialization from the paper's dynamic pretraining analysis. Additional benchmark and model references support the nanoMoE experiments. The related-work section's substantive narrative and first-study positioning otherwise remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix C retain the same routing kernel, fixed-routing and NTK assumptions, generalization bound, and proof. The added empirical analyses introduce no substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 left central threshold and instruction-tuning choices untested and relied on one practical MoE implementation. v4 substantially strengthens the evidence through targeted sensitivity tests, checks of alternative routing explanations, and a second-model study with zero-shot evaluation. Appendix B.1 also makes the core grouping procedure substantially easier to assess and reproduce. The architecture-intrinsic interpretation remains broader than two models establish, but this overreach does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and methodological transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OLMoE grokking study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison; v4 retains the original material and adds further analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds sensitivity tests, cross-domain and entropy analyses, and experiments training and evaluating nanoMoE.

before.justification: v3 reports original OLMoE checkpoint analyses, pathway–generalization correlations, synthetic MoE experiments in Appendix C.4, and parameter dynamics in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the first neural multigraph-routing solvers, their two construction strategies and competitive performance with different scalability tradeoffs. v5's introduction additionally claims that naive extensions of existing single-objective asymmetric solvers perform poorly, extending v3's comparison of existing methods' supported inputs and tasks.

C2.justification: v5 adds explanations involving parallel-edge permutation invariance and graph transformations, and explains the existing omission of MatNet from large-instance evaluations. Appendix H.4 newly attributes the retained FIX10-100 weakness to the selection decoder's growing action space; H.5 qualifies objective-count scalability with the new GMS-DH XASY100 failure. Earlier training-cost and pruning-context limitations remain.

D1.justification: v5 replaces the promised future code release with a stated public implementation link. It also specifies uniform training-preference sampling, evenly spaced evaluation preferences, and construction details for GRBM/GOBM and the added tasks. Existing hardware, hyperparameters, curriculum and parameter counts remain documented as before. Repository contents were not independently verified.

E1.justification: v5 adds MGMOCVRP on FLEX2/FIX2, combining capacity constraints with two conflicting total-distance objectives. It also adds tri-objective MOTSP and MGMOTSP across several distributions and instance sizes (Tables 11, 16–17). v3's multigraph experiments covered TSP-family problems, and all its evaluations were bi-objective.

E2.justification: v5 adds evaluated GREAT-based GRBM and GOAL-based GOBM comparators, including augmented variants, across retained routing tasks and MGMOCVRP (Table 6). It also introduces HGS for MGMOCVRP (Tables 1 and 11). The existing MBM, Euclidean CNH, evolutionary algorithms and relevant heuristics remain.

E3.justification: The existing bi-objective evaluation and training protocols are retained. Added tri-objective experiments use 105 heuristic subproblems and 105 or 1035 neural preferences, with three-dimensional hypervolume reference points (Tables 16–17; Appendix E). MGMOCVRP also receives task-specific reference points. These extend protocols for new experiments rather than revise the earlier evaluations.

E4.justification: The learned-versus-simple pruning and reward ablations, training analyses and zero-shot tests already appear in v3 and are retained. v5 extends the pre-pruning ablation to MGMOCVRP (Table 1) and compares 105 versus 1035 neural preferences on tri-objective tasks (Tables 16–17), adding evidence about pruning and inference-budget sensitivity.

E5.justification: Both versions average hypervolume over test instances and report runtimes. Neither reports repeated training-run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals or statistical significance tests; the added results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Matched earlier benchmark results retain their values and runtimes, but v5 adds substantial results for new tasks and comparators. For example, MGMOCVRP FLEX2-50 yields HV 0.89 for HGS and 0.86 for augmented GMS-EB (Table 1). Tri-objective XASY100 yields 0.64 for GMS-DH versus 0.68 for MBM with 105 preferences (Table 16). These are newly reported settings, not performance changes under v3's settings.

M1.justification: Section 4 and the matched architecture/training appendices retain the GREAT encoders, edge-based and dual-head decoders, preference conditioning, REINFORCE objectives and curriculum. The additional tasks and expanded implementation explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around encoder and decoder incompatibilities, and multigraph-related discussion is consolidated into Section 2.2. A dedicated Extended Motivation appendix reorganizes the architectural rationale, graph-transformation alternatives and technical novelty. Experimental subsections and appendices are reorganized, although most method exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column conference formatting. Architecture diagrams are redrawn with example graphs and autoregressive loops, and a graph-transformation figure is added. Table 1 gains MGMOCVRP, new comparison/result tables appear, and v3's separate time-window tables are merged into v5 Table 12. Training plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Appendix A.2 and new Appendix B substantially expand research positioning, including POCCO, EFormer and hierarchical graph-partitioning work. v5 distinguishes encoding incompatibility from theoretically extendable edge-based methods and develops explicit novelty comparisons against prior AR/NAR combinations and dual-decoder systems. This goes beyond adding citations to the existing review.

T1.justification: v5 explicitly requires the Chebyshev reference value to lie strictly below the minimum of each objective, whereas v3 only calls it an ideal value. New Appendix B.2 provides graph-size and decoding-complexity arguments for line-graph and virtual-node transformations. The Pareto definitions, scalarizations and Proposition 1 remain otherwise unchanged; its proof is still omitted.

improvement.justification: v3's broad applicability claims relied on TSP-family multigraph experiments and one general asymmetric neural baseline. v5 adds capacity-constrained multigraph routing, three-objective tests, two neural comparators and HGS, substantially strengthening tests of generality and comparative effectiveness (Tables 1, 6, 11, 16–17). The expanded architectural rationale and explicit failure cases also improve the argument's clarity and qualification. Evaluation remains synthetic and lacks statistical uncertainty, but these retained limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GMS-EB and GMS-DH research, despite the changed title and format. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 retains those original experiments and adds multigraph capacitated vehicle-routing results, additional neural comparisons and three-objective evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original routing experiments, including hypervolume and runtime comparisons, pruning ablations, training curves and zero-shot generalization results.

C1.justification: v2 introduces counteracting Anti-DreamBooth as a fourth contribution and highlights it in the introduction and conclusion, claiming partial recovery of protected concepts and an overlooked defense weakness. The original SCP diagnosis and training-free TEA contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets Anti-DreamBooth as amplifying semantic collapse and attributes recovery primarily to correcting embedding direction rather than magnitude (Section 4.2 and Appendix C.2). It removes v1's evaluation-limitations paragraph while retaining the prompt-versus-identity tradeoff and limitations of fixed hyperparameters.

D1.justification: The documented code and prompt access location changes from anonymous hosting to a named GitHub repository. A new LLM-use statement identifies ChatGPT among the tools used. Original GPU, batch-size, learning-rate and LoRA details are retained; detailed settings for the added pipelines remain sparse.

E1.justification: The original CC101 and CelebA coverage is retained. v2 adds Relationship tasks involving 'carved by', 'inside' and 'painted on' (Table 2), plus personalization using adversarially masked reference images. These introduce distinct task requirements and training-input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 retains Textual Inversion, DreamBooth and Custom Diffusion, adds ClassDiffusion to the CC101/CelebA comparisons, and evaluates EasyControl and ReVersion with and without TEA (Tables 1–2 and 6–7). These are participating comparators, not merely additional citations.

E3.justification: v2 adds Flux-based EasyControl evaluation and controlled Anti-DreamBooth experiments varying masked-image proportions and TEA adjustment settings. The original Stable Diffusion settings remain documented unchanged. The intermediate masking condition is uncertain: Section 4.2 specifies 20%, whereas Figure 7 labels it 25%.

E4.justification: v2 adds poisoning-induced drift analysis and rotation-versus-scaling sensitivity tests for Anti-DreamBooth (Figures 7–8 and 13–14), plus failure-case comparisons for the added methods. The original multi-concept and hyperparameter analyses are retained and moved into Appendices B and C.1.

E5.justification: New Figures 28–30 explicitly report using the same random seed for baseline/TEA qualitative comparisons. The existing 100-seed and 50-run averages and rotation-ablation ± reporting remain unchanged. No increase in repeated runs or new statistical inference procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds ClassDiffusion scores, EasyControl/ReVersion results and qualitative recovery findings under poisoning. For example, its new EasyControl dog comparison reports CLIP-I of 61.33 without TEA and 64.56 with TEA; ReVersion 'carved by' reports full-prompt CLIP scores of 27.74 and 30.17. Retained TI, DreamBooth and Custom Diffusion table entries are unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same normalization and spherical interpolation procedure, applied to token embeddings for Textual Inversion and contextualized prompt embeddings for DreamBooth. Equations 1–2 remain unchanged; the added applications do not document a new TEA component.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites substantial introduction and evaluation prose, condenses the standalone personalization background into a terminology subsection, and moves the multi-concept and hyperparameter sections into appendices. The title, section hierarchy, citation style and narrative organization also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a results teaser, a TEA framework schematic, Anti-DreamBooth plots and image grids, and qualitative displays for three added methods. It introduces the EasyControl/ReVersion table and expands existing comparison tables. Original figure images are retained, with several displays relocated and the rotation table relabeled as Figure 11.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of anti-personalization, adversarial learning and concept erasure in Appendix A.2. Appendix A.3 adds explicit comparisons with PALP, LEGO and ReVersion, positioning TEA against training-time regularization and token-based personalization approaches.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a constrained bilevel formulation of anti-personalization and a reconstruction/prior-loss expression (v2 Equations 6–7). These extend the mathematical background. Existing TEA equations and distance definitions remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 materially strengthens evidence for TEA's broad applicability through a different architecture, relationship-personalization tasks and ClassDiffusion comparisons, addressing v1's explicitly acknowledged evaluation restriction. The controlled poisoning study and method schematic add explanatory value. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, although the 20%/25% masking discrepancy and Appendix F.3's unchanged claim that all experiments use Stable Diffusion v1.5 limit reproducibility of the expanded evaluation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same semantic collapsing problem (SCP) and Test-time Embedding Adjustment (TEA) work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds ClassDiffusion, EasyControl, ReVersion and Anti-DreamBooth experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original embedding-drift experiments, multi-concept analyses, hyperparameter studies and TEA evaluations on CC101 and CelebA.

C1.justification: The central data-distribution thesis remains, but v2 adds interference magnitude and direction, and the protective role of reasoning trajectories, as explicit main contributions. It also narrows the rollout-SFT claim from avoiding or overcoming catastrophic forgetting to reducing it in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 explains reasoning as connecting novel answers to existing perceptual abilities and reducing interference magnitude. It further argues that perplexity explains why GRPO data preserve knowledge better even when GPT-4o data have smaller LBK. V1's probability-normalization explanation of residual forgetting is dropped. Limitations now cover 3B/7B, and model-selection discussion adds InternVL memory constraints.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the GPT-4o generation prompt and example response, plus the empty-thinking-tag control for answer-only perplexity. Hardware reporting changes from two to four A800 GPUs, while the explicit GRPO gradient-accumulation count is omitted. A new reproducibility statement promises future open-source code without supplying an access link.

E1.justification: V2 adds MMMU validation evaluation, extending prior-knowledge coverage to college-level multimodal problems across six disciplines. COCO-derived 3×3 jigsaws and the existing grounding, document/OCR, general VQA, and hallucination benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds SFT-Rea-4o-Rollout to Table 1, providing an important reasoning-data comparator. Its high-learning-rate Table 2 replaces the SFT-GT comparator with GPT-4o reasoning-data SFT. SFT-GT and SFT-GRPO-Rollout otherwise match the renamed SFT-Non-Rea and SFT-Rea-GRPO-Rollout methods.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B experiments and changes stated SFT defaults from learning rate 1e-6 to 1e-5 and batch size 4 to 16. Table 1 replaces training budgets, including 3B answer-only SFT from 2,738 to 200 steps. New LBK and answer-only perplexity experiments introduce additional measurement protocols and controls.

E4.justification: V2 adds reasoning-versus-nonreasoning interference analysis, answer-only perplexity controls, and reasoning-source Pareto comparisons (Figures 2, 8, and 5). The high-learning-rate analysis is refocused on GPT-4o versus GRPO reasoning data. V1's perplexity-gap distributions and six-epoch rollout analysis are removed; restart analysis and qualitative jigsaw cases are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions show response-distribution boxplots using sampled rollouts. V2 Figure 2 adds shaded bands around LBK curves, but their meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither PDF identifies training-run counts, seeds, or significance tests, so whether the new shading constitutes additional statistical uncertainty reporting is unresolved.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces v1's 3B answer-only and rollout-SFT jigsaw results of 62% and 66% with 53% and 70% under revised settings. It adds 7B results, including 75% for RFT, GPT-4o comparator results, and MMMU scores. The listed 3B RFT OCRBench score also changes from 77.90 to 77.1. Table 2 and new analytical figures substantially expand the findings.

M1.justification: The core procedure retains the same jigsaw construction, three reward components, GRPO objective, and SFT on correct RFT-generated rollouts. Periodic optimizer/reference-policy restarts already appear in v1 and remain in v2 Appendix E. GPT-4o reasoning data serve as an added comparator; LBK is an analytical diagnostic.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and contribution narrative are substantially reframed. Related work is compressed from numbered subsections into thematic paragraphs, and Sections 5.4–5.6 are reordered and rewritten. Limitations move to Appendix B, and ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-usage statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with three training-data paths, Table 1 gains separate 3B/7B blocks, and Table 2 is expanded. New LBK, perplexity, Pareto, and prompt displays replace several earlier plots. The original jigsaw examples and restart plots are retained but relocated to the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 adds Lai et al. on forgetting and RL's Razor, positioning its data-based explanation alongside the latter's KL-minimality account. MMMU and InternVL references are added, while several overview citations, including Jigsaw Clustering, PODNet, and VideoChat-R1, are removed. The principal positioning relative to GRPO and learning dynamics remains.

T1.justification: V2 Section 5.4 adds a Frobenius-norm inequality and the formal LBK definition in Equations 6–7. This extends the existing framework while retaining the one-step decomposition, symmetry theorem, kernel-stability assumption, and appendix proofs, chiefly with updated notation and numbering.

improvement.justification: V1's comparison confounds data source with the presence of reasoning. V2 substantially addresses this through GPT-4o reasoning controls: at 70% 3B jigsaw accuracy, GRPO-rollout SFT retains 84.6 RefCOCO accuracy versus 74.2 for GPT-4o-rollout SFT (Table 1). The 7B experiments and more qualified forgetting claims further strengthen the empirical case. Although the kernel-bound interpretation remains indirect and uncertainty bands are undefined, the improved controls provide substantially stronger support for the central data-distribution explanation.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs study SFT versus GRPO for jigsaw learning and knowledge retention in Qwen2.5-VL. Their complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on 3B and 7B models, benchmark comparisons, and analyses of reasoning data, interference, perplexity, and retention.

before.justification: V1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, jigsaw and prior-task benchmark results, perplexity analyses, and learning-rate and restart experiments.

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions, and central data-distribution explanation remain intact. V3’s conclusion adds the practical claim that even a short RFT phase can produce SFT data yielding RFT-comparable new-task performance while preserving knowledge better than GPT-4o-rollout SFT.

C2.justification: The early-RFT interpretation reverses: v2 describes a clear target-performance ceiling, while v3 Sections 5.8 and 6 argue that a short phase suffices for competitive performance. V3 also interprets mixture experiments as favoring distributional alignment over stylistic diversity and extends its mechanism interpretation to text tasks. Appendix B’s old jigsaw-only scope statement remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 adds preprocessing pseudocode, GPU-hour costs in Table 3, the TRL num_iterations setting, early-RFT budget and data-construction details, and GPT-4o prompts/examples for math and science. These materially expand implementation disclosure, although preprocessing descriptions conflict. The statement promising future code release is unchanged.

E1.justification: V3 adds text-only competition-style math training/evaluation using Open-Reasoner-Zero and scientific multiple-choice QA using Sci-MCQ4. GSM8K, MATH-500, and IFEval become additional retention benchmarks. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained jigsaw and multimodal evaluations.

E2.justification: Tables 7–8 add SFT-Mixture to comparisons with nonreasoning, GPT-4o-rollout, and GRPO-rollout SFT. Table 5 explicitly compares the early self-generated-data variant against RFT and rollout-based SFT. The principal comparator families remain unchanged; newly cited classical continual-learning methods are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added protocols include 90/10 ORZ and Sci-MCQ4 splits, an 8,500-example science sample, Qwen2.5-Instruct experiments, four-rate math sweeps, and GRPO iteration settings of 1, 2, and 4. V3 also specifies the early-RFT budget. Algorithm 1 reports bicubic resizing, conflicting with the retained cropping description in Section 3.1; an actual preprocessing change is unresolved.

E4.justification: V3 adds equal-proportion reasoning/nonreasoning mixture ablations, GRPO iteration sensitivity, and math/science LBK and perplexity analyses, plus math Pareto and learning-rate analyses. The early-RFT study gains quantitative comparisons in Table 5. V2’s large-learning-rate jigsaw analysis is retained in Appendix E, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies independent training-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 16-rollout perplexity boxplots already appear in v2 Figure 4; v3 extends existing graphical reporting conventions without disclosing a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results, including GRPO-rollout SFT ORZ accuracies of 37.8%/53.4% for 3B/7B, Sci-MCQ4 accuracy of 71.7%, and 84.0% jigsaw accuracy for the 3B early-RFT-derived SFT variant. These are newly reported experiments. Original Table 1 is unchanged. In v2 Table 2 versus v3 Table 4, the 7B base MME entry changes from 2334 to 2333; remaining score differences are rounding.

M1.justification: The core GRPO/SFT objectives, jigsaw rewards, periodic restarts, and rollout-supervision approach remain unchanged. Early-RFT trajectories followed by SFT were already described in v2 Section 6; v3 supplies more details and results without establishing a changed core procedure.

P1.justification: V3 locally revises the introduction and learning-dynamics explanation, merges Discussion and Conclusion, and moves the large-learning-rate discussion to Appendix E. New sections and appendices organize the added studies, while the abstract, contribution list, and much of the original narrative remain unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 adds substantial visual reporting for math/science experiments, training costs, early-RFT results, mixture ablations, and GRPO sensitivity, together with Algorithm 1 and new prompt examples. Existing jigsaw figures are resized or relocated, and v2 Table 2 becomes appendix Table 4, producing substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: V3 adds Li and Hoiem and Chaudhry et al. to the existing continual-learning discussion, cites sources for the new tasks and models, and removes the InternVL3 citation and associated discussion. It clarifies that outperforming classical continual-learning algorithms is outside its aim; the main research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Theorems 5.1–5.2, the eNTK/LBK mathematics, and the derivations and proofs in Appendices C–D remain unchanged. V3 adds explanatory prose and explicitly states standard GRPO advantage normalization without revising the formal argument.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially reduces dependence on one unusual visual task through math/science evaluations and adds mixture and GRPO-recipe tests addressing alternative explanations. Table 5 supplies quantitative support for the previously performance-limited early-RFT approach, while cost and implementation disclosures improve practical assessment. Conflicting preprocessing descriptions, the outdated Appendix B scope statement, and overly uniform interpretations of some results reduce clarity, but the broader evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SFT/RFT forgetting study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocations and additions.

after.justification: V3 retains the original experiments and reports additional math reasoning, scientific QA, data-mixture, GRPO-recipe, and early-RFT results.

before.justification: V2 reports original jigsaw-training and prior-knowledge-retention experiments, including Tables 1–2 and learning-dynamics, perplexity, and restart analyses.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that iterative off-policy distillation enables diffusion fine-tuning for potentially non-differentiable rewards, with improved stability, sample efficiency, and biomolecular reward optimization. Removing a repeated PPO-comparison sentence does not materially alter these retained claims or the contribution's scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of low DNA 3-mer correlation and explanations of the stability and computational tradeoffs among argmax, Monte Carlo, and learned value estimates. Appendices C.2 and G expand the limitations discussion to reward-exploitation tuning and the absence of explicit noise-robustness mechanisms, going beyond v2's general warning about imperfect rewards.

D1.justification: v3 maps the existing update-interval choices to individual protein tasks and newly discloses argmax decoding, temperature sampling for the alternative estimator, and generator/reward-model parameter counts. The abstract replaces the direct repository pointer with a project-page pointer. These are limited additions and revisions to reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The protein SS-match, PD-L1/IFNAR2 binder, HepG2 enhancer, and Parp1 molecule-design coverage is retained. Appendix G adds binder training under synthetically corrupted reward signals, introducing a limited new training-environment scenario.

E2.justification: v3 Table 8 adds GLID2E and a KL-regularized DRAKES comparison for DNA generation. The earlier DRAKES numbers reappear as DRAKES w/o KL, so that row is retained under a more specific label. Protein and molecule comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds DNA log-likelihood and binder pTM/pDockQ evaluation, broader update-interval and regularization sweeps, a four-sample Monte Carlo comparison, and noisy-training/clean-evaluation controls. Table 4 also revises reported binder sequence length from 256 to 100. The PDFs do not establish whether that revision corrects documentation or reflects rerun experiments.

E4.justification: v2 already examined DNA update intervals, roll-in mixtures, and reward–diversity tradeoffs. v3 substantially extends sensitivity testing to protein update intervals and DNA/protein regularization, compares argmax-based and Monte Carlo value estimates, and tests reward-noise robustness in Appendices F–G.

E5.justification: Both retain median reporting and the same Table 1 caption describing ± as standard error with a 95% confidence interval. Additional estimates follow the existing practice; v3 supplies no new seed counts, repeated-run information, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Default VIDD benchmark values are retained, but DDPP protein results change: Table 1's β-sheet fraction changes from 0.60 to 0.63, pLDDT from 0.40 to 0.36, and diversity from 0.90 to 0.85. Binder DDPP rows and Figures 5–6 also change. Substantial new results cover added metrics and analyses; for example, v3 Table 23 reports PD-L1 reward 0.4744 at noise=0.1 versus 0.9079 without noise, under the newly tested conditions.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the mixed off-policy roll-in, lazy roll-out updates, and value-weighted forward-KL objective. The argmax implementation disclosure and Monte Carlo comparison expand documentation and analysis without establishing a change to the default VIDD procedure.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the order of Sections 1–7 are retained. Changes include local wording and terminology corrections, expanded derivation explanations, new appendix subsections, updated publication/header text, and moving the generated-sample discussion from Appendix F to H.

P2.justification: The appendix presentation expands substantially through dedicated DNA-comparison, binder-metric, sensitivity, value-estimation, and noise tables. The retained DNA update-interval table gains log-likelihood and another interval, while Figures 5–6 show revised and extended DDPP traces. The document also adopts the ICLR layout and relocates retained displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds Cao et al. (2025), Bryant et al. (2022), and Tang et al. (2025), supporting the additional baseline, pDockQ metric, and inference-time discussion. Appendix E.1 more explicitly distinguishes VIDD from the already cited SVDD. The broader research positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and its Appendix A proof are retained. Appendix B removes v2's final reformulation that absorbs the value normalizer into the roll-in distribution, ending instead at the normalized objective in Equation 5. The additional conditional-KL expansion mainly explains the existing derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 provided limited direct evidence for the value-estimator choice and protein hyperparameter sensitivity. v3 tests these central design choices, expands DNA comparisons and unoptimized binder metrics, and quantifies the reward-noise failure previously discussed only generically. These additions substantially strengthen empirical support and clarify applicability boundaries, although the binder-length revision remains unreconciled with retained scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VIDD study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds empirical comparisons, sensitivity analyses, value-estimation experiments, and reward-noise tests in Appendices E–G.

before.justification: v2 reports original protein, DNA, and molecule generation experiments in Section 6 and Appendix E, including benchmark results and ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central claims: two outlier-robust fidelity and coverage metrics with calibration enabling linear bad-sample degradation and interpretable absolute scores. The additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Appendices J–K newly explain why truncation or guidance can initially increase both scores and produce uncapped Clipped Density above 1. Appendix I replaces v2's criticism inferred from real-data scatterplots with an explicit acknowledgment that those plots cannot establish metric superiority. Section 6 adds the absence of infinite-sample analysis, and Appendix G identifies the FFHQ human-agreement exception.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous code reference with an author-named GitHub repository and explicitly describes reproduction and metric-use access. It adds FMA preprocessing details, including middle-seven-second clips and 1024-dimensional CLAP embeddings, and documents the 2,500-sample mode-dropping exception. Appendix B's core implementation, hardware, and timing information remains unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 retains the image, chest X-ray, and synthetic benchmark coverage while adding Free Music Archive data and toy time-series hallucinations in Appendix P. Appendix O adds distinct scenarios involving an absent rare real mode and incorrect within-mode correlations. The earlier distortion and Gaussian tests are retained under new appendix labels.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Precision/Recall, Density/Coverage, symmetric and probabilistic variants, α-Precision/β-Recall, TopP&R, and Precision/Recall Cover. The new PQMass citation supplies test protocols without adding evaluated comparator results. Human ratings serve as validation criteria.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include StyleGAN truncation levels of 1.0, 0.7, and 0.5 and uncapped-score diagnostics in Appendices J–K. Appendix M introduces an ImageNet sample-size sweep from 100 to 50,000 using an 80% real/20% noise mixture. Appendices O–P add covariance, dimensionality, and signal-amplitude controls. These substantially extend the evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds human-rating validation, truncation and guidance histograms, a final-clipping ablation, calibration and sample-size analyses, rare-mode and correlation failures, and annotated FFHQ artifact inspection. These investigate perceptual agreement, metric mechanisms, stability, and failure sensitivity. Existing component, distortion, and nearest-neighbor sensitivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 already reports means and standard deviations and discusses seed dependence. v3 adds Pearson correlations with p-values in Appendix G, specifies 100 splits for CIFAR-10 mode dropping, and explicitly identifies the music contamination experiment as single-run. The newly stated 100-split count does not establish that runs increased between versions.

E6.justification: New results include human correlations of 0.81–0.96 on three datasets but nonsignificant FFHQ correlations, and score standard deviations below 0.01 at 50,000 samples. Music Clipped Density/Coverage scores are 0.988/0.998 for balanced splits and 0.943/0.875 for genre splits. Figures 4e and 5c change α-Precision mode dropping and β-Recall matched-outlier judgments from fail to pass. Figure 22's fraction/percentage descriptions leave its minimum rare-mode detection threshold unclear.

M1.justification: Section 4, Equations 5–10, and Appendix B retain the same radius clipping, sample-contribution clipping, normalization, and coverage calibration procedures. Appendices J–K examine outputs without the final score cap as diagnostic variants; they do not replace the proposed metrics.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose remain intact, with localized clarifications, an expanded experimental summary, and a rewritten Appendix I interpretation. Appendices are reorganized around the additions: distortions move from G to N, toy tests from J to Q, sensitivity from K to L, and unnormalized results from L to R. Conference headers are added.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: human-correlation panels, truncation and guidance histograms, calibration and failure plots, modality evaluations, and real/generated sample grids with FFHQ defect annotations. Existing plots receive larger, differentiated markers and revised axes or legends, and several appendix figures move. Tables 1–8 retain their structure.

R1.justification: v3 adds Defferrard et al. (2017), Elizalde et al. (2023), Gui et al. (2024), Lemos et al. (2025), and Li et al. (2024). These support music data and embeddings, borrowed failure tests, and fidelity–coverage trade-offs. The main related-work discussion and novelty positioning remain substantively stable.

T1.justification: The metric definitions, Lemma 1's beta-binomial expectation, calibration derivation, and Appendix A proof are unchanged. The new inverse-square-root sample-size behavior is an empirical finding, not an added asymptotic theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's lack of direct human-rating validation and dedicated quantification of absolute-score variability with sample size through Figure 8 and Figures 19–20. Appendices J–K clarify clipping behavior, while Appendix I removes unsupported conclusions from real-data scatterplots. Together these strengthen evidence and interpretation for the central claims. Nonsignificant FFHQ correlations, single-run music results, and Figure 22's percentage ambiguity limit the added support but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Clipped Density and Clipped Coverage research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, with retained material matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments and analyses, including correlations with previously collected human ratings, calibration stability, failure scenarios, and music evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original metric evaluations on synthetic and image datasets, generative-model comparisons, component analyses, sensitivity tests, and computational measurements.

C1.justification: The central PMC, utility and robustness contributions remain. v4 refines the introductory privacy claim by dropping the assertion that PMC avoids private data in its objective and emphasizing independence from fixed ground-truth sequences instead. The change from three to four limitations does not establish another distinct contribution: sampling/prefilling robustness appears twice in the new enumeration.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands the qualifications: outputs can become hallucinations, gibberish or empty responses; generated samples can initially contain sensitive information; and collapse requires accessible higher-reward responses. Section 6 distinguishes output removal from convergence to a retrained model and explicitly disclaims formal unlearning guarantees. The appendices add interpretations of utility drops, approximation trade-offs, checkpointing sensitivity and MUSE evaluation weaknesses.

D1.justification: v4 documents Gemma/DPO hyperparameters, hardware assignments and settings for the new runtime, reward and sensitivity experiments. Appendix A.10 specifies MUSE filtering and prefix-sampling details. It also clarifies greedy reference generation and utility evaluation without the TOFU chat template. Code access already existed in v3; v4 additionally states that experiment configurations are released with the code.

E1.justification: v4 adds MUSE-news-small, containing 454 forget and 1,714 retain sentences, alongside the retained TOFU experiments. This extends LLM unlearning from fictional-author question answering to news sentences using continuation training (Appendix A.10). The existing utility benchmarks and synthetic simulations are retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds DPO to the Phi/Llama TOFU comparisons, epoch ablation and sampling/prefilling evaluation (Figures 3, 4 and 6). The existing GA, GD, NPO, SimNPO and IDK comparators remain. The new Gemma comparison explicitly excludes DPO and NPO because of their reference-model costs.

E3.justification: v4 adds Gemma-3-12b-it configurations and a Llama-2-7b MUSE protocol using sentence-level training, ten epochs and KnowMem evaluation. It also introduces controlled H200 runtime comparisons and additional cross-model experimental settings. The retained TOFU split remains unchanged, while aggregate utility and unlearning scores are normalized by their maximum possible values.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's retained ablations and attacks, v4 adds detailed epoch/runtime sensitivity studies across three models, PMC-fast cost comparisons, empirical reward-convergence checks, alternative-reward tests and gradient-checkpointing ablations (Appendices A.2–A.9). The per-question leakage distributions in Appendix A.5 also examine variation hidden by the previously reported average.

E5.justification: Five-seed reporting remains for the retained Phi/Llama experiments. v4 identifies Gemma comparisons and Appendix B.4 analyses as single-run results, and replaces v3's five-run runtime summaries with individual trajectories. These disclosures do not establish reduced replication of retained experiments. Table 4 still lists five Gemma seeds, inconsistently with the single-run exception in Section 5.1.

E6.justification: v4 adds DPO and Gemma results, MUSE KnowMem outcomes and substantial diagnostic findings, including reported reward convergence within 50 training steps (Figure 25). Table 1 retains the Phi/Llama values and adds Gemma PMC scores of 0.6032, 0.8421 and 0.6934 for ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy and MMLU. Changed runtime figures use different hardware/settings and therefore do not establish a same-setting speed improvement.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 remains unchanged, but v4 substantially extends the implemented procedures: PMC-fast selects reward-improving samples and stops sampling at maximum reward; additional variants use restarts and self-BLEU rewards. Appendix A.10 also adapts PMC to sentence continuations from randomly selected prefixes. These are actual procedural additions, not merely expanded explanations.

P1.justification: The introduction, results explanations and Discussion receive substantial rewriting. Sampling/prefilling attacks move ahead of the side-effect analysis, Section 5.4 becomes a broader experimental overview, and the appendices gain navigation and reorganized experimental subsections. These narrative changes extend beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to distinguish refusal fine-tuning from gradient ascent. Figure 3 expands from two to three panels with a shared legend and normalized axes; Figure 7 redisplays its data with accessible markers. Numerous diagnostic plots are added, attack/ablation displays gain DPO, and tables expand for Gemma. Several retained figures are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v4 adds the Gemma 3 report and Schwinn et al. (2025), removes Cao and Yang (2015), and clarifies positioning relative to distribution matching and alignment. IDK is attributed to Zhang et al. (2024), whereas v3 introduced it as a new baseline. The DPO reference's year/venue update concerns the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 now explicitly requires positive initial probability mass on maximum-reward responses for every forget query. v3 stated convergence without this support assumption. This substantively restricts the theorem's applicability; the categorical proofs, Theorem 2 and the remaining derivations are retained.

improvement.justification: v4 makes PMC's mechanism, computational feasibility and failure conditions substantially more assessable. Compared with v3's brief runtime reporting and limited collapse diagnostics, it adds controlled cost trajectories, direct reward-convergence evidence and targeted reward/checkpointing analyses, alongside stronger comparator and model coverage. The explicit theorem assumption and clearer privacy and evaluation limitations improve precision. Single-run additions, seed/caption inconsistencies and the limited MUSE pilot temper the evidence, but the gains in empirical support and interpretation constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PMC research, with matching core methods, experiments and theoretical appendices. All 23 pages of v3 and 37 pages of v4, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds Gemma experiments, a MUSE-news pilot, and runtime, reward and checkpointing analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original TOFU unlearning experiments, utility evaluations, attack tests, ablations and categorical/Gaussian-mixture simulations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction update the headline GSM8K claim from 78.6-to-80.7 to 78.6-to-81.2 and explicitly frame SDPO as offline alignment. The principal contributions—stepwise decomposition, arbitrary-reward optimization, and an equivalence with a constructed trajectory objective—remain.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 now acknowledges that unbiased model-partition estimation requires conditional posterior sampling that is prohibitive offline, materially qualifying v1's consistency guarantee for the practical loss. Section 4.2 adds an interpretation of the revised transition rewards and their per-step supervision. The reward-model limitation is retained through relocation from Section 6 to Appendix D.

D1.justification: Appendix B.4 newly documents computational and memory scaling, and Appendix C.1 specifies random subset selection followed by two established relabeling stages for the new ablation. Existing hyperparameter tables, GPU information, decoding settings, and code/data access links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same enhancer-design, PDB/Megascale protein, and UltraFeedback language coverage, with GSM8K, IFEval, and AlpacaEval 2.0 evaluation. The added DNA experiment uses smaller random subsets of the existing data, without introducing a different population or task.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add D2-DPO and VRPO to both biological comparisons, retaining the previous comparators. Table 3 adds D2-DPO where v1 compared SDPO only with LLaDA-8B-Instruct. These additions substantially expand direct comparisons with other offline discrete-diffusion alignment methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds sequence entropy as a diversity metric in both biological evaluations. Appendix C.1 introduces first-stage training on random 25k and 50k DNA subsets, followed by the existing two relabeling stages. Previously documented training and language decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C.1 and Table 7 test sensitivity to initial DNA training-data quantity. The existing beta, Monte Carlo sample-count, iterative-labeling, protein tradeoff, and language-response analyses are retained, including material renumbered within Appendix C.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed averages with standard deviations in Tables 1–2 and retain the beta-sweep standard deviations and plotted error bars. Added result entries follow existing reporting practices; no changed experimental run counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are documented.

E6.justification: Table 3 revises SDPO's GSM8K score from 80.7 to 81.2 under unchanged documented settings and adds D2-DPO results. Tables 1–2 add comparator and entropy results while retaining their original biological scores; D2-DPO now leads DNA 3-mer correlation, 0.944 versus SDPO's 0.900. New Table 7 reports predicted activities of 5.56 and 6.02 for the 25k and 50k subsets, substantially expanding the reported evidence.

M1.justification: The operational SDPO loss and implicit reward retain the same form (v1 Eqs. 13–14; v2 Eqs. 11–12), as do forward noising, masking weights, and iterative relabeling. Corrections to theoretical targets and derivations do not establish a changed training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory framing, method explanations, and experimental prose receive localized rewrites. The beta and sample-count discussions are reordered, the contents page becomes an appendix roadmap, and Section 6 becomes a conclusion with limitations moved to Appendix D. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an additional intermediate-step branch and revised reward labels. Tables 1–3 expand for new comparators and metrics, and a data-size table is added. Existing ablation plots and appendix result tables are largely retained with renumbering, resizing, and local page reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds D2-DPO, VRPO/LLaDA 1.5, d1, MMaDA, and Process Reinforcement through Implicit Rewards, and removes Song and Ermon's 2020 Improved Techniques citation. Related work now explicitly contrasts SDPO with pairwise offline and verification-based online discrete-diffusion alignment, within an otherwise retained discussion.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A.1 replace weighted conditional-mean trajectory rewards with log ratios of conditional exponential-reward expectations and substantially revise the proof. Section 4.3 and Appendix A.3 revise the importance-sampling derivation, while Proposition 4.3 and its asymptotic-unbiasedness proof are removed. The pairwise sigmoid algebra is corrected, and Appendix B.4 adds computational and memory complexity bounds.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central justification by revising the trajectory-reward construction and withdrawing v1's blanket asymptotic-unbiasedness guarantee (Theorem 4.1, Section 4.3, Appendix A). Close offline baselines, diversity metrics, and the data-size ablation also address important evaluation gaps. Some appendix equation inconsistencies remain, and new baseline settings and the GSM8K score revision are incompletely explained, but the gains in theoretical qualification and comparative evidence are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SDPO research, with matching title, authors, and experimental domains. All 22 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D, support comparison; moved and renumbered material can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original SDPO experiments across all three domains and adds results including a DNA training-data-size ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original SDPO experiments on DNA design, protein inverse folding, and language modeling, together with ablations and appendix results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapter-based personalized federated adaptation of VLMs, balancing personalization and generalization through selective sharing, and reduced communication. The additional experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations absent from v1: limited few-shot data motivates adapting the last three layers, width 32 balances performance against parameter cost, and inappropriate scaling impairs adaptation or generalization. Appendix E interprets the shared subspace as essential for cross-client coordination and discusses accuracy, computation, and communication tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and E add pseudocode, dataset sizes, the equal base/novel class split, ten-class domain subsets, client averaging, PyTorch and NVIDIA A6000 hardware, layer choices, and resource accounting. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments. Conversely, v1's code-availability statement and repository URL are absent from v2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eleven datasets: seven CLIP recognition benchmarks, CIFAR-10/100, DomainNet, and Office-Caltech10. OxfordPets already appears in v1 Table 1 despite its omission from the dataset description. Added shots, backbones, and partitions vary settings within retained tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The primary benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged. V2 adds evaluated all-global, reversed-sharing, and local-only adapter controls in Tables 5, 13, and 18. Zero-shot CLIP, included in v1 Figure 2, is omitted from the updated learning-curve comparisons in v2 Figures 4–5.

E3.justification: V2 adds systematic 1/2/4/8/16-shot evaluations, Dirichlet concentration sweeps, and one-versus-two-client domain partitions. ViT-B/32 replaces ResNet50 as the stated alternative backbone and receives reported evaluations. The main domain comparison changes from beta=0.3 to 0.5, while retaining the earlier setting in the appendix. New experiments also vary adapter configurations and report relative-improvement and resource metrics.

E4.justification: V1 lacks direct adapter-design ablations. V2 tests adapter width, scaling, insertion depth, alternative sharing arrangements, and removal of federation in Tables 5 and 11–15 and Table 18. It also adds systematic backbone and heterogeneity analyses, expands convergence analysis across shots and datasets, and examines computational and communication costs.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly reports three-seed averaging for Table 1; v2 Appendix C.2 states that every experiment is repeated with three different seeds. This broadens the disclosed run information without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports run dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces pFedMMA's average HM of 82.85 with 84.15 and PromptFL's 82.15 with 83.09; v1's unspecified shot count prevents treating these as controlled same-setting gains. At beta=0.3, CIFAR-10 entries change from 96.79 to 96.92 for pFedMMA and 92.11 to 93.19 for FedPGP. V2 adds extensive shot, backbone, ablation, and resource results. V1's per-domain beta=0.3 scores are retained in v2 Table 10.

M1.justification: Both versions train modality-specific up/down projections locally and aggregate only the shared cross-modal projection, using the same adapter architecture and cross-entropy objective. V2 combines equivalent equations and adds Algorithm 1; these document the existing procedure rather than introduce a new method.

P1.justification: V2 moves the entire Related Work section to Appendix B, compresses displayed equations and bullet lists into inline prose, and reorganizes the experimental narrative into performance, ablation, and learning-curve sections. The appendix structure substantially changes how the paper presents its argument, although much existing prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds radar charts, shot-comparison plots, ablation tables, and resource tables. The four-panel learning-curve figure becomes a dataset-by-shot grid with separate averages. Existing tables are redesigned with shaded rows, colored relative-improvement entries, and separate domain-dataset averages. The architecture overview is retained as Figure 2, within a substantially reformatted document.

R1.justification: V2 adds the OxfordPets reference, Parkhi et al.'s Cats and Dogs, and removes the citation to Ghiasvand et al.'s Decentralized Low-Rank Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models. The substantive related-work discussion and positioning against prompt learning and existing adapters remain largely unchanged; moving that discussion to Appendix B is structural.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds analytical parameter and communication counts, including m[2r(d_v+d_t)+r^2] trainable parameters and m r^2 parameters uploaded or downloaded per round for pFedMMA. Existing mathematical objectives and update equations remain equivalent. No new convergence or generalization theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1 by directly testing the selective-sharing design (Tables 5, 13, and 18), quantifying its previously asserted efficiency (Table 17), and supplying substantial reproducibility details. These additions strengthen the justification for the central method beyond benchmark comparisons. Benefits outweigh the removed code-access statement and remaining overstatements: for example, Table 4 shows one-shot ViT-B/32 HM below FedPGP despite the claim of superiority across all settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pFedMMA work and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. V1 ends after the references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 supplies Appendices A–E. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, ablations, sensitivity experiments, learning curves, and resource measurements in Section 4 and Appendices D–E.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments under federated data heterogeneity, including benchmark accuracies in Tables 1–3 and learning curves in Figure 2.

C1.justification: The abstract's second principal contribution changes from label-weighted conformal prediction to linear quantile interpolation. INTERP-Q is now presented as a method with a marginal coverage guarantee, replacing v1's explicit absence-of-guarantee claim. FUZZY remains an alternative in the appendix, while PAS and the overall long-tailed coverage objective are retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains INTERP-Q's nonlinear set-size response through rare-class score distributions, states that FUZZY does not empirically outperform simpler INTERP-Q, and acknowledges an exchangeability issue when tuning on calibration data. It removes v1's explicit limitation concerning balanced datasets. The main interpretations of coverage and decision accuracy remain broadly similar.

D1.justification: v2 adds the focal-loss implementation source and parameters γ=2 and α=1, plus FUZZY's epsilon-adjustment instructions. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit FUZZY bandwidth rescaling σy=σ/(ny+1) and experimental bandwidth grid, despite retaining FUZZY results. The main code-access information, hardware, and basic training details remain.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist-2018, their truncated variants with 330 and 857 classes, endangered-species coverage, and verifier/guesser decision scenarios. The added focal-loss experiment changes the classifier configuration, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: EXACT CLASSWISE remains in the comprehensive softmax comparison, moving from v1 Figure 4 to v2 Figure 7. However, it disappears from the corresponding PAS-score comparison in v1 Figure 7 versus v2 Figure 9. STANDARD, CLASSWISE, and CLUSTERED remain in that comparison.

E3.justification: v1 Appendix B.2 uses the same validation data for epoch selection and conformal calibration. v2 Appendices C.1–C.2 instead reserve random, disjoint 30% and 70% portions for those purposes, substantially changing the evaluation design. v2 also adds focal-loss training and revises INTERP-Q and WPAS parameter sweeps; the 20-epoch budget and learning rate remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The supplementary analyses are substantially revised. v2 adds a focal-loss robustness check and expands simulated INTERP-Q decision accuracy from one interpolation setting to ten settings. It removes FUZZY's decision-accuracy analysis and the truncated-dataset panels from the class-mapping and PAS-combination analyses, while retaining those analyses on the full datasets.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The displayed verifier/guesser ranges represent alternative decision behaviors rather than statistical uncertainty, and no uncertainty-reporting practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Benchmark and case-study results are revised, with additional focal-loss and interpolation-sensitivity results. For example, PAS coverage for Abeliophyllum distichum changes from 1.00 to 0.00, and for Vanilla planifolia from 1.00 to 0.80 (v1 Figure 9; v2 Figure 12). These are replaced results under the revised experimental protocol, not established same-setting performance declines. The broad size-versus-coverage conclusions remain similar.

M1.justification: PAS, WPAS, INTERP-Q, and FUZZY remain present despite relocation. v2 Appendix A.2 corrects FUZZY's reconformalization rule to include equality at the calibrated transformed-score threshold and specifies an epsilon adjustment when implementing it through Raw FUZZY. This refines the procedure stated in v1 Section 2.2.

P1.justification: The narrative is extensively reorganized and edited. FUZZY moves from the main methods section to Appendix A, while weighted macro-coverage and endangered-species experiments move into the main text. Preliminaries, method summaries, experimental explanations, discussion, and appendix organization are substantially rewritten around PAS and INTERP-Q.

P2.justification: v2 adds Algorithm 1, a method-summary table, numerical results Tables 3–4, and the focal-loss figure. It separates the simpler main comparison from the comprehensive appendix figure and redraws decision-accuracy plots as panels for different verifier probabilities, with method-specific class ordering. Numerous figures also change placement, styling, legends, and captions.

R1.justification: v2 adds Lin et al. on focal loss, Menon et al. on logit adjustment, and Shumailov et al. on model collapse, modestly expanding the positioning against class-imbalance research. The weighted-conformal discussion and its references move into Appendix A rather than disappearing.

T1.justification: v2 Proposition 3 and Appendix B.3 introduce a proof that INTERP-Q achieves marginal coverage of at least 1−2α; v1 explicitly says it lacks a coverage guarantee. v2 also revises FUZZY's coverage statement and supplies the strict-versus-nonstrict threshold argument in Appendix B.5. The weighted-PAS optimality theorem and existing FUZZY results are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: The separate epoch-selection and calibration split resolves v1's acknowledged data reuse that conflicted with a central conformal assumption. Together with INTERP-Q's new coverage bound and the corrected FUZZY formulation, this substantially strengthens the paper's rigor; the focal-loss check adds useful support. These gains outweigh limited losses in supplementary detail and a new reporting inconsistency: Section 3.1 attributes set sizes 7.6 and 55.8 to τ=0.99, whereas Tables 3–4 assign them to τ=0.999.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on the same datasets and simulations, with revised experimental results and an additional focal-loss experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist, including truncated datasets, method analyses, endangered-species results, and simulated human decision accuracy.

C1.justification: v1 presents TLC as a generative CV-learning framework validated on alanine dipeptide. v2 redefines the principal contribution as lightweight extraction of CVs from frozen BioEmu and adds a claimed systematic benchmark on proteins beyond alanine. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion consequently change the method's novelty claim and empirical scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting CVs to protein contacts, committors, and secondary structures, and explains why apparent OPES convergence or high VAMP scores can be misleading. Appendix D.3 motivates RMSD assistance through failures of unassisted SMD, although force constants also differ. These substantially expand applicability and failure discussions beyond v1's alanine-specific interpretations and autocorrelation tradeoff.

D1.justification: v2 adds DESRES sampling instructions, training/validation proportions, activation, dropout and early-stopping settings, software versions, solvation procedures, hardware, and runtime information in Appendices A–B. Its code link changes from the TLC repository to an anonymous BIOEMU-CV resource. Some earlier details disappear from the condensed alanine account, including the explicit 1000-femtosecond training lag; the protein training lag also remains numerically unspecified.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only alanine dipeptide. v2 retains that system and adds DESRES data and explicit-water folding evaluations for Chignolin, Trp-cage, and BBA, substantially expanding molecular and conformational coverage while retaining OPES and transition-path sampling as downstream tasks.

E2.justification: DeepLDA and DeepTDA disappear from the retained alanine comparison: v2 Table 11 preserves DeepTICA, TAE, and VDE from v1 Tables 1–2 but omits both supervised methods. Appendix C.5 additionally evaluates PCA-CVs and TICA-CVs on Trp-cage. These changes alter the comparator families actually tested.

E3.justification: The new protein evaluations introduce 1-microsecond OPES, 500-picosecond SMD, endpoint C-alpha RMSD criteria, PMF MAE, and learned-CV/RMSD mixtures for steering. Appendix C.8 adds approximately 9.8-microsecond OPES. For retained alanine experiments, TAE's stated input changes from aligned coordinates to heavy-atom distances despite identical scores; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that experiments were rerun.
