E4.justification: v2 adds tests of time-lagged conditioning, backbone freezing, encoder size, conditioning placement, and SMD without RMSD mixing, plus four-dimensional CVs and longer-simulation convergence analyses. Committor, hydrogen-bond, secondary-structure, and VAMP analyses substantially expand diagnostic coverage. v1's coordinate-representation and autocorrelation ablations are no longer reported.

E5.justification: Both versions report repeated-simulation averages and uncertainty. v2 additionally reports RMSD uncertainty across 16 protein SMD simulations and explicitly labels standard-deviation bands. More substantially, protein OPES estimates exclude one of four runs for Trp-cage and BBA using a specified deviation-from-mean rule, then recompute statistics over three runs (Appendix B.3); v1 uses all four alanine OPES runs.

E6.justification: The retained alanine values are unchanged, including TLC/TBG-CV's free-energy difference of 9.83 ± 1.15 and THP of 60.93%, while the DeepLDA/DeepTDA rows disappear. v2 adds extensive protein results, including BIOEMU-CV THPs of 100.0%, 31.2%, and 93.8% under RMSD-assisted steering. These are new-condition results, not gains over v1. Added ablations also show mixed outcomes: removing time lag improves PMF MAE but reduces THP in Table 13.

M1.justification: v1 jointly trains a TBG/EGNN flow backbone and CV encoder using flow matching plus autocorrelation on aligned coordinates. v2 introduces BIOEMU-CV, using a frozen BioEmu diffusion backbone, C-alpha-distance inputs, and a trainable encoder/MLP conditioning pathway optimized by denoising score matching without autocorrelation. The original approach remains as TBG-CV in Appendix C.6; this is substantially more than renaming.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. OPES now precedes SMD, interpretability and state discrimination receive dedicated sections, and the original central alanine study is condensed into Appendix C.6. The appendices are reorganized, with new reproducibility and disclosure statements.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column presentation, redraws the method overview around BioEmu, and introduces extensive protein trajectory, TICA, sensitivity, and secondary-structure displays. The original alanine OPES and SMD tables are merged into Table 11, and pathway panels are reconfigured in Figure 16. Several original alanine diagnostic plots disappear.

R1.justification: The central positioning shifts from TBG and continuous normalizing flows to adapting a pretrained molecular foundation model. v2 adds BioEmu, T2I-Adapter, AlphaFold, DESRES, committor, and protein-analysis references, and emphasizes scalability and the absence of systematic protein benchmarks. TBG remains cited for the appendix variant, while much of v1's flow-matching background and associated references disappears.

T1.justification: The mathematical specification changes from explicit flow-matching and autocorrelation losses in v1 to a conditional denoising-score objective in v2 Equation 1, with a no-lag variant in Appendix D.1. v2 also defines thresholded PMF MAE. These are limited changes to formal specifications; neither version develops theorems, proofs, or formal performance guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical conclusions rest on one small molecule. v2 substantially strengthens that foundation through three protein systems, comparisons against long DESRES trajectories, structural validation, and controls examining conditioning, freezing, and failure modes. These additions make applicability and design choices much more assessable. RMSD-assisted SMD, OPES outlier filtering, mixed ablation outcomes, and missing training details limit the strength of performance claims, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and diagnostic transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same time-lagged collective-variable learning project. Despite substantial refocusing, v2 retains v1's alanine results under TBG-CV in Appendix C.6. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulations and analyses for three proteins, extensive ablations, and supplementary evaluations, alongside retained alanine results.

before.justification: v1 reports original alanine dipeptide OPES and steered-MD simulations, quantitative comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and component ablations.

C1.justification: OMA, the navigation-oriented metric and MAT remain the core contributions. v3 broadens the headline performance claim to superiority over learned matching methods and emphasizes real-time GIS/navigation applications under the ONR framing. Its highlighted 34 ms MAT-T result already appeared in v1’s appendix, so this does not establish a new speed contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of geographic and generator transfer, annotation efficiency, corruption tolerance and aggregate-score bias toward simple roads. It identifies geometric complexity as an important failure boundary. It also replaces v1’s explanation of poor CTC-only performance with low-sensitivity language despite retaining the 67.7 versus 78.7 gap, and changes the stated future-work limitations.

D1.justification: v3 adds transition-boundary annotation rules, beam width 4 and expanded release/maintenance plans, while resolving several conflicting training specifications. It no longer discloses v1’s proprietary-Chinese-map MAT preannotation stage or the unoptimized CPU-baseline timing caveat; this does not establish that annotation was redone. Weight decay still conflicts between main text and appendix, and release statements mix present availability with future promises.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluations using MapTR and SeqGrowGraph predictions, nuScenes-C rain/fog/darkness conditions, corrupted SD maps and an occlusion case study. These expand the evaluated input conditions substantially. The original nuScenes/OSM cities and sample counts remain; renaming OMA-GT as OMA Train/Val does not establish additional coverage.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained KNN and HMM comparisons, v3 Tables 1–2 evaluate DeepMM, MTrajRec, GraphMM, EAM3, GMT and FastMAC. Table 3 also adds an evaluated PTv3 baseline. These substantially broaden the comparator set beyond v1.

E3.justification: v3 introduces cross-city training/testing, 1–100% training-data subsets, clean-trained zero-shot corruption evaluation and complexity-stratified scoring. Reported training settings also change: v1 Appendix F.2 gives learning rate 2e-3 and batch size 12, whereas v3 Appendix I.2 gives 1e-4 and 128. These are reporting revisions, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds geographic-transfer and data-efficiency studies, complexity-dependent error analysis, SD-map and weather robustness tests, and occlusion analysis. Tables 13–19 add sensitivity studies of crop size, spatial discretization, loss weights, serialization curves, beam width and metric settings. Existing attention visualizations persist, while the RoPE-specific ablation disappears.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, actual experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3 promises future release of random seeds but supplies no experiment-specific seed or uncertainty information. Its new metric stratification does not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Numerous baseline, transfer, corruption and sensitivity results are added. The MapTRv2-test MAT-L entry changes from 42.3 in v1 Table 1 to 45.0 in v3 Table 2; revised training documentation prevents treating this as an established same-setting gain. The clean-map score remains 78.7, with v3 explicitly labeling validation precision as NR-F1. Threshold-specific scores and MAT-S/M result rows are removed.

M1.justification: The vector encoder, PA/SA attention, association head, CE+CTC objective and beam decoding largely match. However, v1 explicitly applies multidimensional RoPE in both attention modules; v3 removes its description and ablation without clarifying whether RoPE was removed from the model or only from the documentation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, attention explanations and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Terminology systematically shifts from online HD maps and Association P-R to OP maps and NR P-R. The appendices are reorganized with a contents list, dataset Q&A and separate analysis sections, and the repeated bibliography is removed.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the navigation and metric illustrations, restructures comparison tables with method-category and generator columns, and splits the combined ablation table. It adds complexity plots and corruption/generator visualizations. Earlier attention, association and failure-case figures are largely retained but relocated within a substantially revised layout.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially recast around learned map matching, graph/point matching and SD-prior mapping, including SMERF, P-MapNet and TopoSD. Appendix C expands positioning relative to end-to-end planning and NavigScene. Conversely, v1’s explicit PTv3 methodological attribution and RoPE-related citations disappear.

T1.justification: v3 adds a Fréchet-distance-based complexity measure and equally weighted bin-scoring definition, plus computational-complexity assertions for PA and SA in Appendices E.2 and F. Core graph definitions, association mathematics, metric pseudocode and beam-search equations largely persist. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1’s narrow empirical support: KNN/HMM comparisons under one predicted-map generator are expanded to learned baselines, multiple generators, geographic transfer and controlled corruptions. The complexity analysis also exposes an important failure boundary. These materially strengthen assessment of MAT’s usefulness. Reporting weaknesses temper the gain: RoPE and annotation provenance become unclear, weight-decay settings remain inconsistent, and Tables 9–10 disagree with the stated bin-averaging rule. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and failure characterization constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMA benchmark and MAT framework despite changes in title and terminology. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original MAT evaluations and reports additional baseline comparisons, geographic transfer, data-efficiency, corruption and geometric-complexity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original OMA/OMA-GT evaluations, component ablations, model-size comparisons and qualitative analyses in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The central claims of dual-parameter calibration, residual-based aleatoric estimation, combining PCS with CQR, and compatibility with arbitrary estimator pairs remain. The new neural results provide additional support for the estimator-agnostic applicability already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of exchangeability, distribution shift, and the limits of marginal guarantees in Appendix B.1.1. Appendices B.3 and I.1 qualify the earlier favorable interpretation of NCIW by explaining how minimizing width can undermine conditional calibration. New Bayesian and runtime discussions further develop the method's motivation and applicability.

D1.justification: Appendix D.3 supplies neural architectures, diversity strategies, losses, optimization parameters, and stopping rules. Appendix F.5 newly reports hardware, memory, parallelism, and component runtimes. The existing code-access link is retained; moving it to a footnote does not change availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 17 regression datasets, synthetic homoskedastic and heteroskedastic scenarios, multivariate simulations, and Ames Housing feature settings. The neural estimators and additional calibration splits change configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated DE and SQR baselines and their conformalized counterparts in Table 1 and Appendix E. Standard variant (c) gains fixed-gamma1 and fixed-lambda comparisons in Tables 22–26. The earlier UACQR-P/S results are retained unchanged in Appendix G.3 alongside standard and conformalized CLEAR, rather than removed from the paper.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates the shared validation/calibration configuration. v2 additionally evaluates 60% training, 10% validation, 10% calibration, and 20% testing splits across all three PCS variants. Appendix D.3 also introduces neural experimental configurations with distinct architectures, optimization settings, and training budgets. The original standard configuration remains.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds comparisons testing the effect of separating calibration from parameter selection. Fixed-parameter ablations are extended to variant (c), and Appendix F.5 adds component-level runtime analysis. The earlier residual-modeling, model-choice, extrapolation, and housing analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations across 10 seeds, retain the nine-run exception for one naval-propulsion configuration, and report calibration parameters using median and range. Additional result tables follow these practices; changed uncertainty values do not establish a statistical-procedure change.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive neural, separate-calibration, fixed-parameter, and runtime results. Retained scores also receive numerical updates: CLEAR (a)'s insurance NCIW changes from 0.306 ± 0.032 in v1 Table 9 to 0.303 ± 0.029 in v2 Table 15. Results from the new configurations are additional evidence, not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 revises the stated aleatoric estimator from differences of aggregated residual quantiles to ensemble medians of nonnegative, per-member quantile gaps. The central weighted interval and calibration algorithms remain unchanged. Conformalized CLEAR was already defined in v1 Appendix G; its later experimental evaluation does not introduce that method.

P1.justification: The appendix organization changes substantially: coverage theory moves from G to B, algorithm details become B.5, and simulations, implementation details, and result configurations are regrouped. Main-text data subsections are merged, several explanations and the conclusion are tightened, and the appendix narrative gains extensive metric and theoretical discussion.

P2.justification: v2 adds a main-text neural comparison table and extensive neural, runtime, and separate-calibration tables. Variant (c)'s comparator columns are restructured, while UACQR results are redisplayed in Appendix G.3. Existing figures and the housing and abbreviation tables are retained, with some relocation and caption revisions.

R1.justification: Appendix A gains substantial positioning against other calibration methods, distributional regression, MAQR, credal approaches, and uncertainty methods for pretrained models and image generation. It explains additional distinctions and possible integrations with CLEAR. Several time-series references are removed, while the foundational PCS/CQR/UACQR discussion remains.

T1.justification: The original coverage lemmas are retained, but v2 adds mathematical counterexamples concerning interval-width optimization and conditional calibration (Examples B.3–B.6), Bayesian predictive-quantile reasoning and Example B.7, and an explicitly unproved CQR extrapolation hypothesis (B.8). These substantially expand the mathematical analysis.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important empirical gaps by testing modularity with neural estimators and evaluating the separate-calibration variant that v1 only developed theoretically. Runtime breakdowns and explicit analysis of NCIW's limitations further improve transparency and interpretation. Some editorial inconsistencies remain, notably A.1 directing UACQR claims to tables now containing fixed-parameter ablations, but the retained UACQR results in G.3 remain verifiable and these issues do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CLEAR with the same authors, central framework, and identifiable corresponding experiments. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds neural-estimator experiments, separate-calibration evaluations, and measured runtime breakdowns.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, evaluations on 17 regression datasets, and an Ames Housing case study, including detailed appendix results.

C1.justification: The contribution expands from applying discrete diffusion to audio inpainting to introducing two training innovations. The abstract and conclusion now claim performance on MusicNet and MAESTRO through 750 ms, replacing v1's MusicNet results and asserted MTG/500 ms coverage. The abstract also strengthens the performance claim to consistent outperformance for gaps of 150 ms and above.

C2.justification: v3 adds mechanism explanations connecting derivative regularization to temporal continuity and span masking to structured corruption. It interprets subset-trained MAESTRO results as resource-efficient generalization, acknowledges CQT-Diff+'s 150 ms FAD advantage, and explicitly discusses speech and language-model extensions as future work. These extend v1's general token-space coherence argument.

D1.justification: v3 adds selected regularization and span hyperparameters, MATLAB PEA-Q implementation information, MAESTRO subset-selection notes, and code-submission/future-release statements in Supplementary Material A–E. Optimizer, batch size, token length, and hardware were already documented in v1. Exact MAESTRO subset sizes and membership remain unspecified, and the PDFs do not provide the stated code.

E1.justification: v3 adds MAESTRO piano inpainting with 375 and 750 ms gaps. MusicNet reporting shifts from short-gap evaluations including 50 and 100 ms to 150–300 ms. v1's abstract mentions MTG evaluation through 500 ms without corresponding experimental details or results; that assertion disappears.

E2.justification: The MusicNet comparison retains LPC, A-SPAIN-L, CQT-Diff+, and the masked reference from v1 Figure 3. v3 Table 2 adds an evaluated comparator group comprising GACELA, bin2bin, and bin2bin-MIDI on MAESTRO; these were not evaluated against AIDD in v1.

E3.justification: v3 retains MusicNet's 60-segment, four-gap design and the base model's 400,000-step training, but specifies 100,000 steps for new variants. MAESTRO introduces 150,000-step training, six-second evaluation clips with one central gap, and PEA-Q evaluation. The reported inference crossfade changes from 10 to 6 ms.

E4.justification: v3 introduces a dedicated ablation study comparing the DWDSE base, span masking, derivative regularization, and their combination. Table 3 also tests regularization weights, derivative order, and span-distribution parameters at 200 and 300 ms. v1 contains no comparable component or hyperparameter analysis.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without uncertainty estimates. v3 first specifies averaging ten stochastic generations per MusicNet segment and adds ± values in Tables 2–3. It does not define those uncertainty terms or report independent training-seed counts, so this establishes expanded reporting rather than an increase in training runs.

E6.justification: Even the retained DWDSE base has revised MusicNet results: FAD at 200/300 ms changes from 3.0489/3.8067 in v1 Table 1 to 2.802/4.015 in v3 Table 3. Reported protocol differences prevent a clean same-setting performance comparison. v3 also adds variant results and MAESTRO PEA-Q ODG scores of -2.370 and -2.959 at 375/750 ms.

M1.justification: v3 retains the WavTokenizer–DiT backbone but extends DWDSE training with an embedding-derivative regularization loss and noise-dependent geometric span masking (Sections 4.2–4.3). These introduce substantive changes to the training objective and corruption procedure.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, the introduction gains an explicit contribution list, and related work is substantially condensed. v3 removes the standalone tokenizer background, consolidates architecture subsections, and moves inference and evaluation descriptions into the experimental setup. These constitute extensive rewriting and reorganization of existing material.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the separate training and inference diagrams with a redesigned combined Figure 1. MusicNet comparisons move from v1's three-panel Figure 3 and AIDD-only table to a multi-method table. New MAESTRO, ablation, and hyperparameter tables further change the presentation beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds the two Aironi works and references supporting MAESTRO, PEA-Q, and LPC, while removing Anderson and Campbell. It explicitly positions the new training components as extensions of Lou et al. The broader survey and continuous-versus-discrete framing remain substantially the same.

T1.justification: v3 adds mathematical definitions for first- and second-order embedding derivatives, their masked-position regularization loss, and the combined objective. It also formalizes a noise-dependent span-length distribution and masking budget (Sections 4.2–4.3). These substantially extend the mathematical formulation beyond v1's diffusion background; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the empirical support for the central long-gap argument: v1's MTG/500 ms assertion lacked corresponding results, whereas v3 provides explicit MAESTRO comparisons through 750 ms. Table 3 also makes the added training components assessable through component and sensitivity comparisons. Unspecified MAESTRO subsets, undefined uncertainty terms, unequal base/variant training budgets, and an overstated claim of combined-method superiority limit confidence. Nevertheless, the new checkable evidence and clearer experimental account provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AIDD, and their text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v3 includes readable Supplementary Material A–E.

after.justification: v3 reports original MusicNet and MAESTRO evaluations and training-component ablations in Sections 6–7 and Tables 1–3.

before.justification: v1 reports original MusicNet inpainting results using FAD, LSD, and ODG in Section 6, Table 1, and Figure 3.

C1.justification: V3 more explicitly presents the contribution as identifying a case of function induction in the introduction and conclusion. This qualifies the discovery's scope while retaining the central claims about parallel head contributions and reuse across tasks.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of attention sinks, newly identified heads outside the original groups, Llama-2's tendency toward a +2 function, and toy models apparently averaging training tasks. It explicitly limits universality and adds implications for evaluation, training curricula and alignment.

D1.justification: V3 documents the toy model's architecture, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and stopping conditions. Its reproducibility statement additionally describes released data, generation and plotting code, environment instructions and guided notebooks. The existing framework, GPU and path-patching runtime disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: The addition ranges and offsets, six MMLU subjects, Caesar-cipher tasks and base-k addition coverage are retained. The new toy-model study uses existing addition tasks; its training mixtures and model configurations change experimental design rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain their comparison methods and controls. The additional cross-model ablations reuse intact-model and random-head controls; zero/mean ablation comparisons and the Todd et al. FV-head comparison already appeared in v2.

E3.justification: V3 introduces a controlled training-and-evaluation design for randomly initialized toy transformers: five-shot inputs, three training mixtures and evaluation at offsets 0, 1 and 2 (Appendix G). It also adds model-specific causal-validation protocols in Appendix E.1. The original experiments' stated settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 substantially extends mechanistic validation with a search for omitted circuit heads, FI-head ablation and causal-transfer tests in three additional models, and toy-training analyses of whether models learn the contextual rule. V2's cross-model evidence primarily consisted of circuit discovery and attention patterns.

E5.justification: V3 Table 6 explicitly reports means and standard deviations over five runs for the new toy-model study. Figure 32 also displays error bars for PT-ablation controls previously presented as point values in v2 Table 5. Neither establishes increased runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: The main results are retained, but substantial new results appear. V3 reports 89% and 82% faithfulness for augmented circuits, alongside the unchanged original 78.4%; adds cross-model ablation and causal-effect results in Figures 27–30; and reports toy-training outcomes in Table 6, including 75.7±4.2% accuracy at k=1 after training on k=0 and k=2.

M1.justification: The original path-patching procedure and three-group mechanism remain. V3 Appendix D.1 adds a local-search refinement that tests excluded heads individually for their effect on faithfulness and constructs augmented circuits C6 and C7.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. V3 refines terminology and scope wording, expands the conclusion, moves Limitations before the references, and adds reproducibility and language-model-usage statements. The new experiments do not entail a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V3 adds an annotated circuit diagram, four cross-model validation figures and two experimental tables, and highlights relevant positions in existing attention plots. V2 Table 5 becomes the PT-ablation chart in v3 Figure 32. These substantially expand the visual presentation; most existing result graphics are retained.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning through a detailed comparison with Minegishi et al. (2025), acknowledging closely aligned circuits and emphasizing two-step reasoning and cross-task reuse as distinctions. It also adds discussion of semantic induction heads, attention sinks, compositional reinforcement learning and alignment-related research.

T1.justification: The logit-difference equations, circuit-evaluation definitions and base-8 algorithm remain unchanged. The new constant-versus-linear-function explanation is conceptual framing; no substantive theorem, proof or mathematical derivation is added.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism by adding causal validation across three models beyond v2's cross-model circuit-discovery evidence. Local search addresses the acknowledged faithfulness gap, while the Llama-2 exception and explicit scope qualifications improve calibration. Expanded circuits trade simplicity for greater coverage, and the toy study remains preliminary, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation and clearer research positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same function-induction study. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains these empirical results and adds circuit-refinement experiments, cross-model causal validation and original toy-transformer training results.

before.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations, circuit-discovery experiments, causal interventions and task-generalization analyses in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The central claims about on-policy value learning, joint entropy/KL tuning, stability, and efficiency remain. The introduction removes the continuous-action qualification from its first contribution and tempers its comparison with tuned baselines from superiority to competitiveness. The conclusion retains essentially the same principal contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4.1 newly distinguishes benefits of learned Q values from pathwise estimation, discusses applicability to non-reparameterizable policies, and attributes difficulties with GAE-based tuning to variance. Appendix B adds qualified explanations involving exploration and Atari return variance. v3 also acknowledges undiscounted empirical state occupancy and expands the framework-specific limitations of wall-clock comparisons.

D1.justification: Most architecture, optimizer, normalization, and code-access information is retained. v3 corrects the documented critic lower-bound rule, supplies the Atari lambda exception, and expands the JAX/PyTorch runtime discussion with sampling and CPU-related details. Atari-specific architecture and preprocessing information remain sparse.

E1.justification: v3 adds actual evaluation on ten Atari games with discrete actions, substantially extending coverage beyond continuous locomotion and manipulation. The original 23 DMC tasks, eight ManiSkill tasks, and toy experiment remain. Diffusion policies are discussed but not evaluated.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4 adds evaluated RPO and DPO comparators, while Appendix B introduces a reported PQN comparison. PPO and FastTD3 reference rows disappear from the component-ablation comparison, although both remain elsewhere. Despite mentioning PPO in the Atari prose, the corresponding Figure 8 and Table 1 report only REPPO and PQN.

E3.justification: v3 introduces gradient-estimator controls and an Atari protocol with human-normalized scores, curves through 200M timesteps, and lambda 0.65 instead of the continuous default 0.95. Table 2 changes the stated critic lower bound from max r/(1-gamma) to min r/(1-gamma), without establishing rerunning. A ManiSkill budget change remains unresolved because Figure 4 labels PPO as 200M while its caption states 100M.

E4.justification: New Section 4.1 compares pathwise REPPO with score-based variants using either learned Q values or PPO-style GAE, directly investigating whether benefits arise from value learning or gradient estimation. The original HL-Gauss, normalization, auxiliary-loss, KL, and buffer-size analyses are retained in Appendix D; their relocation is not an additional experiment.

E5.justification: The reported seed counts increase from 10 to 20 for REPPO and from four to 20 for PPO, substantially increasing stated replication of the central comparisons. FastTD3 remains at five seeds, and the existing 95% bootstrapped confidence-interval practice is retained.

E6.justification: v3 adds estimator-ablation, RPO/DPO, and Atari results. Atari Table 1 reports human-normalized means of 2.98 for REPPO and 3.35 for PQN, with IQM 1.64 for both. Existing benchmark and component-ablation curves also change. The joint objective is now reported slightly worse than clipping, whereas v1 reported no measurable difference. These are revised findings, not established same-setting performance gains across versions.

M1.justification: Appendix B introduces D-REPPO, computing finite-action expectations for policy value, entropy, and KL terms instead of differentiating through sampled continuous actions. This substantially extends the procedure to discrete policies. Continuous REPPO retains its principal components; its now-preferred clipped objective was already an optional variant in v1.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites and condenses the introduction, background, and method exposition. It reorganizes the algorithm around value learning, policy learning, and architectures, places estimator comparisons first in the evaluation, moves HL-Gauss mathematics into the main text, and regroups implementation details and existing analyses within the appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds an estimator schematic, a gradient-comparison figure, and Atari plots and a results table. The component ablation is split into separate batch-size panels and relocated. The selected-task main-text grid disappears while full per-task appendix plots remain. Existing figures receive substantial rearrangement, legend changes, and revised axes, including 50M rather than 200M timestep ranges in the continuous-control appendix plots.

R1.justification: v3 substantively expands positioning around joint entropy/KL optimization, projection-based trust regions, and differentiable trust-region layers, including Akrour et al. and Otto et al. It adds relationships to discrete SAC and diffusion policies and changes PQN unification from future work to an evaluated extension. The retained reliable-success metric also receives new attribution to Chan et al.

T1.justification: v3 adds finite-action objective formulas in Equations 18–20 and revises existing mathematical expressions: the TD-lambda normalization changes, and the KL-multiplier update replaces v1's duplicated entropy residual with a KL residual. These are limited algebraic extensions and corrections, without new theorems or proofs. The HL-Gauss equations are relocated from Appendix A to Section 3.3.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central empirical argument: Section 4.1 separates value-learning and estimator effects that v1's comparisons between complete algorithms could not isolate. Increased reported replication and additional baselines further improve confidence in that argument, while Atari results test a meaningful extension. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Algorithm 1 differs from the preferred clipped objective, the discrete entropy sign conflicts with the continuous loss, and ManiSkill horizon labels disagree. These issues limit the gains but do not outweigh the substantially stronger evidence for the main contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe REPPO with the same authors, core algorithm, and continuous-control benchmarks. All pages, including appendices, equations, tables, and rendered figures, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original continuous-control evaluations, additional gradient-estimator comparisons, and new Atari-10 results for discrete REPPO.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy optimization experiments, DMC and ManiSkill evaluations, component ablations, and memory and training-stability analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add ARMOR-Think as a contribution claiming improved utility and reasoning efficiency. They replace the emphasis on human-like structured reasoning with the argument that recovering explicit intent addresses out-of-distribution jailbreaks. The original ARMOR safety and unseen-strategy generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops an OOD-to-in-distribution intent explanation and adds the interpretation that policy analysis can correct some erroneous intent extractions. It newly specifies a service threat model excluding attacker access to reasoning and system prompts. Limitations shift from unresolved general-reasoning integration and overhead to residual overhead despite ARMOR-Think.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5 documents ARMOR-Think teachers, output formats, training hyperparameters, preference thresholds and per-round data quantities. Tables 8–10 newly disclose the existing ground-truth scoring prompts, and Table 11 supplies the reasoning-refinement prompt. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original ARMOR settings.

E1.justification: Utility coverage changes from four MMLU subjects, TruthfulQA and MATH to GSM8k and MATH, removing knowledge and truthfulness evaluations while adding elementary mathematical reasoning. This substantially narrows the kinds of utility assessed. Training instruction sources and safety/jailbreak coverage remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as an evaluated comparator while retaining the existing main baselines. New Table 13 additionally compares ARMOR adaptations against their unmodified Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-14B bases. These extend the comparator set without replacing the existing comparison framework.

E3.justification: New settings include ARMOR-Think training with three DPO rounds and about 10k preference pairs per round, a control trained without strategy analysis, and evaluations using 8B and 14B base models. New analyses measure safety-reasoning length and condition safety on intent-extraction correctness. Original attack budgets, judging procedures and decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds intent-extraction analysis (Figure 2), a training ablation testing the necessity of strategy analysis (Table 3), reasoning-length analysis (Figure 5), architecture/scale checks and two ARMOR-Think case studies. It removes three original correlation analyses: strategy-to-safety, intent-to-final-answer and safety-to-final-answer. The other three panels survive in Figure 7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional DPO rounds in v2 describe optimization, not replicated evaluation or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds ARMOR-Think results, including average attack ASR 0.050 and harmfulness 0.009; retained ARMOR values remain 0.060 and 0.002. New utility, ablation, intent, efficiency and base-model results substantially expand the evidence, while MMLU/TruthfulQA results disappear. Retained MATH scores only change rounding. ExHarm SFT prose changes from 0.72 to 0.74 despite retaining the original plot.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 introduces ARMOR-Think: shortened safety reasoning, separate distilled chain-of-thought reasoning for benign instructions, and preference learning with safety, helpfulness and structure rewards. These change training targets, reward construction and response generation. The original ARMOR pipeline remains.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, related work is compressed, and analysis paragraphs and headings are recast. Training-format exposition moves into the appendix, while ARMOR-Think and additional-results sections reorganize the narrative. These exceed local wording corrections.

P2.justification: v2 adds intent and reasoning-length plots, ablation and base-model tables, and appendix prompt/example displays. Tables 1–2 are restructured, the correlation figure contracts from six panels to three, and several displays are relocated or compressed. The original framework and data-construction diagrams are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GSM8k reference and three works concerning inference efficiency, while removing the MMLU and TruthfulQA references. The core safety-alignment and jailbreak literature remains substantially the same; the additions provide limited new efficiency context.

T1.justification: Equations 7–8 and Appendix A.5 add the ternary reward definition, safety/helpfulness selection masks and component score vectors. This is a limited formal extension; the original SFT/DPO mathematics is retained, and no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the strategy component through a direct training ablation and improves reproducibility through explicit scoring prompts. ARMOR-Think also provides a tested response to v1’s open reasoning-integration and overhead limitations, with shorter safety reasoning and improved math utility. These gains outweigh the loss of knowledge/truthfulness coverage and the new ExHarm text/figure inconsistency. ARMOR-Think’s higher average benchmark harmfulness remains a material tradeoff alongside the retained original model.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ARMOR, with v2 extending the work through ARMOR-Think. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated and new content.

after.justification: v2 retains original ARMOR experiments and adds ARMOR-Think evaluations, a strategy-step training ablation and additional base-model experiments, including Tables 1–3 and 13.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and utility evaluations, test-time scaling, ablations and unseen-strategy experiments in Tables 1–5 and Figures 4–5.

C1.justification: The agreement-bias and SGV claims remain, but v2 broadens its advertised contributions to demonstrated self-refinement, verifier-evaluation guidance, and an upgraded benchmark release. It also revises headline performance claims, including a 20-percentage-point advantage over prior VisualWebArena results rather than 16 points. These materially expand the abstract and introduction's contribution scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds an RLHF/sycophancy hypothesis, explains calibration failures through concentrated confidence scores, and discusses the label requirements, domain matching, and cost limiting sampling-based calibration. It also explains trajectory-length results through failure difficulty and examines when periodic intervention helps. These extend the retained discussions of strictness, imperfect oracles, and perceptual limitations.

D1.justification: v2 adds Reflexion and scoring-template prompts, calibration fitting and threshold-selection details, prior-generation configurations, and extensive documentation of oracle corrections and environment resets (Appendices A, B, E, F). It also announces model availability alongside code and data. Some reproducibility precision is lost through omitted snapshot identifiers and less explicit model-specific decoding settings.

E1.justification: The three core environments and robotic tool-hang task remain. v2 adds external, human-annotated VisualWebArena trajectories from AgentRewardBench, including BrowserGym execution-error cases (E.1), extending the represented verification data within the existing web domain. VisualWebArena-Lite is the earlier 305-task representative subset renamed, not new task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands comparisons with WebJudge, Platt and isotonic calibration, and web-search-grounded verifiers (Tables 10–13 and 20). Its main offline model comparison adds GPT-5, Qwen3, and smaller model variants while dropping GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL-72B. Pan et al.'s verifier and the Search Agent/R-MCTS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 changes model versions, replaces universal zero-temperature settings in Table 1 with model-recommended parameters, and revises oracle labels and evaluation rules. OSWorld's main supervision results use verification every five steps instead of only at termination; the documented downstream verifier token limit becomes 8192. New protocols include bias/skewness metrics, calibration trained on 605 trajectories and tested on 305, and a 60-step trajectory-length study.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained two-step and weaker-model ablations, v2 adds extensive tests of scoring templates, calibration, verification frequency, trajectory length, generator–verifier strength, prior diversity, noisy priors, and grounding tools (E.2–E.8). Figure 3 newly quantifies beneficial and harmful intervention outcomes. These substantially broaden the questions tested about reliability and mechanism.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports a bootstrap-estimated percentile threshold in its calibration experiment (E.3.2). Three-run averages for digital environments and 50 robotic rollouts were already documented in v1; there is no stated increase in those counts. Neither version provides systematic confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Many digital results are replaced or added. Online SGV success changes from 50% to 54% in VisualWebArena and from 24.5% to 27% in OSWorld under revised conditions (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4). New Reflexion results reach 53.9%, versus 46.2% without SGV after three refinements (Figure 2). v1's dedicated GPT-4o results disappear, while robotic results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The original two-stage SGV algorithm is retained. v2 adds optional implementations using concatenated priors or different models for prior generation (E.8), and integrates verification into a Reflexion loop with persistent reflections (A.2). These extend the inference procedure without replacing its central mechanism.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and much of the methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. SGV moves from Section 4 into the problem setup, evaluation principles receive a dedicated subsection, and Section 5 expands into downstream applications. Appendices are reorganized around detailed results, ablations, and environment documentation, while substantial earlier material is retained.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns and compresses Figure 1, restructures the main tables with additional metric columns and compact domain summaries, and adds a self-refinement plot, intervention-flow diagrams, response-distribution charts, and numerous analysis tables. Existing qualitative figures are largely retained and relocated. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 substantially extends its positioning through new engagement with AgentRewardBench and BrowserGym, RLHF sycophancy, evaluation-template biases, and tool-grounded critique. It uses these connections to distinguish agreement bias, motivate stronger evaluation controls, and position its benchmark repairs. This goes beyond the retained agent, test-time-scaling, and self-bias literature.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of trajectories and multimodal verifiers, and the two SGV generation equations, retain their substance. The added formulas concern standard evaluation statistics; the calibration studies are empirical. Neither version supplies new theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 acknowledged unreliable oracles without human-label validation; v2 documents corrections and reports 98% accuracy against external annotations versus 85.1% for the original oracles (Table 9). New calibration, robustness, and self-refinement experiments substantially strengthen the evidence for SGV's mechanism and practical value. Removing the matched-GPT-4o control and introducing reporting inconsistencies, such as Table 15's incompatible sample totals, weaken parts of the revision, but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SGV research, with matching authors, core method, and environments. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original verification, self-refinement, and online-supervision results, plus calibration, robustness, and oracle-validation experiments in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original trajectory-verification and agent-supervision experiments in Tables 1–4, with additional ablations and benchmark experiments in Appendices D–E.

C1.justification: v1's explicit non-extrapolation claim concerns RS. v2 extends it to BoN and makes the impossibility of extrapolating either method a central abstract and introduction takeaway. The ROC characterization and shared asymptotic-accuracy claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds a qualified interpretation connecting verifier-limited RS accuracy to RL, distinguishes per-query guarantees from aggregate observations, and discusses distributional assumptions and budget-specific verifier training (Sections 4.4, 6–7). v1's generation-versus-verification hardness interpretation is removed; the main ROC-based explanations remain.

D1.justification: Appendices F–G add MATH500 answer parsing with math-verify and its boxed-answer prompt, disclose GSM8K exact-match checking, and explicitly state that Qwen3 thinking mode is unused. Existing GSM8K/verifier prompts and chat-encoding code are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual MATH500 evaluation alongside GSM8K (Section 6, Figure 5). v1's empirical evaluation is confined to GSM8K, so the second benchmark substantially broadens the evidence's dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain RS versus BoN and the same Qwen3 and Llama verifier alternatives. The earlier four-verifier Qwen comparisons and two-verifier Llama comparisons remain in v2 Figure 4 and Appendix F. No new competing resampling method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The reported per-question generation pool changes from 10,000 responses in v1 to 1,000 in v2. New full-test-set evaluations cap RS at 25 attempts with an incorrect null fallback; MATH500 generation and verification also have 5,000-token limits. These are substantial revised and added evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds GSM8K question 58 as another case study of similar early scaling followed by divergent performance. It also explicitly assesses theory–simulation discrepancies for the Llama example, reporting absolute errors below one percentage point (Section 6, Figure 4). Earlier synthetic ROC demonstrations and other question-level analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and specifies 1,000 bootstrap resamples for its empirical experiments. v2 removes the per-question intervals and bootstrap-count description, while its new aggregate Figure 5 reports exact 90% confidence intervals. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds question-58 results and aggregate GSM8K/MATH500 accuracy curves, showing RS's early compute advantage and BoN approaching its performance later. Matched results also change, including the Llama question-7 curves (v1 Figure 9; v2 Figure F.5), and numerical AUROC annotations disappear. Changed reported settings preclude interpreting these as same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v2 Section 6 adds a verification variant that averages five scoring responses, alongside retained single-CoT verifiers. This changes the verification procedure modestly; the core RS acceptance and BoN selection rules remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten. RS/BoN definitions are consolidated in Section 3.1, related-work background moves to Appendix B, corollaries become equations or inline statements, proofs are reorganized, and a Discussion section is added.

P2.justification: Empirical plots are substantially redrawn with changed axis ranges, legends, marker/line encodings and Llama panel order. v2 adds aggregate Figure 5, replaces the main Figure 1 example with question 58, relocates v1 Figure 4 to Figure F.3, and expands the notation table.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on verifier failures, calibration, MATH and RL, including Petrov et al., Bavaresco et al., Tian et al. and Rafailov et al.; the bootstrap reference disappears. Positioning relative to pass@N, imperfect-reward BoN and ROC analysis largely remains, with background moved to Appendix B.

T1.justification: v2 adds results and proofs connecting KL-regularized RL to RS, establishing RS dominance at matched expected compute, and showing BoN non-extrapolability (Propositions 4, 6 and 7). Proposition 3 gains stronger limiting-accuracy and concavity cases; Appendix C adds a mixture characterization of BoN scaling (Theorem 2). v1's hardness Remark 1 disappears. The compact BoN integral and discrete-score smoothing already existed in v1's appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies a matched-compute dominance proof where v1 relied mainly on initial-slope comparisons and empirical examples, and tests key conclusions across full GSM8K and MATH500 datasets. These additions substantially strengthen the paper's formal foundation and empirical support. Removing per-question bootstrap intervals and resampling details is a reporting regression, but it does not outweigh those gains and the clearer organization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ROC-n-reroll study. Their text, figures, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix F report original per-question experiments and aggregate GSM8K and MATH500 evaluation results.

before.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D report original GSM8K generator/verifier experiments and empirical RS and BoN scaling results.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction explicitly condition RS dominance on a query having a concave verifier ROC curve, replacing unqualified wording or references to weak assumptions. The central ROC characterization, shared limiting accuracy, and impossibility of extrapolation remain. The discussion now treats hybrid methods as implemented approaches needing further refinement.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands applicability qualifications: a common threshold can spend excessive compute on hard queries, while difficulty-dependent thresholds require information unavailable in practice. Section 6 motivates capped hybrids as a remedy. Appendix E qualifies empirical superiority through overlapping uncertainty and dependence on the sample cap, and explains how the seed issue could affect response diversity.

D1.justification: V3 adds GPQA and HumanEval+ generator prompts, a code-specific verifier prompt, and correctness-evaluation details using letter matching and EvalPlus (Appendices E–F). Existing temperature, few-shot count, MATH500 token cap, and GSM8K prompt code are retained.

E1.justification: V3 retains GSM8K and MATH500 and adds GPQA STEM multiple-choice reasoning and HumanEval+ code generation (Figures E.7–E.8). This substantially broadens evaluation beyond mathematical question answering.

E2.justification: BoN remains the comparison method for RS, and matched experiments retain the existing Qwen3 and Llama verifier comparisons. The new RS variants extend the studied method; newly cited alternative approaches are not empirically benchmarked.

E3.justification: The main aggregate evaluation changes from constant thresholds and a null output after 25 failures to accuracy-dependent threshold groups and capped sampling with a fallback. New protocols include HumanEval+ comparisons at caps of 10 and 25, and a threshold-1 runtime diagnostic capped at 10,000 generations. These materially change the evaluated conditions.

E4.justification: V3 adds a focused diagnostic of extreme RS runtimes across queries (Figure E.1) and a HumanEval+ sensitivity comparison between sample caps of 25 and 10 (Figure E.8). Existing per-query ROC and scaling case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix E newly discloses a seed issue: aggregate experiments resample few-shot examples once per question, whereas individual GSM8K experiments resample them per generation. This adds seed information without establishing additional runs or a correction of the issue. Exact 90% confidence intervals remain the reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 Figure 5 is replaced by aggregate results for different RS procedures in v3 Figures 5a–b, so these are not performance gains under unchanged conditions. V3 adds GPQA and HumanEval+ results, including occasions where BoN beats RS capped at 25 on HumanEval+, while the cap of 10 appears more favorable. Figure E.1 reports 16 queries failing to reach threshold 1 within 10,000 generations. Retained per-query curves are unchanged.

M1.justification: V2 uses constant-threshold RS and returns an incorrect null output after 25 unsuccessful samples in aggregate experiments. V3 introduces difficulty-dependent thresholds, using t or t/2 according to a 1% base-accuracy cutoff, and Capped RS, which returns the highest-scoring sampled answer when the cap is reached. These change acceptance and output procedures.

P1.justification: Most narrative and the main section order are retained. V3 makes terminology and copy edits, expands the aggregate-experiment explanation, subdivides Appendix C, and integrates the former standalone discrete-score discussion into the formal setup and proofs. Empirical and prompt appendices are consequently relabeled.

P2.justification: The aggregate-results presentation is substantially expanded: Figure 5 becomes separate rows for variable-threshold and capped RS, with Bo25 reference lines replacing maximum-RS lines. Three new appendix figures display runtime diagnostics and GPQA/HumanEval+ comparisons. Original Figures F.1–F.5 reappear as E.2–E.6, with empirical-versus-predicted caption corrections in the first four.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds discussion of Chen et al. on compound AI systems and provable scaling, and Stroebl et al. on imperfect verifiers. Appendix B adds Wu et al. on reasoning length. New mathematical and benchmark references accompany the revision, while Rafailov et al. and Lan are removed. The central positioning around exact ROC characterization remains.

T1.justification: V3 replaces Assumption 1 and the separate discrete-score smoothing treatment with randomized threshold definitions and a distributional-transform proof (Sections 3 and D.6). It generalizes Proposition 4 to measurable sets, adds the token-cost derivation using Wald's theorem, restricts Theorem 2 to finitely many linear pieces, and requires 0 < c < 1 in Proposition 7. Corrections throughout Appendix D revise extrapolation constructions, convex decomposition, and convergence arguments.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the paper's mathematical reliability by unifying tied-score treatment and repairing important proof gaps, including the unjustified global Lipschitz argument in v2 Appendix D.11. It also addresses the aggregate sampling problem with tested alternatives and validation beyond mathematics. Explicit concavity conditions and new failure analyses better delimit the conclusions. Unknown query difficulty, overlapping confidence intervals, and the disclosed seed issue still limit empirical interpretation, but the gains in rigor and practical understanding support a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ROC-based analysis of rejection sampling and Best-of-N. Their main text, mathematical statements, proofs, figures, notation table, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original per-query experiments and reports revised aggregate comparisons, additional diagnostics, and GPQA and HumanEval+ results in Section 6 and Appendix E.

before.justification: V2 reports original Qwen and Llama experiments on GSM8K and MATH500 in Section 6 and Appendix F, including empirical scaling curves and aggregate accuracies.

C1.justification: The central noise-free vision-to-action flow and action-autoencoder/FLD contributions remain. v3 broadens the architecture claim to include spatial features and transformers, adds quantified memory savings of 18.6%–28.7%, and revises the advertised inference advantage from 1.5×–2.3× to 1.5×–2×. Efficiency receives stronger emphasis without replacing the core contribution.

C2.justification: Appendices B.5–B.8 substantially expand interpretation. v3 attributes DP/ACT failures to precision errors and stringent multi-stage success criteria, connects stochastic visual encodings with lost precision, and explains conditional MLP-FM's difficulties. It also explicitly discusses FLD's additional training time and memory as a tradeoff for inference efficiency, beyond v2's shorter observations.

D1.justification: v3 documents frozen-autoencoder pretraining, the MLP-FM construction, spatial-feature dimensions, and peak-memory measurement using torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated with the shared visual encoder excluded. It adds demonstration counts, camera configurations, and randomization details for the new tasks. It also corrects the DP table to specify the already-described ten-step sampler and explicitly advertises code, datasets, and demos through the retained project-page link.

E1.justification: v3 retains the earlier tasks and adds RLBench CloseBox plus three real-world single-arm tasks: PickBall, ToothBrush, and StoreDrawer. Appendix E additionally evaluates manual disturbances during PickBall and four unseen objects during StoreDrawer, substantially expanding task and test-environment coverage.

E2.justification: FM, DP, and ACT remain the principal comparators. v3 adds MLP-based FM with AdaLN to the existing efficiency comparison and evaluates it against MLP-based VITA (Table 1 and Figure 11). Transformer and U-Net FM comparators already appeared in v2; their appearance here is not a new baseline addition.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes VITA's stated training budget from 50K to 25K–50K steps, DP's from 200K to 100K, and ACT's from 200K to 100K–200K. New analyses introduce architecture controls, reward/action-MSE measurements, memory and training-cost benchmarks, and a four-object OOD evaluation. These are substantial reported protocol changes, although v3's DP hyperparameter table still lists 200K steps, leaving that budget inconsistent.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative evidence for the previously asserted frozen-autoencoder failure, MLP-FM and transformer-VITA architecture comparisons, and FLD training-cost analysis. It also adds DP failure cases, reward and action-MSE analyses, online perturbation examples, and unseen-object tests. Earlier zero-padding, contrastive-loss, variational-encoder, and hyperparameter ablations are largely retained and relocated.

E5.justification: v2 already reports three-seed averages and standard-deviation bands in appendix learning curves. v3 additionally reports mean ± standard deviation for each simulation-table entry (Table 2). The stated seed count remains three; no increase in repetitions or new significance-testing procedure is established.

E6.justification: Many existing simulation results change: DP's ThreadNeedle success rate changes from 0% to 59.33%, and VITA's Square result from 100% to 95.33%. v3 also adds CloseBox, single-arm real-world, OOD, architecture, and resource results. VITA's 0.2215 ms MLP latency and the two original real-world task results remain unchanged. Revised training budgets prevent treating the changed simulation scores as established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 adds a transformer-based VITA variant using 9×512 spatial features (Section 5.1 and Appendix B.6.2). The original vector-based MLP implementation, action autoencoder, FLD/FLC objectives, and flow procedure remain, making this a bounded architectural extension.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the efficiency motivation and architecture explanation, condenses the preliminaries, and reorganizes Section 5.2 into efficiency-first and success-rate subsections. The appendices consolidate formerly separate objective discussions and learning-curve sections into an expanded Appendix B, while relocating task and implementation material. This constitutes substantial narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: The efficiency table is redesigned into vector/grid groups with memory reporting, and the simulation table gains uncertainty entries. Figure 4 is rebuilt around five real-world tasks, while the earlier detailed two-task rollout panel moves to Figure 18. New architecture, failure, perturbation, and OOD displays substantially expand the visual evidence; many earlier ablation figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including π0.5 and Helix for latency motivation, RLBench, and Diffusion as Self-Distillation, with a targeted discussion connecting the latter to latent collapse. The Attention Is All You Need and contrastive predictive coding references are removed. The overall positioning relative to diffusion and cross-modal flow matching remains largely intact.

T1.justification: The FLD/FLC assumption, theorem, lemma, corollaries, and Appendix A proofs are retained. The added Euler update in Section 3 explicates the existing solver, and the repaired assumption cross-reference is editorial rather than a mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central efficiency claim through comparable-architecture FM controls, vector/grid comparisons, and explicit memory and training-cost measurements beyond v2's parameter/latency table. Comparative real-world experiments, quantitative frozen-autoencoder evidence, and main-table uncertainty reporting also address important validation gaps. The inconsistent DP training budget and small OOD evaluation limit some conclusions, but the stronger controls and more transparent tradeoff analysis establish a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VITA research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original results on nine simulation and five real-world tasks, efficiency benchmarks, ablations, and perturbation and unseen-object evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original results on eight simulation and two real-world tasks, inference benchmarks, and appendix ablations.

C1.justification: v3 makes dependence of reasoning-capacity changes on training-data difficulty a principal contribution and presents an implemented curriculum as central to QuestA. v2 principally claims that fixed partial-solution augmentation expands capacity. The overall state-of-the-art and sample-efficiency claims remain, with revised headline results.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations linking easy-prompt RL to shallow-pattern overfitting, decreasing hints to training–evaluation alignment, and no-hint training to neglect of the hardest problems (Sections 2, 5.2, C.1). It qualifies OpenMathReasoning experiments as first-stage-only. Section 5.1 also strengthens the 32B comparison to superiority on every benchmark, although Table 1 contradicts this on AIME24.

D1.justification: v3 newly states access to code, data, and models through a project repository; its availability is not independently verified here. It supplies post-augmentation filtering thresholds, easy/hard selection rules, and exact curriculum budgets. Existing optimizer and decoding details largely persist, although v2's explicit identification of the DeepScaleR comparison baseline as Stage 3 is omitted.

E1.justification: Both retain OpenR1-Math-220K and OpenMathReasoning, the same five mathematical benchmarks, and GPQA Diamond, Zebralogic, Code Contests, Codeforces, and LiveCodeBench V5. Cross-domain results move to v3 Appendix C.2. New difficulty splits and smaller training subsets change sampling within existing coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Easy-Nemotron and Hard-Nemotron RL comparators (Figures 2 and 17), plus a same-data RL comparator without hints (Table 5). These provide substantial comparisons absent from v2. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, included in v2 Table 2, is removed; DeepScaleR's own before/after comparison remains in v3 Table 6.

E3.justification: The main Nemotron training budget changes from 500 steps to 2,000, allocated as 100 steps with 50% hints and 1,900 with 25% hints. Additional filtering reduces the augmented pool from 26K to at most 10K problems. New easy/hard controls use approximately 4K questions each and 1,000 steps. Core benchmark decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled analyses of easy versus hard training prompts, training with versus without hints, fixed 50% hints versus the two-stage curriculum, and extension to zero hints (Section 2, Section 5.2, Appendix C). The existing dataset ablation remains, with its OpenR1 comparison updated to the new fixed-50% run.

E5.justification: Both report pass@1 averaged over 32 completions and retain the same unbiased pass@k estimator and sampling condition in Appendix A.2. Neither introduces training-run repetitions, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new variance-based data selection concerns training design, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main Nemotron scores change from 67.08/59.50/35.52 to 72.50/62.29/41.67 on AIME24/AIME25/HMMT, and the five-benchmark average changes from 59.01 to 63.26 (v2 Table 2; v3 Table 1). These results use revised training conditions. v3 also adds control and curriculum results and updates training-set success and unsolved-problem findings. DeepScaleR and cross-domain table values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 uses fixed 50% hints and describes curriculum training as future work. v3 implements a 50%-to-25% curriculum and adds difficulty filtering after augmentation at each stage (Section 3, Appendix A.5). These substantially extend the training procedure; the underlying GRPO objective and reward remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten, and a new difficulty-versus-efficiency section reorganizes the argument. Related work, benchmark descriptions, and much DeepScaleR discussion move into expanded appendices. Citation style, author presentation, headings, and appendix organization also change substantially.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes its displayed model series, and the original four-panel pass@k presentation is reorganized into controlled comparisons and separate appendix plots. The main mathematical table is split, training plots are redrawn with revised colors, legends, and panel ordering, and new ablation tables and figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Gao et al.'s 'One-shot entropy minimization' and Wang et al.'s work on RL with one training example to motivate sample selection, and removes the infinite-monkey reference. The broader related-work discussion and positioning against approaches such as StepHint remain substantially intact in Appendix A.3.

T1.justification: v3 removes the 'LLM as Infinite Monkey' proposition and its appendix proof. The central capacity definitions, null-gradient assumption, sampling bounds, and tabular policy-gradient proof remain substantively unchanged. The hinted-sampling lemma leaves the main text but remains in Appendix B.1.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important weakness in v2: comparisons against initial checkpoints did not isolate hints from continued RL training. The same-data/schedule no-hint control and equal-2,000-step curriculum ablation directly test these contributions (Tables 5 and 3: average 63.26 versus 60.44 and 60.26). Added filtering and schedule details also improve reproducibility. These substantial evidential gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including the incorrect all-benchmark 32B comparison and Figure 5's description of entropy as increasing despite its decline after an early peak.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QuestA, with matching research identity and substantial shared content. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and additional controlled experiments testing prompt difficulty, hints, and curriculum design, including Tables 1, 3, and 5.

before.justification: v2 reports original QuestA training experiments, mathematical and cross-domain evaluations, and training-dynamics analyses in Tables 2–4 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the 17.7× average/449× peak claim with 3.12×/120× against default references and add claims against compiled and CUDA Graph baselines. The introduction adds contributions concerning released Graph references and reward-hacking detection, and expands optimization discovery to mathematical simplifications. The central contrastive-learning and generalization claims remain.

C2.justification: V1 celebrates extreme stream-related gains as evidence of optimization synergy. V7 identifies asynchronous-stream timing exploitation as producing artificial approximately 18× results and explains why prompt restrictions are insufficient. It adds the need for careful human inspection and replaces the strongest-complex-task interpretation with baseline-dependent effectiveness and mathematical-shortcut explanations.

D1.justification: V7 adds synchronization pseudocode, specifies the checker model, three retrieved hacking examples and clipping threshold 1.5, and documents Claude 4's Graph-reference construction with up to ten attempts and an announced release location. Appendix B replaces the GRU/standard-convolution listings with LSTM and constant-output implementations, including a timing harness.

E1.justification: Both versions train and evaluate using the same 250 KernelBench tasks across three levels. V7 removes H800 from the GPU portability coverage while retaining the other five architectures. Its replacement case studies and generated reference implementations concern existing benchmark tasks.

E2.justification: V7 adds evaluated reference comparisons using Torch Compile, Torch Compile Reduce Overhead and Claude-4-generated CUDA Graph implementations in Tables 4 and 6. The vanilla LLM, evolutionary LLM and CUDA-L1 variant membership in Table 5 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V7 Section 3.1 specifies synchronization of additional CUDA streams before recording the end event, addressing an explicitly demonstrated timing loophole. It also introduces a speedup threshold above 1.01 and conversion-dependent CUDA Graph comparison denominators, including 229 tasks on A100. The 20-minute evaluation window and 1,000-input correctness checks remain.

E4.justification: V1's GRU and standard-Conv3D ablations are replaced by LSTM and mathematical-short-circuit ablations involving different optimization combinations (v7 Tables 8–9 and Appendix B). V7 also adds a diagonal-matrix case study and quantifies timing exploitation. The training-stage and exemplar-selection ablation families remain.

E5.justification: The main repeated-timing, variance-control and best-of-five procedures remain unchanged. V7 Appendix B.1 newly includes an example timing harness averaging 100 forward passes; v1's replaced GRU listing has no equivalent timing loop. This is limited repetition information, without evidence of additional independent training runs or new confidence-interval reporting.

E6.justification: Table 4's reported A100 mean/maximum change from 17.7×/449× to 3.12×/120× alongside timing and training revisions, rather than establishing a same-setting performance decline. Tables 5–6 also change extensively, and the highest default mean shifts from RTX 3090 to H100. Compiled/Graph results are added, while v1 Tables 7 and 11's detailed per-level comparisons disappear.

M1.justification: The three-stage training framework, backbone and contrastive exemplar selection remain. However, v7 Section 3.2 introduces a DeepSeek-R1 reward checker, retrieval from a dynamic hacking-case database, and normalized reward clipping. These substantially extend reward validation and modify training beyond v1's prompt-based prohibitions.

P1.justification: The abstract, results discussion, portability discussion and case-study narrative are substantially rewritten. Reward hacking moves from a method subsection into a standalone section, dataset and evaluation descriptions are merged, and appendix organization changes after removing the former Appendix A. Much of the original training exposition remains.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a grouped comparison of four reference configurations across five GPUs. The speedup-distribution and execution-timeline figures disappear, and a diagonal-code figure is added. Tables 4 and 6 gain configuration blocks. Retained generic appendix snippets are reformatted from three dense four-column tables into five three-column tables.

R1.justification: The 33 referenced works are retained. V7 Section 6.1 removes v1's characterization of The AI CUDA Engineer [13] as a retrieval-based non-RL comparator, its assertion that this work was evaluated as a baseline, and the direct superiority claim. Broader positioning against evolutionary LLMs remains.

T1.justification: V7 adds Equation 6 defining normalized, clipped rewards and a short algebraic/complexity argument for diagonal multiplication in Section 5.1. The original exemplar-sampling, reward-aggregation and GRPO equations remain substantively unchanged; no theorem or proof framework is introduced.

improvement.justification: V7 substantially improves transparency and evaluation design by exposing the timing loophole behind the earlier approximately 18× claim, specifying corrected synchronization, replacing the headline results and adding compiled/Graph comparisons. This addresses a central validity defect in v1. Removed breakdowns and remaining inconsistencies limit reliability: Section 4.4 claims a 96% bucket-method speedup rate despite Table 5 reporting 226/250, and Appendix B.1's reference and optimized LSTM listings return different outputs. These problems are material, but the measurement correction and broader comparisons provide a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CUDA-L1. Their methods, equations, results, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V7 reports original benchmark comparisons, GPU-transfer results, reward-hacking observations and optimization ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original KernelBench evaluations, GPU-transfer experiments and optimization ablations, including per-level comparisons in Appendix A.

C1.justification: v1's central contributions are the geometric equivalence, error guarantee and ordering heuristic. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion additionally claim practical no-clipping quantizers with better accuracy than original GPTQ and efficient GPU inference kernels. This substantially expands the claimed contribution beyond theoretical analysis and prospective applications.

C2.justification: v2 explains why enlarging scales to eliminate clipping can worsen the error bound and motivates explicit outlier handling. It qualifies min-pivot's practical benefit as modest and recommends act-order as an inexpensive approximation for well-conditioned Hessians (Sections 4.5–5). Appendix D.4 adds kernel tradeoff interpretations, although its claim of superiority in every setting conflicts with sub-baseline results in Figure 5.

D1.justification: v2 adds scale-search pseudocode and boundaries, calibration and evaluation processing details, a typical damping formula, and extensive SSQR CUDA/C++ implementation information.
