These are additional protocols; the existing benchmark search spaces, including the 60,000-sample threshold, are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative split-method and temperature ablations, including runtime tradeoffs (E.1–E.2), a large-dataset RFM comparison (E.3), benchmark-overlap analyses (E.14–E.16), portfolio analyses (E.17), and performance versus dataset metafeatures (F.3). These substantially expand investigation of the method's design and behavior beyond v2's benchmark and interpretability evidence.

E5.justification: Table E.13 newly reports asymmetric Elo uncertainty bounds, whereas v2's corresponding table contains point estimates only. Their confidence level and estimation procedure are unspecified. The existing Wilcoxon comparison and five-split averaging for the retained meta-test results remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v2's binary TabArena Table B.10 duplicates its regression Table B.8; v3 replaces it with distinct binary results in E.13, including xRFM (T) Elo 1251 instead of 1504. This is a reporting correction. Numerous supplementary results are also added, while matched TALENT, original meta-test, and TabArena regression/multiclass tables retain their values.

M1.justification: v2 routes each prediction to one leaf. v3 Appendix B adds optional temperature-tuned routing that averages predictions from up to eight leaves using products of node weights. Appendix D also introduces validation-based selection among xRFM and GBDTs. These add substantive prediction procedures, while the original leaf learner and Algorithms A.1–A.5 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Main section order and most prose remain intact. v3 expands selected results paragraphs, introduces focused appendix sections B–D and F, and updates author affiliations, acknowledgments, headers and citation style. These are localized editorial and organizational changes.

P2.justification: Figure 3 expands from six to nine panels, adding normalized-error versus training-time plots. Seven supplementary tables and Figures F.1 and F.3 are added; existing tables and figures are redistributed under the ICLR layout. The original runtime Figure B.1 is retained as F.2, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: The cited works and principal positioning relative to RFMs, scalable kernels, GBDTs and tabular foundation models remain unchanged. Switching from numbered to author-year citations does not add related work.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces mathematical definitions for temperature-scaled sigmoid node weights and path-product leaf weights, relating hard routing to zero temperature. Existing kernel, AGOP and metric definitions remain unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves important evidential and reporting weaknesses: it quantifies split-design alternatives and their computational costs, investigates benchmark dependence, and replaces the duplicated binary TabArena table with task-specific results and uncertainty bounds. These substantially improve support and auditability while preserving the main benchmark evidence. The added tables also expose increased routing costs and nonuniform portfolio gains, although uncertainty-estimation details remain sparse.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same xRFM work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds split-method, temperature-tuning, dataset-characteristic and model-portfolio analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original xRFM benchmark results, runtime measurements and synthetic and real-data feature analyses.

C1.justification: V4 expands the stated contributions to include NegGenBench and trained negation-aware evaluators. Its abstract now claims effective Flux Schnell integration, and its conclusion adds creative, abstract, and unconventional-aesthetic applications. The central claim of stronger negative adherence with low computational overhead remains.

C2.justification: V4 explains why near-ceiling MLLM quality scores poorly distinguish quality, supported by human comparisons (Appendix F). It adds evaluator insensitivity as an explanation for unchanged bias-ablation results and interprets artistic generation as countering preference-induced style homogenization. Failure discussions change substantially, including removal of v1's conclusion that Wan VSF and NAG outputs are overall comparable.

D1.justification: V4 adds VSF pseudocode, explicit VSF preset hyperparameters, Flux embedding-processing instructions, and QLoRA training and annotation/splitting details. It first specifies 28 steps for the retained CFG baseline. Conversely, v1's available-code/ComfyUI statement and link are replaced by promises to release code, data, and models after publication.

E1.justification: The existing 200-prompt component-removal benchmark is retained and named NegGenBench. V4 expands evaluated tasks to style avoidance and abstract/unconventional-aesthetic generation (Appendices M–N), and adds supervised negation/quality judging on a newly annotated image collection (Appendix O).

E2.justification: V4 adds Nano Banana to the external generation comparison and introduces evaluator comparisons against LLaMA Maverick and Qwen-2.5-VL-32B, each with and without chain-of-thought prompting (Table 7). The Wan qualitative comparison drops NAG, retaining only original generation versus VSF. The main image comparators remain, with NAG++ renamed NAG Strong.

E3.justification: V4 adds a VSF Quality setting, human scoring of four methods on ten prompts with two seeds, and a prompt-level 90/10 split with three-level annotations for evaluator training/testing. Table 7 binarizes partial adherence, whereas Table 8 retains fractional scores. Wan qualitative evaluation changes from 1.3B to 14B; the runtime experiment still uses 1.3B.

E4.justification: V4 adds quantitative alpha/beta sensitivity on 30 prompts (Figure 19), human–MLLM agreement and quality-score analyses (Table 4/Figure 9), CLIP negation diagnostics, and new failure cases. The original trade-off and component-ablation curves remain unchanged in Figure 6. Image and Wan case studies are substantially replaced.

E5.justification: V1's McNemar-test description and Table 2 p<10^-6 annotations disappear. V4 adds linear/logarithmic regression fits and R-squared reporting for human–MLLM quality agreement (Figure 9). The main benchmark still uses two seeds, without newly reported confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Existing Table 2 scores remain unchanged after renaming. V4 adds VSF Quality scores of 0.980/0.420/0.986 and Nano Banana scores of 0.985/0.498/0.980 for positive/negative/quality metrics. It also adds Flux, human-validation, evaluator-benchmark, and rescoring results (Tables 3–8), and replaces qualitative examples. These additions do not establish improvements under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The core sign-flip attention, masking, duplication, and padding removal remain. V4 adds negative-embedding extrapolation for Flux Schnell using a mean-padding reference and scale 8 (Appendix G), following v1's unsuccessful Flux application. It also introduces QLoRA-trained NegAwareQwen-7B/32B evaluation models (Appendix O).

P1.justification: V4 extensively reorganizes the narrative into separate experiments, results, and discussion sections, moving substantial background, implementation, evaluation, and qualitative material into appendices A–S with a contents list. Method explanations and results prose are substantially rewritten, and reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: V4 combines the existing trade-off and component-ablation plots into Figure 6 and relocates the hyperparameter grid and quality examples. It replaces image/video montages, removes the WEF gallery, and adds style, failure, agreement, and sensitivity figures plus several evaluation tables. Table 1 gains open-/closed-weight groupings and metric-direction indicators.

R1.justification: Positioning expands into trained negation evaluators, machine unlearning, and aesthetic/preference alignment, citing Qwen2.5-VL, QLoRA, Gandikota et al., VisionReward, LAPIS, and human-values literature. The core CFG/NASA/NAG/Dynamic Negative Guidance lineage remains. V1's separate Feedback Guidance citation is removed.

T1.justification: V4 introduces explicit attention-derived token weights and weighted-subtraction equations (6–8), followed by Appendix B's algebraic equivalence proof. V1 only asserted that equivalence after Equation 6. This is a limited formal addition concerning an already-stated identity.

improvement.justification: V1 acknowledged unreliable MLLM scoring but only mentioned human comparison without reporting its results. V4 supplies human validation and judge-agreement analysis (Tables 3–4/Figure 9), benchmarks a trained negation evaluator, and provides additional generator ratings (Tables 7–8). This substantially strengthens validation of the central negative-guidance finding. The small human sample, removed significance reporting, deferred code-release statement, and Table 8 positive scores that contradict claimed reuse from Table 2 remain meaningful drawbacks, but the stronger validation provides a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VSF research and contain readable main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Matching methods, benchmark results, and figures support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains original experiments and adds human validation, Flux results, trained evaluator benchmarks, sensitivity analyses, and artistic-generation experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-generation evaluations, hyperparameter sweeps, component ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative Wan video results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: identifying shift-readapt-overfit dynamics, introducing dual-control integration of expert data and on-policy learning, and claiming advantages over sequential SFT-then-RL and other baselines. The additional experiments chiefly support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands interpretation and qualifications concerning threshold sensitivity, potentially task-dependent weighting choices, expert style versus expert strength, and weaker models' difficulty absorbing demonstrations. It also discusses continued RL benefits after scaling SFT and explicitly acknowledges configuration dependence and the primarily empirical understanding of pattern shifts (Appendices B and D; Section 6).

D1.justification: v3 supplies technical details for added studies, including weighting cutoffs, synchronization and training budgets, the Qwen3-30B-3A-Instruct medical judge, and 5,000 aligned expert demonstrations for LUFFY/SRFT. Existing software, GPU disclosures and the implementation hyperlink are retained; the new reproducibility statement does not establish changed code availability.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original mathematics, general-reasoning and tool-use coverage, and adds non-verifiable medical question answering on RaR-Medicine with English medical-o1-reasoning expert demonstrations (Appendix B.4). Appendix B.3 also introduces tool-use demonstrations generated by Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct.

E2.justification: LUFFY, whose tool-use results were omitted in v2, is now evaluated on BFCL; SRFT is newly evaluated there (Table 12). Appendix B.2 also adds evaluated comparisons against Entropy Top, Entropy Norm, IS Clip and Focal Loss, substantially expanding the comparison set.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 400-step mathematical training with synchronization every two updates and 16 rollouts, model-judged medical evaluation, Qwen2.5-3B and Phi-mini-MoE policies, and a 20k-example SFT condition. Appendix A.1 also changes the reported tool-use mu decay from 0.6 to 0 over 20 steps to 0.9 to 0.05 over 30 steps. This establishes a reported setting revision without independently proving a rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds adaptive-threshold sensitivity, alternative token-weighting tests, expert-source sensitivity with qualitative examples, weaker-model and MoE robustness studies, and an investigation of whether scaling SFT eliminates RL's benefit (Appendices B.1-B.3, B.5-B.6 and D.3). The original joint-scheduling analysis and bus-trip case studies are retained in B.7 and E.

E5.justification: Both versions retain avg@32 reporting for AIME and avg@8 for AMC in Appendix A.2. v3 adds no repeated-training-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures. Its new discussion of RL variance does not change statistical reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous results are added, including RaR-Medicine scores of 81.3 for CHORD-phi versus 76.8 for pure RL, and Phi-mini-MoE BFCL scores of 61.6 versus 58.9 (Tables 7 and 9). Original main-table mathematics and CHORD-phi scores remain unchanged. CHORD-mu's BFCL overall score changes from 78.1 to 77.6 and tool-use response length from 130 to 197 (Tables 1-2), alongside the revised reported schedule; these are not established same-setting performance declines.

M1.justification: The hybrid objective and default token weighting phi(p)=p(1-p) remain unchanged. Section 4.3 and Appendix B.1 add an implemented optional variant that updates the mixing coefficient using mu=max(0, threshold-mean_reward), extending the procedure beyond predetermined schedules.

P1.justification: Most shared exposition is retained. v3 condenses the preliminaries and main related work, adds Section 4.4, expands the conclusion with future directions, and separates appendix setups/prompts from experimental results. Conference headers, author-year citations, acknowledgements and disclosure sections also change the presentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds eight result tables and a medical training-curve figure, revises the tool-use plots, and relocates existing supplemental displays. The manuscript also adopts the ICLR layout, changing title treatment, headers, text width, typography and placement of figures and tables. The framework diagram and many original plots are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting medical experiments, focal loss and the MoE evaluation. It explicitly connects loss mixing to scheduled sampling and expands discussion of SimpleMix's dataset-level mixing. The main positioning around instruction-tuned policies versus base-model Zero-RL remains intact.

T1.justification: The principal objectives and assumptions in Equations 1-6 remain unchanged. Appendices B.1-B.2 add limited mathematical definitions for reward-adaptive mixing and alternative token-weighting functions, without adding proofs, theorems or theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind CHORD: alternative-weighting and expert-source studies test previously limited aspects of its rationale, while actual LUFFY and SRFT tool-use comparisons address an important comparison gap. Medical and additional-model experiments broaden the empirical support, and explicit qualifications better delimit the conclusions. These gains outweigh the remaining lack of training-run uncertainty and the insufficiently specified SFT-scaling results in Appendix D.3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CHORD, with matching core objectives, original experiments and case studies. The text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, allowing new material to be distinguished from revisions and relocations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds weighting comparisons, expert-source experiments, medical question answering and additional policy-model evaluations.

before.justification: v2 reports original mathematical-reasoning and tool-use experiments, training-dynamics analyses, ablations and generated-response examples.

C1.justification: The central claims of a fast robustness diagnostic and ranking sensitivity to very few preferences remain. v2 broadens the stated scope to Bradley–Terry variants and Arena derivatives, and qualifies the human-versus-LLM conclusion from being 'just as sensitive' to neither being systematically more sensitive (abstract and Section 4.3).

C2.justification: v2 explicitly explains that unsuccessful searches cannot certify robustness and that masking can cause false negatives (Appendix H). Appendix A distinguishes worst-case sensitivity from sampling uncertainty. v1's five examples motivate a similar-response explanation, whereas v2's two new examples motivate an outlier-preference interpretation, although Section 4 retains the old similarity statement. Score-margin mechanisms and benchmark-design implications are also expanded.

D1.justification: v2 adds weighted-model implementation details, dataset identifiers and sports filtering instructions, exact deleted indices in Table 4, and the GPT-5.1 judging prompt and access mode. It removes v1's public-code and reproduction-scripts statement and repository link; this does not establish that the repository itself was withdrawn. The hardware and runtime disclosure is retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench and adds search-augmented dialogue, web development and visual question answering through Search, Webdev and Vision Arenas. NBA team rankings and ATP tennis player rankings add distinct non-LLM domains (Section 4.1, Appendix D).

E2.justification: Appendix A.3 and Table 3 introduce an evaluated uniform-at-random deletion control for comparison with targeted worst-case deletion. This comparator is absent from v1; the newly cited leaderboard attacks are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Retaining tied preferences changes the existing evaluation samples, including Chatbot Arena human judgments from 39,716 to 57,477. v2 also introduces bootstrap-based top-set evaluation, random deletion at 1% and an additional 0.1% Chatbot condition, sports filtering protocols, competitor-removal experiments and GPT-5.1 judging procedures (Appendices A, D and F).

E4.justification: v2 adds bootstrap-ranking robustness checks, random-deletion controls, competitor-removal tests of score-margin sensitivity and explicit verification of AMIP-selected subsets. It replaces v1's five manually inspected examples with two cases assessed by GPT-5.1. The player-involvement analysis is updated in Appendix E, while the original score-gap scatterplot is retained as Figure 18.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates and deletion counts without uncertainty intervals or repeated-trial results. v2 Appendix A adds bootstrap confidence-interval plots and stability estimates from 100 random-deletion trials. Bootstrap resample counts, confidence levels and seeds remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes Chatbot Arena human results from 9/39,716 deletions to 2/57,477 and MT-Bench human results from 83/2,575 to 92/3,355. These use revised tie handling, so they are not same-setting robustness gains. v2 adds results for five datasets and several new analyses, while removing v1's head-to-head win percentages. Some reports conflict internally: v2 Table 2 gives 40/2,400 as 4.00%, and Section 4.4 and Appendix F disagree on the GPT-4 model involved in the inspected losses.

M1.justification: v1 excludes ties and analyzes unweighted Bradley–Terry models; v2 adapts the framework to weighted models with win/loss weight 2 and tie weight 1 (Section 2, Appendix C.2). This changes the fitted objective and supported outcomes, while retaining the AMIP subset search, pairwise-to-top-k procedure, optional additive one-step Newton approximation and exact refitting.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are substantially rewritten. v1's platform-deviations subsection is incorporated into the setup, while proofs, logistic formulations, dataset descriptions and case analyses are redistributed across appendices. A dedicated related-work section and extensively reorganized appendix narrative change the document's structure beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a denser conference layout and adds a conceptual schematic, pseudocode, paired bootstrap-interval plots, sports ranking plots and random-deletion and verification tables. Table 1 is restructured, and v1's five-example table is replaced by full-response figures and judge-output blocks. Existing involvement and model-count plots are relocated or redrawn; the score-gap plot is largely retained.

R1.justification: Section 5 substantially expands positioning relative to vote manipulation, attacks on LLM judges and apathetic annotations, adding works including Huang et al. (2025b), Raina et al. (2024) and Zhao et al. (2025). Additional uncertainty-quantification and masking literature broadens the statistical context. The earlier comparison with Shiffman et al. is retained.

T1.justification: v2 formalizes the weighted tie-handling objective and logistic representation, and introduces the bootstrap-based rank and top-set criterion. Pairwise reversal changes from the non-strict inequality in v1 Equation (8) to a strict inequality in v2 Equation (7). The top-k proposition and proof are retained as Proposition B.1, as are the logistic influence formula and complexity bound.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by incorporating tied preferences, evaluating confidence-interval-based rankings and distinguishing targeted fragility from random-deletion stability. Explicit false-negative and masking limitations also clarify what the diagnostic establishes. These substantially strengthen applicability and evidential support, despite the removed code link and unresolved numerical and model-attribution inconsistencies in Table 2 and Section 4.4/Appendix F.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization. Image-only content was visually inspected.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original ranking analyses on LLM and sports datasets, bootstrap and random-deletion experiments, and a GPT-5.1-assisted qualitative study.

before.justification: Sections 4.2–4.5 report original data-dropping and refitting analyses on Chatbot Arena and MT-Bench, including numerical ranking changes and inspections of influential evaluations.

C1.justification: Both retain the first unified LLM-based 3D understanding/generation claim, geometric-semantic encoder and Spatial-VAE contributions, and the 17.9% relative VSI-Bench advantage claim. The additional evaluations and limitations do not redefine the principal contributions.

C2.justification: V3 substantially expands applicability qualifications: it acknowledges gaps against 3D-enhanced methods, explains extreme-view failures through training coverage and reduced overlap, and tentatively attributes color errors to competing encoder objectives. It also interprets separate-training results as an acceptable unification tradeoff and explicitly states missing language control, freeform editing, and interactive multi-round generation.

D1.justification: V3 adds training hardware and elapsed times, inference precision and latency, and training-pair filtering thresholds. It clarifies projector optimization, corrects loss-weight documentation, and removes the statement extending unified-training learning rates to VAE training. The code-release-upon-acceptance promise is deleted; the retained project link does not establish actual code availability.

E1.justification: V3 adds SQA3D and ScanQA scene question answering and ScanRefer text-guided 3D object localization, substantially extending evaluation coverage to grounding. It also adds extreme-view generation scenarios reaching 140 degrees. The previously evaluated datasets and tasks are retained.

E2.justification: New Table 9 adds comparisons with 3D-LLM, Chat-3D v2, LEO, LL3DA, Scene-LLM, LLaVA-3D, and Video-3D LLM, plus grounding comparators including ScanRefer, MVT, ViL3DRel, and Grounded 3D-LLM. Figure 11 newly compares feature matchings with MASt3R, explicitly distinguishing its access to the target image. Existing comparator sets remain intact.

E3.justification: V3 introduces supervised fine-tuning for the added 3D tasks, EM/BLEU-4/CIDEr and grounding accuracy evaluation, separate-task training controls, and tests at specified 60–140-degree rotations. Appendix A.2 also replaces the L2/SSIM weight listing with LPIPS and matching/RGB weights consistent with the existing equations; this revises reported settings without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and simplified variant, v3 adds joint versus separate optimization (Table 10), grounding with versus without refinement (Table 9), feature matching (Figure 11), extreme-view generation (Figure 12), and color failure cases (Figure 13). These substantially expand analysis of task interference, geometric consistency, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Both versions retain generation examples with different seeds, but neither reports benchmark repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added results follow the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 retain their values. New Table 9 reports UniUGG SQA3D EM of 51.3, ScanQA EM of 24.4, and ScanRefer Acc@0.25/0.5 of 23.2/7.8 without refinement versus 41.9/36.6 with refinement. Table 10 adds separate-training results, including VSI 42.2 for understanding-only versus 40.1 jointly trained. Figures 11–13 add correspondence and failure observations.

M1.justification: The core encoder, Spatial-VAE, LLM/diffusion architecture, and objectives are retained. Appendix A.3.2 newly applies a grounding refinement procedure on ScanRefer, with refined and unrefined results in Table 9. This is a limited procedural addition, although its implementation is unspecified.

P1.justification: V3 adds a pipeline overview subsection, distinguishes the overall training stages from steps within unified training, expands appendix subheadings, and revises the conclusion into 'Conclusion and Limitations.' Conference headers and acknowledgments are added. Most existing prose and the overall section progression are retained.

P2.justification: V3 adds an overall pipeline diagram and combines the earlier separate training/inference explanations into a revised Figure 4. It adds Tables 9–10 and diagnostic Figures 11–13, and reformats retained visualization panels. The earlier simplified-variant Figures 11–12 survive as Figures 14–15; these are relocated material rather than new analyses.

R1.justification: V3 adds references supporting the new 3D benchmarks and comparison methods, including SQA3D, ScanRefer, Scene-LLM, and Video-3D LLM. Appendix A.3.2 extends positioning around 2D inputs and a 3B backbone versus 3D-enhanced methods. Section 2's research framing and the central novelty claim remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical representations, Equations 1–4, Spatial-VAE objective, and autoregressive VQA loss are retained. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs, and v3 adds no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important gaps in v2's validation: Table 10 directly measures the performance tradeoff from joint training, Table 9 adds relevant 3D comparisons, and Figures 11–13 examine consistency and failure conditions. Together with clearer training explanations and resource disclosures, these substantially improve assessment of the central unification claim and its limits. The grounding refinement remains underdocumented, and claimed computational savings lack a direct separate-training cost comparison, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniUGG with the same authors, core architecture, and original experiments. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and redrawn material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds 3D benchmark evaluations, separate-task optimization experiments, and qualitative robustness and failure analyses in Appendix A.3.

before.justification: V2 reports original encoder evaluations, spatial question-answering results, 3D generation experiments, and component ablations in Section 4 and Appendix A.3.

C1.justification: The central claims remain annotation-free self-play, sustained entropy and diversity, improved large-k reasoning performance, and generality across 3B–32B models and 12 reasoning benchmarks. The abstract retains the same 18.3- and 22.8-point AIME Pass@32 gains; new analyses support these retained contributions.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's entropy explanation and integer-answer overfitting discussion, v3 interprets additional negative samples as encouraging exploration, easier-problem augmentation as accelerating overfitting, and synthesis training as regularization through complementary generation and solving tasks. Appendix D and the cases further connect longer responses and systematic reasoning to continued exploration, substantially expanding the mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies Clip-Higher epsilon as 0.28 and explicitly describes the baseline training recipe. Appendix F supplies a separate problem-solving prompt display, and the first-page project-site address changes. Most learning-rate, batch-size, sampling, training-duration, and verification details were already reported in v1 and are relocated.

E1.justification: Both versions use MATH-12k, DAPO-17k, the DeepMath supplement, and the same mathematical, general-question-answering, and coding benchmarks. The new IID/OOD analysis groups existing benchmarks by answer format; it does not introduce new data or task requirements.

E2.justification: v3 Table 3 adds a substantive alternative-strategy comparison: extended RLVR training (Ext), additional rollouts on underperforming problems (Eup), and easier-problem augmentation (SvS-Asp). These controls were absent from v1. The original Table 1 comparators, including SimpleRL-32B and ORZ-32B, remain.

E3.justification: The new Table 3 experiments match total problem-solution pairs for Ext or per-step pairs for Eup, test a 37.5%–75.0% augmentation-accuracy range, and select checkpoints by average AIME 24/25 scores. Section 5.4 adds a condition using only 20% of synthesis pairs for updates and reports grouped IID/OOD accuracy. Previously stated default settings are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds training-volume controls, easier-problem and synthesis-fraction ablations, response-length analysis, benchmark learning trajectories, and detailed response/workflow cases. These substantially expand investigation of why SVS works. The instance-level accuracy analysis already shown in v1 Figure 7 is retained as v3 Figure 9, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 32-generation Pass@1 averaging, unbiased Pass@k estimation, and the 1024-generation instance-level comparison. No new training-seed information, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the general-task table retain their scores, but substantial results are added. v3 Table 3 reports average Pass@1/Pass@32 of 24.6/46.3 for Ext, 21.7/50.9 for Eup, and 22.8/42.8 for SvS-Asp, alongside retained full-SVS scores of 27.9/53.1. Figure 7 adds worse OOD performance with reduced synthesis training; appendices add response-length, checkpoint, and case outcomes.

M1.justification: The proposed SVS procedure retains solution-conditioned problem synthesis, reuse of original reference answers, difficulty-based synthesis rewards, and joint training on three experience types. The relocated algorithm and expanded walkthrough document the existing method; the new experimental variants do not replace it.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: GRPO background, pseudocode, and detailed settings move into Appendices A–C, accompanied by an expanded algorithm walkthrough and appendix contents page. The analysis narrative gains separate controls and mechanism sections, while contributions are consolidated and terminology edited. Sentence-level rewriting of retained scientific passages is mostly light.

P2.justification: v3 adds an ablation table, synthesis-fraction plots, response-length and benchmark learning curves, and case displays. Existing tables are packed together, Figures 2 and 5 are redrawn with smoothing, the instance-level plot is relocated and recolored, and the synthesis prompt is restyled. New Figure 8 incorrectly labels response-length axes as Policy Entropy.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted context, including Cheng et al. (2024) as closely related self-play work, dual learning for the regularization explanation, and ProRL for prolonged training. It also adds latent-reasoning citations and a reference for the already evaluated SimpleRL baseline. The overall research positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The GRPO definitions and objective move from v1 Section 3.1 to v3 Appendix A, while SVS reward definitions remain mathematically equivalent. No new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee is introduced. Mathematical workings in the new cases are sampled model responses, not new theoretical contributions.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked controls addressing whether SVS gains merely reflected additional training examples and how synthesis training contributed. v3 Table 3's training-pair-matched alternatives and Section 5.4's synthesis ablation directly address these important evidence gaps, substantially strengthening support for the retained claims. Expanded walkthroughs improve transparency. Remaining uncertainty-reporting limitations and minor editorial defects, including Figure 8's mislabeled axes, do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SVS research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison; rendered-page inspection resolves text-extraction ordering artifacts.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds controlled comparisons, synthesis-training ablations, learning-curve analyses, and generated-response case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original SVS and RLVR training experiments, reasoning and general-task benchmark results, entropy trajectories, and Pass@k analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the applicability and efficiency claims to direct code-generation training. The central self-play, entropy-maintenance, and reasoning-boundary contributions remain, including the unchanged 18.3- and 22.8-point AIME Pass@32 gains.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations of synthetic-problem validity and difficulty preservation, attributing validator rejections partly to unusual wording. It also explains potential complementarity with entropy regulation and relates computational overhead to the prevalence of underperforming problems. Existing interpretations concerning answer-format overfitting and synthesis-based regularization are retained.

D1.justification: v4 adds coding-synthesis and validity-audit prompts, Clip-Cov parameter values, a disclosure of 32 H100 GPUs for the timing experiments, step/update-time measurements, and a Resources link. These extend reproducibility information while leaving the established mathematical implementation recipe largely unchanged.

E1.justification: v4 adds direct RL training on 12k coding problems from PRIME-RL and evaluation on APPS, CodeContests, TACO, and Codeforces. This substantially extends training and evaluation coverage beyond mathematics. v3's HumanEval evaluation of mathematically trained models is retained and is distinct from this new coding-training scenario.

E2.justification: Appendix F newly evaluates RLVR plus Clip-Cov against SvS and against SvS plus Clip-Cov in Figures 16–17. Existing comparators, including initial models, standard RLVR, SimpleRL, ORZ, and the Table 3 augmentation alternatives, remain.

E3.justification: v4 introduces coding evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 100 validation instances per benchmark, and Avg@16 for CodeContests. It also adds protocols for auditing 6,000 synthetic problems, analyzing 2,000 original–variant pairs, and comparing Clip-Cov variants. Section 4.2 newly specifies 32-inference evaluation for models below 8B on AIME-level tasks. Existing mathematical training and decoding settings are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds synthetic-validity and paired-difficulty analyses in Appendix E.5, empirical testing of the previously described reward-hacking failure in Appendix G, computational-overhead analysis in Section 5.5, and checkpoint curves for existing augmentation ablations in Figure 7. The earlier 20%-synthesis ablation and general-task analysis are retained in Appendices E.2–E.3.

E5.justification: Appendix E.5 newly introduces OLS regression estimates relating original and synthetic problem accuracies. The existing unbiased Pass@k estimator and repeated-generation reporting remain. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across independent training seeds.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 3, and 4 retain their numerical results. Table 2 fills previously blank 3B/8B AIME-level entries; for example, 3B SvS now reports 10.5, 7.8, and 2.8 on AIME24, AIME25, and Beyond-AIME. Its revised averages include additional tasks and do not indicate same-setting performance changes. Substantial new results include coding, Clip-Cov, timing, and failure curves, plus 80.0–87.1% model-judged validity in Figure 13.

M1.justification: The core three-stage SvS algorithm and mathematical reward rules remain unchanged. v4 adds an implemented SvS-plus-Clip-Cov variant in Appendix F and a programming-specific synthesis adaptation in Section 5.4 and Figure 20. The unsuccessful reward scheme discussed in Appendix G was already described in v3.

P1.justification: The main narrative is substantially reorganized: related work moves to Appendix B, and former Sections 5.4–5.5 move to Appendices E.2–E.3. Coding and computational analysis take their places in the main text. Contributions, cross-references, headings, and some explanatory passages are also edited.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a wider layout, colored headings, and a boxed title/abstract presentation. It adds numerous analysis plots, consolidates Figure 6's separate AIME panels, and relocates retained displays. The response-length plot's incorrect 'Policy Entropy' axis label becomes 'Response Length.' The standalone problem-solving prompt display is removed, while its instruction remains documented in prose.

R1.justification: v4 adds references to PRIME, Duan et al.'s geometry work, and Zhang et al.'s multi-teacher synthesis work, while removing Wen et al.'s paper on implicitly incentivizing correct reasoning. Appendix F develops the relationship to Clip-Cov as both a comparator and complementary approach. The broader self-play and data-augmentation positioning remains.

T1.justification: The mathematical reward definitions, GRPO advantage normalization, and optimization objective in Equations 1–6 are substantively unchanged. v4 adds no formal theorem, proof, or theoretical derivation; its regression analysis is empirical.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny of the paper's central claims. Direct coding RL tests applicability beyond mathematical training, Clip-Cov comparisons examine the relationship to dedicated entropy control, and timing and failure analyses clarify costs and reward-design requirements absent from v3's evidence. These are meaningful gains in support and transparency. Limitations remain: the validity audit does not independently establish reference-answer preservation, and the coding efficiency claim concerns training steps rather than matched computational cost.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SvS research work. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds coding experiments, synthetic-problem audits, entropy-regulation comparisons, timing measurements, and failure-mode experiments.

before.justification: v3 reports original mathematical-reasoning experiments, entropy measurements, augmentation ablations, general-task evaluations, and model-response analyses.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on language-dependent English pivoting, multilingual pretraining, and training-data quality versus quantity. v2 reframes the contribution around scaling, pretraining, post-training, and inference. Its central claims now include persistent target-language reasoning deficits at larger scales, harm from specialized mathematical pretraining, translation outperforming direct distillation overall, and distinct language-dependent failure modes.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations separating conceptual and generation failures from reasoning failures, and attributes efficiency disparities primarily to script/tokenizer effects using the byte analysis. Appendix B.1 explicitly acknowledges that accuracy conflates reasoning ability with language compliance. Section 6.2 also qualifies translation-versus-distillation recommendations by language and notes that their relative effectiveness may change with larger datasets or stronger teachers.

D1.justification: v2 documents the compliance pipeline's cleaning, chunking, classifiers, and thresholds, plus error-labeling prompts and human-review sample sizes. Training tables are revised, and hardware changes from two A6000 or A100 GPUs to four L40S GPUs. The release statement expands from planned code/data access to claimed release of models, datasets, and code. The translation prompt is retained; external availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from four to nine non-English languages, adding Chinese, Afrikaans, Thai, Marathi, and Telugu. MMLU-ProX introduces broader multidisciplinary reasoning coverage in place of GPQA's PhD-level science evaluation; IMO is removed. MATH-500 remains. The English-input/target-language-reasoning scenario evaluated in v1 Table 1 is also absent from v2.

E2.justification: v2 adds Qwen2.5-Math-7B to the backbone comparison and Distilled-s1k and Qwen3-8B (Thinking) to the post-training comparisons. Qwen3-8B was explicitly excluded in v1, while v1's Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct comparator disappears. The Qwen3 English-s1k comparison survives in v2 Table 10. The three translation-system comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Training context and maximum inference output increase from 16,384 to 32,768 tokens. v1 specifies GPT-4.1-Mini answer verification; v2 specifies extracted-answer matching plus mandatory language compliance (Appendix A.5). Backbone comparisons now use 20,000 English OpenThoughts3 traces rather than s1k. AIME evaluation expands from 30 questions from 2024 to 60 questions combining 2024 and 2025, and new experiments evaluate multiple model scales.

E4.justification: v2 adds compliance and code-switching analyses, a five-category error analysis with human checks, a shorter-versus-longer reasoning comparison, validation with larger Llama-based models, and byte-based efficiency analysis. The English-s1k versus translated-s1k control is retained and expanded in Appendix B.4, rather than entirely new. v1's s1k-versus-Bespoke-Stratos-17k quality/quantity analysis is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports eight responses per AIME 2024 and IMO question. v2 reports five independent responses per AIME-Combined question and explicitly averages correctness over 300 generations (Appendix A.5). This revises repeated-sampling information and clarifies aggregation. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Most reasoning results are replaced or expanded under revised conditions. For example, translated-s1k Qwen3's Swahili MATH-500 result is 73.2 in v1 Table 3 and 64.4 in v2 Table 2; changed training and scoring prevent interpreting this as a same-setting regression. New results include average MATH-500 scores of 78.3 for Translated-s1k versus 72.8 for Distilled-s1k. The four original FLORES translation rows remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: v1 constructs training traces through translation and applies supervised fine-tuning. v2 retains this approach, renaming M-s1k to Translated-s1k, but adds a distinct direct-distillation pipeline: elicit target-language traces from DeepSeek-R1 and resample until 1,000 pass a language-compliance filter (Section 6.1; Appendix A.7). This substantially expands the data-generation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusions, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. v1's consolidated Experiments section becomes separate scaling, pretraining, synthetic-data, and inference sections. Related work moves from Appendix A into the main text, and experimental appendices are reorganized. Terminology shifts to En-Only, En-CoT, Target-CoT, and Translated-s1k.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a reasoning-example diagram, multi-panel scaling plots, error-distribution plots, and a byte-efficiency plot. Result tables are redesigned with broader language coverage, multiple benchmark blocks, averages, and colored differences. The token-efficiency figure is redrawn for the revised experiment. The translation prompt is relocated, while the verification prompt is removed and an error-analysis prompt is added.

R1.justification: v1 positions the work mainly around English pivoting and multilingual fine-tuning. v2 positions it as a study across model-development stages, complementary to recent language-control and language-mixing research by Qi et al. and Mingyang Wang et al. It adds substantial context on multilingual scaling, specialized pretraining, and tokenizer disparities. These changes exceed the relocation of related work or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Appendix A.7 newly defines a language-compliance score as the ratio of target-language chunks to valid chunks, with a 90% acceptance threshold. This adds a limited mathematical scoring definition absent from v1. Neither version develops theorems, proofs, or substantive theoretical derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence behind v1's broad cross-language conclusions through model-scaling controls, the specialized-pretraining comparison, and explicit compliance and error diagnostics. These address v1's limited model coverage and lack of measured language adherence. The gains outweigh removal of the 17k-data study, although numerical reporting needs correction: Appendix B.4 claims a 14.6-point AIME improvement where Table 10 shows 20.8 minus 8.0, or 12.8 points. Such inconsistencies limit confidence in exact summaries without negating the substantial methodological and diagnostic gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching title, authors, and central question. The complete main texts, appendices, tables, and figures support comparison despite substantial changes in scope and experimental settings.

after.justification: v2 reports original scaling, pretraining, synthetic-data, and multilingual evaluation results, alongside compliance, efficiency, and error analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, multilingual benchmark evaluations, translation evaluations, and inference-efficiency analysis in Tables 1–9 and Figure 1.

C1.justification: The central HeteroRL/GEPO contributions and the 1800-second/3% performance-loss claim remain. v6's introduction explicitly extends the stated tolerance to 'arbitrary delays,' broadening the applicability language. Its new 85% best-to-last-gap statistic in the abstract quantifies the retained stability claim rather than introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: v6 adds substantive interpretations of reasoning-length, truncation, exploration and efficiency tradeoffs, including recommendations for non-think GEPO in latency-sensitive settings. It expands the shared-denominator gradient explanation and analyzes repetition and ineffective reflection in a response case study. Defensive sampling becomes a future hypothesis, conflicting with the retained author-contribution statement claiming experimental benefits. Earlier qualifications about estimator bias and high-latency performance dips remain.

D1.justification: v6 states that code is released and supplies a repository address. It newly documents 8,290 training samples, input/output limits, model provenance, the non-think prompt, A100/Ascend hardware labels and local reward aggregation. It drops v1's bfloat16, Flash Attention-2 and vLLM memory-cap 0.45 disclosures. Most simulated-delay and ZeroMQ details are retained in Appendix C rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: v1 trains on MATH levels 3–5 and evaluates on MATH500. v6 retains this coverage and adds actual AMC2023, AIME2024 and AIME2025 evaluations in Tables 1–5, substantially broadening mathematical benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates GRPO and GSPO. v6 adds BNPO, explicitly identified as Beta Normalization Policy Optimization, and Dr.GRPO to online comparisons and the 1.7B supplementary online/heterogeneous comparisons (Tables 1, 3 and 5). GRPO and GSPO remain, including in the 8B heterogeneous comparison.

E3.justification: v6 adds 8B experiments and separate 2k/4k-output and think/non-think configurations beyond v1's 1.7B setup. Figure 1 also changes the displayed GRPO/GSPO advantage normalization to retain the standard-deviation divisor, although Listing 1's claim that only importance weights differ leaves implementation controls unclear. Pass@1 over eight responses, three epochs and the online/heterogeneous KL rules are retained. Newly disclosed token limits do not establish that v1's limits changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Bernoulli/Gaussian and latency/correlation analyses, v6 adds think/non-think performance and rollout-length/truncation analyses (Appendix B.5, Figure 9), a dedicated weighting ablation with additional variant results (Table 4), a 128-token distribution check (Appendix A), and a comparative response case study (Appendix G). These substantially expand diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: v6 adds an A summary of 0.432 ± 0.36 from 128 generated tokens in Appendix A, although its dispersion terminology is unclear. v1's explicit shared-random-seed statement disappears. The correlation analyses retain their 95% confidence intervals and alpha = 0.05; neither version establishes repeated-training-seed uncertainty for the benchmark tables.

E6.justification: The result tables are substantially replaced and expanded. v1 Table 2 reports GEPO MATH500 best/last scores of 78.5/77.3 online and 75.3/74.4 at delay 64; v6 Table 3 reports 80.4/78.1 and 79.6/79.6 under its explicitly specified 1.7B, 2k setting. Numerous 8B, competition-benchmark, ablation and non-think results are added. Incompletely matched generation settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. The 0.76/0.96/0.78 correlations are retained.

M1.justification: The core group-expectation weight and GEPO coefficient code remain unchanged. v6 removes v1 Section 3.3's explicit defensive-mixture component and recasts it as future work in Appendix H; Appendix D introduces local group reward aggregation without global gathering. v1 explicitly excluded defensive sampling from its reported comparisons, so its removal does not establish changed experimental GEPO updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, results discussion, related work and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. The method narrative foregrounds group-level weighting and gradient comparison, while implementation, network descriptions, token/sequence explanations and RL-paradigm comparisons move into thematic appendices. A contents page and reorganized appendix structure substantially change the reading order.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned into separate algorithm blocks and stacked training plots; the HeteroRL schematic and training plots are redrawn. v6 adds rollout-length and communication/local-reward diagrams, restructures performance tables across models and benchmarks, and moves v1's paradigm table to Table 7. Persistent laboratory headers, a narrower text block and colored case-study panels further change the layout.

R1.justification: v6 adds an IMPALA/V-trace comparison and references supporting the new baselines, datasets and reasoning-efficiency discussion. It removes the detailed Online DPO discussion and Calandriello citation; Noukhovitch remains cited in the introduction, while Section 5 now assigns the earlier theoretical-exploration claim to Wu. Positioning HeteroRL around unpredictable heterogeneous-network latency remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: The variance formulas, lemma, theorem and n-squared-plus-one bound in Appendix A are essentially retained. v6 adds the token-gradient matrix comparison in Section 3.2, Equation 5. Conversely, v1's explicit defensive-mixture Equation 15 and its epsilon-equals-one policy-gradient equivalence argument are removed.

improvement.justification: v6 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support by testing whether the findings extend beyond one model size and MATH500, and by examining reasoning-mode, truncation and response failures. More explicit generation settings and code-access information also improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting problems: Section 4.2 claims a 1.5-point margin where Table 1 gives 51.1 minus 49.9 = 1.2, and baseline controls and defensive-sampling status remain inconsistently described.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GEPO and HeteroRL. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v6 reports original Qwen3-1.7B/8B benchmark results, weighting ablations, think/non-think experiments and training diagnostics. Appendix A also adds a sampled-token analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen3-1.7B reinforcement-learning results on MATH500 under different delays, training diagnostics and synthetic distribution experiments.

C1.justification: The central claims of improved accuracy, efficiency, and search scaling through HDS-QA-supervised hybrid search remain. v2 adds an explicit first-dataset claim concerning more than two parallel subqueries integrated into sequential reasoning, and makes robustness to increasing evidence requirements a headline contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops a synthesis-bottleneck explanation for baseline failures and interprets the new controls as evidence for hybrid search behavior. It newly discusses fixed question templates, successful trajectories containing incorrect intermediate steps, and reduced dependence on large teachers or summarizers. Section 6 adds a substantive accuracy-efficiency tradeoff: GRPO increases search depth and generally lowers AUC despite higher final accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies the question-generation model, discloses a 95/5 training-validation split, and explains how excess parallel queries are truncated to the remaining call budget. Appendix A adds GRPO hardware and training settings, and the title page adds a project-page link. Most existing implementation details and generation prompts are retained; downloadable resource availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use Natural Questions-derived HDS-QA and evaluate MuSiQue, FanOutQA, FRAMES, MedBrowseComp, and BrowseComp. Expanding BrowseComp from 50 to 150 questions retains the same o3-solvable-within-five-minutes criterion. The new controls and analyses use retained tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The seven main named baselines are retained; Directly Gen is renamed Naïve Gen. v2 adds an HDS-QA-trained single-query comparator in Table 4. Appendix F adds RAG-R1 to all three case comparisons and removes Search-o1 from the MuSiQue case.

E3.justification: BrowseComp evaluation expands from 50 to 150 questions. FanOutQA gains BLEURT and switches its judging prompt from Zheng et al. to the dataset-specific Zhu et al. prompt. The reported fine-tuning batch size changes from 4 to 32, without establishing that retained results were rerun. New experiments vary backbone, query parallelism, GRPO training, model size, and summarizer configuration.

E4.justification: v2 adds matched-backbone and single-query controls, GRPO experiments, model-size and summarizer ablations, accuracy grouped by evidence requirements, trajectory-diversity statistics, and RAG-R1 failure cases. These substantially expand tests of attribution and robustness. v1 Figure 5's evidence-coverage-versus-turn analysis is removed; its turn, call, and token-budget analyses are retained elsewhere.

E5.justification: Both versions report four trajectory-generation attempts per HDS-QA question with the same success counts. v2's pass@4 uses those existing outcomes. Neither version reports benchmark evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: BrowseComp results are replaced for the larger sample: HybridDeepSearcher reports 17.2 F1 and 16.0 judged accuracy in v1 versus 15.1 and 13.3 in v2. FanOutQA judged accuracy changes from 25.1 to 20.0 under the revised prompt, while F1 remains 44.1. These replacements use changed conditions. v2 additionally reports BLEURT, controlled-variant results, robustness curves, and trajectory statistics; Table 3's evidence-coverage values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core dataset-generation pipeline, supervised training objective, and reasoning-querying-retrieval procedure remain unchanged. Evidence aggregation was already requested in v1's response-generation prompt. v2 Section 6 adds an optional GRPO training extension using binary correctness rewards from Qwen3-4B-Instruct.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around search scaling and structured aggregation. v2 introduces a separate Discussion section and organizes the appendices into sections A–F. The title and affiliation header also change, while much of the method description and the generation prompts remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout, with extensively reformatted tables and plots. v1's motivation diagram and evidence-coverage-versus-turn plot are removed; v2 adds robustness and ablation displays. The appendix budget plots are merged, and retained case-study continuations receive individual table captions rather than representing entirely new cases.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises positioning around decomposition and synthesis, adding discussion of GenDec, Plan*RAG, ReDel, ADaPT, and synthetic web-agent data. v1's discussion of APR, Multiverse, and adaptive parallel-reasoning termination is removed. The revised account distinguishes HDS-QA through broad parallel retrieval followed by evidence synthesis for sequential reasoning.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the evidence-coverage numerator from |Ui| to |Ui ∩ Di|, aligning the formula with the already stated intersection of retrieved and gold evidence. This fixes a mathematical definition without establishing a changed retrieval procedure. The added AUC equation formalizes an existing metric; neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central contribution through the matched-backbone comparison and single-query control in Tables 2 and 4, addressing attribution gaps in v1. Model-size and summarizer ablations further test important dependencies. These gains outweigh the removed coverage-versus-turn analysis and new reporting inconsistencies, including conflicting BrowseComp baseline accuracies between Tables 2 and 8 and summarizer average-drop claims that do not match the displayed rows.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HDS-QA and HybridDeepSearcher. All 23 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, prompts, and appendix case studies, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds controlled experiments, robustness analyses, trajectory statistics, and model-size and summarizer ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results in Table 2, evidence-retrieval results in Table 3, and additional search-budget analyses and model-output examples in the appendix.

C1.justification: v1 explicitly highlights targeted candidate-query generation among its principal innovations. v2's abstract, introduction and conclusion concentrate the contribution framing on model factorization, belief updating and EIG estimation. The central deployment-time BED approach, novelty claim concerning proper EIG, and benefits on both tasks remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets similar Split/Entropy performance as evidence that nondeterministic likelihoods help through the proper EIG objective, and explains why good candidate samples alone cannot replace explicit optimization. It removes the interpretation accompanying v1's EIG-by-turn diagnostic. Most existing applicability boundaries and model-mismatch discussion are retained.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the 0.2 filtering threshold, exact hypothesis-generation and user-profile-generation prompts, and shared hyperparameters across models. Conversely, it removes v1 Appendix D.2's checkpoint repository identifiers, dated GPT model identifiers and chat-template information. These materially alter reproducibility documentation without establishing that every newly documented detail is an implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Animals, Celebrities and Things in 20 Questions and MovieLens-100K-derived film-preference profiles. Matched and mismatched questioner–answerer scenarios are retained. Different backbone models do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Split, ICL Beliefs and Implicit Maximization comparators. Data–Estimation participation expands beyond v1's single Qwen2.5-72B/Celebrities comparison. Entropy remains a distinct comparator rather than being renamed Split; Naive QA is simply renamed Naive.

E3.justification: The 20 Questions model lineup replaces Mistral-Large with Llama-3.1-8B. v2 Appendix E specifies temperature 1 for preference-hypothesis generation, whereas v1 Section 3.3 states 1.3. Target counts, user counts, turn budgets and candidate-pool sizes remain. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 directly tests replacing filtered beliefs with in-context beliefs and replacing explicit EIG computation with prompted question selection. It also broadens the joint-factorization ablation. The model-mismatch tests and hypothesis-collapse example remain, but v1 Appendix E.1/Figure 11's EIG-by-turn diagnostic is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors across 100 targets per 20 Questions dataset and 200 preference profiles, retaining the same success-rate uncertainty formula. Additional result rows follow this existing practice; no new seed, repeated-run or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new comparators and Llama-3.1-8B while removing Mistral-Large results. Retained Table 1 entries also change: Qwen/Animals BED-LLM goes from 94% to 95%, and GPT-4o-mini/Celebrities Entropy from 53% to 55%. Qwen/Celebrities Data–Estimation changes from 39% in v1 Figure 4 to 34% in v2 Table 1. Some preference curves also change. These are revised reports, with setting revisions preventing an unqualified same-setting performance comparison.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated candidate-question procedure from independent sampling in v1 to joint sampling in v2. The prior–likelihood construction, EIG estimator, hypothesis filtering, retention and uniform weighting remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, background, method explanations and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Detailed algorithmic discussion, the former Section 4.4 analysis, related work and experimental settings are reorganized into thematic appendices with a new contents page.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands from three to seven method columns. Separate matched/mismatched experiment figures are merged into compact grids, with changed colors, legends, axes and panel arrangements. v2 adds a fuller ablation plot and prompt displays, reformats existing prompt figures, and relocates the EIG illustration into the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 refines prior-work comparisons around Split, distinguishes Wang et al.'s meta-training and Chan et al.'s calibration requirements, and adds potential complementarity with policy-based BED. Several references are removed, including Goda et al. (2022) and Rainforth et al. (2018). The central research positioning and most cited work remain.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Section 3.2's explicit finite-sample bias discussion, O(N^-1/2) convergence-rate statement and MLMC qualification, retaining only a conditional convergence observation. The principal EIG mathematics and belief-update alignment analysis remain, often relocated or equivalently reformulated.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct controls separating the effects of belief filtering and explicit EIG selection from candidate generation. v2's ICL Beliefs and Implicit Maximization ablations, additional Split comparator and broader factorization comparisons substantially strengthen evidence for these central design choices. The clearer organization also helps assessment. Removing exact model identifiers and the EIG diagnostic loses useful detail, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BED-LLM research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original results for both tasks and reports additional baseline and ablation experiments in Table 1 and the appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original 20 Questions experiments, simulated-user film recommendations, model-mismatch tests and diagnostic analyses.

C1.justification: The introduction and contribution summary revise the claimed competitor-size advantage from 10× to 5× and focus that outperformance statement on ImgEdit. The central role-rebalancing argument, dataset contributions, and abstract/conclusion claims of state-of-the-art or competitive editing performance remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of designer adaptation, initialization, and differing responses to CoT inputs. It substantially expands applicability boundaries through failures involving extensive object manipulation, text, geometry, and transformations that break source-image alignment. Appendix B links text-rendering limitations to 32× VAE compression and discusses the efficiency–fidelity tradeoff; Appendix D interprets annotation errors.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents the flow-matching objective, UltraEdit filtering thresholds (CLIP and DINOv2 above 0.9; SSIM above 0.8), exclusion of rainbow prompts, and detailed annotation prompts for all 21 DIM-T2I dimensions. These clarify existing construction procedures rather than establish changed datasets. The abstract also changes the reported dataset/model release status from planned to available.

E1.justification: Original training corpora and benchmarks remain. v3 adds MagicBrush test evaluation against human-edited targets and substantially broadens demonstrated task requirements through knowledge-dependent, temporal, geometric, and reference-free editing scenarios (Appendix B), including implicit prime-number counting, rusting nails, and map-to-photo generation.

E2.justification: The original generation, ImgEdit, and GEdit comparator sets are retained after relocation. The new MagicBrush comparison evaluates FluxEdit, FLUX.1 Fill, RF-Solver Edit, ACE++, and ICEdit alongside previously compared methods (v3 Table 5), substantially expanding the editing approaches compared.

E3.justification: Existing training budgets, learning rates, batch sizes, GenEval prompt rewriting, and GPT-4.1 benchmark judging remain unchanged. New protocols include MagicBrush L1/CLIP-I/DINO evaluation, raw-prompt and initialization controls, timing over 100 samples at 1024×1024 with 30 generation steps, and quality assessments using 30K GPT-4.1-rated pairs plus 100 samples assessed by three humans.

E4.justification: v3 preserves the original data-composition and CoT-component ablations while adding designer-free inference, additional designers, internal-designer fine-tuning, and initialization comparisons. Appendix A tests identical CoT blueprints on Janus-4o and Step1X-Edit; Appendices B and D add extensive mechanism-oriented examples, six failure cases, and automated/human annotation-quality analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated model runs, random-seed information, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3 adds sample and annotator counts and aggregate quality percentages, but these describe new evaluations rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Retained headline results remain 0.77 GenEval, 5.50 MJHQ-30K FID, 3.67 ImgEdit, and 6.18 GEdit full-set overall. New results include MagicBrush L1/CLIP-I/DINO of 0.065/0.928/0.882, a 3.61 ImgEdit score for the fine-tuned internal designer, and human-assessment rates of 89% optimized-instruction preference and 81% perfect EII alignment. These are additional evaluations and variants, not improvements to unchanged-setting headline scores.

M1.justification: The core architecture, four-step blueprints, and staged training procedure remain. v3 adds lightweight fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL-3B on DIM-Edit blueprints and describes internal self-play inference (Section 4.3, Table 7). The frozen Q3B row reproduces v1's externally labeled Q3B results, so that relabeling alone does not establish a new method.

P1.justification: The title and author wording change, DIM-T2I motivation expands, and several passages and captions are tightened. Ablations gain named subtopics, while GEdit details and annotation dimensions move into organized appendices. Most original section ordering and prose remain; much of the expansion consists of additional scientific content.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is extensively redrawn and relocated, Figure 2 replaces an illustrative example, and Figure 3 reorganizes the retained images with color-coded columns. GEdit tables move or split between the main text and appendix. Numerous new comparison, failure, and quality-assessment displays are added, and the original dimension list expands into Figures 19–20.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens the literature grounding for its annotation dimensions through understanding, OCR, mathematics, science, and instruction-following benchmarks in Appendix E. It also introduces references supporting new editing comparisons and designers and supplies citations for previously named baselines. Section 2's original connector-versus-integrative positioning remains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems, proofs, or mathematical derivations. v3's newly stated flow-matching objective and expanded curriculum-learning and CoT explanations do not introduce new formal mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for the central blueprint and data-quality argument through designer controls, initialization experiments, same-blueprint baseline comparisons, and automated/human annotation audits. Filtering details and annotation prompts improve reproducibility, while concrete failure cases clarify applicability beyond v1's limited discussion. These address important gaps despite unchanged headline scores. Some designer fine-tuning and timing details remain unspecified, and uncertainty reporting is still absent, but the overall evidential and transparency gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIM datasets and DIM-4.6B framework. Text, tables, figures, and other material support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v3 includes readable Appendices A–E. Relocated and renumbered content can be matched.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds MagicBrush evaluation, designer and initialization experiments, annotation-quality assessments involving human raters, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original DIM model evaluations on generation and editing benchmarks, data-composition and CoT-component ablations, and qualitative editing results.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from interpreting and improving Shampoo to a unified treatment of Shampoo and SOAP, including the new KL-SOAP method. The abstract and introduction additionally claim KL-Shampoo outperforms KL-SOAP and that the practical techniques can make trace-scaled Shampoo competitive without grafting.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of eigenvalue averaging as correction for outdated eigenbases in Kronecker-factored versus augmented diagonal spaces, a matrix-Gaussian whitening interpretation, and discussion of KL versus VN applicability. It also explicitly qualifies exact optimality when expectations are approximated and identifies limited computation as the reason appendix experiments cover only two models.

D1.justification: Table 1 and its associated footnote newly disclose bfloat16 storage and updates, with QR/eigendecomposition performed in float32 before casting. Section 6 further identifies tuned parameters and implementation sources. These improve documentation; v1 does not establish that a different precision regime was previously used.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate NanoGPT and NanoRWKV7 on FineWeb, Llama on C4, and NanoMoE on OpenWebText, with the same stated model sizes and token subsets. The additional analyses use NanoGPT and Llama from this retained coverage; they introduce no new dataset, task, or domain.

E2.justification: v1 compares KL-Shampoo with Shampoo using powers 1/2 and 1/4, with and without grafting, and SOAP. v3 adds KL-SOAP to the runtime comparison and evaluates two-sided Frobenius-based F-Shampoo and trace-scaled VN-Shampoo variants (Figures 5, 7, 9, and 10). Figure 5 also evaluates an adapted Shampoo comparator using QR and eigenvalue averaging.

E3.justification: The stated hyperparameter-search budget increases from 120 to 150 trials per method; v3 specifies two stages of 75 trials, first broad and then refined. Separately, new experiments introduce controlled comparisons of instantaneous versus averaged eigenvalues and align implementations and QR/EMA procedures across estimation schemes. The retained model sizes, token subsets, batch sizes, and default decomposition interval remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds an explicit eigenvalue-averaging ablation under outdated eigenbases (Figure 4), controlled comparisons of one-sided and two-sided estimation and divergence choices (Figure 5), and analyses of QR/EMA adaptations for F-Shampoo and VN-Shampoo (Appendix H). These investigate component contributions beyond the grafting comparisons already present in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The change from 120 to 150 runs concerns hyperparameter-search trials and does not establish a change in repeated-run statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds KL-SOAP training curves, reports KL-Shampoo outperforming KL-SOAP, and supplies new findings about eigenvalue averaging and the relative performance of F-Shampoo and VN-Shampoo. The reported unsuccessful ungrafted Shampoo 1/2 searches on RWKV7 increase from 120 to 150. The revised main curves accompany a changed search budget, so they do not establish performance gains under an unchanged evaluation protocol.

M1.justification: Alongside the retained KL-Shampoo approach, v3 introduces KL-SOAP, which applies Adam/RMSProp in KL-Shampoo’s estimated eigenbasis (Section 5). It also adapts the QR and eigenvalue-averaging procedures to Frobenius-based and trace-scaled Shampoo variants, with explicit update schemes in Figures 6 and 8.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around the joint Shampoo/SOAP framework. Background and method explanations expand considerably, while the short preliminary-results narrative becomes a discussion organized around four experimental questions and additional appendix analyses.

P2.justification: The original runtime and step-wise plots become v3 Figures 1 and 2, with revised colors, legends, and axis presentation. Figure 3 gains a SOAP/KL-SOAP panel. v3 also adds the memory table, algorithm diagrams in Figures 6 and 8, and analysis plots in Figures 4, 5, 7, 9, and 10.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens positioning through connections to KL-based BFGS/DFP interpretations, matrix-normal maximum-likelihood estimation, Bregman matrix divergences, and Adafactor. Added references such as Fletcher, Dutilleul, Kanamori and Ohara, and Shazeer and Stern support these substantive relationships.

T1.justification: v1’s eigenvalue Claim 3 and proof become v3 Claim 4 and Appendix D. v3 adds Claims 3, 5, 6, and 7 with derivations covering proximal-gradient averaging, augmented SOAP eigenvalues, Frobenius estimation, and VN/Adafactor relationships. Claims 2 and 4 are qualified as conditions satisfied at an optimum. The new Appendix C formal update nevertheless omits dimension-normalization factors present in Equation 5 and its own subsequent derivation.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly supports its design through aggregate preliminary training comparisons. v3 Figures 4–5 and Appendix H add component analyses and matched comparisons that substantially strengthen evidence for eigenvalue averaging and the choice of estimation rule. Memory and precision disclosures also improve assessability. Appendix C introduces a normalization inconsistency between its formal claim and derivation, but this localized defect does not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.
