A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KL-Shampoo research, with v3 expanding its scope to SOAP and alternative estimation schemes. Text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–C and v3 Appendices A–H.

after.justification: v3 Section 6 and Appendix H report original training comparisons and component analyses, including results for KL-SOAP, F-Shampoo, and VN-Shampoo.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 and Figures 1–2 report original language-model training experiments, including test-loss curves against training steps and elapsed time.

C1.justification: The central claims of inference-time guidance without conditional retraining, independent attribute control, and compositional control persist. v2's abstract and conclusion add an explicit claim of demonstrated applicability across cardiac, vascular, and skeletal systems, extending v1's cardiovascular demonstrations.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies disentanglement through size–shape correlation and replaces v1's blanket inference that implicit models require retraining with an explanation based on dropout-configuration imbalance. It adds a limitation concerning within-class localized features, discusses transfer of guidance weights, and interprets topology and extreme-editing failures. Empty-segmentation instability remains documented in Appendix 8.4 despite leaving the main limitations section.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial additional reproducibility information: new datasets' label sets, case counts, resolutions and crops; ellipsoid-generation distributions; increased model width and adjusted guidance weights; and alternative-loss weights in Table 10. It also explicitly documents the EDM denoiser parameterization and revises the softmax-temperature specification. Core training hyperparameters and biomechanical-solver details are retained.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained cardiac dataset, v2 evaluates separately trained models on branched aortic segmentations, CTSpine1K vertebrae, and ShapeMedKnee distal femur/cartilage segmentations (Sections 5.8 and 8.2). Appendix 8.9 also adds procedurally generated ellipsoids, substantially expanding anatomical and synthetic test coverage.

E2.justification: The principal comparators remain explicit concatenation with ANG, implicit concatenation with CFG, cross-attention with CFG, and the implicit component-dropout baseline. v2 additionally evaluates VAE reconstruction as a diagnostic reference against unconditional and guided generation in Appendix 8.10, Table 8.

E3.justification: v2 adds a training-fraction sweep with fixed validation data, a 24-case reconstruction/topology comparison introducing connected-component Betti error, a 64-case mass-editing sweep, and 32-sample alternative-loss evaluations. The ellipsoid experiment also changes model width and guidance weights. Separately, Appendix 8.4 revises the stated softmax temperature from 0.01 to 1; this establishes a reported setting change, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test dependence on training-set size, guidance behavior without anatomical complexity, reconstruction versus diffusion contributions to error, tolerance of extreme mass edits, and independent extent/stretch/orientation control (Appendices 8.8–8.12). The original component-loss and compositional analyses remain, although v1's numerical loss-ablation table is omitted.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bars. The additional sample counts and 'seed label maps' in v2 describe experimental inputs, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial qualitative and numerical findings in Figures 12–14 and Tables 8, 9, and 11. For example, new Table 8 reports PA Betti error of 0.583 for unconditional versus 1.042 for guided generation. Retained compositional scores are unchanged, but v2 Table 1 omits v1 Table 2's two-component rows. v1 Table 1's numerical loss-ablation results are also omitted, while Figure 9 remains. New results should not be read as performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: The core latent-diffusion procedure and mass, centroid, and normalized-covariance guidance remain. Appendix 8.12 adds a bounded extension: separate extent and stretch MSE losses and a sign-invariant eigenvector-alignment loss for orientation. These enable finer control within the existing guidance framework. Boolean-union substructures were already demonstrated in v1.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution statements, background, and much explanatory prose are rewritten. Terminology shifts toward 'substructures'; moment extraction and loss computation are consolidated, dataset and training sections are combined, and the appendix is reorganized and expanded. Algorithm 1 is removed, with its procedure retained in prose and Figure 2.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column layout with a predominantly single-column format and extensively rearranges, resizes, and recaptions displays. v1 Figures 5 and 6 move to appendix Figures 15 and 16. New Figures 12–14 and Tables 8–11 accompany the additions, while the original ablation table is removed and the compositional table is shortened.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantive discussion of HUG-VAS and its fixed-connectivity restriction, adds A-SDF, EDM, and CTSpine1K citations, and trims several morphometry and statistical-shape references. The central positioning against conditional training remains. The anonymous ProtComposer reference becomes Stark et al.; this is the same cited work, not a new addition.

T1.justification: Appendix 8.12 adds mathematical definitions for decomposing covariance into extent, normalized stretch, and orientation, with corresponding losses and a sign-invariant eigenvector-alignment formula (Equations 6–8). The original moment definitions remain equivalent. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 acknowledges topology problems without quantifying them; v2 Table 8 distinguishes reconstruction, diffusion, and guidance errors, while Table 9 establishes degradation under extreme enlargement. These diagnostics, broader anatomical demonstrations, and more qualified baseline interpretation substantially improve understanding of applicability and failure conditions. The new anatomical demonstrations remain mainly qualitative, and omitted older result entries plus the unexplained temperature revision reduce traceability, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CardioComposer. Their complete main texts and appendices, including rendered figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison despite the changed title, format, and expanded experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original cardiac experiments and simulations and adds anatomical-system demonstrations, synthetic-ellipsoid experiments, and quantitative scaling, reconstruction, topology, and editing analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original cardiac-generation experiments, conditional-baseline comparisons, disentanglement and compositional-control evaluations, and biventricular biomechanical simulations.

C1.justification: The central efficiency-bias claim remains, but v3 adds major claims about widespread English-naming failures and systematic associations with size and instruction tuning. Its abstract emphasizes that only Gemini among tested models spans the human complexity range. The introduction and discussion also add tentative applicability beyond color, supported by Shepard circles, expanding v2's contribution scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's brief size/modality speculation, v3 interprets low English alignment as potentially compatible with other human color systems, discusses in-context capacity and collapse, and tests a simple clustering explanation. It explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about the bias's origins, the absence of communication pressure and limited cross-domain evidence. These substantially develop mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 supplies model IDs, example prompts, allowed labels, decoding details, 6k-example training sets, the ten-interaction history window, generation limits and stopping rules. Its reproducibility statement identifies source code/data access and promises experiment-code release upon publication. These greatly expand v2's sparse implementation disclosures without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v3 adds an actually evaluated semantic domain: 64 Shepard-circle stimuli varying in radius and spoke angle, categorized through Gemini IICLL (Section 4.3, Figure 5). This substantially extends the color-only coverage of v2. The WCS, English naming and human color-learning reference datasets remain.

E2.justification: English naming comparisons expand beyond Gemini and Llama to include Gemma, Qwen, OLMo and GPT-2; the main IICLL comparison adds Gemma and Qwen. Appendix M also evaluates a new nearest-neighbor sRGB classifier, NN-rgb, against the four main LLMs for k=14. Human and IB reference comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v3 systematically evaluates model-size and base/instruction-tuned variants, OLMo training checkpoints, CIELAB inputs and history-window settings of 0, 10, 20 and 50. These introduce substantial additional evaluation designs. Color IICLL is restricted to sRGB features, whereas v2 also reports Gemini image-input chains. Newly specified defaults for retained experiments are documentation rather than established setting changes.

E4.justification: v3 adds CIELAB sensitivity tests, OLMo training-trajectory analysis, history-window ablations, smaller-model failure analysis and a nearest-neighbor test of the clustering explanation (Appendices C, F, K-M). Its explicit rotation analysis develops the hypothetical-variant check briefly mentioned in v2. Conversely, v2's reported robustness to imperceptible input noise is omitted.

E5.justification: v2 Table 1 reports English naming means and standard deviations across ten random seeds; v3 does not retain equivalent seed/SD reporting for its naming plots. Both versions show 95% confidence intervals for IICLL. v3 additionally specifies a normal-distribution assumption for rotation-analysis intervals, without establishing an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The result set expands substantially beyond v2's two-model study. New outcomes include single-category collapse in 19 of 20 smaller-model chains (Appendix L), Gemini outperforming NN-rgb on all three reported k=14 metrics (Appendix M), and increasingly structured Shepard-circle categories (Figure 5). v2's Gemini image-input color-IICLL results are no longer presented. These are added or removed findings, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same core IICLL procedure: learn sampled stimulus-pseudoword pairs in context, label the full stimulus space and transmit sampled outputs to subsequent generations. v3 documents constrained decoding and conversation history, but does not establish that these revise v2's underlying procedure. Shepard circles use the existing paradigm.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction and explanatory narrative. Background becomes separate motivation, IB and iterated-learning subsections; experimental setup and results are separated; the short conclusion becomes an extended discussion. Organized technical appendices and a reproducibility statement substantially restructure the document.

P2.justification: v2's composite Figure 1 is reorganized and redrawn across separate overview, naming, trajectory and time-course displays in v3 Figures 1-4. v3 adds numerous domain and appendix figures, including model-specific panels and category maps. The numerical results table is removed, while a model-inventory table is introduced, substantially changing visual organization.

R1.justification: Sections 2.1-2.3 substantially expand positioning against previous LLM color studies, neural iterated learning and emergent communication. Added discussions include Abdou et al., Patel and Pavlick, Marjieh et al., Ren et al. and Carlsson et al. The unresolved I-ICL citation in v2 is replaced by an explicit relationship to Zhu and Griffiths (2024).

T1.justification: v3 adds Bayesian iterated-learning convergence conditions and the stationary-prior result in Section 2.3. Appendix A explicitly specifies the meaning prior, Bayesian listener and accuracy/KL-distortion relationship, beyond v2's shorter mathematical account. The central IB objective remains unchanged, and no new original theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidential support and reproducibility of v2's two-model study. Broader comparisons reveal failure boundaries, while history-window tests and the NN-rgb baseline directly examine alternative explanations for category formation. Detailed procedures and clearer limitations make the conclusions easier to assess. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit English-naming seed/SD reporting and image-input color-IICLL results. The Shepard-circle extension remains preliminary, and experiment code is still only promised.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same authors' IB-based color-naming and IICLL research. The text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v2 has no appendices; v3 includes Appendices A-M.

after.justification: v3 reports original multi-model naming experiments, IICLL simulations, Shepard-circle results and additional empirical analyses in its appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original English color-naming measurements in Table 1 and simulated IICLL outcomes in Figure 1.

C1.justification: The central contribution of informative retriever scores and three-objective denoising training remains. V3 explicitly claims generality across reranker backbones and foregrounds retriever-aware reranking. Its conclusion drops v1's specific assertion that the posterior is Beta and potentially preferable to Gaussian noise.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations concerning diversity through bias denoising, diminishing opportunities with stronger retrievers, missing textual inputs for LLM rerankers, online engagement tradeoffs and measured computational overhead. Discussion expands to multiple retrievers, joint stage optimization and end-to-end recommendation, replacing earlier future directions concerning KL estimation and analytical Beta parameters.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies a two-layer MLP generator, dataset-specific hyperparameters, dropout, batch size and fixed controls for existing sensitivity experiments, and announces code access. Algorithm 1 now explicitly documents the previously described warm-up update. Conversely, removing the explicit regularization surrogate leaves that implementation detail less precise.

E1.justification: Both versions use ML-1M, Kuaivideo and Amazon Books, with unchanged dataset statistics, and the same industrial video-feed A/B setting. The online experiment already appears in v1 Appendix D.4. Added backbone and retriever configurations remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds MG-E to Table 1 while retaining all original comparator rows. Table 2 adds an explicit PRM reference, and Table 3 replaces its Pier reference with PRM. These are limited changes to comparator membership.

E3.justification: The original splits and top-50-to-top-6 evaluation remain. Added experiments introduce PIER backbones, 10-layer PRM, Beta(2,5) initialization and dual-tower retrieval, alongside coverage metrics, per-epoch timing and additional online metrics. Sensitivity plots also change their reported cutoff from NDCG@20 to NDCG@6, without establishing that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 already contains objective ablations, noise-distribution visualization and sensitivity studies. V3 adds retriever-versus-reranker noise analysis in Figure 1e, backbone generality tests in Table 2, and analyses of Beta parameters, scaling, stronger retrievers, diversity and training cost in Appendix E. These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains its Student t-test reporting at p < 0.05. V3 adds metric-wise online significance flags and a bracketed DAU uncertainty range of [-0.012%, +0.012%], without new seed or repeated-run counts. DAU reporting is inconsistent: Table 11 marks significance, whereas Appendix E.6 says it nearly reaches significance.

E6.justification: All 15 original Table 1 rows retain their numerical values, and the online realshow gain remains 1.089%. V3 adds substantial results for MG-E, PIER-based DNR, alternative noise initialization, larger models, dual-tower retrieval, diversity, timing and other online outcomes. For example, the new 10-layer comparison reports ML-1M NDCG@6 of 76.09 for PRM and 78.72 for PRM+DNR; these are additional settings.

M1.justification: The denoising, adversarial generation and regularization framework remains. However, v1 Eq. (8) and Algorithm 1 specify an explicit instance-level regularization surrogate; v3 replaces this with an unspecified distributional-difference approximation. The PDFs do not establish whether the implemented loss changed or only its description. The added warm-up update in Algorithm 1 was already described in v1's prose.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten, especially to distinguish the noise generator from its induced posterior and emphasize retriever-awareness. Terminology and section titles change, a notation appendix is introduced, and acknowledgment, ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from four panels in one row to five panels across two rows, and Figure 2 gains model labels. Table 2 becomes a two-backbone comparison, and numerous notation, hyperparameter and evaluation tables are added. Sensitivity axes are relabeled, and figures and tables are redistributed under a different document template.

R1.justification: V3 adds references concerning LLM recommendation, additional diffusion recommenders, OneRec and MiniOneRec, supporting limited new applicability and positioning discussions. Covington et al. (2016) and Yang et al.'s diffusion survey are removed. Most related work and the complementary earlier-stage-to-later-stage positioning remain.

T1.justification: The two likelihood decompositions and their appendix derivations are largely retained. V3 removes v1's explicit regularization surrogate and its claimed control over KL divergence, drops the assertion that L1 is non-positive and minimized at matching predictions, and revises the stated dependence of ground-truth distributions on the reranker. These are limited mathematical revisions rather than new proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's PRM-based DNR with MF retrieval through PIER, larger-model and dual-tower tests. It also quantifies training costs and expands reporting for the existing online experiment, addressing important generality and practical-evaluation gaps. Added hyperparameters and code access information improve reproducibility support. These gains outweigh the less precise regularizer specification and contradictory DAU significance reporting, which remain material weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DNR research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on alternative backbones, retrievers, noise distributions, diversity and computational cost.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark experiments and ablations in Tables 1–3, plus an industrial online A/B test in Appendix D.4.

C1.justification: VisualTableQA becomes a principal contribution in the abstract and introduction, extending the paper's claims to joint visual and tabular reasoning on a newly introduced benchmark. v3 also explicitly includes Gemma fine-tuning and changes the stated state-of-the-art coverage from 10/14 to 11/15 benchmarks. The original dataset, extensibility, and transfer claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 emphasizes that existing benchmarks inadequately test visual information and explicitly cautions that mixed-training gains could reflect additional samples. v3 adds interpretations about transferable compositional visual reasoning, robustness across architectures and training regimes, and resilience to visual complexity. Its rewritten mixed-training discussion gives a more definite attribution to realism and scale, while the limitations section remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix 12 supplies detailed Gemma TABLET-M settings, including NF4 quantization, LoRA rank/alpha, trainable modules, optimizer, batch size, and learning rate. v3 also documents benchmark curation and complexity computation, revises Qwen gradient-accumulation information, and updates the dataset example's path fields and metadata structure (Figure 4).

E1.justification: v3 introduces VisualTableQA: 306 held-out questions on tables from six existing seed datasets, curated to require reasoning over visual cues and tabular content. This adds a substantive capability requirement beyond the retained benchmarks, while the existing training instances remain unchanged (Sections 3.1–3.3 and Table 1).

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Gemma 3-4B zero-shot and MMTab-trained comparators. For the already evaluated Table Recognition task, v3 Table 10 adds DocOwl2, InternVL3-8B/14B, and Gemma-3-12B comparisons. Conversely, the one-shot comparator disappears from the held-out comparison in Table 4, although it remains in Table 3.

E3.justification: v3 adds Gemma 3-4B LoRA experiments, with quantized, one-epoch TABLET-M training documented in Appendix 12, and introduces complexity-based evaluation using 20 bins with sparse bins omitted. Appendix 8 also changes the stated gradient accumulation for 16-GPU runs from 4 to 8; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of performance across visual-complexity levels and robustness across backbone and training regime (Figure 2, Appendices 10–12). The earlier size and task-removal ablations remain, but much of the TABLET-B held-out visualization comparison in v2 Appendix 8.3 is removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly states that VisualTableQA results are averaged over three random seeds (Section 5). The existing bootstrap significance reporting at p < 0.05 is retained. Neither PDF establishes an increase in repeated runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: v3 adds VisualTableQA scores, including TABLET-M 47.8%, zero-shot Qwen 42.4%, and MMTab 41.1%, plus Gemma fine-tuning and additional Table Recognition results. Earlier TABLET-B entries for TabMWP, TAT-QA, TabMCQ, AIT-QA, and PubHealthTab disappear. Table 2 changes the TABLET-B_synth WikiTQ original-image score from 56.5 to 56.4. Most retained Qwen scores and the relocated degradation scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core TABLET retrieval, rendering, highlighting, and instruction-construction pipeline remains unchanged. Gemma/LoRA provides an additional experimental configuration; the new complexity score supports benchmark curation and evaluation rather than changing the proposed model or its inference procedure.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, contribution list, experimental questions, and visualization discussion, and shortens some dataset explanations. It adds acknowledgments and conference headers. These are focused narrative revisions; the main section order and most existing appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 consolidates original-image scores and previously separate degradation results into a revised display. Tables 3, 4, and the open-weight held-out table change structure. v3 adds complexity plots, a component-weight table, and VisualTableQA illustrations; existing task examples are largely retained and relocated.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 adds the specific criticism that TableVQA-Bench questions can be answered from textual content alone, sharpening the positioning of the new VisualTableQA benchmark.

T1.justification: Appendix 10 introduces a mathematically defined visual-complexity score, with component definitions, normalization rules, and a weighted aggregation in Equations 1–12. This is substantial new formal metric content, although it adds no learning-theoretic guarantees. The earlier degradation-score definition remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses two important evidence gaps acknowledged in v2: benchmarks poorly suited to testing visual cues and reliance on one fine-tuned backbone. VisualTableQA provides direct evaluation with documented Qwen gains, while Gemma experiments and complexity analyses substantially strengthen the dataset's empirical foundation. These benefits outweigh the removed subsidiary results and reporting defects: the rewritten discussion reverses the HiTab/TabFact comparisons shown in Table 2, and Section 9 still incorrectly describes fine-tuning as limited to one model.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TABLET research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, equations, and figures are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds VisualTableQA evaluations, Gemma 3 fine-tuning results, and performance analyses by visual complexity.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning experiments, held-in and held-out evaluations, and ablations comparing visualization styles, dataset sizes, and task inclusion.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list extend the explicit state-of-the-art claim from three named benchmarks to five, adding TFB and EPF. The central contributions—multimodal zero-shot forecasting, modality-guided attention and prototype-guided probabilistic generation—remain the same.

C2.justification: v1 gives a general explanation that modality guidance focuses attention on useful historical tokens. v3 Figures 18–21 add case-specific interpretations linking stronger patch relationships to relevant trend transitions. No substantive new discussion of limitations or failure boundaries is added.

D1.justification: A.1 newly documents dataset-specific point counts and sources, GPT4-based quality checking, manual sampling and additional prompt examples. A.4 adds baseline-context details, and A.6 revises model configurations. v3 also adds explicit code/checkpoint release information and GitHub/Hugging Face links, materially expanding provenance and reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: v3 adds short-term evaluation on five EPF electricity-price datasets and the broad univariate TFB collection spanning yearly-to-hourly and other frequencies. It also adds NYSE deterministic and ILI probabilistic evaluations. These substantially extend the represented data and forecasting scenarios beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: TTM joins the retained TSFM-Bench comparison in v3 Tables 2 and 13. New comparisons also evaluate supervised deterministic methods such as TimeKAN, AMD, TimeXer and PatchTST, classical LR/RF baselines on TFB, and small unimodal baselines on TimeMMD (Tables 10–11 and 15–16).

E3.justification: Added protocols include EPF's 168-step input and 24-step output, TFB evaluation using MASE/msMAPE, and additional 10%/20% downstream training comparisons. Figure 9 introduces timing with batch size 64. A.6 also revises the reported model size from 418.6M to 210.8M parameters; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original component ablations and sampling curve are retained. v3 adds tests of prototype-bank size, modality combinations, individual modality guiders and removal of W (Tables 17–19). Appendix C adds history/future, prototype and attention case studies, while Figure 9 extends efficiency analysis across datasets.

E5.justification: v3 introduces forecast bands labeled '80% Confidence Interval' in Figures 15–21, without specifying their construction. The 100-sample CRPS estimation remains unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, seed information or uncertainty intervals for aggregate benchmark scores.

E6.justification: Existing forecasting-error entries are retained, but v3 adds substantial benchmark, baseline, ablation and case-study results. For example, Tables 10–11 newly report TFB mean MASE/msMAPE of 2.134/19.964 for Aurora and 2.158/20.096 for Sundial. These are additional results, rather than demonstrated performance gains over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The reported encoder depth changes from 3 layers in v1 Table 7 to 1 in v3 Table 8. This is a limited architectural configuration revision; Section 3's attention mechanisms, prototype retrieval, loss and sampling procedure remain unchanged. The PDFs do not explain whether the revision reflects retraining or a correction.

P1.justification: Most introduction and method prose is retained. Local revisions include a shorter conclusion, expanded corpus and related-work explanations, new short-term/showcase/analytics sections, and ethics and reproducibility statements. The related-work appendix moves from C to E, without wholesale restructuring of the main narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: benchmark and timing charts, a prototype-bank montage, forecast plots, attention heatmaps and comparison/ablation tables. The corpus figure gains source/count columns, and the prompt figure expands from one example to four. Algorithm 1 is relocated; Table 20 redisplays existing TimeMMD zero-shot results.

R1.justification: v3 adds references including TTM, TimeXer, iTransformer, FLAME and SRSNet, removes MagicScaler, and expands appendix background to other time-series analysis tasks. The central positioning against unimodal foundation models and supervised multimodal models remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The method equations (1–25), metric definitions (26–29) and mathematical content of Algorithm 1 are unchanged. Neither version contains additional formal theorems or proofs; v3's new analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of Aurora's generality and component contributions. Short-term evaluations broaden applicability, Tables 15–16 and 21 add supervised and downstream-data-fraction comparisons, and Tables 17–19 isolate modality, attention and prototype-capacity effects that v1 did not test separately. Expanded corpus provenance and release documentation also improve assessability and reproducibility. The unexplained configuration revision and absent aggregate run uncertainty limit interpretation, but do not outweigh these gains. The improvement concerns stronger evidence and documentation, rather than an established cross-version accuracy or efficiency gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Aurora and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Shared methods and results can be matched reliably across the expanded evaluations, renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds EPF and TFB evaluations, further baseline comparisons, ablations and visual case analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting results on TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench and ProbTS, together with component ablations, sampling analysis and efficiency measurements.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding discussion retain the central contributions: unifying matching-model distillation and incorporating real data without additional GAN losses or discriminators. The claimed framework coverage and exclusion of DMD from UID remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds a conditional explanation of teacher-error correction and emphasizes beta/alpha when interpreting real-data influence. Unlike v1's recommendation of alpha_SiD in [1,1.2], v2 discusses degradation or instability at 1.2 and limits theoretically justified guidance to 0.5. It also explains fine-tuning as requiring stronger real-data influence.

D1.justification: V1 promises a future code release; v2 reports available code and checkpoints and supplies access links. It adds implementation information about reversed codebase time conventions, dropout, adversarial-loss time ranges, teacher provenance, CelebA training, and EMA choices. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although linked resources were not independently checked.

E1.justification: V1 restricts image experiments to conditional and unconditional CIFAR-10 at 32×32 resolution. V2 retains these tasks and adds CelebA face generation at 64×64, substantially broadening the represented image domain. The additional SiD experiments reuse CIFAR-10.

E2.justification: V2 adds sCD, sCT, IMM, MeanFlow, and FACM to the unconditional comparison in Table 3. It also adds direct SiD-versus-RealSiD comparisons in Appendix A.3 and includes GAN methods in the fine-tuning comparison in Table 6, which previously evaluated only RealUID.

E3.justification: Reported CIFAR-10 settings change from AdamW to Adam, and unconditional teacher provenance changes from an authors-trained teacher to an existing checkpoint. Coefficient searches and fine-tuning configurations are revised, and GAN fine-tuning is added. New CelebA protocols use batch size 64 and 800,000/1,600,000 iterations. The PDFs do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 expands coefficient and fine-tuning sensitivity studies, adds a corrupted-teacher Gaussian case study in Figure 4, and tests real-data incorporation into SiD at alpha_SiD=0.5 and 1.2 in Figure 5. These investigate teacher errors and transfer of coefficient recommendations beyond the original flow-model experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions report three independent FID evaluation runs with empirical variance below 0.01 and average inference timing over 10,000 iterations. V2 does not introduce seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Best reported CIFAR-10 RealUID FIDs change from 2.03/1.91 to 1.98/1.87 under revised coefficient and fine-tuning configurations, rather than identical settings. V2 adds fine-tuned GAN results of 2.10/1.88. New CelebA results in Table 8 are 0.96 for UID, 0.87 for UID+GAN, and 0.89 for RealUID; Figure 5 adds SiD convergence and instability findings.

M1.justification: The core objectives and architecture remain intact. Algorithm 1 corrects the update condition from n % K to n % (K+1), aligning the written procedure with the already stated K fake-model updates per generator update. This establishes a pseudocode correction, not that the implementation changed.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence are retained, with explanatory rewrites and terminology refinements. V2 moves Lemma 2 into Section 3.4, consolidates experimental Appendices D–E into organized Appendix D subsections, and adds publication, broader-impact, and LLM-use text.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 6 are substantially restructured around beta/alpha, with expanded grids, GAN fine-tuning blocks, and revised highlighting. Figure 2 is redrawn; Figures 4–6 and CelebA sample grids are added. CIFAR-10 grids use larger thumbnails, while the unchanged inference table moves into Appendix D.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting newer comparators, CelebA, Adam, and EMA, and removes the AdamW reference. The central positioning relative to FGM, SiD, IBMD, inverse optimization, and DMD remains stable. Tong et al. changes from preprint to publication metadata for the same work.

T1.justification: The original UID and RealUID theorems are retained, but Appendix A.1.4 newly derives the objective for corrupted teachers and analyzes possible error correction under additional assumptions. Appendix A.2 extends coefficient-domain analysis, including conditions yielding unbounded objectives. Moving and algebraically rewriting the existing Lemma 2 is not itself new theory.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow empirical validation through CelebA and diffusion-model experiments, extends fine-tuning controls to GAN comparators, and reports a meaningful failure case for heuristic SiD. Expanded implementation and access information also improves reproducibility. These gains improve the paper beyond its small FID changes. The teacher-error argument remains conditional, and uncertainty reporting is unchanged, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger validation and clearer applicability boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RealUID research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renamed material.

after.justification: V2 retains original CIFAR-10 experiments and adds CelebA results and direct diffusion-model experiments in Appendices D.3 and A.3.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 generation experiments, coefficient ablations, convergence curves, fine-tuning results, and inference measurements in Section 4 and Appendices D–E.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand from W[1]-hardness for two- and three-layer networks to hardness at increasing levels of the W-hierarchy for arbitrary fixed depths. v3 additionally claims hardness parameterized by depth in constant dimension, resolves a deep-network injectivity question, and strengthens the claimed optimality of enumeration with respect to depth and dimension jointly.

C2.justification: v3 develops a substantive interpretation connecting network depth to the W-hierarchy and discusses possible computational depth separation. Its conclusion replaces several earlier open questions with W-/Th-hierarchy membership questions and qualifies the sparse, small-weight discussion to two-layer constructions. v2's explicit worst-case limitations paragraph disappears, although practical applicability caveats remain in the conclusion.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 in v3 documents region representations, sign-pattern enumeration, matrix updates and dimensionality tests for the enumeration approach previously sketched in v2's Appendices A.1 and B.2. This provides additional implementation-oriented detail for an existing algorithmic approach.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or test scenarios for training or evaluation. The expanded coverage concerns formal decision problems and network classes.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates comparison methods. DeepZ, DeepPoly, ZonoDual and other verification methods appear as related-work citations.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, preprocessing, training budgets, sample sizes or testing protocols. Changes to network dimensions and depth concern theoretical constructions.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness experiments, error analyses or empirical case studies. The function plots illustrate mathematical constructions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals or statistical tests. The randomized approximation statements concern theoretical success guarantees.

E6.justification: Neither version contains empirical measurements, performance rankings or experimental result entries. The added table and plots present theoretical classifications and constructed functions; changed mathematical bounds are assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The reduction constructions change substantially. v3 replaces v2's homogenization-and-scaling construction for Lipschitz hardness with h(x,y)=f(x+Ty1) in Theorem 7.3, generalizes homogenization to deeper networks, and introduces Boolean-formula simulation and digit-extraction networks in Theorems 5.4 and 9.1. These change the constructed networks and computational procedures.

P1.justification: v3 integrates v2's appendix preliminaries and proofs into the main argument, creates a separate algorithmic-upper-bounds section, and reorganizes the Lipschitz and ICNN discussion. The abstract, contributions, proof explanations and concluding research agenda are extensively rewritten around depth as well as dimension.

P2.justification: v3 adds the complexity overview Table 1, an algorithm display, and new Figures 5, 6, 7 and 9. It expands v2's zonotope illustration into the network-to-zonotope diagram in Figure 8 and moves appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 3. The document also adopts a different article layout throughout.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around Boolean circuits, interpretability, ICNN expressivity and threshold-circuit complexity. Section 8 cites Cao et al., Dewasurendra and Jayawardhana, and Das et al. (2026) as resolving the norm-maximization questions left open in v2, including deterministic approximation. This changes the research frontier against which the contribution is presented.

T1.justification: v3 adds W[P] membership results, depth-dependent W-hierarchy hardness, injectivity and other decision-problem results, and constant-dimension and joint-parameter lower bounds, including Corollary 9.4. Lemma 7.2 and Theorem 7.3 replace v2's flawed unit-ball argument in Appendix B.7 with regional-gradient reasoning and a new hardness reduction. Homogenization is generalized, norm-oracle assumptions become explicit, and the p=0 approximation claim is removed.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs an important weakness in a core contribution: v2's Lipschitz-hardness proof relied on an invalid identification with maximum function magnitude on the unit ball, while v3 supplies regional-gradient reasoning and an explicit separating construction. The new membership and depth-sensitive hardness proofs substantially sharpen the complexity classification. Integrated proofs and Table 1 improve verifiability. These gains outweigh the loss of the explicit worst-case limitations paragraph.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures and supporting material are readable. v3 integrates material from v2's Appendices A and B into an expanded main text, allowing reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 likewise reports theoretical algorithms, reductions and proofs without experimental, simulation or data-analysis outcomes. Its new Table 1 summarizes complexity classifications.

before.justification: v2 explicitly describes the work as purely theoretical. Its main text and appendices report constructions, complexity proofs and mathematical illustrations, without original empirical outcomes.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: four goal-aligned non-collaborative behaviors, exposed agent vulnerabilities, and an extensible simulation framework. The added experiments principally support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 replaces the explanation of weak combined tangential realism as a truncation effect with an explanation based on unnatural behavior pairings. It also adds substantive interpretations of alignment filtering, excluded tasks, reasoning-budget robustness, training-mixture choices, and differing behavior effects in feedback-based tasks. Appendix A clarifies behavioral scope exclusions.

D1.justification: Appendix D.7 documents collection of successful GPT-4.1-mini dialogues and explicit training-mixture proportions. Listings 1–2 remove the persona placeholder, although the PDFs do not establish whether this reflects an execution change. Existing QLoRA hyperparameters, hardware information, and the promise to release code and data upon publication remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds ColBench backend programming and MINT's HotpotQA, HumanEval, TheoremQA, and GSM8K tasks, extending evaluation beyond service transactions to coding and feedback-assisted problem solving. Appendix D.5 also evaluates single-domain MultiWOZ tasks and previously excluded tau-bench human-transfer scenarios.

E2.justification: New Table 16 includes GLM-4.5 and DeepSeek-Chat-v3.1 alongside GPT-4.1-mini in the human-transfer comparison. The five agents in the main benchmark comparison and the PBUS simulator comparator remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds a 50-step reasoning-budget experiment, training comparisons holding dialogue count at 1,308 while varying behavior mixtures, and separate single-behavior human evaluations. It also introduces a balanced 40-dialogue human validation of goal-alignment judgments. These extend the evaluation design; the original main experiments retain their 30-step limit and scenario counts.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether failures persist with a longer reasoning budget, audit causes of goal misalignment, validate the alignment judge against a human, and compare uniform versus nonuniform training mixtures. Single-behavior human evaluation further examines realism separately from behavior combinations. The original error analyses and dialogue examples are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix D.3 introduces Matthews correlation coefficient estimation for agreement between human and automated goal-alignment judgments. Existing four-trial averaging and the human-evaluation sampling seed of 42 remain. Neither version reports confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2, Figure 4, and the earlier error-analysis results retain their values. Substantial new results include Table 20's average scores of 86.9 and 86.6 for mixed-data training versus 78.8 for collaborative-only training, judge–human MCC of 0.77, and new domain evaluations. Figure 5b adds isolated tangential realism preference of 66.7%; the original combined-setting result remains, so this is not a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: The original architecture and four behavior modules remain. Appendix F.1 adds procedural adaptations: ColBench changes unavailable-goal generation and removes failure-triggered impatience; MINT triggers impatience through negative feedback and removes complaints about ignored tangential utterances. These are limited adaptations of the existing framework.

P1.justification: The behavior-grounding and human-evaluation passages are revised, and the appendices gain taxonomy and extensibility sections plus separate human-evaluation subsections. Most existing prose, the main section sequence, prompt wording, and dialogue examples remain, making the rewriting and reorganization limited.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the empirical displays with tables for reasoning budgets, excluded scenarios, mixed-data training, and new domains. Figure 5 becomes a relocated two-panel human-evaluation figure. Figure 4 is enlarged and recaptioned without changing its plotted results, and Figure 3 replaces 'Fragment Dumping' with 'Incomplete Utterance.'

R1.justification: Section 3.1 and new Appendix A substantially expand the taxonomy's grounding in customer-service research, including rapport, entitlement, and abusive behavior. v3 adds MINT and ColBench-related references and removes Lei et al. (2022) and Patient-Ψ. The new MINT citation to Wang et al. (2024) is a different work from the removed Patient-Ψ citation.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The existing task-success and goal-alignment definitions remain; the added taxonomy rationale and explanation of MCC introduce no new formal derivation or mathematical property.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation and practical usefulness: alignment audits and human agreement address previously unchecked measurement reliability, the longer-budget experiment tests a potential confound, and mixed-data training demonstrates a concrete benefit of the simulator. Coding and feedback-task evaluations also substantiate the existing extensibility claim. Sparse protocol details for the added domains and an untested explanation of unnatural behavior pairings remain limitations, but the gains outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same simulator framework. Their main text, figures, tables, prompt listings, and complete appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds training comparisons, validation studies, and evaluations on additional tasks.

before.justification: v1 reports original MultiWOZ and tau-bench simulations, fine-tuning experiments, human evaluations, and agent-error analyses.

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims to be the first study of asymmetric structure in TTA, strengthening the explicit novelty claim. The central contributions concerning efficient collapse prevention, biased-signal regularization and vision/language adaptation retain their earlier scope.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations of shortcuts, alpha's balancing role and gradient interference from norm inflation. Appendix E.6 adds a concrete limitation: entropy-based Gaussian calibration may fail for ConvNeXt. E.11 further develops applicability arguments, while the original limited success of collapse recovery remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a ZeroSiam source-code link, explicitly identifies the main evaluations as one epoch, and supplies calibration sample counts, learning-rate settings and A100 measurement details. Appendix C's existing optimizer, model and LoRA specifications are largely unchanged; the new reproducibility statement mainly organizes existing information.

E1.justification: The datasets and vision/language tasks are retained. Table 11 adds actual evaluation at ImageNet-C severity levels 1 and 3, extending the severity-5 alpha study in v1 Table F to milder corruption conditions.

E2.justification: New Table J evaluates SPA and TTE on ResNet50-GN and ViT-Base, and REM on ViT-Base. These directly relevant multi-branch comparisons substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set; the original comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds distinct supplementary protocols: three- and five-epoch adaptation, calibration using 6,400 Gaussian inputs, and accuracy/memory/time comparisons with efficiency measured on an A100 at batch size 64. The original RTX 3090 timing experiment and main adaptation settings remain, so these are added evaluations rather than replacements.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis with entropy-versus-divergence trajectories, Swin-Tiny learning-rate sensitivity, noise-based calibration validation, adaptation-duration robustness and a norm-inflation diagnostic. The alpha study gains additional severities. Existing collapse-recovery and stop-gradient analyses are retained, with the latter moving to E.8/Table H.

E5.justification: v1 does not disclose repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. Appendix E.9 explicitly reports five-seed reruns of the label-shift comparison for DeYO and ZeroSiam across five architectures, with means and standard deviations in Table I, adding substantial statistical support for stability.

E6.justification: DeYO's Table 3 overall average changes from 44.4% to 43.1%, and its Swin-Tiny average in Table A changes from 43.1% to 36.5%. New results cover calibration, uncertainty, efficiency and longer adaptation, including ZeroSiam's 65.7% at epochs three and five in Table G. The earlier alpha=3 result of 61.0% is omitted.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the architecture and the adaptation objective remain unchanged. Appendix E.6 adds a supplementary procedure for selecting the predictor learning rate by minimizing prediction-entropy change after adaptation on Gaussian noise; it does not replace the fixed rates in the main experiments.

P1.justification: The title changes from 'Efficient Siamese' to 'Efficient Asymmetry', with selected abstract, introduction and mechanism paragraphs rewritten. The alpha discussion moves into the main text, and acknowledgments, ethics, reproducibility and LLM-use statements are added. Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds two plots and new calibration, epoch, statistical and multi-branch comparison tables. Old Table F becomes the expanded main-text Table 11; old Table G becomes Table H, and Table 2 is relocated. These substantially expand the visual presentation while retaining the original architecture and principal result displays.

R1.justification: New Appendix E.11 substantially positions ZeroSiam against SPA, REM and TTE through differences in architecture, augmentation, collapse assumptions and efficiency. REM, TTE, OT-VP and DPCore references are added, several other TTA references are removed, and the introduction strengthens the first-in-TTA novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, both lemmas, the formal assumptions and Appendix B proofs are retained. Appendix E.10 adds mathematical definitions of decision margin and relative boundary sharpness, together with scaling reasoning about logit-norm inflation.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's central stability and efficiency argument through five-seed uncertainty estimates and direct multi-branch comparisons in Tables I and J. Additional duration and sensitivity tests strengthen practical reliability evidence, and the source-code link improves reproducibility information. Figure F's evaluation scope remains ambiguous, but this localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical substantiation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ZeroSiam research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds sensitivity, adaptation-duration, repeated-seed and multi-branch comparison results.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-C adaptation experiments, mathematical reasoning evaluations, efficiency measurements and ablations in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The central claim of stable, competitive normalization-free deep E-I SNN training remains. The abstract and conclusion replace explicit Dale's-law compliance with capturing cortical E-I architecture. The conclusion drops its explicit sparse-representation claim and adds a claim of compatibility with analog or mixed-signal neuromorphic platforms.

C2.justification: v2 adds digital-hardware deployment limitations and analog-platform applicability discussion (Section 6), and interprets measured computational costs as a biological-fidelity tradeoff (F.5). Appendix F.1 newly explains gradient amplification and averaging effects in different pathways. Section 5.3/F.4 also refine the distribution interpretation and soften categorical sparsity language.

D1.justification: v2 specifies convolution kernels, fan-in, classifier exceptions, first-batch initialization pseudocode, global average pooling, time-averaged logits, validation selection and no dropout (E.1/E.2/F.6). It also documents the added datasets' settings. Conversely, v1's explicit channel-normalization and direct-encoding instructions disappear. Code release remains promised upon publication.

E1.justification: Beyond retained CIFAR-10/100 coverage, v2 evaluates TinyImageNet, CIFAR10-DVS and DVS-Gesture (Table 1). This substantially broadens static image coverage and introduces event-stream object classification and gesture recognition, providing temporal-input evaluations absent from v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds BNTT, NeuNorm, TEBN, tdBN and TAB to the retained CIFAR-10 comparison, and BNTT, TEBN and TAB to CIFAR-100. These expand evaluated comparisons beyond citations in related work. Existing comparators remain; v1's SNN with default BN becomes Vanilla BN.

E3.justification: Reported CIFAR peak learning rates decrease from 0.01/0.02 to 0.001/0.002 (v1 A.6.1 versus v2 F.6). Added evaluations introduce TinyImageNet downsampling, event-data resizing and augmentation, batch size 32, and 10/16 simulation steps. Appendix F.5 adds a controlled runtime/memory protocol. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds gradient-scaling sensitivity across 1/sqrt(d), 1/d and 1/d² (Table 3), and computational-overhead analysis across five architectures (Table 4). Table 2 replaces v1's clamped Kaiming initialization of all three weight matrices with unconstrained initialization of W_EE and W_IE, changing the ablation question.

E5.justification: v1 reports point accuracies without run-count or significance information. v2 adds ± values, explicitly identifies five independent runs for starred BN/DANN reproductions, and introduces error bars and significance reporting in Figure 6. The uncertainty measure, statistical test and run count for unstarred proposed-model results remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds results including 77.66% on CIFAR10-DVS, 94.86% on DVS-Gesture and 50.29% on TinyImageNet. Retained results are revised: CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 changes from 92.12% to 92.05±0.11%, and CIFAR-100 VGG-16 from 65.53% to 64.95±1.14%, with different reported settings. New sensitivity and overhead results include 2.32–2.50× training-time and 1.12–1.57× memory costs.

M1.justification: The core circuit equations, dynamic initialization and E-I Prop operations are retained. However, v1 Appendix A.6.1 describes a single linear logits head, whereas v2 Appendices E.1/F.6 specify an E-I classifier without output divisive inhibition. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents an implementation change or fuller documentation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 edits grammar and author information, reframes the Dale's-law subsection, and rewrites selected experimental and concluding passages. Appendix A's subsections become Appendices A–F, with implementation material regrouped and experimental details moved after supplementary results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, and new Figure 3 illustrates stabilization and STE. Tables 1–2 are restructured, including an ablation-component matrix, while Tables 3–4 are added. Distribution and gradient plots are revised, and the DANN comparison gains error bars and significance annotations. The feature-map example is retained as Figure 8.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for NeuNorm, TAB, the three added datasets and DYNAP-SE2 hardware. These extend comparison and applicability context, while the principal positioning against normalization-dependent SNNs and Cornford et al.'s E-I-constrained ANNs remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's current-variance and initialization-rate derivations are retained in v2 D.3/D.4. v2 additionally supplies an analytical fast-inhibitory-neuron derivation (D.1), parameter-by-parameter backpropagation formulas (D.5), and explicit moment-based initialization formulas (E.2). These substantially expand the mathematical treatment beyond relocated equations.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support was limited to static CIFAR datasets and point comparisons. v2 substantially strengthens validation through event-based tasks, TinyImageNet, broader normalization comparisons and scaling sensitivity. Explicit computational costs and fuller implementation details also make the framework easier to assess and reproduce. Undefined statistical quantities, changed CIFAR settings and classifier ambiguity remain limitations, but the added evidence substantially improves support for the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DeepEISNN framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments, including event-based datasets and TinyImageNet, alongside ablations, gradient-scaling sensitivity and computational-cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10/100 experiments, component ablations and appendix analyses of gradients, architecture depth and feature representations.

C1.justification: The original three contributions remain. V4's abstract adds a claim about signature semantics differing from human conceptual organization and qualifies coding's isolation through its relationship with missing-information detection. It also replaces v3's multilingual/cultural characterization with culture- and humanities-oriented benchmarks.

C2.justification: New Section 5 distinguishes predictive signatures from semantic resemblance and proposes explanations involving auxiliary skills, proxy cues and statistical co-occurrence. The appendices interpret task specificity and corpus stability, acknowledge computational limits and corpus-representativeness requirements, and discuss smaller-scale applicability. The conclusion adds qualifications concerning open-ended scoring and causal understanding.

D1.justification: V4 newly links a reported code/data release and supplies explicit benchmark-labeling rules, alternative-regression hyperparameters, robustness-test settings and computational timings. Appendix A.8 reports approximately two hours per model for perplexity extraction and 30–40 minutes per benchmark for filtering/regression. The original hardware, context construction and core preprocessing details were already present in v3.

E1.justification: V4 adds AbsenceBench's missing-information task across numerical, poetry and GitHub material, evidenced by Figure 1's new tell_missing row and Appendix A.5.5. Appendix A.7.3 also evaluates Dolma as an alternative signature-source corpus. Existing benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V3 mentions Lasso and Elastic Net as possible regressors; v4 actually compares them with AIC and a random-feature baseline. Appendix A.7.2 also compares Thrush screening against Spearman correlation and mutual information, substantially expanding evaluated alternatives for both pipeline stages.

E3.justification: V4 adds separate held-out-model and cross-task prediction protocols, preselection-ratio sweeps from 10^-6 to 1, and corpus-size sweeps from 100K to 10B tokens. It also adds adjusted R-squared to the granularity comparison and a signature/function semantic-similarity evaluation. These extend evaluation design without replacing the original extraction settings.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's LOOCV and granularity comparison, v4 tests unseen-model generalization, task specificity versus shared confounds, alternative regularizers and screening methods, corpus dependence, threshold sensitivity and scale stability. Section 5 and Appendix A.9 additionally examine signature meaning through semantic comparisons and concrete textual examples.

E5.justification: Appendix A.6 adds 10,000-bootstrap significance tests for within-category versus cross-category overlaps, with p-values in Table 5 and stars in Figure 4. V4 also first reports ± quantities for prediction errors. Their statistical meaning is unspecified, and additional repeated runs are not established; v3's semantic bootstrapping and Mann–Whitney tests remain.

E6.justification: V4 adds substantial generalization, robustness and qualitative results, including RedPajama–Dolma matrix agreement of 0.895 and adjusted R-squared entries in Table 1. Figure 1 retains existing pairwise values but adds AbsenceBench; the reported cross-function mean changes from 0.087 to 0.105 under expanded coverage. LOOCV reporting changes from 0.075/0.180 to 0.076/0.181 for method/mean baseline, with v4 explicitly specifying 27 BBH tasks rather than establishing a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains contextual token perplexities, Thrush screening, AIC forward selection and normalized signature correlations. Algorithm 1's added 30-segment context explanation was already documented in v3's appendices. Alternative estimators are evaluated as ablations rather than adopted as a changed method.

P1.justification: V4 rewrites the abstract and final remarks, makes localized explanatory edits, relocates LOOCV to the robustness appendix and reorganizes appendices A–E as A.1–A.5 before adding new sections. Most existing introduction, method and results prose remains closely matched; the added scientific content does not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: The ICLR format substantially reflows the document: Figure 1 moves onto the opening page, Figure 4 shares a page with discussion, Figure 5 has surrounding text, and previously separate algorithm/table pages are consolidated. Figure 1 gains a task row, Figure 4 gains significance annotations, Table 1 gains an adjusted R-squared column, and new statistical and sensitivity tables appear.

R1.justification: V4 adds citations including AbsenceBench, Dolma, Humanity's Last Exam, LESS and semantic-representation studies. It briefly positions signatures against benchmark saturation and connects interpretations to representation research, while retaining the existing related-work organization and central positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix A.7.4 adds an asymptotic argument that downstream regression scales as O(m d'^2), using dimensionality reduction to justify filtering. The signature definitions, correlation equations, sparsity assumption and SIS conditions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially addresses v3's limited validation of generalization and dependence on construction choices. Held-out-model checks, alternative-estimator comparisons, Dolma agreement of 0.895 and threshold/scale analyses directly strengthen the empirical basis for signature robustness. Concrete examples and the code/data link improve interpretability and reproducibility. Undefined ± quantities and the unexplained 27-model training subset limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same benchmark-signature research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and can be matched despite reformatting and added material.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical analyses, expands to 89 benchmarks, and reports additional generalization, robustness, statistical and qualitative results.

before.justification: V3 reports original results from 32 models and 88 benchmarks, including overlap analyses, leave-one-out prediction errors and token/chunk/document comparisons.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims about label-free three-role self-play, improvements across diverse models, and the 7.6-point pass@8 gain. The added experiments expand supporting evidence without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning suppression of incorrect references, reward-width selection, the verifier's dependence on the available judge, task diversification, and alignment with CEM judgments. Appendix D.6 explains questioner stagnation, responder substring exploitation, and verifier self-delusion. The original limitations in Appendix A remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The advertised code repository changes from Tongyi-Zhiwen/SPELL to Tongyi-Zhiwen/Qwen-Doc. Appendix D.4 adds baseline reproduction details involving sampled short documents, DeepSeek-R1-generated QA pairs, consistency filtering, and training configurations. D.3 adds the MRCR dataset reference. Existing hardware, runtime, and core implementation disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds MRCR with two, four, and eight needles and HELMET RAG, in-context learning, and summarization evaluations. This substantially extends the long-context coverage, particularly through multi-needle retrieval and summarization. The original training sources, six long-context QA benchmarks, and short-context suite are retained.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds evaluated LongPO, SoLoPO, and QwenLong-L1 reimplementations plus the official LongPO checkpoint. These methods were discussed but not evaluated in v1. Table 4 additionally compares external-judge variants with and without the internal verifier; existing baseline comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain unchanged. Added controls vary rollout group size, Gaussian reward width, and judge/verifier configuration. The new benchmark and alignment comparisons specify 16K input and 4K output limits, with document-matched data construction for reimplemented baselines. These extend the experimental settings without revising the original protocol.

E4.justification: Sections 5.5–5.6 add sensitivity tests for group size and reward width and investigate verifier usefulness under an external judge. Appendix D.5 adds task-distribution and verifier-disagreement trajectories, while D.6 adds qualitative reward-hacking failure analysis. These substantially expand investigation beyond the retained component and reward-mapping ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the eight-response/averaged-run evaluation descriptions and the same pass@k estimator. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, seed disclosures, or uncertainty-reporting procedures appear. The new group-size and Gaussian-width sweeps concern training settings, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original results are retained, while Tables 3, 4, 8, 9 and Figure 8 add substantial findings. Table 9 reports SPELL at 47.2 versus 46.1 for QwenLong-L1, 44.2 for SoLoPO, and 42.8 for reimplemented LongPO. Table 4 reports 47.2 with either judge. Table 8 shows higher SPELL averages but some HELMET losses, including 7B summarization at 13.7 versus RLVR's 14.3.

M1.justification: The proposed three-role algorithm, reward equations, history memory, grounding filter, and policy updates remain unchanged. Section 5.6 tests an external-judge comparison variant. The stricter CEM criterion discussed in new Appendix D.6 was already explicitly defined in v1 Section 4.2.

P1.justification: v2 adds Sections 5.5–5.6 and groups supplementary material under Additional Analysis, moving the old cost and short-context sections into D.1–D.2 and renaming prompt Appendix F to E. Author order and several explanatory passages change, but most existing prose and all prompt templates are retained.

P2.justification: The displayed evidence expands substantially through new tables for sensitivity, judge substitutions, additional benchmarks, and alignment comparisons, plus the two-panel training-dynamics Figure 8. Existing figures and tables are retained; the cost plot and short-context table move, and the cost-plot caption expands. The overall visual style remains consistent.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Michelangelo and HELMET and supplements its positioning with direct comparisons against previously discussed long-context alignment methods. The related-work taxonomy, discussion in Section 2, and central novelty positioning remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, and derivations remain unchanged. Section 5.5 adds a three-sigma motivation for the existing choice of sigma = 0.5/3; it does not establish a new theoretical result, proof, or guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens comparative credibility and generalization evidence by adding direct long-context alignment comparisons and evaluations beyond the original QA-focused suite. The sensitivity and judge-substitution controls also make central design choices more assessable. These address important gaps in v1's empirical support. Some new superiority and noise-suppression interpretations exceed the demonstrated evidence, and additional benchmark protocols remain briefly documented, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SPELL. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds hyperparameter experiments, judge comparisons, additional benchmarks, alignment baselines, and training-dynamics analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across 12 models, component ablations, training analyses, and short-context benchmark results in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions qualify arbitrary-loss generality by distinguishing exact likelihood-style equivalence from induced non-likelihood surrogates whose objectives may differ. Reliability recovery is explicitly restricted to the population/full-batch setting under perfect calibration. These materially narrow two central theoretical claims; the up-to-7-point empirical improvement claim remains.

C2.justification: Sections 3–4 clarify the surrogate interpretation and population-versus-finite-sample boundary. Direct likelihood optimization changes from 'intractable' to feasible but coupled and non-convex. Appendix H attributes apparent speedups to system variance instead of seed/padding variance. The existing miscalibration failure limitation remains.

D1.justification: V4 adds a project-page link in the abstract and a reproducibility statement identifying a public code repository. V3's resource appendix provided model and dataset links only. Existing experimental implementation and hardware disclosures remain unchanged; repository contents are not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same UltraFeedback-derived datasets and MultiPref, evaluate on AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard, and retain the same synthetic-noise scenarios and qualitative task examples.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains standard DPO, IPO, SimPO, CPO, their label-smoothing variants, base models, rDPO, and Hölder-DPO. Tables 3 and 7 retain DPO versus RE-DPO. Corrections from 'HöldeRE-DPO' and 'R-DPO' in prose do not change comparator membership.

E3.justification: The backbones, single-annotator and MultiPref settings, evaluation metrics, hyperparameter sweeps, synthetic-noise procedures, alternative judge, and controlled runtime protocol remain unchanged. The population-level theorem revision does not revise the experimental protocol.

E4.justification: Both retain Table 4's sensitivity study, Figure 2's noise experiments, Figure 3's annotator histograms, Tables 5–6's low-confidence examples, Appendix G's judge comparison, and Appendix H's runtime analysis. No analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: Appendix H and Table 8 retain means and standard deviations over three seeds/runs. Figure 3 retains distribution means and standard deviations across 227 annotators. No repeated-run information or uncertainty-reporting procedure changes.

E6.justification: The measured results in Tables 2–8 and Figures 2–3 are unchanged. Appendix H corrects the numerical finding that all overheads are within roughly 20%, reporting SimPO overhead of about 32–40% instead. This matches the retained base/RE-PO times of 5383/7557 and 5384.2/7117 seconds.

M1.justification: Table 1, Equations (1)–(7), and Algorithm 1 retain the same preference probabilities, posterior weighting, policy objective, and EMA reliability updates. The new induced-surrogate qualifications explain the existing construction without changing its procedure.

P1.justification: V4 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, contributions, methodological explanations, proof, and conclusion, and corrects method-name inconsistencies. It adds a reproducibility statement and Appendix J on editorial LLM use, and updates author information. The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact.

P2.justification: V4 adopts ICLR title and running-header formatting, restyles headings and table spacing, and reflows existing content. Figure 1 changes 'RPO Loss' to 'Robust Loss'. All three figures and eight tables remain, with the same empirical plots and comparison structures.

R1.justification: The cited works and Section 2's substantive positioning remain the same, including connections to Dawid–Skene and Crowd-BT and comparisons with robust losses and data filtering. Citation-style changes and removal of generic novelty wording do not establish changed research positioning.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix D replace the finite-dataset update operator and likelihood with population expectations, revise the nondegeneracy assumption, and establish the fixed point through total expectation. This substantially changes the convergence guarantee and removes v3's unjustified equality between a finite empirical average and its population expectation.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses an important validity problem in the central theorem: v3 claims finite-dataset recovery using an invalid empirical-average equality, whereas v4 formulates the argument at population level and uses total expectation. The guarantee becomes narrower but substantially more defensible. Clarifying non-likelihood surrogates and correcting the runtime overstatement further improve consistency between claims and evidence, while retaining the empirical results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RE-PO work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Appendices A–I are present in both; v4 adds Appendix J. No material gaps prevent comparison.

after.justification: V4 retains original experimental results, including AlpacaEval 2 comparisons, MultiPref evaluations, reliability-estimation experiments, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: V3 reports original alignment evaluations, synthetic-noise experiments, hyperparameter studies, annotator analyses, qualitative examples, and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendices E–H.

C1.justification: The simulator and benchmark contributions remain, but the headline empirical message changes substantially. v1 emphasizes GPT-4.1's leading 54% overall success and general capability deficits. v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion distinguish lightweight, standard, and reasoning models and introduce performance versus latency as a central deployment trade-off.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning framework versus model limitations, limited self-correction, memorization, and deployment latency. Appendix G explicitly qualifies oracle-assisted recovery as optimistic. Appendix I attributes part of GPT-4.1's QT2-F weakness to transition timing, qualifying the intent-inference interpretation. Appendices J and K discuss future pre-validation and richer environmental interactions.

D1.justification: Appendix N replaces a model-name paragraph with exact API endpoint identifiers.
