Other additions document tool arguments, user-simulator models, and construction of the 204 training trajectories. These improve implementation specificity, although training hyperparameters remain unreported. The promise to release code and data upon publication is unchanged.

E1.justification: The main benchmark retains 600 episodes and the same twelve query types. Appendices F and G extend existing QT2-F and QT4-F tasks to simulated user clarification, corrective dialogue, and explicit post-execution failure feedback. The additional fine-tuning episodes reuse existing query coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains all eleven original models and adds Llama3.2-1B-it, Llama3.2-3B-it, Gemma3-4B-it, Gemini2.5-Pro, and GPT-5.1, substantially extending comparisons to lightweight and reasoning models. Section 5.2.4 also evaluates HiAgent against ReAct, and Table 13 compares fine-tuned and untuned Gemma3-4B-it.

E3.justification: New protocols include episode-completion-time measurement, callback-triggered self-review, simulated-user feedback, and recovery evaluation on initially failed episodes. Appendix H introduces training on 204 gold trajectories from separate generated episodes; Appendix I tests a three-second scoring delay. These are additional experimental settings, not evidence that the retained main-table experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained error taxonomy and tool-feedback analysis, v2 tests framework dependence with HiAgent, autonomous self-review, clarification and correction dialogues, oracle failure notices, memorization through fine-tuning, and sensitivity to delayed state checking. These analyses directly investigate alternative explanations for benchmark failures.

E5.justification: Both versions report three judge calls per case, seeded episode generation, and the same annotation-agreement and judge-validation statistics. v2 adds no repeated-agent-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original eleven Table 1 rows and GPT-4.1 error counts are unchanged, but substantial results are added. GPT-5.1 reaches 100% on QT4-1-IF; HiAgent obtains 40%, 52%, and 40% on QT4 feasible tasks. New latency, dialogue, recovery, and fine-tuning results appear. Appendix I reports 62% versus 44% for GPT-4.1 QT2-F when scoring is delayed three seconds, a changed-condition result.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 expands the reported agent interface from 13 to 17 tools. Appendix B adds environmental-control-rule retrieval, user questions, workflow cancellation, and workflow-status inspection. The core simulator dynamics and ReAct prompt remain unchanged; Appendix J's simulation-based pre-validation architecture is a future proposal.

P1.justification: The results narrative is rewritten from query-by-query discussion into model-capability groups. Evaluation methods move into benchmark design, and analysis becomes part of experiments. The appendix is extensively reorganized into A–Q, grouping error analyses and prompts, while the abstract and conclusion are rewritten around the new empirical narrative.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains model-category divisions; v2 adds the HiAgent figure and latency, self-review, oracle-recovery, and fine-tuning tables. Appendix tables and prompt listings undergo extensive font, spacing, and multipage-layout changes. The original QT3 error-distribution figure is retained as Figure 7 with changed placement and size.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Llama 3, GPT-5.1, and HiAgent, including a substantive comparison with HiAgent. The related-work section and positioning against household simulators and smart-home benchmarks are otherwise retained. Updated metadata for existing model references does not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation in Section 3.3 and additive Aggregator equation remain unchanged, with the latter moving from Appendix A.12 to Appendix P. The new discussions of pre-validation and environmental interactions introduce no formal definitions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's failure interpretations relied largely on one framework and descriptive error analysis. v2 directly tests framework choice, feedback availability, training, and scoring time, substantially improving the evidence available to assess benchmark validity. Reasoning-model and latency comparisons also strengthen deployment relevance. Sparse experimental settings and broad causal and memorization conclusions remain weaknesses, but the new controls and disclosed scoring-time confound provide substantial diagnostic gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SimuHome simulator and benchmark. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the substantial appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds model evaluations, latency measurements, planning and feedback experiments, fine-tuning results, and scoring-time sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 11 agents on 600 episodes, error analyses, and human validation of LLM judging.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims: a bi-Lipschitz functional representation, its existence and biological analogues, training-free extraction, relationship detection and phylogenetic reconstruction. The new experiments primarily support these existing contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning input and encoder robustness, template fairness, fine-tuning effects and model-size independence. Appendices D–E substantially expand applicability and limitations, including governance, risk tracing, adaptive attacks, contamination and uninterpreted DNA subsequences. Appendix C.7 also qualifies the comparison with PhyloLM's intended tasks.

D1.justification: v2 adds source-code, interactive-demo and PyPI access/install information, alongside specifications for the new experiments. Model-size documentation is extensively revised: for example, Mixtral-8x7B changes from 7.0B to 47B, and previously unknown Flan-T5 sizes are supplied. These are documented changes, not independently verified corrections.

E1.justification: v2 adds synthetic random-word inputs, mathematical fine-tuning using OpenMathInstruct-2, and relationship evaluation restricted to models sharing Qwen2Tokenizer. These substantially extend the tested conditions beyond the retained six extraction benchmarks, routing dataset and 305-model roster.

E2.justification: v1 compares relationship detection only against Random and Greedy. v2 adds PhyloLM distance signatures with an RBF-SVM in Table 1 and evaluates its same-tokenizer variant in Appendix C.7, introducing a directly relevant research comparator. The routing comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds accuracy reporting, alternative encoder configurations, template controls, embedding/DNA dimension sweeps, and full-parameter fine-tuning with 10–10,000 examples. New encoder-distance analyses sample 10,000 pairs. The model inventory also substantially revises reported parameter sizes, without establishing that model identities changed or existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Sections 5.5–5.7 and Appendices C.3–C.7 add tests of random-input robustness, chat templates, fine-tuning intensity, encoder choice, embedding dimension, DNA dimension, model-size bias and shared-tokenizer performance. The earlier dataset-stability test, phylogenetic analysis and false-positive case study are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed means and standard deviations; no increased run count is documented. v2 adds Spearman-based encoder-distance comparisons and point-biserial correlation plus logistic-regression significance testing for model-size effects.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises existing scores: Qwen3-based DNA AUC changes from 0.957 ± 0.044 to 0.979 ± 0.027, while the newly evaluated BGE variant reports 0.992 ± 0.023. Random and Greedy scores also change. New robustness and fine-tuning results substantially expand the evidence; Table 2 routing scores remain identical.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same response generation, sentence embedding, concatenation and Gaussian projection procedure. RepTrace is a new name for the existing pipeline; alternative encoders and template settings are evaluated as ablations rather than introduced as a revised method.

P1.justification: v2 consolidates definition and existence into one section, moves inheritance/determinism and Hilbert-space development into Appendix A, and reorganizes the appendices, including a separate model-details section. Related-work and experimental narratives are substantially expanded, and the extraction pipeline receives the name RepTrace.

P2.justification: v2 adds a fine-tuning heatmap, encoder-distance plots, two dimension-sensitivity figures and four result tables. Table 1 gains an accuracy column and additional method rows. Existing displays are reflowed; the earlier phylogenetic figures are retained as Figures 6–7 rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning around PhyloLM, explaining its tokenizer-dependent distances and contrasting them with sentence-level DNA representations. It replaces v1's assertion that no existing method reliably handles the heterogeneous comparison. Related work also expands to HybridLLM and MetaLLM, with additional literature supporting the broader-impact discussion.

T1.justification: v2 introduces Definition A.1, formally defining evolution as an operation bounded in Hilbert distance. The existing DNA definition, inheritance and determinism theorems, existence argument, projection corollary and concentration proof are otherwise retained through relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: The PhyloLM comparisons and systematic extraction controls address important weaknesses in v1's baseline coverage and largely untested configuration choices. Access information and explicit limitations further strengthen the paper. Some new interpretations overreach: Section 5.7 claims monotonic growth although Figure 5 falls from 0.7860 to 0.7001 between 100 and 1,000 examples, and Appendix C.6 treats nonsignificance as proof of independence. These weaken particular conclusions, but the overall validation is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM DNA work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, controlled fine-tuning experiments and extensive robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original relationship-detection, model-routing, distance-correlation and phylogenetic results involving 305 LLMs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contribution: constraining key and residual vectors to edit-relevant subspaces improves knowledge preservation while maintaining edit efficacy and general capabilities. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses the weakness of gold-referenced zsRE scores and the leniency of references reset before each batch. Appendix J qualifies the subspace interpretation: both subspaces respond to entity identity, but the entity-specific space responds more strongly. New discussions also address threshold transfer, sampling-cost tradeoffs, larger-model applicability, and ripple effects.

D1.justification: Appendix I supplies a previously absent account of precomputation resources: NVIDIA A100 80GB PCIe hardware, separate key-vector and SVD timings, peak memory across subject counts, and reuse of cached factors per model and layer. v2 also documents threshold selection and controlled-analysis procedures. These are documentation additions; code and data release remains promised upon publication.

E1.justification: Appendix F.7 adds RippleEdits POPULAR, testing propagation to logically and compositionally implied facts, subject aliases, and preservation after individual edits. This substantially extends task coverage beyond direct factual editing, contextual robustness, and general-capability benchmarks retained from v1.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Table 1 and the extended CounterFact comparisons remain unchanged. Added larger-model and RippleEdits experiments reuse MEMIT and AlphaEdit, already evaluated against SUIT; no comparator is removed from a retained comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix E.2 revises the stated zsRE reference from the pre-edit model to immediately before each batch, without establishing that experiments were rerun. New protocols include preservation of the original answer's first 1–4 tokens after all edits, LLaMA2-13B with 500 edits, 100 individual RippleEdits edits, additional models for spectral analysis, and controlled subject-count and entity/context experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds zsRE metric diagnostics and stricter preservation tests, RippleEdits robustness evaluation, spectral comparisons across models, sensitivity to the number of subjects used for SVD, and controlled entity-versus-context interventions. These substantially expand validation beyond the retained component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps, perturbation measurements, and heatmaps.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new sample averages, layer averages, and distance contrasts extend the analyses without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises the Qwen zsRE results: SUIT's S changes from 88.2 to 89.3 and specificity from 96.6 to 81.7; AlphaEdit's S changes from 89.6 to 73.9, reversing their S ranking. These revisions do not establish gains under identical settings. New tables report stricter preservation, larger-model, RippleEdits, cost, and subspace results; Table 5 also adds S scores.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the SVD-based key projection, two-direction residual update, directional penalty, and AlphaEdit-based weight update. Additional tuning explanations and precomputation details do not establish a changed editing algorithm.

P1.justification: Changes include localized rewrites of Section 6.3, expanded dataset and metric explanations, standardized model names, and a corrected weight-decay parameter label. New appendix subsections organize the additions, while the main narrative and section order remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds dedicated zsRE, larger-model, RippleEdits, and cost/subspace tables, plus a twenty-panel spectral figure. Table 1 shades the S columns and Table 5 gains an S column. Existing plots and the five heatmap examples are retained, with some relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for RippleEdits, LLaMA 2, and the Kneedle algorithm, and explicitly critiques prior zsRE specificity evaluation. The main related-work section and SUIT's positioning within knowledge-editing and linear-representation research remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix J introduces mathematical definitions for within-entity and between-entity distances, norm-normalized distances, and entity-effect contrasts. These are limited formal additions for the new analysis; the editing mathematics, assumptions, and derivations in Appendices A–C remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central preservation and subspace claims. Compared with v1's first-token zsRE reporting and variance comparisons, it provides stricter preservation tests and controlled entity/context interventions, alongside practical cost measurements and broader evaluation. These gains outweigh a localized reporting defect: Section 5.2 still claims the highest Qwen specificity at 96.6%, although the revised Table 1 reports SUIT at 81.7% and FT-L at 89.7%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SUIT research work. Text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, including the heatmap examples. Added material can be distinguished reliably from relocated or renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds preservation tests, RippleEdits results, larger-model evaluation, and further subspace and computation-cost analyses.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and the appendices report original knowledge-editing experiments, capability evaluations, ablations, and subspace analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statement and conclusion retain the same central claims: network-dependent canonicalization, continuity, symmetry preservation, universal approximation and superior classification performance. Additional applications and supporting experiments do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning spectral normalization, band selection, backbone robustness, crop selection and stabilization of canonical poses, plus an argument about specialization versus separately learned canonicalizers. G.10 explicitly leaves continuity of the entropy-based segmentation variant unresolved. The earlier regression and per-class optimization-cost limitations remain.

D1.justification: The rewritten tutorial adds pseudocode, explicit candidate counts of 32 for graphs and 50 for point clouds, projection/Riemannian refinement options, and fuller spectral and cropping instructions. New experiments disclose frozen-backbone training and runtime/parameter information. Conversely, v1's explicit instruction against differentiating through refinement and its node-level construction equation are omitted; Appendix F's existing hardware and hyperparameter details remain.

E1.justification: V2 adds natural-image classification on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and point-level part segmentation on ShapeNet, extending both domain and prediction-task coverage. The original toy, TUDataset, OGB and ModelNet40 evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original benchmark tables is retained. New comparisons introduce unmodified PointNet++ and RSCNN alongside their adaptive variants in Table 10, and a vanilla pretrained ResNet-18 control in Table 11. Reusing existing point-cloud comparators on ShapeNet is chiefly a coverage extension.

E3.justification: Original Appendix F protocols remain, while v2 adds frozen-backbone classifier training on CIFAR, category-mean-IoU segmentation evaluation, controlled sensitivity sweeps and consecutive-epoch rotation measurements on 1,500 training examples. Its spectral implementation also replaces the previously stated maximum-eigenvalue-scaled dyadic bands with boundaries anchored at 2. This reported setting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retained G.1–G.3 analyses, v2 tests uniform versus dyadic bands, alternative graph shift operators and additional point-cloud backbones. It adds hyperparameter sensitivity, runtime/parameter comparisons, canonical-rotation stability and a visualization of 20 canonicalized chairs (G.4–G.9), substantially expanding investigation of design choices and behavior.

E5.justification: Table 3 newly supplies ± uncertainties for augmentation, canonicalization and adaptive-canonicalization rows that previously had point estimates only. G.6 specifies ten independent CIFAR runs. The existing TUDataset ten-split reporting practice remains; increased run counts for retained ModelNet40 results are not documented.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2 and 5–7 retain their results. Table 3 revises AC-PointNet from 81.3 to 81.1, AC-DGCNN from 91.7 to 91.6, and augmentation baselines from 76.4/89.3 to 75.8/89.0 under the retained stated protocol. Tables 8–13 and Figures 2–4 add substantial new findings, including CIFAR gains and mixed segmentation performance: AC-DGCNN scores 80.9 versus VN-DGCNN's 81.4.

M1.justification: The original prior-maximization framework remains, but v2 adds crop-and-resize canonicalization (E.5) and a segmentation variant that selects transformations by minimizing entropy summed over points (G.10). The spectral implementation is also reported with Jk-dimensional rotations after padding, versus Mk-dimensional rotations before padding in v1. These are substantive procedural extensions beyond expanded explanations of the existing search.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes and rewrites the supporting narrative: it adds a main related-work section, subdivides Appendix A's comparisons, and rebuilds Appendix E as a practitioner tutorial with consolidated classification and optimization explanations. It removes the appendix roadmap and shortens G.2, while largely preserving the main theoretical exposition.

P2.justification: V2 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 8–13 and Figures 2–4, introducing sensitivity plots, a training-stability curve and canonicalized point-cloud examples. Table 3 gains a provenance caption and source markers, and existing tables are relocated or reflowed. The original framework schematic remains.

R1.justification: A new main-text related-work section and expanded Appendix A substantially develop comparisons with energy-based canonicalization, weighted canonicalization/frame averaging and test-time transformation search. Newly discussed works include Shumaylov et al., Schmidt and Stober, and Basu et al. V2 also adds cognitive-psychology positioning while elaborating distinctions from previously cited Kaba and Dym.

T1.justification: The principal continuity, symmetry and universal-approximation theorems and proofs remain unchanged. V2 adds auxiliary volume-retaining assumptions and a cited concentration inequality (Definition 21, Lemma 22), an epsilon-plus-search-error approximation argument, and a formal continuity check for truncation. V1's Appendix D automorphism derivation is removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support that v1 lacked: G.4–G.9 examine design choices, sensitivity, computational cost and canonicalization behavior. Broader task evaluations, newly reported uncertainty and fuller implementation and related-work discussion improve assessment of generality and reproducibility. Some implementation details are lost, and segmentation continuity remains unresolved, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive canonicalization framework and retain identifiable matching methods, theorems and experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds ablations, CIFAR classification, ShapeNet segmentation, computational measurements and stability analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original graph and point-cloud classification results in Tables 1–3, with additional implementation comparisons and rotation-generalization experiments in Appendix G.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions and claims about unsupervised semantic-aware and visibility-aware UV parameterization. The added evaluations support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v2 expands v1's brief assurances of minor geometric degradation into explicit discussion of distortion-versus-perception tradeoffs, partitioning effects, and the greater equiareality loss of global visibility optimization. Appendix A.3 adds qualifications about segmentation-dependent outcomes and substantial training overhead, alongside proposed computational remedies.

D1.justification: v2 newly reports total and per-iteration training times, explicitly distinguishes per-mesh training from inference, and discloses sequential per-part execution and inspection of 3–5 neighbors during seam detection. Existing architecture specifications and the code-access statement remain unchanged; hardware and detailed training budgets remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 adds human perceptual evaluation with 115 participants, comprising 45 industry experts and 70 general participants. This introduces population-based assessment of semantic alignment and seam visibility beyond v1's mesh metrics and qualitative renderings.

E2.justification: PartField joins ShDF and SAMesh in the partitioning comparison, and a new packing comparison evaluates Maya, Blender, and Houdini (Tables 5–6). The existing headline UV-parameterization comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The new user study specifies 11 comparisons per participant: five semantic and six visibility questions, with separate expert/general reporting. Appendix A.3 also introduces a controlled seven-chart cow packing comparison using texel density and UV-space utilization, plus total and per-iteration training-time measurements. These supplement the retained evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands supplementary analysis through packing-efficiency comparisons, PartField partitioning ablations, and computational-cost analysis identifying seam extraction as the main visibility-training bottleneck. The original semantic/visibility-objective ablation is retained as Table 7; its expanded discussion does not represent new measurements.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty estimates. The added preference percentages and timing averages provide new descriptive results without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The existing headline scores remain unchanged: v1 Tables 1–2 become v2 Tables 1 and 3. New results include expert preferences of 93.70% for visibility-aware and 80.22% for semantic-aware outputs, PartField conformality/equiareality of 0.8999/0.6921, packing-efficiency measurements, and training-time comparisons. These are additional results, not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds evaluated pipeline variants using PartField partitioning and Maya, Blender, or Houdini packing in place of existing components. These are optional adaptations; the default ShDF/grid pipeline, neural architecture, and training losses remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 introduces qualitative/quantitative subsections within Section 4, expands seam-detection explanations and Appendix A.3 discussion, and removes the acknowledgments. These are localized structural and prose revisions; the overall organization and most foundational exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds preference and training-time tables, a packing table and visualization, and a questionnaire figure. The partitioning figures expand to include PartField rows and revised captions. Most earlier figures are retained unchanged, including those relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to PartField and Houdini for the new comparisons. Section 3.2 also explicitly disclaims backbone novelty and locates the contribution in integrating semantic and visibility objectives, clarifying the attribution already present in v1.

T1.justification: Around Eq. 7, v2 corrects the contradictory local AO convention and loss reasoning: zero denotes occlusion and one exposure, so high-AO seams increase the loss. This aligns the reasoning with the existing Eq. 4 definition. The equations and remaining mathematical development are retained.

improvement.justification: The user study supplies direct human evidence for perceptual benefits that v1 supported through proxy metrics and renderings. Correcting the AO contradiction and documenting distortion and training-cost tradeoffs also materially improve correctness and transparency. Missing uncertainty estimates and incomplete timing controls limit the new evidence, but the gains in validation and practical understanding are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same framework. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these experiments and adds original user-study, packing, partitioning, and training-time results.

before.justification: v1 reports original mesh-parameterization experiments, quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–2, and ablations in Appendix A.3.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain unchanged. The introduction and conclusion narrow the reported accuracy-gain range from 2.36%-10.37% to 1.74%-8.89%; the conclusion also revises HV improvements over LQ-LoRA from 3%-8% to 2%-7%.

C2.justification: New discussion attributes guided search's advantage to candidate quality after comparison with random extension. Added integer, larger-model and rank results are interpreted as broader applicability and low-bit stability. The rationale for NormalFloat changes from blockwise expressiveness to preservation of small-magnitude weights.

D1.justification: New Appendix A.1 specifies seven 8-dimensional embeddings, a two-layer MLP with hidden dimension 128, LayerNorm, SiLU, learnable output scaling and parameter counts. v2 also clarifies configuration-specific SVD construction, discloses layerwise baseline configuration assignment, provides explicit bit accounting and adds an implementation-repository link. These substantially improve documentation of previously unspecified implementation choices.

E1.justification: C4, the four GLUE tasks and the seven zero-shot tasks displayed in Table C.3 are retained. Added backbone sizes, ranks and integer quantization change model settings rather than represented data or task requirements.

E2.justification: Figure 8 adds a random-extension comparator to the existing search/no-search ablation. QLoRA, LQ-LoRA, GPTQ-LoRA and Shared-LoRA remain in their corresponding comparisons; Q-LoRA becoming QLoRA is a naming change.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 extends the stated baseline evaluation grid to include 6 bits, while Table 2 changes baseline solution counts from four to six. Added protocols include integer mixed precision, LLaMA-2-13B at rank 64, additional LLaMA-2-7B ranks and ten randomly added configurations per epoch. However, v2 inconsistently lists five baseline budgets, reports six solutions and retains a four-budget accuracy-gap description.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands the diagnostic evidence: guided search versus random extension, integer-quantization robustness, LLaMA-2-7B rank sensitivity, adapter-similarity analyses across ranks and decoder backbones, and configuration-set size trajectories. Existing unseen-configuration and segment-count analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The additional correlation heatmaps measure adapter similarity, rather than statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises accuracy gaps, HV and baseline runtimes: Shared-LoRA's QNLI HV changes from 0.45 to 0.60 and its gap from -15.93% to +2.90%. Expanded baseline budgets prevent treating these summaries as established same-setting gains. Table C.2 changes GPTQ-LoRA's Qwen2.5-1.5B HV from 0.535 to 0.427, reversing its ranking against CoA-LoRA's unchanged 0.479. Integer-quantization, 13B-model and additional rank results are added; Tables 3 and C.3 retain their values.

M1.justification: Both versions use configuration-conditioned r×r LoRA adjustments, the expected task-loss objective and alternating GP search with segmented Pareto filtering. v2 documents mapper internals and configuration-specific SVD factors; residual SVD already appears in v1 Appendix A.1. These disclosures do not establish an underlying algorithm change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained. Changes include localized NormalFloat explanations, clearer C/Q terminology, baseline-name standardization, additional related-work and appendix subsections, and publication-header, corresponding-author and acknowledgment additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4, A.1, C.4 and C.5, expands the similarity heatmaps, adds a configuration-size plot and introduces a third curve in Figure 8. Figures 2-3 are redrawn or relabeled, plot axes are clarified as average bits, and numerous displays are relocated. Existing zero-shot and RoBERTa rank results remain identifiable.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 substantially expands positioning against parameter and LoRA generation, discussing P-diff, G.pt, CONDP-DIFF, ICM-LoRA and LoRA-Gen and their reliance on trained parameters or expert adapters. The quantization discussion and citations are also revised, including LowRA; the GPT3.int8 and SmoothQuant references are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 9 swaps the arguments of the nondominance predicate, and Appendix Equation 11 revises the storage constraint into average-bit units. These are localized formal revisions without new theorems or proofs. Algorithm 1 retains the earlier predicate ordering, so the Equation 9 revision is not consistently propagated.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves the central mapper architecture largely unspecified and compares configuration search only with no search. v2 supplies concrete implementation details and tests guided search against random expansion, substantially strengthening reproducibility and evidence for the central mechanism. Integer-quantization and larger-model/rank tests further support applicability. Inconsistent baseline bit counts and incomplete propagation of the Pareto correction limit some comparisons, but the implementation and experimental gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoA-LoRA work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, despite some internal reporting inconsistencies.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds random-extension comparisons, integer-quantization experiments and further model-size and rank evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original GLUE accuracy and training-time measurements, C4 perplexity, zero-shot evaluations and ablation results.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the claimed demonstrated applicability to general-chat distillation with Qwen2.5 and Gemma2, including a 9B teacher. The central claims concerning shift invariance, linear-time computation, flexible weighting, and fidelity–diversity trade-offs remain intact.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly reports and interprets CSD(S,S) failure under limited-data task-specific distillation, motivating teacher–student weighting through calibration. It adds explanations linking uniform weighting to minority-vocabulary learning and high-temperature performance, and explains adaptive weighting behavior. Sections 3.2 and 4.4 also qualify Monte Carlo's convergence disadvantage and discuss its broader modeling flexibility.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository link, explicit Monte Carlo pseudocode in Algorithm 2, and general-chat implementation information. Table 9 newly documents profiling configurations, including sequence limits, LoRA use, microbatch/accumulation settings, A100 hardware, and resource costs. The original code snippet and existing training details are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds general-chat distillation using 50,000 UltraChat prompts and evaluation on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval (Sections 4.3 and C.3). The existing instruction-following, dialogue summarization, low-resource translation, and arithmetic-reasoning coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds DLD comparators within the retained on-policy and task-specific experiments, including centered and standardized variants (Tables 2, 3, 5, and 10). It newly evaluates DPKD and DistiLLM-2 in Table 4 and extends the probability-loss comparison to weighted KL, TV, and SRKL in Table 8.

E3.justification: New protocols include Qwen2.5-7B-to-1.5B and Gemma2-9B-to-2B distillation using teacher/student-generated responses, GPT-4/GPT-4-Turbo judging, and AlpacaEval win rates against text-davinci-003. V2 also introduces calibration measurements and a separately specified single-A100 efficiency comparison. Existing Dolly and task-specific settings are largely retained and relocated into Appendix C.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's weighting, decoding-temperature, offset, and Monte Carlo analyses, v2 tests normalized DLD variants and weighting-temperature sensitivity. It adds calibration comparisons, offset dynamics during training, adaptive weighting, gradient-coefficient entropy, and a DLD generation-failure example (Section 4.4 and Appendix D).

E5.justification: V2 adds standard deviations to existing weighting-ablation results in Tables 5 and 8, corresponding to v1 Tables 4 and 6. Both versions already specify the same five evaluation seeds; the additional uncertainty reporting does not establish an increase in training runs.

E6.justification: Many chat, calibration, efficiency, and ablation results are added, while retained scores in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged. New DistiLLM+DLD achieves 17.69 on GPT-2-0.1B Vicuna Eval versus the best CSD score of 17.18, changing the expanded comparison's winner. Table 4 reports Qwen MT-Bench/GPT-4 scores of 7.69 for CSD(S,S) versus 7.28 for DistiLLM-2. Probability-L2 U/S result assignments also swap: their averages change from 11.35/11.13 in v1 Table 6 to 11.13/11.35 in v2 Table 8.

M1.justification: The core pairwise logit objective, analytic gradient procedure, and reference implementation remain unchanged. Appendix D.2 introduces tested adaptive weighting variants: geometric interpolation between student and teacher probabilities controlled by two epoch schedules or a token-specific entropy rule.

P1.justification: Existing experimental setup and evaluation descriptions are consolidated into Appendix C.1–C.2, with shorter main-text summaries. Related work and supplementary analyses gain subheadings; the abstract is edited, and conference headers and acknowledgments are added. Most introduction, method, and conclusion prose is retained.

P2.justification: Several comparison tables are substantially expanded, and new chat, calibration, efficiency, and task-specific tables are added. Figure 5 becomes a three-panel display; v1's two-panel offset Figure 8 becomes v2's four-panel Figure 9. New Figures 10–13 present additional analyses, while v1's training-curve Figure 9 is retained as v2 Figure 8.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds AMid and a subsection distinguishing CSD from BPO's sequence-level preference matching and ARD's diffusion-to-autoregressive distillation. References also add logit standardization and works supporting the new chat experiments. The original positioning as a logit-level alternative to f-divergence objectives remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds mathematical definitions of normalized DLD variants and Remark 4's weighted-centering equivalence argument. Appendix A.5 newly derives how weighted KL changes the target distribution. Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 replace the sufficient-capacity wording with an explicit infinite-capacity assumption; their underlying proofs are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: The added shift-aware DLD controls, Qwen2.5/Gemma2 chat evaluations, and disclosure of CSD(S,S) failure substantially strengthen empirical assessment and guidance on weighting choices. Mechanism analyses and reproducibility information address important gaps in v1. These gains outweigh localized inconsistencies: Table 2 no longer supports the retained claim of winning every benchmark, and Remark 4's exact gradient equality misses a factor of two under Equation 8's normalization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Concrete Score Distillation work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and expanded material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds general-chat evaluations, calibration and gradient analyses, adaptive-weighting experiments, and computational resource measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original teacher–student distillation experiments, instruction-following and task-specific results, weighting ablations, and generation examples in Section 4 and Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract and central contributions remain the same. The introduction narrows the novelty framing by acknowledging existing probe-to-LLM cascades, replacing v1's suggestion that dynamic computation had yet to bring comparable flexibility to safety monitoring.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of transfer errors through differing harm policies, qualifications about untuned external monitors and speculative model sizes, and explanations of layer-selection sensitivity. The conclusion newly acknowledges nonmonotonic performance with additional compute and the need for layer search, while retaining the earlier small-data and interpretability limitations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the external-monitor system prompt and model access references, transfer-dataset selection details, and an explicit shared classification threshold of 0.5. The original code link, training grids, optimizer, hardware and epoch budgets remain; the new reproducibility statement mostly points to existing information.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained WildGuardMix and BeaverTails evaluations, v3 tests WildGuardMix-trained monitors on HarmBench, ToxicChat and OpenAI-moderation (Appendix F.2). These introduce substantial coverage of different textual styles, class distributions and harm-labeling policies.

E2.justification: v1 compares TPCs with linear, bilinear, MLP and early-exit MLP probes. v3 retains these comparisons and adds evaluated external monitors: gpt-4o-mini, claude-3-haiku, o3-mini, Llama-Guard-3-8B and shieldgemma-2b (Table 4).

E3.justification: The original splits and degree-5, rank-64 setup remain. Added protocols include cross-dataset testing with accuracy, precision, recall and false rejection rate; prompted external-monitor evaluation; and six-layer sweeps on Llama-3.2-1B/3B and Llama-3.1-8B. Table 1 also introduces a validation-selected layer summary of existing results, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix F.2 adds distribution-shift tests and selected false-positive cases examining incompatible harm-labeling policies. Appendix F.4 adds systematic model-size and layer sensitivity analyses. The original calibration, progressive-training, latency, rank, maximum-degree and symmetry analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-seed averages for the main comparisons and seed-0 cascade experiments. The added layer sweeps follow the existing five-seed averaging practice; no new statistical uncertainty estimation, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: The original plotted results and ablations are retained, while Tables 3–7 add substantial transfer, external-monitor and layer-wise results. For example, ToxicChat F1 is 57.66 for fifth-order TPC, 52.97 for EE-MLP and 46.27 for the linear probe. These are newly reported evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1; Table 1 summarizes existing full-depth results.

M1.justification: The mean-pooled inputs, polynomial architecture, symmetric CP factorization, progressive training loss and cascading algorithm remain unchanged. The corrected confidence-condition prose agrees with the already-correct Algorithm 1 in v1; input-driven terminology and transposed matrix conventions do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are retained. Local revisions clarify input-level monitoring, correct the cascade explanation and harmonize notation. v3 separates static and dynamic results discussion and adds ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage disclosures, alongside the new appendix subsections.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the result displays with the main-text static summary (Table 1), transfer table and plots (Table 3/Figure 7), external-monitor comparison (Table 4), and layer-sweep Tables 5–7. It also adds boxed examples and a system prompt. Earlier figures are largely retained and renumbered rather than replaced.

R1.justification: A new Cascades & ensembles discussion substantially expands positioning, especially relative to McKenzie, Cunningham and Hua and earlier cascade literature. It distinguishes TPCs from probe-to-external-LLM pipelines and explains their possible complementarity. References also expand to support the new datasets and monitor comparisons.

T1.justification: The polynomial definitions, progressive loss, feature-attribution derivation and parameter/FLOP analyses remain mathematically equivalent. Factor-matrix transpositions and corresponding index changes revise notation; no substantive theory, assumption or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the paper by addressing v1's limited evidence about cross-dataset transfer and layer selection, while correcting an important gap in positioning against existing monitoring cascades. The new analyses expose labeling-policy mismatch and layer sensitivity, and the expanded limitations better qualify applicability. External-LLM comparisons carry less weight because tuning is unmatched and some parameter counts are speculative, but the broader evidence and clearer boundaries provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same truncated polynomial classifier (TPC) research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds cross-dataset evaluations, external LLM monitor comparisons and model-family layer sweeps.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on WildGuardMix and BeaverTails, cascade evaluations, feature attribution and multiple training and computational ablations.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain DiVeQ, SF-DiVeQ, and improved codebook replacement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the empirical performance claim to DAC-based speech coding. The introduction and Table 1 soften the claim of no hyperparameter tuning to avoiding complicated tuning, and the conclusion drops the blanket tuning claim.

C2.justification: v1 recommends custom SF-DiVeQ initialization; v2 adds substantive explanations of its benefits and limitations, including worse performance with random initialization at larger codebooks and recovery through higher codebook learning rates. Sections C.6–C.7 interpret replacement and convergence effects. Section 4 also limits t-SNE interpretation to intuitive within-method visualization and explains the deliberately simplified speech evaluation.

D1.justification: New Section A.3 documents the speech codec architecture, single codebook, 512-dimensional quantization space, optimizer settings, and VCTK preprocessing, including 16 kHz resampling. v2 adds detailed initialization experiments, explicit SF-DiVeQ inference instructions, a project code URL, and a reproducibility statement describing implementation materials. Existing vision implementation details are largely retained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image compression and generation on five image datasets. v2 retains that coverage and adds speech coding on CSTR VCTK, covering English speech from 109 speakers with different accents using a simplified DAC-based codec (Sections 4 and A.3). This introduces a substantially different modality and task.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain STE, EMA, RT, ST-GS, and NSVQ. The residual quantization comparisons retain their narrower STE, RT, and NSVQ comparator set. The added speech and robustness experiments introduce no new baseline method.

E3.justification: v2 adds VQGAN training at learning rate 2.5e-4 and batch size 32 alongside the retained 2.5e-5/batch-8 configuration. Speech evaluation introduces speaker-disjoint 80/20 splits, four speech metrics, 300-epoch training, and 10–13-bit codebooks. Sections C.6–C.7 add common initialization without replacement, 100/150/200-epoch comparisons, and codebook learning-rate multipliers of 10–50.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations, v2 tests whether DiVeQ's advantages persist without codebook replacement and how SF-DiVeQ depends on initialization, training duration, and codebook learning rate (C.6–C.7, Figures 22–25). It also extends variance sensitivity to VQGAN, adds speech batch-size ablations, and tests VQGAN stability under larger learning rates and batches.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages for image reconstruction and identify selected analyses as individual runs. v2 continues these practices without adding seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Its speech tables report test-sample averages without specifying a new repeated-run or uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Original VQGAN FIDs are retained in the corresponding configuration columns, while v2 adds another configuration, speech results, variance sweeps, and replacement/initialization results. For example, new Table 3 reports 13-bit, batch-64 speech PESQ values of 1.75 for SF-DiVeQ, 1.64 for DiVeQ, and 1.67 for EMA. These are newly reported evaluations with no v1 counterpart.

M1.justification: The DiVeQ and SF-DiVeQ constructions, detach variants, and importance-based codebook replacement algorithm remain unchanged in Sections 3 and B. v2 explicitly describes SF-DiVeQ's curve-based inference, consistent with its existing construction; this does not establish an algorithm revision. The new initialization experiments vary training settings.

P1.justification: The main narrative and existing appendix organization remain recognizable. v2 makes targeted grammatical edits, systematically replaces misleading bitrate terminology with codebook bits or size, and revises the misalignment discussion. It inserts speech-related subsections, acknowledgments, a reproducibility statement, and an LLM-use disclosure without extensively rewriting the retained exposition.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with new Tables 3 and 8–10 and Figures 22–25. The existing VQGAN tables gain grouped training-configuration columns and failure highlighting. Existing plots receive revised axis labels, variance plots use revised colors, and retained figures and image grids are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Vali's 2025 thesis, Vali and Bäckström's 2023 stochastic quantization work, and the VCTK corpus reference. It also foregrounds the already-cited SFVQ inspiration in the introduction. The broader related-work taxonomy and positioning against existing quantization methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 2 extends the existing two-dimensional NSVQ overshoot argument by asserting that the probability approaches 1 in higher dimensions, without supplying a new derivation. The method equations, gradient expressions, limiting calculations, distortion metric, and appendix RVQ derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 did not separately test dependence on codebook replacement and custom initialization. v2's common-initialization comparison without replacement and initialization sweeps (C.6–C.7) substantially strengthen the evidence while exposing conditions needed for good performance. The additional VQGAN configuration, speech evaluation, and implementation information further improve validation and reproducibility. The main-text summary of random initialization remains broader than Figure 24 supports, and uncertainty reporting remains limited, but the added controls and qualifications provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiVeQ research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing material can be matched reliably across the expanded appendices and renumbered displays.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original speech coding experiments, additional VQGAN configurations, and replacement and initialization ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original image compression and generation experiments, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, training analyses, and residual quantization experiments.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion extend the empirical success claims to sparse-view CT. The central claims concerning single-operator self-supervision, the equivariance definition and MMSE optimality retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive guidance on transformation choice and approximate invariance, interprets near-equivariant operators as a failure condition, and discusses noise-misspecification stability and computational tradeoffs (Appendices A.2 and B.4). However, its blanket claim that ES outperforms EI with unknown noise conflicts with the high-noise MRI results in Table 8.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-availability link, reproducibility statement, training/inference pseudocode, an explicit 0.8 split ratio, ten inference samples, additional processing details and per-method timing/epoch information. These substantially expand disclosure without establishing changes to the core procedure. Table 10's ES MRI timing implies about 92 hours, conflicting with the retained 50-hour maximum.

E1.justification: v4 adds LIDC-IDRI sparse-view CT simulations and acquired FastMRI k-space measurements to v1's coverage (Sections 5.3-5.4). Appendix B also adds noisy inpainting with random and periodic column masks and a Gaussian-prior decimation simulation, substantially expanding acquisition conditions and test scenarios.

E2.justification: FBP is newly evaluated as a CT comparator in v4 Table 1. Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged, including the pseudo-inverse baseline already present in v1 Figure 4. Most added evaluations reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50-view CT with noise standard deviation 0.001 and a 900/110 training/test split, sinc resampling of acquired MRI data, controlled use of noiseless ES/EI losses on noisy data, and a 256-sample MAP equivariance test. These are added evaluation designs; retained benchmark splits and metrics remain stable.

E4.justification: v1's architectural ablations, noise-dominated MRI comparisons and training curves are retained. v4 adds structured-mask tests probing failure under near-equivariant operators, known-versus-unknown noise comparisons, empirical MAP-equivariance verification and computational-cost analysis (Tables 7-10). These substantially broaden the questions investigated.

E5.justification: Both versions report reconstruction scores using averages and standard deviations. v4 introduces no repeated-training run counts, seed disclosures, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. The 256 samples in its MAP experiment specify evaluation sample size rather than repeated training.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark values agree, including v1 Table 5 matched to v4 Table 6 apart from equivalent rounding. New results include CT PSNR of 32.62 for ES versus 28.61 for EI, and acquired-MRI PSNR of 28.30 versus 27.88 (Table 1). Table 7 exposes periodic-mask failure, while Table 8 shows ES below EI under unknown high MRI noise: 25.73 versus 26.02. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The ES and noisy R2R objectives, equivariant reconstructor definition, architectures and split-averaged inference remain unchanged. Algorithms 1-2 document the existing procedure. Testing the existing noiseless loss on noisy measurements does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section sequence are retained. v4 makes localized explanatory rewrites, particularly for forward operators, subdivides Appendix A, expands the metrics discussion, introduces additional appendix subheadings and adds a reproducibility statement. This is a limited narrative reorganization rather than a pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: Table 1 expands from one MRI panel to three medical-imaging panels. New Tables 5 and 7-10 display transformation guidance, mask/noise analyses, MAP validation and timings, while Algorithms 1-2 add pseudocode blocks. Figures 1-8 retain their content with several relocations; v1 Table 5 becomes v4 Table 6. The evidence displays are substantially expanded.

R1.justification: v4 adds Armato III et al. (2011) for LIDC-IDRI, Portilla and Simoncelli (2000) for texture distributions, and Xu et al. (2016) for push-broom acquisition. The relationship to splitting, equivariant imaging and equivariant-network research, including the principal novelty claims, remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: The main definitions, assumptions, theorems and Appendix C proofs are substantively retained. v4 Appendix B.4.2 adds a Gaussian-prior/decimation setup and a closed-form MAP expression (Equation 25). As printed, its zero-mean conditional likelihood is inconsistent with the stated nonzero MAP formula.

improvement.justification: Acquired-MRI validation and targeted mask/noise tests substantially strengthen the evidence for practical applicability and reveal failure conditions absent from v1's evaluation. Explicit training/inference instructions and reported code access also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized defects in the additions: the overstated unknown-noise comparison in Table 8, inconsistent timing documentation and the likelihood/formula mismatch in the MAP example.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Equivariant Splitting work. Their main texts and Appendices A-C are readable, and corresponding methods, proofs, tables and figures can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds CT, acquired MRI measurements, structured-mask and unknown-noise experiments, MAP simulations and training-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on MNIST, DIV2K and FastMRI, including architectural ablations and additional noisy MRI results in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The main distribution-matching, smoothness, uniqueness and application-performance claims are retained. The Introduction refines the claimed disadvantage of geometry-based approaches toward piecewise interpolation, and Section 5 adds a claim that adversarial training can reduce interpolant-training complexity relative to baselines.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes failure from time-independent geometry from failure attributed to nonsmooth, time-dependent piecewise interpolation. Appendix D.3.1 adds explanations for why stronger piecewise regularization can increase path energy while stronger second-derivative regularization generally decreases it. The new RBF discussion identifies numerical instability and computational burdens, substantially expanding the mechanism and tradeoff analysis.

D1.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add implementation information for the new comparisons, including precomputed OT maps, training budgets, LAND parameters, RBF cluster and epoch choices, and regularizer-weight grids. v2 reports approximately 400 minutes to fit 1199 RBF metric networks on an RTX 3080. It also specifies knot sampling more explicitly; existing code and data access links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same knot distribution, U373 cell-tracking data, EB/Cite/Multi single-cell datasets and breast-cancer tissue sections. The added studies vary marginal counts, couplings, metrics and regularization within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The central knot comparison replaces time-independent LAND OT-MFM with time-dependent LAND OT-MFM in Figure 2. The cell-tracking comparison additionally evaluates the time-dependent variant while retaining the earlier variant. These substantively revise an important comparator in two principal experiments; comparator membership in Tables 1–3 is unchanged.

E3.justification: The revised knot MFM comparison trains interpolants using intermediate data and uses a 32-unit SELU vector-field network, replacing the earlier end-marginal interpolation setup with a 64-unit ELU vector-field network. Added protocols sweep K from 30 to 1200 and regularizer weights, evaluate interpolant EMD and path energy, and train the additional cell MFM variant for 75,000 epochs with precomputed successive OT maps.

E4.justification: v2 adds marginal-count sensitivity analysis in Figure 8, independent-versus-OT coupling analysis in Figure 9, and time-dependent MFM failure analysis in Figure 11. Appendix D.3.1 adds piecewise-linear and second-derivative regularizer ablations across weights and Cite dimensions. Appendix D.1 also investigates RBF metric-fitting failures and computational cost.

E5.justification: The new Figure 9 loss plot includes a seed=42 label, providing seed information absent from v1. The five-run single-cell reporting and existing ± entries remain unchanged. Tables 4–6 provide point estimates without stated repetition counts, and Figure 9 does not define its shading as a particular uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values and rankings, but v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative findings. Tables 4–6 report interpolant EMD, CFM EMD and path energy; for example, Table 4 reports path energy increasing from 300.01 to 87052.14 as the piecewise regularizer weight increases from 0.01 to 10 for the first held-out time. Figure 2 replaces MFM results under changed conditions, and Figures 8, 9 and 11 add further findings.

M1.justification: The interpolant parametrization, adversarial objective, two-stage ALI-CFM procedure and three regularizers remain unchanged. R3GAN training and LAND-based single-cell regularization were already documented in v1 Appendix D.3. Newly evaluated MFM variants are comparators.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits grammar, terminology and citations, revises the abstract's wording, updates the conference header and author information, and expands selected explanations. The main section order and appendix organization remain, with the regularizer study added as subsection D.3.1.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-panel Figures 8, 9 and 11 and Tables 4–6, and replaces the MFM panels in Figure 2. The earlier tumour-prediction Figure 8 moves into the main text as Figure 6; the raw histology and bifurcation figures are retained as Figures 7 and 10. The author block, link colors and page layout also change.

R1.justification: Section 3 revises v1's characterization of MFM as time-independent to acknowledge both time-dependent and time-independent metrics. Section 2.1 explicitly credits existing work for the neural interpolant parametrization. The central distribution-versus-pointwise positioning and cited-work set remain; the Albergo reference update concerns the same work's publication.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 explicitly conditions the GAN/Jensen–Shannon equivalence on an optimal discriminator. Appendix B replaces generic coordinate-distribution statements with an explicit isotropic joint Gaussian specification. The two uniqueness theorems and their Appendix A proofs retain their mathematical content apart from numbering.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1's central MFM comparisons by acknowledging and directly evaluating time-dependent MFM on knot and cell data. The added coupling and regularizer studies substantially strengthen evidence for key design choices and expose accuracy/path-energy tradeoffs. Main benchmark scores remain unchanged. Unspecified uncertainty in the new ablations and RBF timings limited to metric fitting constrain some conclusions, but the comparative evidence and diagnostic depth improve substantially.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ALI-CFM research, with matching methods, datasets and core experiments. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–D, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds MFM evaluations, coupling and marginal-count studies, and numerical regularizer ablations in Tables 4–6.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-knot, cell-tracking, single-cell and spatial-transcriptomics experiments, including learned trajectories and numerical EMD results in Tables 1–3.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: principled early balanced truncation preserves useful SSM dynamics, improves training efficiency and extends to selective systems. The additional variant and experiments do not materially redefine the advertised core contributions.

C2.justification: v3 substantially extends v1's discussion of size–accuracy dependence, recovery time and selective-system caveats. It interprets truncation ablations, explains CPU/JIT overheads, proposes SISO structure as an explanation for weak Mamba size benefits, and discusses the pragmatic variant's tradeoff between simpler tuning and unpredictable final dimensions.

D1.justification: v1's hyperparameters and reduction schedules are retained. v3 newly provides a code repository address, RTX 6000 timing context, CPU/GPU placement and JIT overhead information, JAX/PyTorch implementation distinctions, Mamba transform/kernel details, and HNN stabilization and distillation hyperparameters. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: The same MNIST/sMNIST, CIFAR10, ListOps, AAN, IMDB and Pathfinder tasks are used. MNIST becomes sMNIST without evidence of changed data or task requirements. Additional architectures, compression methods and timing studies do not establish new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares compressed LRUs with models trained directly at fixed dimensions. v3 actually evaluates HNN-regularized, subsequently truncated LRUs on sMNIST and knowledge distillation on CIFAR10 (Tables 2, 6 and 7). It also introduces random-HSV and top-HSV truncation controls; merely cited alternatives in v1 were not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The retained LRU benchmark settings remain unchanged. New protocols include controlled 256-to-32-state ablations varying reduction counts and windows, validation-based acceptance of pragmatic reductions, Mamba state-size sweeps, and operation-level timing benchmarks. Appendix F specifies full-size HNN training followed by truncation and teacher–student distillation experiments.

E4.justification: v1's HSV-trajectory analyses are retained as Figures 21–24. New Appendix C tests bottom versus random versus top HSV removal, reduction frequency and early versus late reduction windows. Appendices B, D and E additionally analyze pragmatic compression variability, computational bottlenecks and Mamba's weak size–performance relationship.

E5.justification: The main experiments retain five-seed, top-3/top-1 reporting. New ablations specify ten-seed averages, and Tables 6–7 state ten seeds without establishing that retained results were rerun. Figure 18 adds summaries excluding the best and worst runs, although its mean-versus-median labeling is inconsistent.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical results remain unchanged, but v3 adds comparator, pragmatic, Mamba, ablation and timing results. For example, Table 2 reports CIFAR10 accuracy of 79.4% for KD versus the retained 84.4% for CompreSSM at approximately 57 states. Table 4 also replaces v1 Table 3's MNIST zero entries with 12.7±3.0 states and 96.1%/93.3% compressed/baseline accuracies.

M1.justification: The original tolerance-based algorithm remains. New Section 3.2 adds fixed-fraction truncation with validation checks, checkpoint rollback and stopping after degradation. Appendix E.3 extends v1's mean-system suggestion into a Mamba procedure using calibration, cached per-channel transforms and rank-aware selective-scan execution.

P1.justification: Much main-text wording remains, but the appendices undergo substantial narrative reorganization. Implementation and results material is regrouped, the HSV-stability explanation is rewritten and expanded, and the brief selective-system outlook develops into detailed SISO/MIMO and Mamba explanations. Dedicated variant and comparator subsections also change the main-text organization.

P2.justification: v3 adds extensive ablation, timing and Mamba plots, architectural and distillation diagrams, and comparison/variant tables. Figure 3b changes from normalized training time to speedup. Original HSV Figures 5–8 are retained and relocated as Figures 21–24, rather than constituting new visual evidence.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused discussion of HSV regularization by Schwerdtner et al. (2025), initialization by Yu et al. (2024), and additional selective/linear-attention architectures and distillation references. It sharpens comparisons with existing compression approaches while retaining the original literature categories and first principled in-training MOR positioning.

T1.justification: The central assumptions, truncation bound and HSV-continuity lemma remain. v3 corrects Equation 14's observability numerator from CC^T to C^T C and adds wall-clock accounting and reduction-complexity derivations in Appendix D. Appendix F adds an HNN objective and differentiability argument, although Equation 28 incorrectly identifies the sum of HSVs as the nuclear norm of PQ.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly validates compression against fixed-size training and HSV trajectories. v3 addresses important validation gaps through controlled truncation/schedule ablations, evaluated compression alternatives, a Mamba implementation study, and substantially better timing and reproducibility documentation. New inconsistencies in norm notation, seed counts and timing labels limit confidence in some details, but the added evidence substantially strengthens understanding of why and when the method helps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CompreSSM work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison. Retained material can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and reports additional compression comparisons, controlled ablations, pragmatic-variant results, timing measurements and Mamba experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original LRU compression experiments, including accuracy, state dimensions, training times and HSV trajectories in Section 4 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: optimizing latent thoughts at test time without model-weight updates, using an intrinsic confidence reward without optimization-time decoding, and improving robustness on difficult reasoning tasks.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the extended-budget results as complementarity with explicit reasoning, attributes speed savings to shorter generated answers, and proposes that a latent workspace can neutralize redundant tokens. These extend existing explanations; the confidence-versus-correctness limitation remains unchanged, and the workspace account is not separately tested.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the official LatentSeek implementation and code reference, accompanied by its optimization-step setting in Table 3. Existing LTPO hardware, hyperparameters, selection protocol, and prompt templates remain unchanged. Moving the LTPO code link to a footnote does not change access information.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning only. V2 adds StrategyQA commonsense reasoning and BIG-bench Date Understanding symbolic reasoning on two models, substantially extending task and domain coverage while retaining the five mathematical benchmarks.

E2.justification: V2 adds LatentSeek with two prompt variants to Table 1 for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, the timing comparison in Table 3, and the fixed-configuration comparison in Table 7. This introduces a directly related test-time optimization comparator that v1 only cited.

E3.justification: V2 retains the original 4,096-token evaluation and adds a 64,000-token Qwen-3-14B AIME evaluation in Section 4.7, substantially extending the generation budget tested. Its new LatentSeek timing comparison specifies 10 optimization steps versus 20 for LTPO; Appendix D additionally measures generated length and optimization time.

E4.justification: V2 adds a focused generation-budget scalability check and an analysis separating optimization overhead from savings in generated length. Existing token-count, best-reward, top-k, fixed-configuration, and failure-case analyses remain. Appendix E expands interpretation without adding another measured ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments use a fixed random seed and timing results average three runs. V2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice, significance test, confidence interval, or stated increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Existing matched result entries are retained, but v2 adds substantial comparator, cross-domain, extended-generation, and cost-breakdown results. New Table 5 reports average AIME accuracy of 75.00% for Zero-Shot CoT versus 80.00% for LTPO at 64,000 tokens. Table 8 reports Date Understanding accuracy of 64.40% versus 76.40% with Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. These are newly reported comparisons under their respective settings.

M1.justification: The frozen-model framework, Gaussian exploration policy, confidence reward, REINFORCE update, and final decoding procedure remain unchanged. Appendix E offers a conceptual explanation of latent-token behavior without introducing another method component.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized revisions to comparator and efficiency discussions, adds Sections 4.6–4.7 and Appendices C–E, and renumbers the retained prompt-template and LLM-use appendices. The introduction, method, theoretical discussion, and conclusion are largely preserved rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 5, 8, and 9, expands existing comparison tables with LatentSeek rows, and relocates Figure 2 and several tables through reflow. The original figures and overall visual design remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds Geva et al. (2021) and Srivastava et al. (2023) for the new tasks and expands the distinction from the already-cited LatentSeek around decoding costs. The broader related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: Section 3's mathematical formulation and policy-gradient derivation, along with Theorems B.1–B.2 and their proofs, remain unchanged. The new latent-workspace discussion supplies no additional formal result.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's missing direct LatentSeek comparison and testing whether LTPO remains useful when CoT receives a much larger generation budget. Non-mathematical evaluations and the cost breakdown further support breadth and efficiency. These gains outweigh the limited reporting weaknesses, including unexplained LatentSeek Prompt 1 GSM8K values of 53.15% in Table 1 versus 49.89% in Table 7 and the untested workspace interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LTPO research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, moves, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds LatentSeek comparisons, non-mathematical evaluations, extended-generation results, and an inference-cost breakdown.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark accuracies, inference timings, component ablations, hyperparameter robustness results, and qualitative examples.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and concluding summary retain the same central contributions: a mechanistic explanation involving similar low-rank updates and biased rounding, a minimal FlashAttention mitigation, and a diagnostic workflow. Additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 proposes that QK normalization and Gated Attention disrupt structurally aligned error updates, interprets rising maxima counts as a leading indicator of failure, and explicitly cautions that the Llama patterns do not demonstrate BF16 training failure. The existing GPT-2-focused and precision-format limitations remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies Muon hyperparameters and parameter assignments, Llama probe details, and an explanation of absorbed attention scaling. Its pseudocode repairs the overwritten stabilization maximum and the backward dK update. These improve the documented implementation; the PDFs do not establish corresponding changes to previously executed code. The code link and original hardware details remain.

E1.justification: OpenWebText language modeling remains the dataset/task coverage. The additions vary model size, architecture and optimizer, and inspect existing attention-pattern questions on illustrative English text; they do not establish a distinct data domain, language or task requirement.

E2.justification: Original FlashAttention remains the comparator against stabilized FlashAttention in Figure 7. The standard-attention and high-precision substitution comparisons in Section 3.2 are retained. Muon supplies an optimizer setting for both attention methods, rather than an additional competing stabilization method.

E3.justification: v1 Figure 7 shows training through 20K steps with beta = 7. v3 reports 600K-step GPT-2S experiments with beta = 2 under AdamW and Muon, plus 100K-step GPT-2M training under AdamW. These substantially extend the evaluation budgets and configurations; the original Section 3.1 setup remains documented.

E4.justification: v3 adds optimizer/model-size robustness checks in Figure 7, Llama-3.1-8B case studies of similar update structures and multiple maxima in Appendix D, and a temporal analysis of maxima occurrences versus loss in Appendix E.1/Figure 13. The original operation-, layer- and head-localization analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 7 explicitly displays Trial 1 and Trial 2 for each attention method. v3 replaces these with one displayed curve per method in each configuration without identifying repeated-run counts or uncertainty aggregation. Explicit replication information is therefore removed; this does not establish that fewer runs were performed.
