E6.justification: Figure 7 replaces the original two-trial results with longer trajectories across three configurations, reporting stable modified-attention training and loss explosions with original attention. New appendix results show corresponding attention patterns in Llama and a temporal relationship between maxima and loss. These are new or replaced results under different settings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 4 changes repeated-maximum detection from exact equality to a tolerance condition, rowmax(S) − S ≤ epsilon, with 10^-3 given as an example. This broadens when stabilization activates while retaining the same conditional softmax-shift mechanism.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section sequence remain largely intact. v3 locally rewrites the rounding and mitigation explanations, clarifies gradient notation, and expands supporting explanations through Appendix A.3, the detailed Equation 1 derivation and diagnostic workflow. It also adds future-work, acknowledgment and LLM-use text.

P2.justification: Figure 7 changes from one plot with labeled trials to three configuration panels with logarithmic training-step axes and revised legends. v3 adds two multipanel Llama figures and a dual-axis maxima/loss figure. Existing Figures 8–10 become Figures 10–12, and algorithms and several figures are repositioned; these retained displays are not new results.

R1.justification: v3 adds the Muon references by Jordan et al. (2024) and Liu et al. (2025), removes Hao et al. (2025), and adds an explanatory FlashAttention subsection in Appendix A.3. The broader related-work positioning and central novelty claim remain stable.

T1.justification: Section 3.3.2 substantially revises the central rounding argument. v1 incorrectly rounds the exact tie −4.703125 to −4.71875; v3 introduces an accumulated FP32 residual, giving −4.703990459442139 and a valid rounding-up example involving the sticky bit. Claim 3 and Remark 1 are correspondingly revised. Appendix E.2 expands the already-existing Equation 1 without changing its mathematical result.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves important correctness and reproducibility deficiencies: Section 3.3.2 repairs the invalid ties-to-even example, and the stabilized algorithm now preserves its adjusted maximum. Longer training across optimizer and model-size configurations substantially strengthens empirical support. The loss of explicit two-trial reporting reduces transparency, and the Llama evidence remains illustrative, but these limitations do not outweigh the central corrections and stronger validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FlashAttention training-failure analysis and mitigation. Their main text, equations, figures, algorithms and appendices support a reliable comparison; relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical analyses and reports longer GPT-2 training experiments, Llama-3.1-8B representation probes, and the relationship between multiple maxima and loss.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-2 training experiments, precision-substitution interventions, representation and gradient analyses, and stabilization trials, including Figures 2–7.

C1.justification: The central ACE contributions and headline gains of 10.6% on agents and 8.6% on finance remain. However, the introduction changes from matching IBM-CUGA overall and surpassing it on test-challenge to an unqualified claim of surpassing the top-ranked agent. The original scores and narrower abstract/Section 4.3 account remain, making this a limited strengthening of the leaderboard claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of transfer across model families, tolerance to weak and corrupted reflections, excessive reflection, pruning tradeoffs, and raw versus cache-discounted token costs (Sections 4.5–4.7 and Appendix A). A new Section 4.3 footnote qualifies CUGA as a contextual reference. The original limitations are retained in Section 5, alongside these expanded applicability and mechanism discussions.

D1.justification: v3 documents additional experiment-specific sample sizes, model assignments, adaptation budgets, corruption frequencies, threshold ranges and use of GPT-5.1's default prompt caching. These extend the technical record, while the existing role prompts and code-access destination remain unchanged. The new reproducibility statement mainly consolidates existing disclosures.

E1.justification: v3 retains AppWorld, FiNER and Formula and adds offline evaluation on StreamBench's DDXPlus medical diagnosis and BIRD-SQL text-to-SQL tasks (Section 4.1 and Appendix A.2). These introduce substantially different domains and task requirements beyond the original agent and finance coverage.

E2.justification: The original accuracy comparisons retain their baseline membership. The new evaluation-stage cost comparisons include Base ReAct alongside GEPA and ACE (Tables 14–15), extending v2's cost comparisons against GEPA and DC in Table 4. Added accuracy studies reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1 and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct configurations. New domain evaluations use 1,000 training examples, specified GEPA validation sets, and GPT-4o-mini judging for BIRD-SQL. Appendix A also introduces controlled reflector and hyperparameter variations and a cost study using one epoch and one reflection round. These are additional protocols; the original main-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Reflector, multi-epoch and warmup ablations, v3 tests removal of incremental updates, varying Reflector capability, adversarial feedback frequency, reflection rounds, deduplication thresholds and pruning triggers (Appendices A.4–A.6). It also adds component-level adaptation/evaluation cost analyses and measured prompt-cache reuse, addressing previously untested mechanisms and tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added tables continue reporting point estimates; their signed differences indicate changes relative to baselines, not uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, while Tables 5–21 add substantial new findings. For example, DDXPlus accuracy is 90.2 for ACE versus 75.2 for the base model and 76.4 for GEPA. BIRD-SQL averages are 52.9, 47.8 and 52.2 respectively, with GEPA ahead on Moderate and Challenging subsets. Further additions quantify model-dependent gains, robustness, ablation effects and token costs.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the Generator–Reflector–Curator workflow, itemized context bullets, deterministic delta merging and grow-and-refine mechanism. The prompt contents in Figures 6–14 match across versions. Additional model configurations and ablations evaluate the existing procedure; no algorithm revision is established.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and most existing method and prompt language are retained. v3 makes localized rewrites, adds explanatory subsections and conference statements, moves limitations into Section 5, and integrates the previous caching discussion into cost analysis. Citations switch to author–year formatting, and the appendices are reorganized around extended results and discussions.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–21 covering model comparisons, new domains, cost breakdowns and sensitivity tests. It also adopts the ICLR layout, resizes and relocates existing displays, and changes Figure 1's axis ranges and tick spacing. The original figures, including the leaderboard snapshot and prompt displays, are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new benchmarks, judging procedure, caching discussion and robustness discussion, and Appendix C expands comparisons with GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet. Explicit acknowledgment of building on Dynamic Cheatsheet is removed from the abstract and introduction, although Section 3 retains the connection. The broader positioning around context adaptation remains stable.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The procedural account of ACE is retained, and the new appendices add empirical analyses and conceptual discussion without new mathematical definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: The direct incremental-update ablation and reflection stress tests address important gaps in v2's evidence for ACE's mechanism and failure conditions. Additional model and domain evaluations substantially strengthen generalizability, while measured caching and token breakdowns clarify serving-cost tradeoffs. These gains outweigh localized overclaims, including the strengthened CUGA statement and Appendix A.1's assertion that online adaptation is consistently strongest, which Tables 7–9 do not support. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ACE framework and retain matching core experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 23 pages of v2 and 32 pages of v3, including figures, tables and appendices, without material reading gaps.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds experiments across models and domains, robustness tests, sensitivity analyses and detailed cost measurements in Appendix A.

before.justification: v2 reports original AppWorld, FiNER and Formula experiments, component ablations, and adaptation cost and latency measurements in Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: The abstract's claimed average gain changes from +4–8% to +4–10%. The introduction revises gains over vanilla and KD from +7.96%/+6.0% to +9.94%/+8.5%, while retaining +4.4% over TransLoRA. The central contribution remains selective token-level LoRA knowledge transfer.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting excess scores to likelihood ratios and informative gradients, claims error-free alignment and robustness to synthetic-data imperfections and weak experts, and explains selected tokens through semantic structure. Appendix L hypothesizes cleaner-data generation during refinement and discusses its remaining gap to supervised targets. The original seed-example and fixed-threshold limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises future code release; v2 reports the code as publicly available. v2 also explicitly documents sampling 100 MMLU instances before the 90/10 split, mentions a length filter, supplies an alternative generation prompt and GPT-4o-mini grading details, and provides stage-wise runtime measurements. These substantially expand the documented reproduction and resource information.

E1.justification: BBH, MMLU, LaMP 4/5 and the existing other-user, mixed-user and cross-task coverage are retained. Appendix J adds a deliberately degraded synthetic-training-data scenario using the lowest-rated samples. The larger-model experiments change model configurations without adding benchmark tasks.

E2.justification: The original vanilla, KD/MinED, TransLoRA and five-shot KD comparators are retained. v2 adds fully supervised target-expert references in Table 18 and explicit source-LoRA comparisons in Table 19. The additional Alpagasus citation supports data grading, not a newly evaluated transfer baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include 4-bit Mixtral and 70B evaluations, top/bottom/random 20% token controls, and one-to-one-only alignment experiments. The stated retained BBH synthetic-set size changes from 250 to 225 in v1 Appendix F versus v2 Appendix H; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun. v2 Appendix D.3 also describes source-generated data for the TransLoRA comparison, inconsistently with its retained target-query description.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, representative sensitivity curves and external-data tests, v2 adds token-subgroup and expert-agreement analyses, alignment diagnostics, comprehensive selection-ratio sweeps, degraded-data and prompt tests, synthetic-quality ratings, self-refinement, weak-source diagnostics, runtime profiling and highlighted-token case studies.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without reporting random-seed counts or dispersion. v2 Table 1 reports three-seed means, Table 11 adds standard deviations across the main comparisons, and Section 4.3 identifies supplementary analyses as using one fixed seed. The unspecified v1 run count prevents establishing an explicit increase from a known earlier count.

E6.justification: Many Table 1 estimates are replaced by three-seed means: TiTok BBH accuracy changes from 0.432 to 0.424 for Mistral-to-Mistral and from 0.510 to 0.488 for Llama2-to-Llama3. These are revised reported estimates, not established same-protocol performance losses. Numerous new results cover controls, larger models, robustness, refinement and timing; the original component-ablation, external-data and five-shot comparison values are retained.

M1.justification: The core procedure, Algorithm 1 and Equations (1)–(7) remain unchanged. Appendix L adds an evaluated iterative extension: the transferred target generates new synthetic data, the original source expert/base pair scores it, and a fresh target LoRA is trained again.

P1.justification: v2 polishes wording, standardizes 'token-wise contrastive excess,' tightens the conclusion, reorders the selection-ratio and query-source discussions, and reorganizes appendices. It also updates the publication header and adds acknowledgments. The main narrative and section structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic tables, a comprehensive sensitivity grid, a mean-plus-standard-deviation table, runtime breakdowns and Figure 5's highlighted examples. It also replaces v1 Figure 3(a), which repeats the headline-task curve under a BBH label, with a BBH curve in Figure 2(a). Other original diagrams and plots are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Li and Babu (2019) and Neyman and Pearson (1933) for its statistical motivation, and expands the contrast with TransLoRA regarding external, non-synthetic data. The main related-work positioning remains stable. The additional Alpagasus reference represents the same work already cited in v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations (1)–(7) remain unchanged. The new likelihood-ratio/Neyman–Pearson discussion in Section 3.2 invokes established theory as motivation and interpretation; it supplies no new formal theorem, derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through three-seed uncertainty reporting, direct token-selection controls, broader robustness checks and measured runtime breakdowns, addressing important evidential gaps in v1. It also corrects the duplicated sensitivity panel. New inconsistencies temper these gains: Table 7's baseline values conflict with its labeled target, and Appendix D.3 contradicts the main TransLoRA generation description; some optimality and bias interpretations also exceed their evidence. These weaknesses limit particular additions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical scrutiny and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TiTok research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original transfer results and reports additional experiments on token selection, alignment, synthetic-data robustness, larger models, self-refinement and runtime.

before.justification: v1 reports original transfer experiments on BBH, MMLU and LaMP, including component ablations, external-data experiments and a five-shot KD comparison.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contribution: architecture-agnostic query refinement using complementary retrievers to improve retrieval efficiency and quality. The headline 14-fold speed and 54-fold memory claims remain. The broader benchmark evidence supports these retained claims without redefining the core contribution.

C2.justification: Section 2.4 and Appendix G expand the explanation of geometry-constrained, document-dependent updates; Section 4.1 adds a latency–stability interpretation. Applicability changes from v1's explicit exclusion of zero-shot use to evidence for transferred settings. V2 removes the dedicated limitations paragraph, including its acknowledgment of missing theoretical foundations.

D1.justification: Tables 20–25 newly disclose selected GQR and fusion hyperparameters for each ViDoRe 2 model pair/subset. V2 also specifies ViDoRe 3 markdown inputs and transferred configurations. The existing optimizer, tuning grids, K=10, Docling version and code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 retains ViDoRe 1/2 and adds ViDoRe 3 evaluation across eight subsets: cs, energy, fin_en, fin_fr, hr, industrial, pharma and physics (Table 2). This substantially expands the evaluated document corpora and domain coverage within visual document retrieval.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain Average Ranking, RRF, Min-Max and Softmax score aggregation, their tuned variants, the same single retrievers and the MonoQwen2-VL-v0.1 reranker. ViDoRe 3 uses existing comparison methods; Llama-Nemo is excluded only from this newly added benchmark.

E3.justification: The original tuning protocol remains, but v2 adds evaluation on ViDoRe 3 without target-benchmark tuning, transferring a fixed GQR learning rate of 10^-4 and T=50 across six model pairs. It uses supplied markdown for that corpus and adds a T=5–100 sensitivity sweep and controlled latency measurements at T=25/50.

E4.justification: V2 adds GQR learning-rate/step sensitivity tests, component-level latency analysis, baseline fusion-weight sweeps and query-level rank trajectories (Figures 4, 5, 7 and 8). These investigate stability, computational costs and differences from score fusion. The earlier search, candidate-pool, loss and role-swapping ablations remain.

E5.justification: V2 adds standard deviations across nine retriever pairs to the retained ViDoRe 2 comparison (Table 3), and reports the same statistic across six pairs on ViDoRe 3 (Table 5). These describe configuration variability, not repeated-run uncertainty. The existing 100-run latency statement is unchanged; no new seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: The earlier result tables retain their numerical values. New ViDoRe 3 results include Colnomic/Jina at 57.4 versus its 55.7 primary baseline, and average relative gains of 2.89% for GQR versus 2.66% for Min-Max fusion. Two fin_fr entries decline by 0.1 despite the universal-improvement prose. New sensitivity curves, query trajectories and fixed-step timings add further findings.

M1.justification: The GQR procedure and Algorithm 1 are unchanged: combine retrieved candidate pools, optimize the primary query embedding using KL divergence from the consensus distribution, and rank candidates with the refined embedding. Fixed hyperparameters for the new evaluation do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: V2 lightly rewrites the introduction, separates method rationale into Section 2.4, divides single-retriever and hybrid comparisons, and moves storage and selected design-choice discussions into appendices. Much of the existing prose remains verbatim; the reorganization is focused.

P2.justification: V2 adds benchmark and parameter tables, sensitivity plots, a latency breakdown and query-rank heat maps. It moves the existing architecture diagram into the main text and Algorithm 1 and the reranker plot into the appendix. The main latency plot is redrawn with direct labels and fewer displayed model series, while the hybrid comparison gains a Std column.

R1.justification: The cited works and related-work discussion are retained. Positioning relative to multimodal late interaction, dense–sparse fusion and cross-encoder-guided query refinement is substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: The method's mathematical formulation remains unchanged, with no new theorem, proof or substantive derivation. Appendix C's added weighted-fusion equations explicitly state rules already described in v1.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly depended on in-domain tuning; v2 provides substantive evidence that one transferred configuration works across six model pairs on ViDoRe 3. Sensitivity analyses, runtime decomposition and disclosed selected parameters strengthen practical validity and reproducibility. Removing explicit limitations and overstating improvement across every subset weaken qualification, but these localized shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GQR research work. All 22 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison; retained equations, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds ViDoRe 3 experiments, parameter sensitivity analyses, latency breakdowns and query-level case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original ViDoRe 1/2 retrieval experiments, latency measurements, reranker comparisons and method ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free mode switching, overthinking suppression, accuracy, and token efficiency. The additional appendix evidence does not revise these main claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning difficulty-adaptive switching, latent reasoning's contribution beyond stopping control, and convergence-timing tradeoffs. Appendix C.6 introduces rigid geometric constraints as a specific failure condition and attributes the example's error to latent smoothing; that causal explanation remains tentative evidence from one case.

D1.justification: v2 documents how the top-five embedding-similarity diagnostic is calculated, how the explicit-only ablation retains stopping triggers, and which switch caps correspond to reported accuracy/length pairs. Algorithm 1, Table 4, and listed code/data links remain unchanged. Hardware and timing implementation details are still unspecified.

E1.justification: v2 retains the five mathematics/STEM benchmarks and adds coding on HumanEval, LeetCode-Contest, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench; multi-hop QA on LongBench's 2WikiMultihopQA; and commonsense reasoning on CommonsenseQA (Appendix C.3). This substantially broadens evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: Sampled CoT, greedy CoT, and Soft Thinking remain the external comparators, including in the new benchmark evaluations. v2 additionally evaluates controller-retaining SwiR without latent reasoning and component-removal/symmetric-window variants as ablation comparators (Tables 8–9).

E3.justification: Original evaluation settings remain unchanged. New protocols add Qwen3-32B evaluation, latency/TFLOP comparisons at fixed accuracy, entropy and top-five embedding-similarity diagnostics, and controlled trigger/window/component variations. Appendix C.4 labels its runtime model 'Qwen-3B' without resolving its precise identity.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's window-size, mixing-coefficient, and budget analyses, v2 adds exploration diagnostics, switch-count distributions by difficulty, a spatial-reasoning failure case, convergence-timing tests, and controls isolating latent reasoning and window asymmetry/removal (C.1 and C.5–C.9). Some original window and budget results are reused, but the additional controls address previously untested questions.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly reports descriptive variability through switch-count boxplots, medians, and ranges across problems. This concerns problem-level variation, not repeated-run accuracy uncertainty. The eight-repeat AIME averaging statement remains unchanged; no new seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results: Qwen3-32B averages of 84.30% for SwiR versus 82.38% for CoT, broader-domain averages of 81.24% versus 78.54%, and runtime, diagnostic, and ablation findings. These are newly reported evaluations. Original main results and all detailed rows in v1 Tables 5–19 are retained in v2 Tables 11–25.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same entropy-based switching, asymmetric dwell windows, signal mixing, and convergence/termination controller. New ablation variants test components without revising the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are almost unchanged, with limited citation, bibliographic, and cross-reference edits. Appendix C gains organized subsections C.1–C.9, while its original detailed-results subsection becomes C.10; existing prose undergoes little rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Figures 6–8, Tables 5–10, and a boxed, annotated reasoning trace spanning two pages. These include diagnostic curves, latency/compute plots, switch-count boxplots, and comparison/ablation tables. Original figures remain unchanged, and original appendix tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: New references support the added coding and QA benchmarks. Appendix B.4 also explicitly discusses COCONUT and Long⊗Short as training-based efficiency approaches. The central positioning as a training-free alternative to purely latent reasoning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of latent embeddings, switching, signal mixing, controller behavior, and token efficiency are unchanged. The added empirical diagnostics and illustrated erroneous model solution introduce no new theoretical result, proof, or formal assumption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the paper. The controller-retaining explicit-only comparison in Table 8 addresses whether latent reasoning contributes beyond early stopping, while new component controls, broader tasks, and Qwen3-32B evaluation strengthen mechanism assessment and generality. Runtime measurements and a concrete failure analysis add practical perspective. The timing setup remains underspecified and the failure's causal attribution is tentative, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SwiReasoning framework. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds larger-model and broader-domain evaluations, runtime measurements, diagnostic analyses, and ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original reasoning accuracy, token-efficiency, Pass@k, and ablation results in Section 4 and Appendix C.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion now emphasize SSFT plus GFPO and claim superiority over SFT with GRPO across math reasoning and execution-based coding. v2's headline empirical claims concern SSFT versus SFT. Distributed implementation remains documented but loses its place as a headline contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations attributing RL gains to preserved reasoning modes, interpreting coding gains through a larger search space, and acknowledging difficulties theoretically justifying the selection heuristic. It also qualifies generality through smaller gains on other model families and a coding shortfall for Qwen3-4B. These extend the earlier discussion of matching-induced specialization.

D1.justification: Appendices A.3–A.5 and Table 9 document coding-data construction and GFPO implementation, including four-token tag spans, learning rate, batch size, rollout count, KL coefficient, and hardware. Existing SSFT implementation details and access information remain. Coding RL data size is internally inconsistent: the prose and Table 5 state 1000 questions, while Table 9 states 1280.

E1.justification: v3 adds execution-based LiveCodeBench v5 evaluation, coding fine-tuning data constructed from Open-Thoughts questions, and RL training data from DAPO-Math-17k and Intellect-2-RL. It evaluates transfer from math to coding and from coding to math. The original s1k, Open-R1, and reasoning-benchmark coverage remains.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces the single-<think> SFT-mixed-distill-32B comparator with SFT-mixed-distill-32B-tags, which assigns distinct tags without replacement. The original comparator remains in the coverage plot. Appendix A.3 additionally evaluates tagged SFT with full-sequence GRPO or GFPO and random-matching SSFT with GFPO, substantially expanding the controls.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce a 10-step math RL protocol, sampled-token Pass@1 evaluation, Qwen3-4B and Llama3.1-8B configurations, and a matching-length sweep over 0, 100, 1000, 2500, and 3500 tokens. Coding evaluation executes generated programs against tests. The original SSFT training budgets and main math evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 7 newly tests matching-prefix length against training time and accuracy. Section 4 and Appendices A.3–A.6 add RL controls, robustness across model families and training domains, and bidirectional domain-transfer analyses. The earlier random-matching, 93k-data, training-dynamics, and qualitative reasoning analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 2 and 5 newly specify averaging 16 generations for coding Pass@1. The existing 32-generation math averages and 11-set Cons@6 reporting remain. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the addition concerns documented generation counts.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial RL, coding, model-family, and matching-length results, including SSFT-GFPO AIME24/25 scores of 64.22/58.80 and code-trained SSFT's LCB score of 52.07. Original SSFT scores of 64.06/58.13 and the 93k results remain unchanged. Table 1 replaces untagged-baseline scores of 55.73/51.56 with tagged-baseline scores of 58.23/51.96, which are different-comparator results, and removes cross-task averages.

M1.justification: v3 introduces Global Forking Policy Optimization in Section 2.3: reinforcement learning applies policy gradients only to forking-token positions, using complete generations to compute advantages. This adds a training stage and question-conditioned token sampling for Pass@1. The original SSFT matching loss, algorithms, and graph-based selection alternative remain.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion, condenses background and figure-related prose, promotes robustness to a standalone section, and moves implementation material later in the appendix. Much of the original explanatory wording and narrative order remains; the larger expansion primarily adds scientific content. Headers, affiliation text, and acknowledgments are also edited.

P2.justification: v3 removes the opening comparison diagram, compresses the inference illustration, relocates learned-matching diagrams to the appendix, and expands boxplot axes to display full whiskers. It adds the matching-length figure and tables for coding, RL, model families, and hyperparameters. Table 1 replaces its average column with LCB and adds GFPO rows.

R1.justification: Appendix A.7 substantially develops positioning relative to RL-based length control, discussing objectives, token budgets, training-data differences, and complementarity. New references also support GFPO and RLVR discussion. Conversely, v2's Parallel-R1 and multi-paradigm reasoning discussions and several associated citations are removed. The DETR-inspired positioning remains.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 newly asserts matching complexity O(NM/k), with k = Tr/L, whereas v2 discusses truncation efficiency without this formal scaling statement. The matching definitions, Hungarian loss, selection equation, and Algorithms 1–2 remain mathematically equivalent. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: Section 4, Figure 7, and Appendices A.3–A.6 substantially strengthen evidence for generality, matching efficiency, and adaptive token selection through coding execution, domain transfer, additional model families, and RL controls. These address important questions left untested in v2. Stale Table 1 gain statements, conflicting coding scores in Tables 2 and 5, and inconsistent coding RL sample counts weaken reporting precision, but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSFT research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, and retained content can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original GFPO, code-generation, model-family, and matching-length experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning evaluations, matching ablations, training-dynamics analyses, and generated reasoning examples, including Tables 1–2 and the appendix.

C1.justification: The central RICH claim and recommendation to combine training and inference defenses remain. However, contribution 3 now claims creation of the first adversarially robust RL-tuned reasoning VLM, and the abstract foregrounds its robustness gains. This adds a substantial model contribution beyond v1's experiments with existing models; the earlier no-RL findings remain in the body.

C2.justification: Appendix B newly qualifies the specification benefit through meaningful prefill and proposes a termination-probability explanation; Appendix C argues that token meaning matters. Section 5 adds clean-performance costs and limits the training recommendation toward security applications. Figure 8 attributes uneven scaling possibly to degraded capabilities. v1's broader representation-based extension of RICH is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds a substantial training recipe: 16,000 iterations, the 9,000-iteration checkpoint, four H100 GPUs, batch size 12, two PGD steps, attack epsilon 4/255, step size 2/255, and clean-loss weight 0.5. It also identifies the system-message source and inherited defaults. Figure 7 documents all four existing white-box images; the original prompts are retained in Appendix D.

E1.justification: Attack-Bard, visual prompt injection, and shape/color/texture classification remain the main evaluation coverage; Figure 7 identifies the four previously used images. New Table 1 lists COCO, Flickr30k, VQAv2, and TextVQA results, but their attribution and protocols do not establish whether these represent additional evaluations by this work or a summary of prior results.

E2.justification: Figures 1 and 8 add unmodified InternVL 3.5 gpt-oss 20B as the comparator for its adversarially finetuned variants. The original LLaVA, FARE, Delta2, Qwen, Llama, and frontier-model comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The original main-text protocols remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce prefill and token-content controls, an 8/255 attack budget, and budget-forced reasoning up to 64K tokens with 9,000- and 16,000-iteration finetuning checkpoints. InternVL Figure 1 uses the Attack-Bard label subset, whereas Figure 8 uses all 1,000 ImageNet classes. Tables 7 and 8 also use different sample coverage.

E4.justification: New Appendix B tests goal-only versus security specifications, prefill removal, and length-matched random prefills. Appendix C tests the less leading 'object' prompt and random versus meaningful added tokens. Appendix E examines finetuning checkpoints and long reasoning budgets, while Figure 1 adds a weevil reasoning case study. These substantially expand tests of mechanisms and sensitivity.

E5.justification: v1 already reports standard deviations, standard errors, and McNemar tests. v2 additionally specifies two replicates for Tables 7–8 and at least ten runs per configuration for Figure 8's standard errors. These are new reporting details for added experiments, not evidence that the original experiments received more runs.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–4 are numerically unchanged as v2 Tables 2–5. v2 adds InternVL accuracy curves, prefill and prompt-control results, and multi-benchmark robustness scores. The cited VQAv2 example changes from FARE 31% and Delta2 59.5% to 23.0 and 61.0 in new Table 1; insufficiently matched evaluation details prevent interpreting these as performance changes under the same conditions.

M1.justification: v1 primarily uses existing robust models with prompt repetition and CoT. v2 additionally constructs a robust InternVL 3.5 gpt-oss 20B through adversarial finetuning of its vision encoder and introduces budget-forced reasoning for this model. Section 4.4 and Appendix E establish a substantial new training and inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, methodology, reasoning-experiment discussion, limitations, and author contributions receive selective edits. The main five-section narrative and most existing prose remain intact. New analysis appendices move the original prompts from B to D and the color example from C to F, with corresponding reference updates.

P2.justification: v2 adds the first-page overview and reasoning plot, the prompt-injection comparison grid, an image gallery, and the long-budget plot, plus Tables 1 and 6–8. Retained tables are restyled and the RICH statement receives a new box. All five original figures remain, with changed placement and numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds the s1 budget-forcing and InternVL 3.5 references, removes the Goyal et al. VQAv2 reference, and adds the robust reasoning-VLM novelty claim. Its broader positioning relative to Zaremba and adversarial training remains stable. The Delta2 reference changing from Wang et al. 2025b to 2025c is only relabeling.

T1.justification: RICH remains a qualitative hypothesis. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and v2 adds no mathematical derivation or substantive formal definition. Reformatting the hypothesis and revising its conceptual discussion do not constitute theoretical changes.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a directly robustified RL reasoning VLM and controls separating useful token content from token quantity. v2 adds both, substantially strengthening tests of its central hypothesis through Section 4.4 and Appendices B, C, and E. The training recipe and explicit prefill and clean-performance qualifications also improve reproducibility and interpretation. Uneven long-budget behavior and differing coverage in the token controls still limit universal or causal conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RICH research work. All 17 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including their figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison. The original experiments can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds InternVL adversarial finetuning and reasoning experiments, together with prompt and prefill controls.

before.justification: v1 reports original PGD attack experiments, Attack-Bard classification results, and VLM-description-to-Claude experiments in Appendix A.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: an Explain-then-Detect system outperforming direct detection, the same three method components, and state-of-the-art binary, fine-grained, and reasoning performance. Additional validation supports these retained claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 develops the interpretation of CDE as promoting calibration, discusses evaluator strictness and reproducibility, and explains hyperparameter failure regimes. Appendix J.2 newly identifies implicit hate and missing contextual/world knowledge as persistent failure conditions, with targeted annotation and retrieval proposed as future remedies. V1 primarily discussed successful cases and general deployment caveats.

D1.justification: V2 adds the complete Explain-then-Detect prompt, specifies one-time expert conversion of guidelines into policy manuals, documents CDE validation tuning and transfer, and supplies new evaluator identifiers and annotation instructions. Existing software versions, hardware, LoRA settings, training duration, and prospective code/artifact release arrangements remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use HatefulMemes, MAMI, PrideMM, and the Hatred rationale annotations for the same binary, fine-grained, and explanation tasks. The new human evaluations, calibration measurements, and error cases concern retained data and model outputs.

E2.justification: Matched comparisons retain zero-shot, SFT, DPO, GRPO, RA-HMD, LOREHM, and U-CoT+, with unchanged comparator membership in Tables 1–3. Additional LLMs in v2 serve as evaluators; the new diagnostic comparisons use existing baseline methods.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported fine-grained metric from macro F1 to micro F1, although the original table values remain identical; this does not establish rerunning. New evaluation protocols add alternative judges, BERTScore, ECE with 10 bins, Brier scores, and randomized human coherence/helpfulness assessments by three annotators per example.

E4.justification: V2 adds judge and prompt sensitivity tests, human validation of explanation quality, calibration analysis, CDE hyperparameter sensitivity findings, per-class diagnostics, and three shared failure cases. These substantially extend v1's component/warmup ablations, CDE distribution analysis, and successful correction examples.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly reports inter-annotator reliability, with Krippendorff's ordinal alpha of 0.71. The three-seed, 60-point correlation analysis and its significance reporting are unchanged. V2 does not document an increased repeated-run count or add confidence intervals for the retained performance tables.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain all numerical entries. V2 adds judge/BERTScore results, human coherence of 96% versus 100% and helpfulness of 1.6 versus 2.2 for GRPO versus ExPO-HM, calibration results, per-class scores, and failure examples. Table 12 gives 3B GRPO Brier 0.441 versus ExPO-HM 0.283; the 0.590 cited in Section 4.6 belongs to zero-shot.

M1.justification: The policy-manual SFT warmup, 50/50/50 GRPO curriculum, CDE reward design, and default parameters are retained. Corrections to the displayed GRPO loss sign and CDE cutoff notation do not establish a changed implemented training or inference procedure.

P1.justification: V2 corrects typos and terminology, updates affiliations, adds explanatory subheadings, and reorganizes Appendix B to separate ordinary prompts, policy-manual construction, and statistics. Most existing main-text prose and the overall narrative remain intact; the expansion mainly consists of new scientific material.

P2.justification: V2 adds evaluator, prompt-sensitivity, human-rating, calibration, and per-class tables, an annotation-interface figure, and a failure-case display. Original Figures 1–3 are retained, with sizing/layout adjustments. The six existing success cases move from Tables 9–10 to 15–16, and appendix table captions are repositioned above their tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds HelpSteer, cited for the human helpfulness rubric, and BERTScore, cited for explanation evaluation. The related-work narrative and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged. Publication updates for HatefulMemes and RA-HMD refer to already cited works.

T1.justification: The original CDE estimator and chain-rule derivations move unchanged from Appendix E to G. New Appendix H.2 derives confidence constraints and sample-level and dataset-level Brier bounds under an idealized binary CDE-maximizing policy, including Eqs. 16–31. V2 also corrects the GRPO loss expression and the final cutoff in Eq. 11.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central explanation-quality evidence through human ratings and checks across judges and prompts, addressing v1's reliance on one automatic judge and CDE. Per-class results and explicit failures also clarify applicability. The unspecified human-evaluation sample size, unreconciled macro/micro reporting change, and misattributed calibration baseline limit particular findings, but do not outweigh the broader corroboration and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ExPO-HM and retain the same research framework. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across additions, reorganizations, and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds human evaluations, alternative-judge evaluations, calibration measurements, per-class results, and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification and reasoning results across three meme benchmarks, component ablations, warmup comparisons, and CDE analyses.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion extend explicit validation claims to Llama3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B, including their reported 2.61- and 2.50-point gains. The central contributions concerning selective nested computation, routing control and post-training integration remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 interprets entropy and hidden-state findings as evidence that DND revisits uncertain tokens and improves their representations. It also attributes ITT's limited gains to routing-related training/inference mismatch and emphasizes complementary router and threshold controls. These refine the mechanism discussion; the limitations are retained, moving from Appendix E to F.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly discloses that all parameters are trainable with the same learning rate; v1 did not specify this. Appendix B adds two-epoch, 64-H100, approximately 1–2-day training details for Llama and Gemma, while Table 3 supplies BF16 and vLLM-kernel information. Existing Qwen settings and the promised future code release remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The described SFT data sources and benchmark suite are unchanged. v2 Table 1 uses the eleven tasks already evaluated in v1 Table 2; the added backbones, throughput measurements and diagnostics expand configurations and evaluation procedures rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds ITT as an evaluated comparator for Qwen3-1.7B, whereas v1 only discussed ITT in related work. This is a targeted addition to one model's comparison; the original comparators remain, and MOR is still compared descriptively rather than through reported benchmark results.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma3-1B configurations and a reportedly compute-matched ITT comparison. It also introduces throughput testing across four input/decode-length combinations on one H100 with a single batch, plus entropy and hidden-state diagnostic measurements. These substantially expand the evaluation design without revising the retained Qwen protocols.

E4.justification: New Figure 4 tests whether frequently selected tokens have higher original logit entropy and larger entropy reductions after DND. New Appendix D and Figure 8 examine selection against hidden-state changes. These add substantive tests of the selection mechanism; the original ablations, control analyses and qualitative examples remain.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 4 newly reports fitted linear trends and Pearson correlations, adding statistical estimation to the diagnostic analyses. Appendix B retains the same 16 inferences per AIME question; neither additional run counts nor new benchmark confidence intervals are reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds Llama average scores of 45.37 versus 47.98 with DND, Gemma scores of 47.08 versus 49.58, and an ITT score of 59.58 against Qwen DND's retained 61.41. Table 3 newly reports DND throughput at 91.6–93.1% of vanilla speed. New diagnostic findings include Pearson correlations of 0.3359 and -0.5831. The original Qwen benchmark and ablation values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same token-choice routing, same-layer nested processing, normalized fusion, router losses, buffer proportional control and EMA synchronization. Applying DND to additional backbones introduces no documented change to its procedure.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the MOR discussion and ablation interpretation, organizes main results into base, scaling and throughput discussions, and inserts an appendix subsection for token-selection analysis. Most introductory and methodological prose remains unchanged, so this is a limited narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: v2 adds a consolidated dense-model performance table, a throughput table, two entropy scatterplots and a hidden-state violin plot. It also expands the MOR table with a Purpose row and relocates retained displays and appendix material. This substantially expands the visual evidence beyond simple renumbering or numerical cell updates.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 and the expanded MOR comparison table distinguish MOR's parameter-efficiency objective from DND's enhancement of existing pretrained models, adding discussion of from-scratch training costs. v2 also adds Ma et al. (2025), Estimating LLM Uncertainty with Evidence, to support the entropy interpretation. The broader related-work positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(10) and Appendix A's computational assumptions and FLOPs derivation, including the 6.27% overhead estimate, are unchanged. The new diagnostic plots introduce empirical measurements and fitted relationships, not new formal definitions, theoretical results or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's efficacy evidence was confined to Qwen models and its overhead assessment was analytical. v2's Llama/Gemma results, direct ITT comparison and measured throughput address important gaps in generalizability, comparative effectiveness and practical cost. The new diagnostics also strengthen evidence about token selection, although correlations and lower entropy do not prove better representations as the text suggests. The broader empirical support provides a substantial overall improvement despite that interpretive overstatement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DND work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Llama and Gemma evaluations, an ITT comparison, measured inference throughput, and entropy and hidden-state analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Qwen3 benchmark results, architectural and training ablations, and token-selection analyses in Tables 1–2 and the main-text and appendix figures.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: action representations influence exploration and optimization, and local-tangent actions provide the most reliable general choice. The added studies support and qualify these retained contributions.

C2.justification: V2 develops an algorithm-dependent interpretation of identity centering and recommends centered relative actions for unstable systems, extending v1's discussion of problematic initialization. It adds cautious explanations of 6D-versus-matrix differences and explicitly excludes discrete-action algorithms. Section 3.3 also softens the description of unscaled SAC failures, although the appendix retains failure examples.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 replaces withholding code pending acceptance with a repository link and a statement that code, training scripts, and reproduction instructions are public; the abstract adds a project link. Appendices A.3–A.4 specify centering formulas and the six-output Gram-Schmidt implementation. Existing code listings and network/tuning details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the idealized rotation task, drone tracking and racing, nine RoboSuite tasks, and ReachOrient/PickAndPlaceOrient. The new representation studies reuse these environments; the added RoboSuite average represents existing tasks.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluated representation variants. Appendix A.3 compares additive and scaled identity-centered quaternion/matrix actions against existing global and delta variants. Appendix A.4 evaluates Zhou et al.'s 6D representation against matrices across the idealized settings and drone tasks; v1 cited this work without evaluating that representation.

E3.justification: Section 3.1 changes the stated sparse-reward angular tolerance from pi/10 to 0.1 radians. The corresponding original results remain unchanged, so the PDFs do not establish whether experiments were rerun or the description was corrected. New drone-centering comparisons select the additive variant and explicitly retune hyperparameters using the original sweep settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic ablations testing whether identity centering explains quaternion/matrix performance: uncentered, additive-bias, and scaled-bias variants are compared across algorithms and reward settings in Appendix A.3. Additional drone experiments test centered relative actions against global actions. V1's projection, scaling, exploration, and entropy analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The original run counts and uncertainty displays are retained, including 50-run idealized comparisons, 25-seed drone curves, and five-seed robot benchmarks. The new idealized studies also specify 50 runs. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure or formal significance test is documented.

E6.justification: Table 2 and the original learning curves retain their values. V2 adds substantial results in Figures 21–31: centering benefits PPO but has mixed effects for SAC/TD3, while 6D-versus-matrix rankings depend on algorithm and action frame. Figure 5 also adds an across-task RoboSuite average. These are additional results, not demonstrated improvements between versions under identical settings.

M1.justification: Sections 2.4.1 and A.3 introduce additive and componentwise-scaled identity biases before quaternion/matrix projection, changing the action-generation procedure. These are localized adaptations; the underlying PPO, SAC, TD3, and recommended local-tangent procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section order are preserved. V2 inserts a centering subsection and hypothesis, adds concise hypothesis summaries, renames Appendix A.2, and inserts two appendix sections before the retained implementation material. Additional changes include localized wording edits, publication headers, and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: V2 adds extensive comparison plots in Figures 21–31 and repeats one centering panel as Figure 3. Table 1 gains a delta-action column, the RoboSuite chart gains an average group and revised styling, and noise-distribution figures receive clearer tangent-coordinate axes. Boxed hypothesis summaries also change the main-text presentation; existing figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds Schuck et al. (2025b) on differentiable SciPy transformations. It also expands discussion of the already-cited Zhou et al. (2019) and Geist et al. (2024), explaining the relationship between 6D and matrix representations and the choice of matrices for the primary comparison.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds mathematical definitions of the two centering maps and range/reachability arguments under bounded network outputs. The existing SO(3) definitions, projection equations, and manifold-entropy argument remain unchanged; no new theorem or substantial proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses two important gaps in v1's comparative evidence: whether initialization contributes to quaternion/matrix disadvantages, and whether the omitted 6D alternative changes the recommendations. The controlled centering ablations and direct 6D comparisons substantially strengthen the practical guidance, including its algorithm-dependent qualifications. Concrete code-access information further improves reproducibility documentation. The unexplained sparse-reward tolerance revision remains a protocol-clarity weakness, particularly because the original results are unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the additional analyses in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds empirical comparisons of identity-centered actions and 6D rotation representations.

before.justification: V1 reports original reinforcement-learning experiments in an idealized rotation environment, drone tasks, RoboSuite, and modified manipulation environments, with additional empirical analyses in the appendix.

C1.justification: The central methodological and transfer claims remain. The abstract and introduction reduce the claimed GPQA gain from 12.5% to 6.6% and add a 3.5% average-gain claim. The revised GPQA claim still conflicts with unchanged Table 1: MAD scores of 37.88 and 45.45 imply 7.57 percentage points, rather than Section 4.3’s 6.57.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking transfer to peer-input use and task focus, cooperative curricula to AutoGen performance, MT-GRPO weaknesses to variable-length normalization, and length penalties to avoiding overlong failures. It also expands N-player limitations. Some interpretation remains problematic: Section 4.4’s approximately 7% reduction in System Design Issues conflicts with Figure 5’s labels of 29.5 and 13.9.

D1.justification: v2 adds project-page and model-collection access links, VS-Bench implementation attribution, normalization reference points, and explanations of the length bounds. However, Appendix C removes v1’s downstream decoding settings: temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, and top-k 20. The core hyperparameter table and prompt listings are retained.

E1.justification: Both retain training on Tic-Tac-Toe, Kuhn Poker, and Mini Hanabi; testing on Connect Four, Leduc Hold’em, and Simple Hanabi; and the same seven reasoning benchmarks under single-agent, MAD, and AutoGen settings. The added experiments reuse this coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds direct MT-GRPO comparisons on games and downstream MAD/AutoGen tasks (Tables 10–11). Tables 7–9 also introduce explicit SPIRAL RAE trained on the full game portfolio and competitive-only MARSHAL controls, substantially expanding comparisons relevant to the algorithm’s contribution.

E3.justification: Appendices D–G introduce Qwen3-8B training and evaluation, controlled algorithm-versus-game-curriculum experiments, and penalty-weight settings of 0, 0.5, and 1. New analyses measure failure categories, response length, and overlong-response losses. These substantially expand the experimental design without establishing reruns of the retained 4B experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative GPQA failure analysis (Figure 5), player-role return distributions (Figure 6), algorithm/curriculum disentanglement (Appendix E), and length-penalty sensitivity and failure analysis (Appendix G). These address mechanisms and robustness questions beyond v1’s retained qualitative examples and component ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The 1000-game evaluation count is retained. New return distributions and failure percentages are descriptive analyses, without a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for 8B models, comparison methods, failure categories, and penalty sensitivity. For example, its new Table 6 reports MAD averages of 82.49 for Qwen3-8B and 85.09 for MARSHAL-8B. Original Table 1 and raw appendix results remain unchanged, while Tables 3–4 replace normalized poker values: the Tic-Tac-Toe specialist’s Kuhn scores change from 42.90/-77.80 to 74.15/3.42 despite unchanged raw returns.

M1.justification: The self-play procedure, turn-level cumulative-return estimator, agent-specific centering, objectives, rewards, and prompts remain unchanged. MARSHAL is a renaming; the 8B experiment and alternative algorithms are experimental configurations and controls.

P1.justification: The title and method name change, competitive/cooperative terminology is standardized, and explanatory prose is edited throughout. Section 4.4 gains an expanded heading, and new appendix sections precede the retained material. The main narrative structure and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1–4 are redrawn with revised styling, labels, and legends; Figures 5–6 and eight experimental tables are added. Main and appendix tables are regrouped and reformatted, including replacing green/red highlighting with bold, underlining, and row shading. These constitute a substantial visual revision.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that SPIRAL’s role-conditioned estimator is analogous to its agent-specific normalization and develops a substantial comparison with MT-GRPO in Section 5 and Appendix F. This materially refines positioning of the central contributions. Additional citations cover the failure taxonomy, VS-Bench, automated workflows, and a self-play survey.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, four numbered equations, and GAE equivalence argument are retained. Appendix F.1 adds conceptual explanations of MT-GRPO’s limitations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical attribution through matched algorithm comparisons and separate curriculum controls in Appendices E–F, addressing an important gap in v1. The 8B experiments and penalty analysis further test scalability and robustness, while revised related work clarifies methodological overlap. These gains outweigh the remaining GPQA arithmetic discrepancy, the new Figure 5 labeling inconsistency, and the loss of evaluation decoding details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same work, renamed from MARS to MARSHAL. The methods, equations, figures, tables, prompts, and retained appendices can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds model-scaling experiments, controlled comparisons, and supplementary analyses in Appendices D–G.

before.justification: v1 reports original game-playing experiments, downstream reasoning evaluations, and ablations in Section 4 and Appendix F.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the sampling-wall diagnosis, deterministic latent-path contribution, efficient self-conditioning, and language-generation/reasoning improvement claims. The added no-unrolling phrase restates a capability already explained in v1.

C2.justification: v1 reports unsuccessful initial attempts to add Loopholing through fine-tuning; v2 removes that limitation and interprets Tables 17–18 as demonstrating successful integration into pretrained checkpoints. New discussion also attributes gains specifically to pre-sampling latent propagation and argues that benefits persist at increased capacity. Section 6.3 narrows the early-TKL interpretation from faster denoising progress to more active prediction updates.

D1.justification: v2 adds a Reproducibility Statement providing a repository link for source code and processing/training/evaluation scripts. It also documents the 424M configuration and checkpoint initialization for continued pre-training. The extensive original hardware, optimizer, preprocessing, and pseudocode disclosures remain largely unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same LM1B/OWT training coverage, zero-shot corpora, downstream language tasks, and Countdown/Game of 24 tasks. The added experiments vary model capacity, training history, or evaluation procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix D.11/Table 19 adds LDDM-M (sampled token) as a control against MDLM and LDDM-M (latent). This is a newly evaluated comparator; the original comparison methods remain present.

E3.justification: New protocols include 100K-step comparisons at 169M/424M parameters, continued pre-training from a 1M-step MDLM checkpoint for 10K–200K steps, and a matched 200K-step propagation-control experiment. Appendix D.12 adds the original MGDM evaluation-and-decoding scheme; v1's Table 4 already tested original decoding with stricter validity checks. Main experimental settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices D.8–D.12 substantially extend the analyses: directly quantifying idle steps, testing capacity scaling and checkpoint adaptation, separating sampled-token from latent propagation, and checking reasoning results under alternative evaluation rules. These supplement v1's existing self-conditioning, propagation-length, MLP, multistep-backpropagation, and compute-budget studies.

E5.justification: The four GPT-4.1 evaluations per sequence, averaging practices, and Figure 4(b) error bars are unchanged. v2 adds no documented training-seed repetitions, confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Original benchmark tables and performance plots retain their results after matching renumbering. Substantial new results include 55.04 versus 93.71 Gen PPL for latent versus sampled-token propagation under the matched 200K-step setting (Table 19), and 51.51 after 200K continued pre-training steps (Table 18). Idle-step counts, scaling results, and original-protocol reasoning scores are also added. The introduction corrects the MDLM/AR Gen PPL ratio from 3.26 to 3.17.

M1.justification: The proposed latent pathway, LayerNorm fusion, two-pass self-conditioning objective, and generation/training algorithms remain unchanged. Section 3 makes sequence notation and conditioning arguments explicit; the new experiments apply the existing method or test a control variant.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and notation explanations clearer, revises the training introduction, adds cross-references and a reproducibility statement, and updates correspondence, acknowledgments, and publication headers. New appendix subsections extend the document without extensively rewriting or reorganizing its existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds six experimental tables (15–20) and the idle-step plot (Figure 8), substantially expanding the appendix displays. Existing sample figures gain colored error annotations and explanatory captions. Original performance plots are unchanged; other edits include loss-label and G-eval-caption corrections, table renumbering, and pseudocode reflow.

R1.justification: The bibliography and main related-work section are retained. Appendix D.11 adds a limited positioning refinement by explicitly contrasting latent propagation with a sampled-token variant described as closer to standard self-conditioning, citing the already included Chen et al. work.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and derivations remain substantively unchanged. Explicit conditioning arguments, positional indices, and renaming the self-conditioning loss to the Loopholing loss clarify notation without changing mathematical content; no new proofs or theorems appear.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis and practical applicability of the paper. The matched sampled-token control tests the central information-preservation mechanism more directly, while successful continued pre-training addresses v1's reported failure to adapt existing checkpoints. Evaluation under the original MGDM rules adds useful robustness evidence. One qualification remains: Table 16 repeats earlier 1M-step small-model scores within a section describing 100K-step training, leaving its cross-scale budget comparability unclear. This limits that scaling evidence but does not outweigh the other substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Loopholing Discrete Diffusion work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on idle steps, model scale, continued pre-training, propagation controls, and reasoning evaluation protocols.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-modeling, text-generation, arithmetic-reasoning, and ablation results in Section 6 and Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same two-stage contribution, rank-aware credit-assignment and importance-weighting claims, REDDIT-V2 performance claims, and proposed broader applicability. The added experiments support these claims without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive applicability discussion in Appendix E, covering movie-specific textual representations, codebook validity in other domains and exclusion of INSPIRE for insufficient data. Appendix D.3 qualifies conclusions about adapted DPO baselines, D.7.4 states the computational restriction of 7B evaluation to REDIAL, and Section 3.6 interprets the new component ablations.

D1.justification: Appendix D.3 documents single-item ground-truth SFT supervision, BIGRec-based catalog scoring and shared-prefix caching for the new baselines. Appendix C revises 1B vLLM tensor parallelism from four to two. Most existing implementation details, prompt templates and code/data/checkpoint access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates on REDDIT-V2 only. V3 adds training and evaluation on REDIAL, with its own seeker–recommender conversations and smaller movie catalog (Appendix D.7). Movie recommendation remains the domain; INSPIRE and other application domains are discussed without evaluation.

E2.justification: Appendix D.3 and Table 3 add evaluated DPO, S-DPO and SPRec baselines across all three original backbones, introducing an RL-free preference-training comparison family absent from v1. The comparator sets in the retained REDDIT-V2 on-policy and off-policy tables remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New studies introduce REDIAL's 20,896/2,612/2,613 train/validation/test split, Claude-3.7-Sonnet demonstrations, a Qwen2.5-7B backbone, single-item DPO training with catalog-ranking inference, and penalty sweeps. Existing REDDIT-V2 splits and Recall/NDCG metrics remain. Appendix C also changes stated 1B tensor parallelism from four to two, without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Section 3.6 and Table 2 add quantitative tests jointly removing remap and reflect, removing reflect alone, and omitting SFT. Appendix D.7.3 adds sensitivity to the list-length penalty over zero and four negative values (Figure 10). V1's qualitative pipeline example, catalog-drift analysis and generation examples are retained.

E5.justification: The standard-error statements in Table 1 and v1 Table 2, retained as v3 Table 4, are unchanged. V3 introduces no seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or new significance-testing procedure. Its additional SFT figure repeats the existing mean/standard-deviation display practice.

E6.justification: All numerical rows in the two original REDDIT-V2 result tables are retained. V3 adds ablation, DPO, REDIAL and 7B results in Tables 2, 3 and 5–7. For example, REDIAL Table 5 reports 3B Rank-GRPO (exp∞) Recall@20/NDCG@20 of 0.4648/0.2405 versus GRPO's 0.4300/0.2168. These are newly reported findings, not gains over v1 under its original settings.

M1.justification: The advantage formula accompanying Eq. (6) changes from normalization across ranks within one response to normalization across sampled responses at a fixed rank. This changes the stated estimator; the two-stage pipeline, rank-level importance ratios and reward constructions remain. The PDFs do not establish whether this correction reflects a training-code change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and methodological exposition are retained. V3 integrates an ablation section and new appendix subsections, consolidates the earlier on/off-policy discussion, moves qualitative examples from Appendix E to F, and updates author/header text. It also introduces an unresolved 'Table ??' reference in Appendix D.5.

P2.justification: V3 adds substantial displays for ablations, DPO comparisons, REDIAL evaluation, scaling and penalty sensitivity: Tables 2, 3 and 5–7 and Figures 7–10. Existing plots are resized and relabeled, captions are expanded, and Figure 6 moves beside its discussion. V1 Table 2 is retained as Table 4.

R1.justification: Appendix D.3 adds focused positioning against DPO, S-DPO and SPRec, distinguishing candidate selection from generative ranking and adding supporting BIGRec, Bradley–Terry and in-context ranking references. Appendix E adds INSPIRE context. The main related-work sections and novelty positioning against earlier CRS and GRPO-style methods remain intact.

T1.justification: The formal advantage definition below Eq. (6) changes the normalization population from ranks to responses at a fixed rank, a mathematical correction beyond equivalent notation. Appendix B's gradient derivations remain unchanged. V3 also removes the footnote defining the teacher's recommendation space as the union of its generated items.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing v1's single-dataset evidence, lack of quantitative pipeline/SFT ablations and absence of RL-free preference-training comparisons. Tables 2–3 and Appendix D.7 make component utility and generalization more assessable, while the corrected advantage formula and explicit applicability qualifications improve precision. The ablations do not isolate every component, uncertainty reporting remains sparse, and minor editorial defects appear, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ConvRec-R1 and Rank-GRPO. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables and figures, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds quantitative ablations, DPO-based comparisons and REDIAL experiments, including a 7B backbone.

before.justification: Sections 3 and Appendix D report original training dynamics, recommendation performance and catalog-grounding analyses on REDDIT-V2.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free draft/verdict synthesis, consensus selection, error correction and cost efficiency. The introduction's principal contributions also remain unchanged; the additions mainly expand supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting normalization to selection collapse and expert specialization to complementary reasoning. Appendix J newly identifies SV's limitations: fine-grained extraction, color matching and a verdict favoring verbose incorrect drafts despite correct majority evidence. This substantially qualifies v1's emphasis on successful recovery and competing tool pipelines' weaknesses.

D1.justification: v2 documents the critic's evaluation template and pairwise elimination procedure and expands the explanation of answer-only NLL scoring. Section 7 now states that supplementary material includes anonymized source code, while the abstract retains the same public repository link. Existing SV prompts and structured-image preprocessing details remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 retains the four original benchmarks and adds TallyQA-Complex and MathVista (Table 2, Section 4.4). Relational counting and visual mathematical reasoning substantially broaden evaluation beyond the original information-intensive and high-resolution tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds Pixel-Reasoner to benchmark comparisons, o1 to performance/cost comparisons, and LLaVA-Critic-7B/72B with pointwise and pairwise judging. Conversely, the standalone Qwen2.5-VL-72B comparator disappears from the retained alternative-pool comparisons in Tables 12–13, although it remains in the main comparison.

E3.justification: New protocols include MathVista-testmini, 1000 sampled TallyQA-Complex questions, and 1000-instance-per-benchmark cost comparisons. Appendix G introduces judging controls with three versus five candidates, pointwise versus pairwise decisions, different judge sizes and an alternative verdict sharing the critic's backbone. Table 4 also expands the small-verdict configurations.

E4.justification: v2 adds normalization and answer-only versus full-trajectory NLL ablations, selection-frequency analysis, expert-complementarity analysis and SV's own failure analysis (Appendices F, I and J). It also expands verdict-scale and judging analyses. The earlier visual-input, structured-input, recovery and DeepEyes analyses are largely retained; alternative-pool experiments no longer report the Qwen72B verdict.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. New frequencies and averages extend descriptive results without introducing uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 scores remain unchanged, while v2 adds substantial benchmark, critic, cost and diagnostic results, including SV accuracies of 76.9 on TallyQA-Complex and 82.9 on MathVista. Its verdict-scale table replaces InfographicVQA values, including GLM's 86.0 with 84.7, while dropping v1's 1000-sample qualifier; these are not established same-setting performance changes. The alternative-pool Qwen72B-verdict results of 84.2 and 80.4 disappear. Section 4.2 also corrects the ChartQAPro improvement from 6.6 to 6.7 points.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same normalized answer-NLL consensus score, cross-all expert selection, reasoning drafts and single verdict synthesis call. The structured image input already appears in v1. Newly tested scoring variants are ablations, without a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition, including the abstract, method and conclusion, is preserved. Changes include localized results-paragraph rewrites, reorganized related work, the ensemble discussion's move to Appendix B, and revised ethics and reproducibility wording. Much of the expansion is new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table displays for benchmarks, costs, tokens, normalization, critics, complementarity and failures. Figure 8 gains critic bars, and main and alternative-pool tables gain comparison rows and revised formatting. Existing method, qualitative and prompt graphics are largely retained; the earlier recovery Figure 9 is redisplayed with a Table 11 caption.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through new discussions of general VLM reasoning and LMM-as-a-Judge, including LLaVA-Critic and multimodal evaluation research. SV is explicitly situated relative to selection-based judges. The original language-model ensemble discussion is retained in Appendix B rather than removed.
