T1.justification: The NLL, relative consensus and global consensus definitions remain mathematically unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's added calibration and off-policy discussions remain empirical explanations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of consensus and synthesis through normalization ablations, critic comparisons using a shared backbone, and explicit analysis of SV's failures—important gaps in v1's evidence. Additional tasks and comparative costs further improve assessment of applicability and efficiency. Reporting limitations remain: API/token accounting does not establish full-pipeline cost, the verdict-scale subset becomes unclear, and Section 4.5's stated 72B critic gain range does not match Table 20. These issues limit precision but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Speculative Verdict work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark evaluations, critic comparisons, cost measurements and analyses of consensus selection and failures.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, component ablations, recovery statistics and model-pool experiments in the main text and appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: large-scale synthetic supervision, complementary generative/discriminative features, feedback-driven generation, ambiguity-aware prediction and strong DIS/HR-SOD generalization. The added experiments do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds detailed interpretations of feature failures and complementarity, connects distribution coverage to generalization, and discusses performance relative to SAM adaptations. Appendix G explains regularization through branch collapse and sparse ambiguity. Appendix H newly discusses synthetic-data evaluation boundaries and computational limitations, extending v1's narrower quality and generalization discussion.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the mask decoder's real-data supervision, identifies ImageNet taxonomy as the category source, clarifies 25,000 images in each later generation round, and discloses the absence of a synthetic test split. It also adds a four-A6000, 2.5-day training alternative. These improve documentation without establishing changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds dedicated camouflaged-object detection on COD10K, CAMO and NC4K, including fine-tuning on CAMO and COD10K training sets (Section 5.5). This substantially extends task coverage to detecting foreground objects that blend into their backgrounds. The original DIS/SOD benchmarks and 139,981-image synthetic dataset remain.

E2.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluated comparators: FSPNet in Table 6; SAM, Pi-SAM and DIS-SAM in Table 13; and additional SOD/DIS methods including LDF, HRSOD, DHQ, PGNet, BASNet, U2Net, IS-Net, FP-DIS and UDUN in Table 14. Original comparisons remain. HQ-SAM and SAM-HQ denote the same comparator, not separate additions.

E3.justification: New protocols include zero-shot COD transfer and COD fine-tuning, training BiRefNet and MVANet on S3OD (Table 3), expanded real-only training controls (Table 14), and regularization/decay configurations with diversity metrics (Table 15). Figure 8 adds generative precision-recall and UMAP assessments. The original DIS/SOD evaluation metrics and matched 10,000-image synthetic-data comparison remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's modality, backbone, mask-count, generation-round and prompting ablations, v2 adds feature-complementarity case analyses (Appendix A), image/mask domain-gap analyses (Appendix C), controls testing dataset benefits across architectures, and auxiliary-loss sensitivity tests examining branch collapse and diversity (Appendix G). These address substantial additional analytical questions.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, run-to-run variability or significance tests. The new entropy and average-IoU measurements describe prediction-branch diversity, not uncertainty in estimated experimental performance.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and ablation values are retained, while v2 adds extensive results. Table 6 newly reports fine-tuned COD10K F-measure of 0.911 versus BiRefNet's 0.888, rather than a same-setting improvement over v1. New Table 13 also reports HQ-SAM overall F-measure of 0.859, versus 0.850 for SAM-HQ in retained Table 4, without explaining the evaluation difference.

M1.justification: The architecture, feature fusion, losses, mask selection and iterative weighting remain unchanged. However, the reported generation prompt changes from requiring complex backgrounds to mixing simple and complex scenes, with revised scene-variation instructions (v1 Figure 5; v2 Figure 11). This revises a method input without establishing that the dataset was regenerated.

P1.justification: v2 copyedits prose throughout, introduces S3ODNet naming, revises the prompting text, shortens its example list and updates headers and acknowledgments. Added experimental and appendix subsections extend the document, while the original main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds COD predictions, feature visualizations and a four-panel domain-gap figure (Figures 5, 6 and 8), plus Tables 3, 6 and 13–15. Existing qualitative figures are retained and relocated, the prompt box is revised and moved, and table placement is reorganized. These substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature supporting COD benchmarks, additional segmentation baselines, SAM adaptations, UMAP and generative precision-recall analysis. Appendix F extends positioning against foundation-model adaptations, particularly DIS-SAM. The main related-work argument and novelty positioning in Section 2 remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: The explicit model, objective and sampling equations are retained. Appendix G invokes the existing MHP/Voronoi interpretation to motivate the unchanged decaying auxiliary loss, but introduces no new formal derivation, theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central empirical case: Table 3 tests S3OD with other architectures, addressing v1's limited separation of dataset and model benefits. COD transfer tests and decoder-regularization analyses also examine important previously unsupported aspects of generalization and ambiguity handling. These gains outweigh the added reporting weaknesses, including unexplained HQ-SAM score differences; run-level uncertainty remains absent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S3OD research. All 17 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds camouflage-detection experiments, expanded comparisons, feature analyses and decoder-regularization ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments, cross-dataset evaluations, ablations, synthetic-data quality measurements and efficiency results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a comprehensive visualization-quality benchmark, shortcomings of general MLLM judges, and improved human alignment through specialized training. Reported improvement percentages change, but these update supporting results without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly limits fidelity assessment to visually detectable presentation problems when source data are unavailable, consistent with the retained appendix rubrics. It adds limitations concerning static visualizations, geographic concentration, subjective style categories, and small annotator subgroups. New interpretations attribute complex-chart failures to weak cross-view understanding and ineffective feedback to scoring biases; Appendix E also advances stronger generalization and production-readiness claims.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses 603 annotators and their geographic, professional, and educational composition. It documents consistent training configurations across four backbones and the downstream integration/evaluation procedures. Sections 7 and A.4 additionally promise annotations, quality-control records, statistical analyses, and model weights. Existing core hyperparameters, software information, and benchmark access link are retained.

E1.justification: The original 3,090-image benchmark and its visualization categories remain. v2 adds visualization generation with iterative feedback through MatPlotAgent and visualization recommendation through HAIChart on VizML's user-created Plotly visualizations (Section 5.2.5 and Appendix E). These introduce distinct tasks and input distributions. New style/domain breakdowns characterize existing benchmark samples.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains the seven original baselines and adds Qwen2.5-VL-3B/32B/72B-Instruct, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-v1.6-mistral-7B. The new downstream comparisons also evaluate original systems without VISJUDGE and alternatives using Qwen 7B or 72B feedback/reward models. Qwen-7B's expanded name is a naming clarification.

E3.justification: The original split, 648-sample benchmark evaluation, metrics, and training hyperparameters remain. Added experiments compare more model sizes and backbones under consistent training settings. Appendix E introduces GPT-4o assessment on a 0–100 scale for generated visualizations and Hit@1/Hit@3 for recommendation. Appendix B.6 introduces error-analysis subsets of 139 multiple visualizations and 94 dashboards.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands the existing bias, complexity, case-study, and scaling analyses. Additions include backbone and downstream generalization tests, style/domain and coupled-design-failure analyses in Appendix A.2, annotation-quality audits in A.4, and quantified complex-visualization error patterns in B.6. Earlier illustrated cases are largely retained and renumbered.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 newly quantifies annotation disagreement using crowd–crowd and crowd–expert MAE, including estimates by visualization type and annotator background. This adds statistical characterization of annotation noise. Both versions already average three model evaluations; v2 does not report increased repetitions, new seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 3 revises retained benchmark results: VISJUDGE's overall MAE/correlation changes from 0.442/0.681 to 0.421/0.687, GPT-5 from 0.551/0.429 to 0.553/0.428, and Qwen-7B's MAE from 1.048 to 0.847. Their revision's cause is unexplained. v2 also updates Figure 8's scaling results and adds backbone, annotation, and downstream results. Table 7 supports an average generation gain of 6.07 points, but its actual range is 4.10–8.91, contradicting the stated 5.53–8.91.

M1.justification: Section 4 extends VISJUDGE from a Qwen2.5-VL-7B model to variants using Qwen2.5-VL-3B, InternVL3-8B, and LLaVA-v1.6-mistral-7B. This broadens the model architectures while retaining the scoring outputs, GRPO/LoRA procedure, and accuracy-plus-format reward specified in Appendix D.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify fidelity, condense annotation and case-study descriptions, and standardize model names. Appendix A is reorganized, the scaling subsection becomes Section 5.3, and limitations and extended-experiment sections are added. Much of the original prose and narrative sequence remains; the scientific additions do not amount to wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: Table 3 expands into a substantially larger comparison organized by closed-source, open-source, and VISJUDGE groups. v2 adds application-result tables, with generation results displayed twice as Tables 4 and 7, and subtype boxplots in Figure 12. Figure 5 consolidates legends, Figure 8 changes plotting scales, and Figure 1 moves into the first page. Most appendix case illustrations remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations supporting style, domain, and dashboard analyses, including Bateman, Borkin, Sarikaya, and ChartGalaxy, plus references for newly evaluated model families. Section 2's research positioning and the benchmark's novelty claim remain essentially unchanged. Bibliographic updates and duplicate representations of existing works do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Appendix D retains the same exponential accuracy-reward equation and 0.9/0.1 reward weighting. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. Updated empirical scaling fits and conceptual fidelity explanations do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's single-backbone validation and previously unquantified annotator agreement through expanded Table 3, Appendix A.4, and two downstream applications in Appendix E. Clarifying visual-only fidelity also makes the evaluation scope more accurate. GPT-4o-based generation assessment, incomplete downstream settings, and the incorrect Table 7 gain range limit the stronger deployment claims, but the broader validation and annotation evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisJudge-Bench and VISJUDGE. All 53 pages of v1 and 62 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection allowed matching of retained, relocated, and revised material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations across model backbones, downstream application results, and annotation-quality analyses in Table 3 and Appendices A.4 and E.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, VISJUDGE fine-tuning results, training-data scaling experiments, and dataset analyses, including Table 3 and Figures 4–8.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains distributional optimization that exploits arbitrary junction-tree decomposability through message passing. v2 adds an explicit contribution claiming predictor accuracy is robust to decomposition modifications and broadens the empirical comparison claims to multiple baselines. These extend the supporting claims without redefining the research contribution.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations involving noisy value estimates in large junction-tree nodes, FDA's competitiveness, and reduced overfitting from stronger decomposition under shifted training data. It removes v1's explicit Gcn4 caveat about intrinsic disorder and multiple conformations, instead emphasizing limited, dispersed data. These materially revise the account of applicability, failure mechanisms, and robustness.

D1.justification: v2 documents the FDA/PPO implementations, including PPO clipping at 0.2, clarifies atom-based contact construction, and adds single-GPU runtime and memory/parallel-execution information. Most architecture, optimizer, and predictor-training details in A.8 were already in v1 Section 4, although the within-node decoding and overlapping-variable explanation is shortened. The public code-access statement remains.

E1.justification: v2 extends synthetic task coverage to length L=400 and alphabets D=50 and D=100, testing larger discrete design spaces. All seven protein datasets remain. Gcn4 replacing GB1 in the main figure is a change in emphasis, since both appeared in v1 and remain evaluated in v2.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares DADO with a naive EDA. v2 adds FDA and a PPO-style EDA to the retained main synthetic and protein comparisons. FDA uses DADO's factorization, providing a substantive control for message passing. The new predictor-robustness experiments also include an undecomposed neural-network comparator labeled Naive NN.

E3.justification: Reported protein initialization changes from the 1,000 lowest assay-label sequences to the 1,000 lowest-f(x) sequences, and hyperparameter sweeps are now broadened when optima reach their boundaries. New protocols include reusing L=200 hyperparameters at L=400 and training on bottom-half assay labels against unchanged holdouts. Most significance evaluations now target final-iteration performance instead of trajectory AUC.

E4.justification: v2 adds a message-passing control through FDA, larger-length/alphabet analyses, runtime analysis, and five-protein studies of contact thresholds and random edge perturbations, including bottom-half-label training. The original GB1 threshold case study survives as Figure A6. However, v1's synthetic K=100 versus 1000 and seven-protein K=100 versus 1000 sampling-budget ablations are removed.

E5.justification: The 20-seed, 95% confidence-interval, paired two-sided t-test framework remains. Most tests change from AUC to final-iteration means, and Figures 2–3 compare against the strongest baseline. New graph-mutation studies report ten repetitions and display replicate variability. The retained GB1 case study still uses its original AUC tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds FDA/PPO results, larger synthetic-design results, robustness correlations, and runtime measurements, while removing sampling-budget results. FDA is competitive with DADO on GB1 and exceeds it on ynzC and CreiLOV in Figure A4. Existing protein trajectories and p-values also change. Revised initialization and statistical comparisons prevent treating these revisions as uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: DADO retains the same junction-tree factorization, conditional sampling, distributional value functions, message passing, and per-factor weighted maximum-likelihood updates. Algorithm 1 and the corresponding derivations are substantively unchanged. FDA and PPO are added comparison methods, not new DADO components.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, intuitive method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively edited and condensed. Detailed algorithm sketches move to A.3, implementation material moves to A.8, and the appendix is reorganized into dedicated baseline, implementation, and analysis sections. Terminology, headings, affiliations, and conference formatting also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds the extensive protein-structure/contact-graph/junction-tree Figure A1, robustness figures, and runtime Table 1. Main comparison plots gain FDA/PPO curves and revised legends. Protein plots introduce the -log(c-f(x)) scale, with ordinary-scale counterparts retained in the appendix, and the main protein panels are reordered and reselected. The document is comprehensively reformatted.

R1.justification: FDA and PPO were already cited in v1; v2 expands their discussion as controls for factorization and update stabilization. The Design-Bench reference by Trabucco et al. (2022) disappears with the continuous-design future-work discussion. The broader positioning relative to EDAs, reinforcement learning, and Bayesian optimization is retained.

T1.justification: The decomposition definitions, EDA derivation, distributional-value lower-bound reasoning, and maximum-entropy derivation are retained. v1 Appendices A.3–A.4 correspond to v2 A.4–A.5. The new A.3 largely relocates the earlier algorithmic explanation; equation renumbering and compressed notation do not introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked an evaluated control separating factorization from message passing. v2's matched FDA comparison addresses that central attribution gap, while robustness studies and runtime measurements substantially strengthen assessment of practical applicability and reveal cases favoring FDA. Removing sampling-budget ablations, dropping the explicit Gcn4 structural caveat, and emphasizing endpoint tests lose useful information, but the new controls and boundary analyses provide a clear, substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DADO research, with matching authors, objectives, algorithm, and theoretical development. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 27 pages of v1 and 37 pages of v2, including their appendices, without material comparison gaps.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A.9 report original optimization experiments, additional baseline comparisons, graph-robustness studies, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A.6 report original synthetic optimization experiments, evaluations on seven protein datasets, sampling-budget ablations, and a GB1 decomposition study.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about mitigating reward hacking, preserving diversity and improving live accompaniment. The appendix adds support without redefining those core contributions.

C2.justification: The appendix substantially expands interpretation of mechanisms and failure conditions. It discusses why excessive rule weighting can reduce coverage, why excessive adversarial weighting can weaken melody alignment, and why removing penalties permits invalid outputs. It also introduces a conditional-discriminator overfitting hypothesis and interpretations of critic tracking, chord-density checks and longer-sequence behavior.

D1.justification: Section C.8 newly discloses eight gradient updates per discriminator step and how training logs are averaged. Sections C.12-C.13 document the shared 2,821-symbol chord vocabulary, provide a vocabulary link, and specify long-sequence inference details. Existing architecture, training hyperparameters and release information are retained.

E1.justification: The datasets and existing interaction tasks are retained. Section C.13 adds an explicit fixed-melody extrapolation scenario using sequences of at least 512 frames, beyond the 256-frame training horizon, on the existing test corpora and Wikifonia.

E2.justification: Table 8 adds GRPO with and without adversarial training; the text specifies a Dr.GRPO implementation. Table 9 adds GAPT with a discriminator conditioned on both melody and chords. The original Online MLE, ReaLchords and non-adversarial GAPT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The added experiments substantially extend the evaluation design through reward-weight controls, alternative RL optimization and discriminator-input comparisons. Section C.13 evaluates 137 test sequences and 300 Wikifonia sequences using 512-frame context versus a 256-frame sliding window with an eight-frame hop. Table 10 adds average chord pitch-class count as a diagnostic measure. Existing protocols are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's adversarial-removal ablation, embedding visualization and key-shift probe, v3 adds reward-weight and penalty ablations, optimizer and discriminator-input comparisons, training and critic diagnostics, a check for dense-chord metric gaming, and long-sequence robustness analysis. These examine several previously untested design choices and failure conditions.

E5.justification: Section C.7 and Table 6 newly report means and standard deviations across three RL post-training seeds for GAPT, its non-adversarial ablation and ReaLchords on both dataset settings. This adds policy-training uncertainty to central quantitative comparisons. v1 already reported user-study standard errors and paired tests, but not this seed variability; an increase from a previously specified run count is not established.

E6.justification: Existing results remain unchanged, while Tables 6-10 and Figures 8-12 add substantial numerical and qualitative evidence. For example, the new Table 8 reports test harmony/diversity of 0.459/16.872 for GRPO without adversarial training and 0.478/26.603 with it. These are newly reported experimental comparisons, not improvements to previously reported same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The primary PPO-based GAPT method and two-phase discriminator schedule remain unchanged. Sections C.10-C.13 add evaluated variants using Dr.GRPO, a melody-conditioned discriminator, and extended-context or sliding-window inference. These are auxiliary procedural extensions rather than replacements of the main method.

P1.justification: The existing prose and section organization are essentially unchanged. v3 appends Sections C.7-C.13 with accompanying explanations and expands one author's name from Teng Ma to Aleksandra Teng Ma. There is no extensive rewriting or reorganization of the retained narrative.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with a seed-summary table, ablation and chord-density tables, multi-panel training diagnostics, critic plots and long-sequence curves. Tables 8-9 redisplay original Table 1 results alongside new variants. Existing figures and tables are retained without substantive redesign.

R1.justification: Section C.10 newly discusses GRPO and Dr.GRPO and positions the adversarial-training benefit across alternative RL objectives. This is a limited extension: the existing related-work section and bibliography are unchanged, and the new algorithms' citations remain unresolved question-mark placeholders.

T1.justification: Equation 7 introduces a limited mathematical extension by parameterizing the previously equal-weight three-component reward with separate coefficients for the ablations. The original online factorizations, assumptions and adversarial reward definition remain unchanged, and no new proofs or theoretical guarantees are supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked policy-seed uncertainty and systematic tests of several important design choices. v3 addresses these gaps through Table 6 and the reward, optimizer and discriminator ablations in Tables 7-9, while checking potential metric gaming and behavior beyond the training horizon. These additions substantially strengthen the empirical support and clarify failure conditions without removing existing evidence. The unresolved GRPO citations are a limited drawback.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GAPT research. All 17 pages of v1 and 22 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. The existing material is retained, with additions concentrated in Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds seed comparisons, ablations, training diagnostics and longer-sequence evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original fixed-melody and model-to-model experiments, a study with 12 musicians, and supplementary quantitative results.
